### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/current-events/1370-end-of-the-world/

1.

Why is God angry with the world? Why should God expect righteousness and honor from people who do not know about Him? Where does the honor which should go to their Creator get misplaced? (Romans 1:18-23)

2. What is vengeance? What is retribution? How you feel when you want to take revenge on someone who has

wronged you? Is this the kind of revenge God seeks? What is the difference in the focus or purpose of our seeking vengeance and God’s? (Genesis 4:15, Deuteronomy 32:35-36)

3. Do you ever bear a grudge? What are the scriptural guidelines governing our taking revenge? (Genesis 4:15,

Leviticus 19:17-18, Romans 12:18-19, Proverbs 20:22, 1 Thessalonians 4:4-6, MacLaren’s Exposition quote)

4. Exodus 20:1-7, Commandments 1-3 – These deal with the relationship between God and man

a. Does this present world follow these commandments well? Do you have “idols” in your life?

b. Nahum 1:2-3: Who is God angry with in these verses? Why? Define God’s character. (Psalm 89:14)

c. Nahum 1:3-4: Generally, what do storms and clouds, whirlwinds, the sea, and rivers scripturally

symbolize? (Joel 2:1-2, Isaiah 57:20, 66:15, Jeremiah 25:32, Revelation 22:1,17)

d. Is this vengeance for the sake of revenge? Explain. (“Verifying God’s Vengeance” box)

5. Exodus 20:8,12, Commandments 4-5—These deal with honoring God’s provision for us

a. How well does our present society honor parents, authority figures and teachers? Do you treat others in a

way that will lift them up, help them improve? How does God’s plan use vengeance to help man?

b. Nahum 1:5: What do mountains, hills, earth and the world prophetically symbolize? What is the chief of

the mountains?

c. Nahum 1:6: What does fire do in Scripture? What is God’s vengeance accomplishing?

d. Nahum 1:7-9: Why is it necessary for God to make a complete end to wickedness? Is there comfort here?

6. Exodus 20:8,12; Commandments 6-10—These deal with the relationship between people

a. How are we doing today with these commandments? Are we living up to the integrity the Lord expects?

7. Psalms 46:1-11, Zephaniah 3:8-9, Psalms 76:8-10—Does God’s vengeance bring the end of the world as we

know it? Discuss Psalm 46 in regards to:

a. Verses 1,4,5: Promises—can you hold onto these promises to combat the fear of today’s troubled times?

b. Verses 2,3,6: Trouble—rephrase these verses without the symbolic pictures.

c. 8-11: Accomplishments—what was the purpose for all this trouble?

8. How does the wrath of man praise God? How can you see God’s vengeance in the full picture of His love,

power, wisdom and justice?

## Episode 1371 — Will There Ever Be Peace on Earth?
Published: 2025-02-03
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/current-events/1371-peace-on-earth/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/08123915/CQ_Rewind_02-02-2025_Will_There_Ever_be_Peace_on_Earth.pdf

Psalm 145:13: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures throughout all generations.

In our last episode about God’s vengeance bringing the end of the world as we know it, we examined several Old Testament prophecies that pointed to how God’s vengeance works in the dismantling of all vestiges of our present and sin-ridden world. When these dramatic prophecies are focused on without the context of the rest of God’s character, they are often understood to paint a bleak and harsh picture of who God is. In this episode, we will again focus on Old Testament prophecies.

However, this time, we will be looking at what happens AFTER the vengeance of God is exercised. What we will find is a breathtaking view not only of who God is but also of what His plan REALLY has in store for ALL of humanity. If you truly want to know who God is, then follow along as we unfold the rest of this prophetic story!

We left off in our last episode stating that God’s vengeance brings the end of the world as we know it—and it doesn’t sound good.

For example:

2 Peter 3:10,12: 10 But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with a roar and the elements will be destroyed with intense heat, and the earth and its works will be burned up. 12 looking for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be destroyed by burning, and the elements will melt with intense heat!

Peter is recapping what the Day of Vengeance looks like as the symbolic heavens and earth pass away in the intense heat of the end times. He described it the same way twice so we could feel the impact.

We went through many prophecies that gave us the sense of gloom, doom, fire, destruction, pain, suffering; and then there is nothing left. It seemed as though this was God’s vengeance. Why would God act like this? Let’s look a little further, but from a slightly different perspective.

Here we have a softer description of the vengeance:

Isaiah 40:4–5: 4 Let every valley be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; and let the rough ground become a plain, and the rugged terrain a broad valley; 5 then the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all flesh will see it together; for the mouth of the LORD has spoken.

We see a calmed-down version of all the tumult. God said all flesh will see it together. The glory of the Lord is being revealed and is seen by all flesh.

This is preparing humanity to understand that God’s vengeance is the small and necessary step to dismantle the world’s sinful systems so that God’s true plan can be fully revealed. God’s glory will shine out after all the destruction and trouble.

Mankind has been allowed to do whatever they wanted to do—they made a mess. It must now be taken apart so that the glory of the Lord can shine out AFTER that destruction and trouble.

In Luke 4:18-19, Jesus quoted the following prophecy but stopped in the middle of a sentence:

Isaiah 61:1–2: 1 The spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and freedom to prisoners; 2 to proclaim the favorable year of the LORD...

Jesus stopped reading from Isaiah at this point, saying this was being fulfilled before his audience.

Here’s the rest of the prophecy he did not quote: …and the Day of Vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn.

Why did Jesus leave out the rest of the prophecy? He literally stopped quoting in the middle of a sentence.

Because his purpose at that time was to proclaim the favorable year of the Lord, meaning he would bring them the kingdom, describing what it looks like and how it would operate.

From the Isaiah prophecy, we can see the “happily ever after”—comfort all who mourn— comes after the vengeance. It was not yet time for Jesus to proclaim the Day of Vengeance, as it and the ultimate comforting of all who mourn would not come until after his return.

God’s plan unfolds in stages. First, Jesus came to earth 2,000 years ago and called his disciples who would follow him to a heavenly reward. Then he returns, bringing God’s vengeance, which opens the door to comfort ALL who mourn. There is a process. The time of God’s vengeance is merely a piece in the process that brings us to something greater.

The Lord’s Prayer reflects this two-part approach:

Matthew 6:9–10: 9 Pray, then, in this way: Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed be Your name. 10 Your kingdom come. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.

Jesus taught us to pray for God’s kingdom on earth because it was a reality not yet revealed. What does this mean? Whenever God says something is going to happen, it is a reality. It may not be happening at that moment, but when God says it will happen, it will happen—it’s a fact; it’s guaranteed; it’s as good as done. The kingdom on earth is a reality even though it would happen over 2,000 years in the future.

This is how prophecy works. Prophecy is God’s graciousness in giving us a glimpse of what He knows the future will be. When God reveals the future, it is a fact! The reality of Your kingdom come…on earth (Matthew 6:10)—even though they did not see it, was real. His statements are unequivocal.

The prophet Daniel sums this up for us, reminding us what is presently in place must be removed:

Daniel 2:44: In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, and that kingdom will not be left for another people; it will crush and put an end to all these kingdoms, but it will itself endure forever.

It destroys the other kingdoms (earthly governments). This is part of God’s vengeance. The end result is that God’s kingdom will endure forever.

Moving on, Psalm 145 is a song of praise and prophecy. It is a beautiful prophecy to read for encouragement:

Psalms 145:1–5: 1 I will extol You, my God, O King, and I will bless Your name forever and ever. 2 Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever. 3 Great is the LORD, and highly to be praised, and His greatness is unsearchable. 4 One generation shall praise Your works to another, and shall declare Your mighty acts. 5 On the glorious splendor of Your majesty and on Your wonderful works, I will meditate.

Have we ever seen this magnitude of praise unfold with multiple generations at the same time? No, this has never happened, but this is what we have to look forward to.

I will bless Your name forever and ever. Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever. When the thought of God’s vengeance overwhelms us, this is a great psalm to read to put it into the perspective of eventual never-ending peace. This psalm gives us a foundation of who God is and the purpose of His vengeance. We can’t wait for something this glorious!

God’s kingdom work is to be accomplished through those who are called to follow Jesus. When we put all of the scriptural accounts in one place, we can see how they dovetail together.

1 Peter 2:9,12: 9 But you are A CHOSEN RACE, A royal PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION, A PEOPLE FOR God's OWN POSSESSION, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light; 12 keep your behavior excellent among the Gentiles, so that in the thing in which they slander you as evildoers, they may because of your good deeds, as they observe them, glorify God in the day of visitation.

The day of visitation is another name for the Day of Judgment. It is not a 24-hour day; it is a period of time. As followers of Jesus, what we do now does matter because others are watching, and in the kingdom they will remember our example of Christlikeness later.

It is important for followers of Christ to behave righteously now, but it is also important for those who are not followers.

In our previous episode, we talked about our not taking revenge when we have been wronged, as vengeance belongs to the Lord (Romans 12:19). We left off with questioning, When will I get the justice I deserve? Where is justice for me? If any justice went unfulfilled, the Day of Judgment will put it right. Those who did wrong to others will have consequences and will have to make it right.

This is where true followers of Christ come in. They are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s possession (1 Peter 2:9, KJV). What does a priesthood do? It ministers to the people. They will be working with Jesus from heaven as mediators for the reconciliation of mankind back to God. This is what the call of the church is about—to be with Jesus to do this wonderful work in the day of visitation or Day of Judgment.

So much depends upon how we decide to see what the Bible puts in front of us. Will we complain about the details or glory in the conclusions?

In a way, God’s vengeance is the introduction to His kingdom. What does the foundation that His vengeance clears the way for look like?

The foundation of God’s kingdom has three distinct levels of operation, all of which are put into practice by those proven faithful to God’s will. As we will see, these three levels are designed to accomplish the mighty work of instituting an indestructible system of righteousness that will endure for all eternity.

But first, Psalm 145 continues with praises for God’s mighty acts, greatness, goodness and mercy:

Psalm 145:6–10: 6 Men shall speak of the power of Your awesome acts, and I will tell of Your greatness. 7 They shall eagerly utter the memory of Your abundant goodness and will shout joyfully of Your righteousness. 8 The LORD is gracious and merciful; slow to anger and great in lovingkindness. 9 The LORD is good to all (to just a few? No, to ALL), and His mercies are over all His works. 10 All Your works shall give thanks to You, O LORD, and Your godly ones shall bless You.

Men shall speak of the power of Your awesome acts—they have not done this yet, but this will happen in the future. God is good to not just a few but to all, so all Your works shall give thanks to You, O Lord. It shows a mighty power and governing presence that changes everything. But how?

There are three distinct levels of kingdom foundations:

1. First and foremost, it is built upon the foundation of Jesus Christ the Righteous:

Revelation 11:15: Then the seventh angel sounded; and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ; and he will reign forever and ever.

In our previous episode, we talked about the symbolic destruction on earth, but here we see the world goes on forever. Christ, under God, His Father, will reign forever and ever.

Once the present systems are removed, then the world will see evidence of mankind’s resurrection. Jesus describes how this process will begin:

John 5:28–29: 28 Do not marvel at this; for an hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, 29 and will come forth; those who did the good deeds to a resurrection of life, those who committed the evil deeds to a resurrection of judgment.

The resurrection of judgment will be a time of decision. Mankind will come back and be held accountable for their deeds and words in this life. Again, whatever justice wasn’t met in this life will have recompense. The resurrection brings all from their graves in order to rehabilate and work through all of the issues of life.

The first foundation is Jesus Christ, the righteous—the basis for everything. We get this from the New Testament: the words of Jesus, the words of the apostles and the writers of the New Testament. The amazing thing is that the Old Testament showed us this was going to happen! Some Christians put the Old Testament aside, and by doing so, they miss how the gospel actually works.

2. The kingdom is built upon the faithfulness of Jesus’ true disciples:

Daniel 7:27: Then the sovereignty, the dominion and the greatness of all the kingdoms under the whole heaven will be given to the people of the saints of the Highest One; his kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom, and all the dominions will serve and obey him.

Who are the saints ruling over?

The rest of mankind.

We remember 1 Peter 2:12: Keep your behavior excellent among the Gentiles so that in the thing in which they slander you as evildoers, they may because of your good deeds, as they observe them, glorify God in the day of visitation.

…the Gentiles are the people who Jesus and his faithful followers (the holy people, a priesthood) rule over, as Jesus’ ransom sacrifice “paid” for them. The price was paid to reconcile (pay the penalty for) sin through Adam and bring life through Christ.

Working to bring all of humanity back to God is why we are Christians. We are not Christians to go to heaven and have a good time. We are called to be Christians to follow in Jesus’ sacrificial footsteps, to learn how to be ministers of this amazing reconciliation.

3. The kingdom is built upon the restored nation of Israel on the earth:

Jeremiah 31:27–30: 27 Behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and with the seed of beast. 28 As I have watched over them to pluck up, to break down, to overthrow, to destroy and to bring disaster, (wait a minute – that doesn’t sound good!) so I will watch over them to build and to plant, declares the LORD. 29 In those days they will not say again, the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge. 30 But everyone will die for his own iniquity; each man who eats the sour grapes, his teeth will be set on edge.

We can see the equality of true justice shine out in this. Once the effects of God’s vengeance overthrow and break down the governments that have been based on greed, mankind will realize they do not want to go back to the old order. They will see equity in justice and application—no one will be able to say, It was his fault that I did that. At that time, every human being will be responsible for themselves because they have been redeemed by Jesus from Adam’s sin.

Can we imagine Israel being restored after all they have gone through throughout history? We are seeing this start to unfold now. The Jewish people brought back to their ancient homeland was prophesied.

Jesus and his faithful followers in heaven will oversee this merciful justice for the nation of Israel.

God’s promise to them and through them will be magnificent:

Jeremiah 31:31–33: 31 Behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, 32 not like the covenant which I made with their fathers in the day I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, My covenant which they broke, although I was a husband to them, declares the LORD. 33 But this is the covenant which I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD, I will put My law within them and on their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people.

God is contrasting the old Law Covenant (on which Israel had as its basis and no one could keep but Jesus) with the New Covenant, which will be written on their hearts. This will be an amazing transformation. It will be from the “inside out”—I will put My Law within them, and on their heart I will write it—in contrast to the Law, which worked from the “outside in.” Because of this reverse process with God giving them a basis of righteousness, their hearts can be molded differently. God will give them the basis of righteousness.

Let’s finish this prophecy by adding the last verse:

Jeremiah 31:34: They will not teach again, each man his neighbor and each man his brother, saying, Know the LORD, for they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them, declares the LORD, for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin I will remember no more.

There will eventually be a complete forgiveness of past sins and a clean slate for the world. This is huge! This reconciliation is the ultimate point of Jesus’ sacrifice.

- The first kingdom foundation is built upon Jesus Christ the Righteous. - The second kingdom foundation is built upon the faithfulness of Jesus’ true disciples. - The third kingdom foundation is built upon the restored nation of Israel on earth.

Israel’s transformation of heart and elevation of favor will serve to draw the rest of humanity to God:

Zechariah 8:20–23: 20 Thus says the LORD of hosts, It will yet be that peoples will come, even the inhabitants of many cities. 21 The inhabitants of one will go to another, saying, Let us go at once to entreat the favor of the LORD, and to seek the LORD of hosts; I will also go. 22 So many peoples and mighty nations will come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the favor of the LORD. 23 Thus says the LORD of hosts, In those days ten men from all the nations will grasp the garment of a Jew, saying, Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.

This is a descriptive picture. Nations and all people will see God’s favor upon Israel and will want to be a part of it. There is a magnetism from the grace of God that will work through the Jewish nation, plainly stated in Scripture.

This foundational power is a process that permeates everywhere.

No wonder this foundation cannot be destroyed; it is built on loyalty to God and the divine power that comes with that loyalty.

What will planet Earth look like with the solid foundation of God’s kingdom as its base? Does everything change?

When sin is removed from the world because of Jesus’ sacrifice, things do change. When the curse upon the ground that God put in place as a consequence of Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17) is removed because of Jesus' sacrifice, things do change. Humanity will still be mortal, and the earth will still be the earth, but ALL will grow and develop as God had originally designed them to grow and develop. That’s the difference—that’s the change!

Psalm 145 continues with praise, and now it gets specific about some details of this kingdom:

Psalm 145:11–16: 11 They shall speak of the glory of Your kingdom and talk of Your power; 12 to make known to the sons of men Your mighty acts and the glory of the majesty of Your kingdom. 13 Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures throughout all generations. 14 The LORD sustains all who fall and raises up all who are bowed down. 15 The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in due time. 16 You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing.

To begin to grasp God's character, read these verses over and over again. It says the word kingdom four times and the word dominion once. It clarifies what His kingdom looks like, full of God’s power and mighty acts. He takes care of everyone. All the previous verses of praise in this psalm lead to this.

We will spend the rest of this segment in the book of Isaiah because it has more kingdom prophecies than any other book of the Bible. It gives us an expansive view of what the kingdom looks like.

The kingdom works because of Jesus. It is based on justice and accountability and produces peace:

Isaiah 11:1–5: 1 Then a shoot will spring from the stem of Jesse, and a branch from his roots will bear fruit.

This is talking about Jesus—think about this prophecy with Jesus in mind.

2 The spirit of the LORD will rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD. 3 And he (Jesus) will delight in the fear of the LORD (God), and he will not judge by what his eyes see, nor make a decision by what his ears hear;

Why wouldn’t he do this?

4 but with righteousness he will judge the poor, and decide with fairness for the afflicted of the earth;

We get the sense that justice will be comprehensive, righteous and complete. It won’t be based on just an observation; but rather, on absolute truth.

and he will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will slay the wicked.

There will be a separation of those who willingly do not want to follow God’s rules in the kingdom. They will end up going into what Revelation 21:8 calls the “second death” because, despite every opportunity, they decide they will not follow Jesus’ rule under God.

5 Also righteousness will be the belt about his loins, and faithfulness the belt about his waist.

Righteousness, fairness and faithfulness describes Jesus’ oversight or supervision of this amazing kingdom! There is justice and judgment at that time. Conformity to righteousness will be a requirement for the world.

God’s creation will be brought back to the harmony with Him that was present in the Garden of Eden. How do we know?

Isaiah 11:6–9: 6 And the wolf will dwell with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little boy will lead them. 7 Also the cow and the bear will graze, their young will lie down together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. 8 The nursing child will play by the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper's den. 9 They will not hurt or destroy in all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

Were animals eating other animals in the Garden of Eden?

No. Even though carnivores like lions, leopards and wolves were designed to eat meat, there was no death or disharmony in the garden. Every creature harmoniously lived together.

We aren’t told exactly how this will work in the future kingdom, but we know the descriptions provided are facts. As the facts unfold, we will understand. God put Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, which was His gift to humanity. Sin messed all that up, but not forever. God’s plan has something much better.

In God’s kingdom, each will have ample space and opportunity to support themselves:

Isaiah 65:21–25: (NIV2011) 21 They will build houses and dwell in them; they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit. 22 No longer will they build houses and others live in them, or plant and others eat. For as the days of a tree, so will be the days of My people; My chosen ones will long enjoy the work of their hands. 23 They will not labor in vain, nor will they bear children doomed to misfortune; for they will be a people blessed by the LORD, they and their descendants with them. 24 Before they call I will answer; while they are still speaking I will hear. 25 The wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox, and dust will be the serpent’s food. They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, says the LORD.

Everyone will have shelter and resources for eternal life. But each must make progress in their heart and minds to be in harmony with God. Evil won't be allowed to flourish.

Personal responsibility will be the order of the day, not only for each individual taking care of themselves and helping others, but the personal responsibility that acknowledges this is God’s kingdom run in God’s way, and all are loyal to Him. The beauty of all of this is that each person is given the ability to care for themselves. Again the wolf and the lamb are shown eating together, but not each other. It is not a coincidence or just a poetic expression; it is to show us what the Garden of Eden looked like as a precurser to what God’s kingdom will look like.

God’s government, through Jesus, will assure everyone that war will forever cease!

Isaiah 2:2–4: 2 Now it will come about that in the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD (the government of God) will be established as the chief of the mountains, (the chief of all governments) and will be raised above the hills (above every earthly organization) and all the nations will stream to it.

Everybody will want to go there. Everyone streams towards it.

3 And many peoples will come and say, Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob; that He may teach us concerning His ways and that we may walk in His paths.

Think of the enthusiasm of going here!

For the law will go forth from Zion and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem. 4 And He will judge between the nations, and will render decisions for many peoples; and they will hammer their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will not lift up sword against nation, and never again will they learn war.

What a powerful prophecy! This describes how the kingdom will look nationally and physically. Through God's government, administered by Christ and his faithful ones, wars will cease and humanity will be able to take care of themselves.

Another confirmation:

Revelation 21:1: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth passed away…

The word new in Revelation means “freshness from its former condition.” It's renewed. This is the key. The Garden of Eden was completely lost and cut off from mankind. The prophecies tell us those conditions will be renewed.

This is biblical prophecy repeated again and again, showing the power of God’s word. When we put it all in place, we see the relatively short period of God’s vengeance will become a distant memory, unfolding a lasting, glorious new world.

No wonder the message of Jesus was called the gospel! This is the best news anyone could hope for, and it will become a permanent reality.

What will all of humanity look like when they are raised to life to live throughout the vast expanses of planet Earth?

This really is the key question. After all, 1 Corinthians 15:22 tells us that as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. Made alive to what kind of life and what kind of future? Here we go first back to the breadth of God’s character to form our answer. God is just and loving. He is wise and powerful. Put these attributes together and watch the future unfold!

Unfortunately, we see different Christian denominations misrepresenting God's character by creating a doctrine of eternal torment that contradicts all the scriptures we've just read. (Please search “hell” at ChristianQuestions.com for multiple episodes of in-depth scriptural analysis on the subject.)

How will life work in the kingdom?

Psalms 145:17–21: 17 The LORD is righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds. 18 The LORD is near to all who call upon Him, to all who call upon Him in truth. 19 He will fulfill the desire of those who fear Him; He will also hear their cry and will save them. 20 The LORD keeps all who love Him, but all the wicked He will destroy. 21 My mouth will speak the praise of the LORD, and all flesh will bless His holy name forever and ever.

It doesn’t say “all spirit beings”—it says all flesh will bless His holy name.

The beauty of God’s kingdom is in the details of the prophecies.

This kingdom is everlasting. All will be taught of God through Jesus to comply with godly righteousness:

Daniel 7:13–14: 13 … And behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man was coming… 14 and to him was given dominion, glory and a kingdom,

No surprise here, because we have seen all the pieces come into place.

that all the peoples, nations and men of every language might serve him.

Not most languages, not the most common languages, but ALL people of every language.

His dominion is an everlasting dominion which will not pass away; and his kingdom is one which will not be destroyed.

What a blessing afforded to the whole world! It is in the Bible again and again in multiple prophecies. It keeps showing up. Why? Because Jesus paid the price. He did what needed to be done to right the wrong and satisfy justice for Adam’s sin.

Because Jesus paid the ransom price, the delivery of this kingdom is guaranteed!

Isaiah 9:6–7: (NIV2011) 6 For to us a child is born, to us a son is given, and the government will be on his shoulders...7 of the greatness of his government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on David’s throne and over his kingdom, establishing and upholding it with justice and righteousness from that time on and forever. The zeal of the LORD Almighty will accomplish this.

This is God’s will! This has been His design from the very beginning. 1 Peter 1:19,20 speaks of the provision of Jesus as the Lamb slain even before the foundation of the earth.

The zeal of the LORD Almighty will accomplish this—this is not just wishful thinking on God’s part. The kingdom of God through Christ will be accomplished.

What does this kingdom bring to humanity?

The kingdom brings all manner of physical healing:

Isaiah 35:4–6: (NIV2011) 4 say to those with fearful hearts, Be strong, do not fear; your God will come, He will come with vengeance; with divine retribution He will come to save you. 5 Then will the eyes of the blind be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. 6 Then will the lame leap like a deer, and the mute tongue shout for joy.

Yes, it does start with vengeance, but He will come to save you. THEN the blind will see and the deaf will hear. THEN comes the healing of the nations. God’s vengeance sweeps away what man has put in place through Satan’s influence. The kingdom restores humanity!

The kingdom brings renewal to the earth:

Isaiah 35:6–7: (NIV2011) 6 …Water will gush forth in the wilderness and streams in the desert. 7 The burning sand will become a pool, the thirsty ground bubbling springs. In the haunts where jackals once lay, grass and reeds and papyrus will grow.

The earth will be fruitful just as God designed. The fact that God wrote it means He will do it. He wrote it through the hands and minds of those prophets He touched with His spirit to write the prophecies for us to read.

The kingdom brings reconciliation to all of humanity:

Isaiah 35:8–10: (NIV2011) 8 And a highway will be there; it will be called the Way of Holiness; it will be for those who walk on that Way. The unclean will not journey on it; wicked fools will not go about on it. 9 No lion will be there, nor any ravenous beast; they will not be found there. But only the redeemed will walk there, 10 and those the LORD has rescued will return. They will enter Zion with singing; everlasting joy will crown their heads. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.

Satan won't be able to interfere. No ravenous beast, meaning false religions, will be there to control mankind through fear. Mankind will flourish without hindrances. Gladness and joy will overtake them—what a beautiful promise!

One last quote from a different prophet to sum up what this earthly kingdom will look like:

Micah 4:1–3a: 1 And it will come about in the last days that the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains. It will be raised above the hills, and the peoples will stream to it. 2 Many nations will come and say, Come and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD and to the house of the God of Jacob, that He may teach us about His ways and that we may walk in His paths. For from Zion will go forth the law, even the word of the LORD from Jerusalem. 3 And He will judge between many peoples and render decisions for mighty, distant nations.

The kingdom promises are not just mentioned by one prophet in one circumstance. They are stated again and again.

The power and might of God’s kingdom will be unquestioned as righteousness is put in place!

Micah 4:3b–5: 3 Then they will hammer their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks; nation will not lift up sword against nation, and never again will they train for war. 4 Each of them will sit under his vine and under his fig tree, with no one to make them afraid, for the mouth of the LORD of hosts has spoken. 5 Though all the peoples walk each in the name of his god, as for us, we will walk in the name of the LORD our God forever and ever.

Again, this is a different prophecy at a different time, but with the same view of the future kingdom.

This is the ultimate reason why Jesus came and why sin has been allowed to happen for a period of time. The memories of these painful experiences will stay with humanity as eternal lessons. Retribution was put in place for the purpose of restoring mankind to the relationship Adam had with God at the beginning.

Revelation 21:3–4: 3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne, saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is among men, and He will dwell among them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself will be among them,

Remember how Adam and Eve could hear God “walking” in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 3:8)? This is as if God is saying, “I'm back. I'm back because sin is gone, because Jesus has taken care of it. I am back, and I am present with you.”

4 and He will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and there will no longer be any death; there will no longer be any mourning, or crying, or pain; the first things have passed away.

These first things (former things in the King James Version) are gone because God said so. Jesus did the work he came to do, and the kingdom is the result. This is why God's vengeance is an important, small step in the process of taking down the things of this world, so God's kingdom can be here forever and ever for the benefit of every single human being.

So, will there ever be peace on earth?

For Rick, Jonathan and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Isaiah 55:8–11: 8 For My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways My ways, declares the LORD. 9 For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts. 10 For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there without watering the earth and making it bear and sprout, and furnishing seed to the sower and bread to the eater; 11 So will My word be which goes forth from My mouth; It will not return to Me empty, without accomplishing what I desire, and without succeeding in the matter for which I sent it.

Here are just a few New Testament scriptures that verify this magnificent plan:

Colossians 1:18–20: 18 He is also head of the body, the church; and he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself will come to have first place in everything. 19 For it was the Father’s good pleasure for all the fullness to dwell in him, 20 and through him to reconcile all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross; through him, I say, whether things on earth or things in heaven.

The world will need the body of Christ to work them through the reconciliation process, and even though they don’t know it, they want them and wait for them:

Romans 8:18–19: 18 For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed to us. 19 For the anxious longing of the creation waits eagerly for the revealing of the sons of God.

God’s promises and prophecies carry over from the Old Testament to the New:

Acts 17:30–31: 30Therefore having overlooked the times of ignorance, God is now declaring to men that all people everywhere should repent, 31 because He has fixed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness through a man whom He has appointed, having furnished proof to all men by raising him from the dead.

Justice is a centerpiece. Through him all men will be able to choose the door of true freedom:

Hebrews 9:24–28: (NRSV) 24 For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by human hands, a mere copy of the true one, but he entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. 25 Nor was it to offer himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Holy Place year after year with blood that is not his own; 26 for then he would have had to suffer again and again since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the age to remove sin by the sacrifice of himself. 27 And just as it is appointed for mortals to die once, and after that the judgment, 28 so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

God proclaimed this kingdom to be coming; therefore, it is coming!

Revelation 21:3–4: 3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne, saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is among men, and He will dwell among them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself will be among them, 4 and He will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and there will no longer be any death; there will no longer be any mourning, or crying, or pain; the first things have passed away.

## Episode 1372 — Does God Punish Us When We Break a Promise?
Published: 2025-02-10
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1372-promise/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/13190753/CQ_Rewind_2-10-25_Does_God_Punish_Us_When_We_Break_a_Promise.pdf

Ecclesiastes 9:10: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might...

What is the status of promises these days? Has the making of a promise become a simple figure of speech? When we say, “I promise,” are we really saying, “I’m going to try,” or “I really do intend to accomplish what I said I would do”? Have we lost our connection between our promises and our integrity? It seems as though the power of a promise has gone from being a guarantee of what will happen to a way of showing effort in getting things done. So, what does God see in us when we make a half-hearted promise to someone else? Does this kindle His wrath, or does it just disappoint Him? What should we know and do when it comes to making and keeping our promises?

What does our theme text about doing things with all our might have to do with promises?

Actions are far superior to words! We will explore this as we continue.

You can make a promise without actually having to use the words, “I promise…” You just declare you will or won’t do something, and the other person relies on your word.

Before we focus on our promises made and sometimes broken, we need to ask THE fundamental question: What is the highest purpose of a promise?

- It is made to be counted on! As sinful human beings, we are extremely challenged in this area of life.

If you think about it, God's promises are a statement of a fact even if some have not yet unfolded. When we study them, we can better understand the true meaning of a promise.

God is the Grand Promise Keeper:

Isaiah 55:8-11: 8 For My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways My ways, declares the LORD. 9 For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts. 10 For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there without watering the earth and making it bear and sprout, and furnishing seed to the sower and bread to the eater; 11 So will My word be which goes forth from My mouth; It will not return to Me empty, without accomplishing what I desire, and without succeeding in the matter for which I sent it.

Mirriam Webster Dictionary Promise: noun

1. a declaration that one will do or refrain from doing something specified

2. a legally binding declaration that gives the person to whom it is made a right to expect or to claim the performance or forbearance of a specified act. (“Forbearance” here means not collecting on something due.)

This is emphatically stating that God's promises will always be fulfilled. This is the model we should follow.

There are three closely-related Greek New Testament words for promise.

The first word gives us the sense of a focused intention that precedes deliberate action. Of the 15 uses of this word, four are related to humanity and three of the four are NOT good.

Promise: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1861 epaggello; verb to announce upon (reflexively), i.e. (by implication) to engage to do something, to assert something respecting oneself

Here is the one positive use having to do with women in the church:

1 Timothy 2:9-10: 9 Likewise, I want women to adorn themselves with proper clothing, modestly and discreetly, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly garments, 10 but rather by means of good works, as is proper for women making a claim <1861> to godliness.

Making a claim here is that Greek verb for promise. The Apostle Paul isn’t saying women can’t wear braids in their hair or wear jewelry; instead, they should present themselves in relation to the promise they made—the stated intent of godliness. Being gaudy or showy would be inappropriate and out of place. If it’s too gaudy, it may not be godly.

The same goes for men. As followers of Jesus, we should dress in a way that honors God, not for the purpose of impressing ourselves or others. How are we presenting ourselves if we have promised our lives in sacrifice to follow in Jesus’ footsteps?

Here is an example of this word relating to God’s promises:

Hebrews 6:13-14: 13 For when God made the promise <1861> to Abraham, since He could swear by no one greater, He swore by Himself, 14 saying, I WILL SURELY BLESS YOU AND I WILL SURELY MULTIPLY YOU.

I will surely multiply you—God builds on and expands His original promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:2-3 and others) so His hearer clearly registers and understands His words. This example of commitment is what we should follow in our promises in order to be disciples of Jesus.

The second Greek word used for promise is a noun and expresses an unequivocal commitment to future actions.

Promise: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1862 epaggelma; noun a self-committal (by assurance of conferring some good)

This Greek word is used twice in the Bible, both times regarding God’s promises.

2 Peter 1:4: For by these He has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises <1862>, so that by them you may become partakers of the divine nature…

The divine nature is so far above us that we can’t understand it, but God’s promises open that door for us. This is the power of the concept of “promise” in the New Testament—the clarity, focus and security God provides.

2 Peter 3:12-13: 12 Looking for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be destroyed by burning, and the elements will melt with intense heat! 13 But according to His promise <1862> we are looking for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.

These scriptures start out with a terrible picture of destruction, but they are the introduction to what God’s promises will actually bring—a new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. What a promise!

We can rely on God’s promises. They are indestructible, irrefutable and cannot be questioned.

The last Greek word for promise is also a noun. It is the announcement of a promise as a basis for what people can rely on.

Promise: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1860 epaggelia; noun an announcement (for information, assent or pledge; especially a divine assurance of good):—message, promise

All combined, these three words for promise are used 70 times in the New Testament.

65 of those 70 uses refer to God and His promises.

The other five uses refer to human commitments—and a heads up, they mostly describe negative circumstances.

A negative human application of promise relates to the chief priests’ promised commitment to Judas to pay him to betray Jesus:

Mark 14:10-11: (NASB) 10 Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went off to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. 11 They were glad when they heard this, and promised <1861> to give him money. And he began seeking how to betray him at an opportune time.

Judas was driven by money. He had the promise of payment from the chief priests, and he acted on it by betraying Jesus. This was not a promise that brought glory to anyone. Unfortunately, many human promises end up this way.

Now we compare God’s promises:

Galatians 3:14,16: 14 In order that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we would receive the promise <1860> of the spirit through faith…. 16 Now the promises <1860> were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, and to seeds, as referring to many, but rather to one, and to your seed, that is, Christ.

The clarity of God’s words is shown here. Jesus told his followers the spirit would come to them when he left. This was a reflection and a confirmation of what God had promised Abraham all those years ago. Our promises need to be made with the same gravity.

As a friend of ours once said, “We might be the only Bible someone reads. Are we a good translation?” Are our lives reflecting what the word of God has taught us?

God’s lofty example of perfect promise keeping may seem beyond us. So, how did Jesus handle promises while he was on earth?

Jesus did not make a habit of promising things to his disciples. Instead, he LIVED his commitment to his Father every day in every way:

John 4:31-34: 31 Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, Rabbi, eat. 32 But he said to them, I have food to eat that you do not know about. 33 So the disciples were saying to one another, No one brought him anything to eat, did he? 34 Jesus said to them, My food is to do the will of Him who sent me and to accomplish His work.

Everything Jesus did and said was for the purpose of accomplishing his Father’s work in accordance with His Father’s will. He didn’t need to make a bunch of formal promises; he just did what God put in front of him.

Interestingly, Jesus never specifically taught anything about keeping promises. However, he did talk about being firm and truthful. Jesus LIVED the life of one who kept his promises on a higher level than any other human being ever did. He was absolutely dependable.

Living with focused integrity lessens the need to make promises along the way. Like Jesus, we need to LIVE the life.

Jesus taught us the principles of keeping our word, as some people do and some do not. Here Jesus was chastising the Pharisees:

Matthew 12:33-35: 33 Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit. 34 You brood of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak what is good? For the mouth speaks out of that which fills the heart. 35 The good man brings out of his good treasure what is good; and the evil man brings out of his evil treasure what is evil.

If we have been a “tree” with bad “fruit,” we need to transform ourselves and find new “treasure”! Not keeping our word is symptomatic of a wrong heart motivation and an unrealistic life perspective. If we are portraying ourselves as Christians but we are not keeping our word, there is a fundamental disconnect as others watch us.

Obviously, there is a difference between the promise made in a wedding vow and telling someone I’m going to bring an apple pie to your house on Friday, when we’re not really sure we’ll have the time to bake anything. But in each case, someone relies on what we say to be absolutely true.

Are we talking here about big life promises or our daily interactions with others?

Both. There are levels of promises, but there can be no vacillation when we have made a vow to God. If we say we vow to walk in Jesus’ footsteps and live lives of sacrifice, we have made a high and lofty promise we must keep. The same is true of our marriage vows because scripturally marriage is a covenant of God, made in His presence. These are serious promises.

It is easy to become sloppy in our thinking, words and commitments in everyday matters.

In these next scriptures, notice the clarity with which Jesus says we should speak. Understanding this helps us with promise making and promise keeping.

Jesus taught us that simple speech portrays a clear message and a righteous conscience:

Matthew 5:33-37: 33 Again, you have heard that the ancients were told, YOU SHALL NOT MAKE FALSE VOWS, BUT SHALL FULFILL YOUR VOWS TO THE LORD. 34 But I say to you, make no oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, 35 or by the earth, for it is the footstool of His feet, or by Jerusalem, for it is THE CITY OF THE GREAT KING. 36 Nor shall you make an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. 37 But let your statement be, Yes, yes or No, no; anything beyond these is of evil.

Speak clearly. Base our words on the commitment we have to serving God as a disciple of Jesus! This helps to clarify our thoughts and to grow in spiritual maturity.

With all this in mind, let’s get back to our original question:

Does God punish us when we don’t keep our promises?

If so, what might a “punishment” look like?

We can’t say how God will react. But breaking promises is a sinful act (as we “miss the mark”), and there may be many ways we reap the consequences of that act. We may start to feel guilt and shame. We may lose credibility with those around us. If others can’t rust our words, why would they trust our actions? God allows these and other natural consequences in the way He decides is most appropriate. He doesn’t carry out a vendetta against us, but He may save us from ourselves by providing us with experiences that help us grow through consquences for our untrustworthy tendencies.

Though God will not “hunt us down” (He doesn’t need to look for us) if we break promises, it does not mean we haven’t disappointed Him in one way or another.

He is watching:

Ephesians 4:29-30: (YLT) 29 Let no corrupt word out of your mouth go forth, but what is good unto the needful building up, that it may give grace to the hearers; 30 and make not sorrowful the holy spirit of God, in which ye were sealed to a day of redemption.

That word for corrupt here means rotten, putrefied or worthless. But it also means of poor quality, unfit for use. So, it’s not only vulgar or slanderous words but words that are useless. We want to use “quality” words, not useless ones. When we don’t do what we say we will do, we are not reflecting Jesus very well.

In studying for this, I realized I've been making several commitments to people to do something and hadn't done them. Well, I just haven't had the time.

Of course, I certainly found time to watch my favorite TV shows…

So, I've circled back, and I am doing what I said I would!

Sometimes, we believe in what we say at the time but lack follow-through, which is also a lack of integrity. We want integrity in our follow-through, or else we shouldn’t make the promise!

If we assess our behavior, see a problem and act to correct it, we will develop Christian discipline without having to be corrected.

Necessary Christian discipline comes in degrees, as some disciples respond more easily than others:

Hebrews 12:5-8: (This is in the context of considering what Jesus endured) 5 And you have forgotten the exhortation which is addressed to you as sons... (then the Apostle Paul quotes from Proverbs 3:11,12) MY SON, DO NOT REGARD LIGHTLY THE DISCIPLINE (tutorage, training) OF THE LORD, NOR FAINT WHEN YOU ARE REPROVED (admonished) BY HIM;

- Do not regard lightly the discipline of God—the whole process of helping us grow. Like Julie’s example, she understood she needed to do better and self-corrected. - Do not lose heart when you are reproved by Him—to be scolded with words or a disheartening experience.

We may read the Scriptures or hear something from one of the brotherhood and realize we should apply it to ourselves. This is another way God helps us “right the ship.”

6 FOR THOSE WHOM THE LORD LOVES HE DISCIPLINES (educates, disciplines), AND HE SCOURGES (to flog, literally or figuratively) EVERY SON WHOM HE RECEIVES (accepts). 7 It is for discipline that you endure; God deals with you as with sons; for what son is there whom his father does not discipline? 8 But if you are without discipline, of which all have become partakers, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.

- Whom the Lord loves He disciplines—the actions of discipline may not feel like “love,” but they are. Good parents know that discipline is part of raising their child with love. - He scourges every son whom He receives—scourging seems harsh, the opposite of acceptance, but as a last step in this progression, a stronger type of discipline might be necessary.

Hebrew 5:8 says Jesus learned obedience by the things he suffered. Jesus never needed to be disciplined by God; he only needed direction. We, on the other hand, need correction.

Sometimes a harsh experience can shake us out of our lethargy and enable us to move forward. This is the point of God’s discipline.

If we do not speak truth to others because we promise thing we do not follow through on, we are subject to God's discipline in whatever way He deems necessary.

The desired result of all of this:

Hebrews 12:11: All discipline for the moment seems not to be joyful, but sorrowful; yet to those who have been trained by it, afterwards it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

It is all about nurturing, learning and stimulating us towards Christian maturity. So, when we are not speaking the truth, God will do what is necessary for us to learn the lesson.

As we grow into the high-level integrity of being a disciple of Christ, we need to embrace the scriptural guidelines for who we should be in our everyday lives.

Our focus should be on those things that are eternal:

1 Corinthians 9:24-25: 24 Do you not know that those who run in a race all run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may win. 25 Everyone who competes in the games exercises self-control in all things. They then do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.

This is our big picture. So, in this picture, where does making promises come in?

We should “promise” God our hearts, by living each day with the determination to work at being completely faithful to our calling:

2 Peter 1:10-11: 10 Therefore, brethren, be all the more diligent to make certain about His calling and choosing you; for as long as you practice these things, you will never stumble; 11 for in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and savior Jesus Christ will be abundantly supplied to you.

We promise our hearts to God by living how He has directed us in His word.

We should “promise” the brotherhood our engaged support by living the way Jesus taught us to live:

John 15:12-13: 12 This is my commandment, that you love one another, just as I have loved you. 13 Greater love has no one than this, that one lay down his life for his friends.

Galatians 6:2: Bear one another’s burdens, and thereby fulfill the law of Christ.

Notice these scriptures aren’t about talking; they are about daily LIVING the word of Christ. He showed his love by helping his followers, walking with them and ultimately dying for them and all of humanity. We need to show up for the brotherhood and be there to help them with their burdens.

We should “promise” the brotherhood our prayerful devotion by regularly engaging in prayer for them:

James 5:16: Therefore, confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another so that you may be healed. The effective prayer of a righteous man can accomplish much.

It’s nice to tell the brotherhood you are praying for them, but even better is to make sure you are engaging in frequent, earnest prayer. We need to do the work. If you say you are going to pray for someone, pray for them!

We should “promise” all men our respect and love by living every day after the pattern of Jesus:

Galatians 6:9-10: 9 Let us not lose heart in doing good, for in due time we will reap if we do not grow weary. 10 So then, while we have opportunity, let us do good to all people, and especially to those who are of the household of the faith.

If we live these words rather than just talking about them, we will have achieved a high level of integrity others will see. We will draw people to us because they will recognize the quality of our characters. Promises are one thing, but doing our best to be reliable and trustworthy is what gives people a sense of security about us. Jesus is our example of keeping promises through doing the will of God.

Remember, it comes down to what we do, not what we say. And that's exactly how Jesus taught us to live. What matters is doing the will of God.

That is how we keep our promises.

So, does God punish us when we break a promise?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!
