## Episode 1375 — Are Soul Ties Biblical?
Published: 2025-03-03
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1375-soul-ties/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/07103227/CQ_Rewind_03-03-25_Are_Soul_Ties_Biblical.pdf

Mark 10:6–9: 6 But from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female. 7 for this reason a man shall leave his father and mother, 8 and the two shall become one flesh… 9 what therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.

Human beings are different from all the rest of God’s creation. Of all the creatures on this earth, we were the only ones created “in God’s image.” God was intentional with this, as the human race was meant to be an extension of God’s family here on this planet. He created us as social and relationship-oriented beings. We were created to be connected, not just with our Creator, but with each other. In many spiritually based groups, this connectivity is defined by the phrase “soul ties.” These are often described as the most intense connections people can have between them. They are credited with having their basis on a mystical level. Do these soul ties accurately represent what God intended humanity’s connections to look like, or are they way off-base?

A soul tie is said to be an intense bond between two people that feels all-consuming.

- It differs from the common expression “soul mate” in that it doesn’t have to be romantic or with only one person. It can exist between friends or even enemies, or business associates.
- It is said it can be created by physical intimacy or other shared experiences that form an emotional bond.
- It is said it can be created by making vows or promises to someone out loud, with the thought that those words remain in existence somewhere in the universe and they are binding.
- It is said it can be created in a past life.
- It is said it can be created by casting a magical love spell or a binding spell.
- The idea of being bound by soul ties is very popular on social media.

While it originates from New Age teachings of mystical connections, some Christians have embraced this idea as having its basis in Scripture. We will take an honest look to see if this is true.

Some Christians use the account of Adam and Eve being joined as a basis to justify soul ties:

Genesis 2:21–24: 21 So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and he slept; then He took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh at that place. 22 The LORD God fashioned into a woman the rib which He had taken from the man, and brought her to the man. 23 The man said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. 24 For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother, and be joined to his wife; and they shall become one flesh.

As Christians, we look at these scriptures as a beautiful example of the joining together of a man and a woman in marriage.

Proponants of soul ties say, “two parts of their souls were knit together.” However…

“…when people become ‘one flesh’ they are not combining their souls. A person does not find their ‘better half’ when they marry, because humans are not halves.” – christianity.com

Does the account of Shechem and Dinah verify soul ties?

Genesis 34:1–4: 1 Now Dinah the daughter of Leah… went out to visit the daughters of the land. 2 When Shechem the son of Hamor… the prince of the land, saw her, he took her and lay with her by force. 3 He was deeply attracted to Dinah the daughter of Jacob, and he loved <157> the girl and spoke tenderly to her. 4 So Shechem spoke to his father Hamor, saying, Get me this young girl for a wife.

This royal prince, Shechem, forcibly grabbed Dinah and raped her. But he was deeply attracted to Dinah…and he loved the girl.. He wanted her for his wife. Does this violent connection that soon ended in tragedy describe a soul tie?

Soul ties are often described in a negative sense, as the reason you are being held back in some area of your life. Therefore, the reasoning goes, the tie needs to be severed.

Symptoms of a negative soul tie include:

- You have a hard time letting go after a breakup.
- You can’t see life without this person.
- Your self-worth is based on this other person.
- One of you exhibits manipulative and controlling behavior, or obsessive and possessive behavior.

Your soul tie must be severed, and there are seemingly no limit to the number of “spiritual healers” who can help “unknit” your souls from one another. There are also Christian “deliverance” ministries helping people break soul ties with the fear that demons can travel to and from people connected by a soul tie.

The human mind is very creative, and this quickly steps into the realm of mythology, witchcraft and paganism. It is a warning bell.

Let’s drop in on a few additional scriptures some people use to suggest soul ties are scriptural.

The friendship between Jonathan and David was remarkable. Was it a soul tie?

1 Samuel 18:1: Now it came about when he had finished speaking to Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit <7194> to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved <157> him as himself.

Their souls were “knit together.” It’s definitely poetic, and this sure sounds like this idea of a soul tie. Is it?

Knit: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7194: qashar; a primitive root: to tie, physically (gird, confine, compact) or mentally (in love, league)

This does give the sense that their souls/lives were literally tied together. What do we do with that?

Let’s look further into their relationship:

1 Samuel 18:3–4: 3 Then Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved <157> him as himself. 4 Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, with his armor, including his sword and his bow and his belt.

There is no doubt Jonathan and David had a strong bond of friendship.

In summary, we see strong, positive connections like Adam and Eve and Jonathan and David. We see strong negative connections like Shechem and Dinah.

Do these examples give credibility to soul ties being a scripturally sound concept? No! There are several reasons for this.

In the Dinah account, Shechem loved her. Jonathan loved David. The Hebrew word for love used here is broadly used in the Old Testament.

Love: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #157 āhaḇ; a primitive root; to have affection for (sexually or otherwise):—(be-) love(-d, -ly, -r), like, friend

The King James Version translates this as love 169 times, lover(s) 19 times, friend(s) 12 times, beloved 5 times, liketh 1 time; lovely 1 time, loving 1 time

The word is used to convey admiration and respect.

We are to have a high level of respect for our neighbor and for others:

Leviticus 19:18: …you shall love <157> your neighbor as yourself; I am the LORD.

Leviticus 19:34: The stranger who resides with you shall be to you as the native among you, and you shall love <157> him as yourself, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt.

If we say this word love indicates a soul tie, as in Shechem loved Dinah and Jonathan loved David, then we would have to say everybody in the nation of Israel had to have a soul tie. Everybody is tied to their neighbor, and everybody is tied to the stranger. Everybody is tied to everybody! But we can’t take that word and just focus on this one way it is used. It has a much broader meaning.

Let’s look at Jonathan and David to understand what happened. Why did Jonathan have this great affection for David? Just before the texts we read, David had done something unusual. The young man David, a teenager, stood up against the giant Goliath and killed him in a one-on-one battle.

He did this in the name of God and the name of Israel. When there was no soldier in the entire army who would stand up against that man, this kid comes and kills the giant.

David’s faith and courage had saved Israel, and Israel was King Saul’s kingdom. King Saul was Jonathan’s father. Jonathan watched David save his father’s kingdom in the name of God. Jonathan saw this and was drawn to him because of the clarity of his thinking, his courage and his faith. Jonathan covenanted his friendship to David because David was the kind of person everyone wanted to be!

This was an extraordinary example of friendship. It was incredible because they were both men of a high level of character. This is not some mystical soul tie; this is a tie based on admiration for each other that made them want to be a part of each other’s life.

After King Saul died, David became king. After King David died, his son Solomon became king. He is said to have had 700 wives and 300 concubines as a display of wealth and power. Were his connections with all those foreign women evidences of dangerous and unhealthy soul ties?

Let’s look at how the Bible describes it, but first we want to look at Solomon’s devotion to God.

Remember, before Solomon became devoted to idolatrous women, he was first devoted to serving God:

1 Kings 3:3: Now Solomon loved <157> the LORD, walking in the statutes of his father David…

The distractions and power of kingship overrode Solomon’s devotion to God:

1 Kings 11:1–2: 1 Now King Solomon loved <157> many foreign women… 2 from the nations concerning which the LORD had said to the sons of Israel, You shall not associate with them, nor shall they associate with you, for they will surely turn your heart away after their gods. Solomon held fast to these in love <157>.

These relationships were not soul ties. They were the result of the attraction of power and lust Solomon felt, even though God warned him not to pursue such relationships. Solomon rationalized these attractions into becoming a way of life. This act of defiance would cost him dearly, as his son would lose the royal lineage of the kingdom of Israel. Those who believe in soul ties would argue that this is the danger in them. We say, no, this is the danger of lust! It is the danger of misplacing your life’s dedication.

When we believe in this concept of soul ties, we take our life circumstances and say they are beyond our ability to change. I am a victim of what happens around me, and I have no choice. Solomon later wrote in Proverbs that he learned all is vanity. His actions were not due to some mystical tie; they were the effects of human emotions and desires running wild, resulting in blatant idolatry.

We have noticed a pattern with Christian internet preachers embracing soul ties. They hold up as “proof” whatever scriptures legitimately describe any kind of meaningful relationship, like those we’ve already reviewed.

Two additional “proofs” often cited are 1 Corinthians 6:16—a warning that when sleeping with a prostitute, The two shall become one flesh. Proponents say this proves a soul tie is created through the sexual act. In Colossians 2:2, the Apostle Paul says the hearts of the brethren have been knit together in love. Therefore, they say, we have a soul tie with every other believer.

But being “knit together in love” is a choice. This is not a destiny driven by some mystical power. The believers in Colossae decided to follow Jesus and love the brethren. Our core values are about making choices, not rationalizing our behaviors by claiming to be cosmic victims.

Making and breaking soul ties is an appealing concept:

- It can be an excuse for bad behavior by rationalizing promiscuity because “you have no choice,” as you are supernaturally tied to this person and this person and this person…
- It provides an explanation for why we hurt so much when a relationship goes bad.
- It’s a romantic notion made even more popular by people like the biggest-selling recording artist in the world, Taylor Swift, who has a song called Invisible String with the lyric, “Isn’t it just so pretty to think all along there was some invisible string tying you to me?” Aww. Such a pretty thought!

Are we going down a “pretty” road now? It IS attractive. But sin is attractive. Darkness is attractive. Evil is attractive. Godlessness is attractive. Are we going to get stuck in such things?

Human beings are given free will with the ability to assess situations. Yes, our natural inclinations can draw us into unhealthy situations, but we absolutely have choices in the human connections we make.

We talked some about using mystical means to undo these problems. What does the Bible say about such an approach to this perceived problem?

The principles in the Old Testament Law show a clear-cut response to such approaches:

Deuteronomy 18:10–13: 10 There shall not be found among you anyone who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire, one who uses divination, one who practices witchcraft, or one who interprets omens, or a sorcerer, 11 or one who casts a spell, or a medium, or a spiritist, or one who calls up the dead. 12 For whoever does these things is detestable to the

LORD; and because of these detestable things the LORD your God will drive them out before you. 13 You shall be blameless before the LORD your God.

Beyond the romantic notion of soul ties is the mystical part, where now we allegedly need certain rituals to break the ties that are ruining our life. They look an awful lot like witchcraft involving white candles, salt, cord-cutting rituals, specific prayers, magic spells or incantations and more.

There’s nothing biblical about demons traveling through a metaphorical string between us. This creates an environment of unnecessary fear and feeds into demonology, wanting to look into things we are not supposed to look into.

In Deuteronomy, those who do these things are detestable to the LORD. This is an Old Testament scripture, but Jesus never says in the New Testament that it no longer applies. He doesn’t even have to address it because it was so clearly ungodly and idolatrous.

Stay far away from any situation that requires this or that ritual to cut the soul tie with demons traveling back and forth! This is an ungodly realm, and as Christians, we are to have no part in such things.

What about legitimate relationship issues?

We might need to seek counseling for ways of coping with past or present relationships. The hurt and pain is real. For example, a counselor might suggest we remove from our house physical objects belonging to the person causing us pain, for example. All rituals aren’t evil or demonic.

Professional counseling can certainly help us to move past the pain. Certain physical rituals can help us move past difficult circumstances. Rather than being mystical, these can give our minds clear steps to clean something out of our past so we can move into the present, and then move on by approaching the future. That is an acceptable way to look at things.

But when we tie in the magic spells and spirit realm, we have gone too far. We don’t need those things. We want to focus, make better choices and move forward in a godly way.

Instead of trying to see harmful relationships as driven by mystical powers with mystical threads that connect us, let’s see them as they really are: sin and darkness, rooted in the sin of Adam and the influence of Satan.

Ephesians 6:10–13: 10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of His might. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you will be able to stand firm against the schemes of the devil. 12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the powers, against the world forces of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. 13 Therefore, take up the full armor of God, so that you will be able to resist in the evil day, and having done everything, to stand firm.

Next in this text comes the armor of God—the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the spirit, the shield of faith and the girdle of truth. Mentally “putting on the armor” is not a ritual; it is acknowledging we need God’s help in our struggles.

Let me arm myself with faith—not in meaningless rituals, but in the word of God. Let me arm myself with righteousness—the breastplate of righteousness covers our heart, our vital organs. It is no accident it’s called “righteousness.” Righteousness protects us, not ritual. The Scriptures give us the answers. We are not to go down the road of mysticism.

Handling all challenges comes down to our decision to focus our thinking and resulting actions, both in accordance with clearly-delivered guidance from God’s word:

2 Corinthians 10:3–5: 3 For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh, 4 for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but divinely powerful for the destruction of fortresses. 5 We are destroying speculations and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God, and we are taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.

Taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ—our influences should not be coming from the outside in, but rather with the thought of, I am going to immerse myself in the word of God, in God’s help and direction. I will immerse myself in fellowship with those of like faith. I am going to work on having my thoughts be captive to following Jesus’ example. This should be our driving force. Our reactions need to be scripturally based.

Seeing our own weaknesses helps us see a scriptural path to dealing with them:

James 4:1–4: 1 What is the source of quarrels and conflicts among you? Is not the source your pleasures that wage war in your members? 2 You lust and do not have; so you commit murder. You are envious and cannot obtain; so you fight and quarrel. You do not have because you do not ask. 3 You ask and do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures. 4 You adulteresses, do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.

It comes down to the idea of, “It’s all about me, and what I want when I want it.” Why is this soul ties concept becoming more popular, especially with younger people? Perhaps because of the prevalence of “ethical non-monogamy” or “polyamory,” meaning, having multiple intimate relationships with the full knowledge and consent of all parties involved. This concept does not align with God’s laws against adultery and fornication, so they need another excuse, another reason, Well, this is just the way the universe works!

No, it is not the way the universe works; it’s the way a sinful mind can work. We need to take it out of the “universe” and bring it down to our own responsibility and accountability.

Everyone can live as they choose, but Christians should look inward and decide not to act upon unscriptural desires.

We do not need to be fighting to sever a soul tie; we need to be fighting our own internal thoughts and emotions to be more pleasing to God.

Be wary of those who encourage mystical responses relating to perceived soul ties in the name of Christ.

The Apostle Paul comments on those who preached a different gospel:

2 Corinthians 11:13–14: 13 For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. 14 No wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

We found “healers” online and on social media advising their followers to ask for angelic help in dealing with soul ties. One said, “If you work with archangels, consider calling upon Michael every time you feel the soul tie get triggered.”

We are not to call upon angels! If we claim Christianity and are considering contacting angels, immediately stop and go in the other direction! In the case of soul ties and angels, we are dealing with demonism. Angels don’t respond to us. They are sent when God sends them. They do not come because we call! Do not listen to any who try to guide you down such pathways.

Proverbs 4:23–27: 23 Watch over your heart with all diligence, for from it flow the springs of life. 24 Put away from you a deceitful mouth and put devious speech far from you. 25 Let your eyes look directly ahead and let your gaze be fixed straight in front of you. 26 Watch the path of your feet and all your ways will be established. 27 Do not turn to the right nor to the left; Turn your foot from evil.

Make sure your heart is in the right place. Make sure your words are speaking the right things. Don’t let your eyes wander; look straight ahead. Watch where you go.

This is not mystical; it is all choice. As Christians, we need to daily make these clear and firm choices, and then stand in righteousness.

This is a simple process. While the idea of soul ties might be enticing and feel like a way to get what we want without having to take responsibility, it is all lies. It is a devious lie that take us away from the true meaning and true focus and direction of our lives—to walk in Jesus’ footsteps.

Don’t let soul ties even enter your mind. They are fictitious, they are mythological and they don’t belong!

So, are soul ties biblical?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

and David, and Solomon and his wives support the idea of biblical “soul ties”?

2. Are these considered positive soul ties? Are there negative soul ties according to those that

profess this belief? (Genesis 2:21-24, 34:1-4, 1 Samuel 18:1-4, 1 Kings 3:3, 11:1-2)

3. If soul ties exist, how would Leviticus 19:18 and 34 be interpreted?

4. What are the dangers in living our lives with this idea? How might this affect our personal

responsibility towards our own mistakes? Could this belief in soul ties impact forgiveness? How could it affect looking to God’s word for guidance in repenting and walking again in righteousness? How could it affect your relationship with God and with His son, Jesus?

a. How do we accurately see the problem? How do we arm ourselves? (Ephesians 6:10-13)

b. What should our responses to challenges be based on? (2 Corinthians 10:3-5)

c. What is absolutely necessary when looking at our own weaknesses? (James 4:1-4)

6. What experiences or actions have you had to “stand strong and walk away” from? What thoughts

and ideas from the world are the most attractive to you? How are you fighting against letting them gain a footing in your life?

## Episode 1376 — Do I Really Have to Love My Enemies?
Published: 2025-03-17
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1376-enemies/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/15085207/CQ_Rewind_3-17-25_Do_I_Really_Have_to_Love_My_Enemies.pdf

Luke 6:27-28: But I say to you who hear, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, 28 bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.

Loving the people we know and appreciate can be hard work in general, never mind loving our enemies. There is so much emotion involved in loving others, and let’s face it, sometimes even those we appreciate can act in ways that cause us aggravation! When it comes to how we are to treat ALL of those around us, whether we like them or not, Jesus taught us a very high standard to live by. Luke’s account of his words from the Sermon on the Mount clearly lays out the way we should be striving to live, especially in relation to those who stand against us. If we give it a chance, focusing on what Jesus said and working at practically applying it to our everyday lives can fundamentally change the way we see and treat everyone around us.

While we will use the Luke account as our basis for learning, we will add important details from Matthew 5 to enhance our understanding.

In Matthew 5, Jesus repeatedly compares what his Jewish audience had been taught with what he was teaching:

Matthew 5:43: You have heard that it was said, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR and hate your enemy.

Jesus is quoting here from Leviticus 19:18 that says love your neighbor as yourself, but nowhere did the Law say to hate your enemy.

(Source: James Burton Coffman Commentary) THAT was an addition to God’s word by the scribes and Pharisees. Thus, the people of Jesus’ day had fallen into the old and vicious habit of linking a sublime truth with a ridiculous error…

By the time it filtered down to the people, the popular belief was truth mixed with error.

Matthew 5:44-45: But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, 45 so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven; for He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.

The word for love here is the unselfish, agape kind of love, which means giving without expecting anything in return. That one small point will play an enormous role in understanding this whole subject.

Loving our enemies with this kind of love includes recognizing the evil they do, but not with retaliation in mind. It is okay to recognize the evil, but it is not okay to retaliate.

Luke 6:27-28 presents this by making four specific points: But I say to you who hear...

Jesus gave us four different approaches. Yes, Jesus taught us to love our enemies, but what else did he say? Do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you. By listing these as four different aspects, Jesus is saying, Listen carefully; this is important.

Jesus then gives details as to how to live this specific kind of love:

Luke 6:29-30: 29 Whoever hits you on the cheek, offer him the other also; and whoever takes away your coat, do not withhold your shirt from him either. 30 Give to everyone who asks of you, and whoever takes away what is yours, do not demand it back.

It sounds like he’s stopping the evil by responding in an unexpected way, as in, Here, you must need this shirt more than I do! If someone is in an argumentative mood and we don’t argue back, as difficult as that might be, the argument loses its fire.

Jesus is telling us how to approach such disagreements in a contrary way. But these exhortations seem to go too far! Wait—what do you mean? Just give things away? Isn’t there any standard or justice we are supposed to live by? What does Jesus mean by all this?

Jesus was teaching his disciples about the heart attitude they would be challenged to develop as his followers. He was focusing on what goes on inside our hearts.

This all sounded impossible, but later in Jesus' ministry, he would show them exactly what loving our enemies would look like. He would live what he taught. There are several examples of this, but we want to focus on Judas' example.

Judas had become an enemy, the betrayer of Jesus. He was one of the twelve apostles— Jesus’ closest followers. We may argue that Judas really did not expect the conspiracy against Jesus to unfold fully, and that he knew Jesus had the power to overcome any enemy at any time. Whatever he knew, let’s not forget that Judas still betrayed his friend for a bag of money.

Days before the crucifixion, we get a glimpse of Judas’ dark heart at the home of Jesus’ friends, Lazarus, Mary and Martha, in the town of Bethany. After dinner, Mary took a pound of costly perfume and anointed the feet of Jesus while wiping his feet with her hair. This beautiful act of service symbolized the preparation for his burial.

Continuing with the account:

John 12:4-6: 4 But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, who was intending to betray him, said, 5 Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and given to poor people (about a year’s worth of wages)? 6 Now he said this, not because he was concerned about the poor, but because he was a thief, and as he had the money box, he used to pilfer what was put into it.

During the week before his crucifixion, Jesus had been telling his disciples he would die. Instead of learning from and caring for Jesus in his last days, Judas was thinking about money.

Pilfer means to steal something, typically of small value. Apparently Judas was in the habit of taking a little here and there for himself and thought no one would notice.

Judas’ selfish heart was revealed. From his perspective, this was money being wasted, as his heart was set on personally profiting from the wisdom, kindness and power that Jesus displayed.

When we think of Jesus’ ministry up to this point, we know he went to various places at which he would perform miracles, preach and teach, and people were drawn to him. He was an itinerant preacher with no place to live, so people would contribute and say, Just keep doing your good work! Judas found a way to skim off the top, a little here and a little there, and nobody noticed because he was the bookkeeper and keeper of the money bag.

We see the craftiness and darkness within Judas. He profited off of the crowd's appreciation of Jesus' selflessness in healing, performing miracles and doing the will of God.

We contrast that dark heart with Jesus’ tender and understanding heart, which would also be revealed in this experience:

John 12:7-8: (NLT) 7 Jesus replied, Leave her alone. She did this in preparation for my burial. 8 You will always have the poor among you, but you will not always have me.

Jesus pronounced Mary’s actions honorable and appropriate. He knew Judas’ scolding that the money should be going to the poor wasn’t real, but was coming from a greedy heart.

Jesus honored Mary for her respectful and costly sacrifice. She poured out that costly ointment as a memorial of his death. The contrast between Mary and Judas is dramatic. Jesus recognized the beauty of Mary’s sacrifice. And all he says to Judas is, Leave her alone. He doesn’t go any further than that. Just, No, you are not stopping this.

Jesus doesn’t address Judas’ underlying motivation. This isn’t even the betrayal yet. But in the lead-up to it, we see how Judas is walking in a pathway of darkness that will lead him to become an enemy of the man he had called Master and Rabbi.

Jesus instructs us to live a love that includes our enemies.

This is such an important point. We can see the context of “love your enemies” in how Jesus treated Judas the same way as the other apostles (remember that Jesus could read the hearts of others where we cannot). There was equality in Jesus’ treatment of his apostles—even though Jesus knew of Judas' betrayal, he conducted himself toward Judas in the same manner as he did toward the other apostles. This is a dramatic lesson for us.

By loving Judas all along the way, Jesus was revealing the fundamental principle of humble acquiescence to God’s will. We need to take note!

The plot to betray Jesus would unfold quickly.

How would Jesus respond to its development each step of the way?

What Jesus would do as this heartbreaking plot unfolded showed us in graphic detail just what it means to love our enemies. As we shall see, Jesus would be a shining example of all that he taught in the Sermon on the Mount.

He taught us to:

Jesus illustrated those four points in the way he treated Judas.

Before we highlight what loving our enemy should look like, let’s take a moment to look at what the heart of an enemy can look like, even though it is painful to do so.

Let’s go back to Judas to understand some of the underlying things that are happening:

Matthew 26:14-16: (KJV) 14 Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went unto the chief priests, 15 and said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver. 16 And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him.

Incidentally, 30 pieces of silver was the price to ransom a slave. The irony is how little Jesus was valued. The fact that Judas was skimming off the top of the group’s purse indicates his greed—I need to know what I can get for him. This is dark.

Judas’ question spoke volumes. What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? There is no negotiation, no thinking about his actions—just, I’ll deliver him, pay me. It is stark and deeply disturbing.

*The only recorded words of Judas to Jesus after this bargaining statement were two simple sentences. The first showed his cowardice, and the second actually betrayed Jesus. We will go over these shortly.

Again, remember why we are going through the pain of looking at all this. It is because we want to understand what it means to love our enemies.

We contrast this with Jesus, interacting with the twelve in the upper room the night before his crucifixion. He already knew who would betray him.

Knowing this, Jesus would demonstrate bless those who curse you by blessing Judas, the one who put his death in motion:

John 13:2-5: 2 During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him, 3 Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going back to God, 4 got up from supper, and laid aside his garments; and taking a towel, he girded himself. 5 Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.

In Jesus’ time people wore sandals, and the streets were dusty. When you visited someone, your host would have their servant wash your feet so that you would feel clean and refreshed. This was a lowly job. However, for the night of the Passover supper, only Jesus and his twelve apostles were using the upper room, there was no official host. Surprisingly, no one had thought to do this for him or each other, so they ate their meal with dirty feet. It seems that none of them were willing to take on a servant’s position. But Jesus was.

It is interesting that the scripture starts by saying, During supper, which means Jesus allowed the meal to begin, and when he saw nobody stepping forward to wash their feet, he felt there was a lesson that needed to be taught. He would wash the feet of the twelve, which meant Jesus washed his would-be betrayer’s feet just like everyone else’s. He blessed Judas by humbly serving him; he treated him just like the others.

Shortly after this, Jesus would show them how to do good to those who hate you:

John 13:21-26: 21 When Jesus had said this, he became troubled in spirit, and testified and said, Truly, truly, I say to you, that one of you will betray me.

(Source: Bible Commentary by David Guzik) Judas’ betrayal of Jesus troubled him. Jesus was not unfeeling or emotionally detached from the events… He loved Judas and was troubled for Judas’ sake, much more than his own.

22 The disciples began looking at one another, at a loss to know of which one he was speaking. 23 There was reclining on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved… 25 he (John), leaning back thus on Jesus' bosom, said to him, Lord, who is it? 26 Jesus then answered, That is the one for whom I shall dip the morsel and give it to him...

Matthew 26:25: And Judas, who was betraying him, said, Surely it is not I, Rabbi? ...

*Judas' first statement showed his cowardice: Surely it is not I, Rabbi?

What hypocrisy, knowing the plan of betrayal was already in motion!

...Jesus said to him, You have said it yourself.

Continuing in the John account:

John 13:26-27: ...So when he had dipped the morsel, he took and gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. 27 After the morsel, Satan then entered into him. Therefore Jesus said to him, What you do, do quickly.

Judas knew Jesus understood what was happening, but the account goes on to say the other apostles didn’t understand what Jesus meant, or obviously, they would have stopped Judas from leaving.

There is confusion amongst the other apostles, but Judas and Jesus both knew what Judas was about to do. Jesus basically said, You have betrayed me in your heart; now go do what you set out to do. Talk about loving our enemies! The words of Jesus exposed to Judas that Jesus knew he was the betrayer. Jesus didn’t hold back—What you do, do quickly. The way he exposed Judas was to share food with him, which was a sign of a close friendship in those days. Jesus is showing us how to do what he taught in Luke 6:27.

Jesus didn’t beg or plead for Judas to reconsider. He didn’t stare Judas down or stand in his way. Instead, he allowed Judas to follow what he had already decided to do.

Finally, we are in the Garden of Gethsemane, and Jesus is praying:

John 17:12: While I was with them, I was keeping them in Your name which You have given me; and I guarded them and not one of them perished but the son of perdition, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled.

Jesus said, I was keeping them in Your name. What did he mean by that? Jesus regularly prayed for his apostles. They were under his protection, guidance and direction. Judas was included in that prayer all along the way.

Jesus had always prayed for Judas. He showed us how to:

To see the betrayal unfold in the Garden of Gethsemane, we will combine the accounts in Matthew 26, Mark 14 and Luke 22 and read them as one narrative.

Jesus asked Peter, James and John to stay awake while he stepped away to pray. He returned and found them sleeping. This happened twice:

Mark 14:41-42: 41 And he came the third time, and said to them, Are you still sleeping and resting? It is enough; the hour has come; behold, the Son of Man is being betrayed into the hands of sinners. 42 Get up, let us be going; behold, the one who betrays me is at hand!

Jesus, in the middle of the weight of the upcoming crucifixion and the overwhelming burden of his mission, still had room enough in his heart to warn those who were his followers in the garden—Get up, let us be going; the one who betrays me is at hand!

Jesus’ heart also had room to warn his betrayer:

Mark 14:43-44: 43 Immediately while he was still speaking, Judas, one of the twelve, came up accompanied by a crowd with swords and clubs, who were from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. 44 Now he who was betraying him had given them a signal, saying, Whomever I kiss <5368>, he is the one; seize him and lead him away under guard.

Kiss: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance # #5368 phileō; to be a friend to (fond of an individual or object), i.e. have affection for

This is translated elsewhere as a brotherly kind of love. A kiss was a common greeting among friends. That would be the signal.

Matthew 26:49: Immediately Judas went to Jesus and said, Hail, rabbi! and kissed <2705> him.

*Judas' second statement actually betrayed Jesus: Hail Rabbi!

Kissed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2705 kataphileō; to kiss earnestly

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: To kiss much, kiss again and again, kissed tenderly

This means kissed with strong emotion—not just a peck on the cheek, but eagerly. Kata modifies the verb phileō to make it more intense.

This is the same type of kiss in Luke 7:38 when a different woman anointed Jesus in a Pharisee’s house and cried and kissed his feet. In the context of this verse, Judas Iscariot used this gesture not out of affection, but as a signal to identify Jesus to the authorities.

This was betrayal disguised as affection and respect, calling him Rabbi.

This reminds us of:

Proverbs 27:6: (NIV) Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.

Continuing with the narrative:

Luke 22:48: But Jesus said to him, Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?

In other words, Are you going to inflict such pain on the one you claimed to love?

It's a profound and heartbreaking moment, as the kiss—typically a gesture of love or friendship—is now a signal of treachery.

We can imagine the grief with which Jesus spoke, Are you betraying the son of man with a kiss? In other words, Are you using this sign of affection to turn me over to the enemy? Is that what you are doing here? His final warning goes further than just this question.

Jesus’ final warning was simple: Do you betray me by showing your friendship?

Matthew 26:50: And Jesus said to him, Friend, do what you have come for. Then they came and laid hands on Jesus and seized him.

The last thing Jesus does is call Judas Friend. Jesus doesn’t lie. Judas was his friend, had been his friend. He had protected and guided Judas during his ministry, and now Judas had turned on him. But Jesus did not turn on Judas, and that is the point. Judas betrays him with a sign of affection, with this supposed strong display of love for his brother, but Jesus does not turn on him.

That is loving our enemy. He allowed the sin and the darkness to unfold which helps us to see how loving our enemy works.

Focusing on such a powerful example of Jesus loving his enemies in action is both inspirational and scary! There is so much for us to learn.

We need to get practical. How do we apply the lofty examples of Jesus handling those who stood against him in our everyday lives?

There certainly is much to learn here. Our practical application of loving our enemies really needs to begin with the answer to a simple question: Do I truly want to walk in Jesus’ footsteps and live as a daily example of his wisdom, love and grace? Answering yes— and meaning it—opens the door to elevating the way we behave towards others.

Of course we want to walk in Jesus’ footsteps. But there are a lot of situations where self-protection and boundaries are absolute necessities for our physical or mental health. Loving someone who has hurt or wronged us could leave us vulnerable to further harm.

Sometimes, people commit actions that are simply unjust or harmful, and it may feel wrong to show love or compassion toward those who are not sorry for their actions. This can especially be the case when the enemy's actions have led to serious harm, such as abuse, betrayal or violence.

To take an extreme case, we all agree child abuse is heinous. Once the child comes of age, how would they actively bless their abuser? How could they?

This is a difficult circumstance (along with many others). What would Jesus do or say in this type of case? We truly believe that in a circumstance of abuse, to bless such a person is NOT to overlook what has been done. It is NOT to pretend nothing happened. That is not blessing anyone. When we bless someone, we want what is good for them.

What would be good for such a criminal is to turn them in, to bring them to a place where they can recognize the darkness of the evil they have committed. Then they can begin the process of rehabilitation. In this way, we can bless a person who has committed such an atrocity. We bring them to where they can be put back together, where they can understand the indescribable pain and suffering they have caused. This is the beginning of blessing them. We will expand these thoughts as we go.

Jesus continues his teaching in Luke by reasoning through the differences between how most people act and how he was teaching his followers to act:

Luke 6:31-34: (This is known as the “Golden Rule”) 31 Treat others the same way you want them to treat you. 32 If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. 33 If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. 34 If you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you?

Even sinners lend to sinners in order to receive back the same amount.

This is all about rising above our natural reactions—the baseline of normal human standards—and instead learning to act based on spiritually-driven responses.

According to various writers, this Golden Rule exists in many cultures. However, one difference is that the Christian Golden Rule ethic is expressed positively—we are to do to others what we would have them do to us. This is an admonition to act positively. In other cultures, the Golden Rule often reads, “What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others,” or “What is hateful to thee, do not do to another.”

(Source: Bible Commentary from William Barclay) “It is not unduly difficult to keep yourself from such action, but it is a very different thing to go out of your way to do to others what you would want them to do to you. The very essence of Christian conduct is that it consists, not in refraining from bad things, but in actively doing good things.”

To love others and mean it, we need to give ourselves over to Christ and the will of God as fully as possible:

Philippians 1:19-21: 19 For I know that this will turn out for my deliverance through your prayers and the provision of the spirit of Jesus Christ, 20 according to my earnest expectation and hope, that I will not be put to shame in anything, but that with all boldness, Christ will even now, as always, be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death. 21 For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.

The Apostle Paul was committed to glorifying God exactly like Jesus did. So the question is: how do we live with that same determination?

Christ will even now, as always, be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death—this means the essence of Jesus should shine through us. It should flow through us. It should be exalted in our human form. When people see us, we want them ideally to see a reflection of Christlikeness. And as Paul says, whether by living or by dying, we can be that reflection. This is turning ourselves over to be like Christ as fully as possible.

To love others and mean it, we need to not be afraid to share in and to feel their experiences. Here we see such an example:

Romans 12:14-16: 14 Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. 15 Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. 16 Be of the same mind toward one another; do not be haughty in mind, but associate with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own estimation.

It is easy to rejoice with ones we really like. True love and forgiveness often involve mutual respect and understanding. If our enemy is not open to reconciliation or has no intention of changing their harmful ways, loving them might not be a realistic or healthy expectation. I’m probably not going to rejoice with my enemies, so what is the principle?

First, we are told to Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. How do we bless an enemy if they are a bad person doing evil things? We would treat them with human respect. Typically when we become enemies with others, we show them no courtesy, kindness or respect. Jesus never did such a thing, and we are to follow his example.

Rather than retaliate, think to bless. Keep that blessing attitude in mind even in the midst of controversy. Verses 14-16 above are referring to those with which we have commonality, such as our Christian brethren and our families. Verse 17 refers to actual enemies.

But within our community of faith or everyday life, we should enter into their realities, whether they are happy or sad. Don’t play favorites; don’t be proud; instead, be humble. We have to put ourselves in a position where we can relate to others. This applies to our enemies, too.

This sets the table for appropriately dealing with those with whom we have problems:

Romans 12:17: Never pay back evil for evil to anyone. Respect what is right in the sight of all men.

When someone wrongs us, we naturally want justice. Some people feel that showing love to their enemies might prevent them from seeking justice or standing up for what’s right. This could be particularly important when the actions of the enemy have hurt others we love and we are standing up for them. The core point is that love doesn’t mean accepting or excusing harmful behavior. Loving our enemies doesn’t mean we have to force ourselves to have something in common with them. It is the benevolent love that says, For God so loved the world He gave His only begotten son (John 3:16). It is love that gives to all equally, without condition. It does not demand reciprocal action as in, I take care of you, and you take care of me. Instead, it is, I care about you as a human being. This is the kind of love we want to have.

Is it ever okay to pay back evil for evil—maybe when the evil is really bad?

Romans 12:17: Never pay back evil for evil to anyone. Respect what is right in the sight of all men.

It says NEVER. If we want to be Christlike, we always apply the never.

Again, this does not mean that if there is a serious issue, we do not pursue justice through legal means. We do what is appropriate. We still must stand up for what is right and recognize evil for what it is.

To love others and mean it, we need to be peaceable with all, leaving all revenge in the hands of God:

Romans 12:18-19: 18 If possible, so far as it depends on you, be at peace with all men. 19 Never take your own revenge, beloved, but leave room for the wrath of God, for it is written, VENGEANCE IS MINE, I WILL REPAY, says the Lord.

This takes the responsibility off our shoulders and gives it to God, even if the consequences for them are in this life or God’s future kingdom.

However, thinking of someone who hurt you or someone you love not having significant consequences until after they are resurrected can be pretty unsatisfying. Some people believe that loving your enemy might condone or even enable bad behavior, which could undermine the value of standing up for moral or ethical principles.

We still have to love our enemy appropriately and with benevolence, but not necessarily with brotherly love. That is not what Jesus is telling us to do.

If we truly love someone, we want what is best for them. What is best for someone who is continually doing things that are hurtful to other people is for them to learn the lesson. We want them to learn the lesson in the appropriate way, using the system as best we can. What we feel about the situation is not what should dictate our love of our enemies.

We seek appropriate consequences, not vengefully, but with a sense of clarity in our own hearts and minds that we are seeking these consequences to help them. If they do not get the help now, by God’s grace, they can get the help later. Ultimately, we want what is best for every human being forever. As Christians, we must practice what we preach.

This may include getting away from this person and not interacting with them for our own health. We have to stay above the fray (not be directly involved in a difficult or angry situation).

To love others and mean it, we need to exercise self-control and become positive contributors in all of our interactions:

Ephesians 4:26-27; 29-32: 26 BE ANGRY, AND yet DO NOT SIN; do not let the sun go down on your anger, 27 and do not give the devil an opportunity. 29 Let no unwholesome word proceed from your mouth, but only such a word as is good for edification according to the need of the moment, so that it will give grace to those who hear.

Be angry, and yet do not sin.

It's okay to be angry. We're not suggesting to suppress or avoid our feelings. But it says, do not let the sun go down on your anger. This means our anger should not control us, as it gives the devil an opportunity for us to continue down the path to sin.

Let no unwholesome word proceed from your mouth, but only that which is good...

We want to give grace to those who hear. When did Jesus ever not give grace to those who hear? Even when he was harsh with the Pharisees, he told them what he was angry about and why. He was justified, righteous, clear and honest, and it wasn't about vengeance; it was about teaching.

30 Do not grieve the holy spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

When we dedicate our lives as Christians, we have God’s influence working within us. We want to follow it—not ignore it—because it is there to guide us. When we do not follow God’s influence within us, when we do not follow His providence and instead go our own way, we are not living up to that dedication we said we would give to God. This does not please God. So, what do we need to do to not grieve the holy spirit of God?

31 Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.

We must put these things away from us. This is how we are taught to love our enemies— put aside bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, slander, malice. Learn to live above those. Does this mean people who wrong us get away with everything? NO! It means we love them with that “Jesus kind of love,” the benevolent agape love that rises above our base human emotions and wants what is best for them. If we truly want what's best for someone, we can put aside our emotions.

32 Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has forgiven you.

Isn’t this the point? We have received forgiveness and love, and now we freely give them back. Putting away all bitterness, wrath and anger and not letting the sun go down on our

anger doesn’t mean we don’t address our anger, difficult feelings and resentment. We don't repress or suppress all these feelings. The feelings are not bad, but we have to process them so they are good for our mental well-being. We can be angry—and there are definitely things to be angry about—and not sin, not be vengeful or hurtful.

We can allow ourselves to be angry, but we don’t want that anger to stagnate, fester or grow. We need to treat our anger with Christlikeness. It is okay to visit anger for a time, but it is not okay to live there.

Being a Christian means we need to rise above it, and that is hard. But that is what Jesus did and what he taught us.

Step-by-step changes require small steps, growth as a result of that small step, and building on that step with the next small step.

We have seen how Jesus did it and now we can see what we need to do to follow his example. Get ready because there is work to be done!

So, where does all of this bring us? In this world, working at loving our enemies generally doesn’t change anything. Now what?

Now, we need to look at the whole concept of loving our enemies from the perspective of the BIG picture. Jesus loved his enemies, and he was crucified anyway. To some, that shows failure; however, from the perspective of God’s plan and eternity, Jesus could not have been more successful!

Even to the apostles at the crucifixion, his mission seemed like a failure. It wasn't until his post-resurrection appearances that they understood the magnitude of Christ's sacrifice.

Jesus continues to show us what loving our enemies looks like:

Luke 6:35-36: 35 But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return; and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for He Himself is kind to ungrateful and evil men. 36 Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.

(Source: Bible Commentary from William Barclay) The Christian ethic is based on the extra thing. Jesus described the common ways of sensible conduct and then dismissed them with the question, ‘What special grace is in that?’ So often people claim to be just as good as their neighbors. Very likely they are. But the question of Jesus is, ‘How much better are you than the ordinary person?’ It is not our neighbor with whom we must compare ourselves; we may well stand that comparison very adequately; it is God with whom we must compare ourselves; and in that comparison we are all in default.

Jesus says, Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. Be merciful in that godly, higher sense. God sent Jesus to die for everyone—there is no greater mercy shown in all of the universe and all of history than this! Then, to create a process for reconciliation—what mercy! This is what we are to be about. The message is clear: it is not about what we get from others in this life; it is about what we give to others. It is not about evening the score or converting them into our way of thinking. We need to be an example that rises above the circumstances.

To love others and mean it, we need to be focused on God’s plans and purposes, and not what we want or what we think.

The Apostle Peter applies the principles of this lesson to everyday life:

1 Peter 2:18-20: 18 Servants, be submissive to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but also to those who are unreasonable. 19 For this finds favor, if for the sake of conscience toward God a person bears up under sorrows when suffering unjustly. 20 For what credit is there if, when you sin and are harshly treated, you endure it with patience? But if when you do what is right and suffer for it you patiently endure it, this finds favor with God.

We have to go through difficult times knowing that if we are suffering unjustly, this is something God looks upon, and we will be blessed for that. Maybe the circumstance never works out in the way we would like, but if our going through injustice and difficulty gives us blessing from God—which is more valuable? Getting it to work out the way we wanted it to, or being blessed by God, the Creator of all things?

We are to stand for serving with dignity and respect, even if dignity and respect are not shown to us. This is what Jesus did, and this is our calling.

This is loving those who act as enemies in an everyday environment. Why do this? Why do we love?

1 Peter 2:21-23: 21 For you have been called for this purpose, since Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example for you to follow in his steps, 22 who committed no sin, nor was any deceit found in his mouth; 23 and while being reviled, he did not revile in return; while suffering, he uttered no threats, but kept entrusting himself to Him who judges righteously.

We see the example of Jesus all over again; he committed no sin, nor was any deceit found in his mouth, and while being reviled, he did not revile in return. He uttered no threats or any of those earthly things we would do when we get into circumstances where we are unjustly accused. He rose above it all. We need to do this because Jesus gave us those specific steps to follow. He didn’t just say it; he lived it. We can’t argue when somebody absolutely over and over again lives the life they preach.

We are to do this because Jesus gave us these specific footsteps to follow:

1 Peter 2:24-25: 24 And he himself bore our sins in his body on the cross, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness; for by his wounds you were healed. 25 For you were continually straying like sheep, but now you have returned to the shepherd and guardian of your souls.

This is HOW we stand with Christ! This is HOW we put away our previous lives of sin.

By his wounds we are healed. Do we deserve it? No. Do we get it anyway? Yes. That is how we love our enemies. Remember to see that we ourselves are underserving and yet blessed. Live that blessed life.

To love others and mean it, we need to wherever possible bless those who do evil.

Returning to Romans 12:

Romans 12:20-21: 20 BUT IF YOUR ENEMY IS HUNGRY, FEED HIM, AND IF HE IS THIRSTY, GIVE HIM A DRINK; FOR IN SO DOING YOU WILL HEAP BURNING COALS ON HIS HEAD. 21 Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

How is this blessing someone? The thought of heaping coals of fire on the head of an enemy is a direct quote from the Book of Proverbs:

Proverbs 25:21,22: (KJV) 21 If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.

It is generally thought this referred to the practice of lending coals from your fire to help your neighbor quickly start their own fire.

This blessing, this act of kindness, would make an enemy ashamed of conduct towards you.

Bless, don’t curse. Bless! Don’t wish evil. Bless!

When circumstances (not excuses) make it so we cannot bless those who stand against us here and now in this life, and we cannot conceive of how we could get around to being a blessing to that person, we need to ask ourselves honestly, Did I try? Did I try to apply Christlikeness, or did I say, Ahh, let them rot. Do we make an excuse and rationalize and say we just couldn’t, or are we actually putting the effort in?

When circumstances make it so we cannot bless those who stand against us here and now in this life, we have the marvelous hope of doing so in the future:

Romans 8:18-22: 18 For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed to us. 19 For the anxious longing of the creation waits eagerly for the revealing of the sons of God. 20 For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope 21 that the creation itself also will be set free from its slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. 22 For we know that the whole creation groans and suffers the pains of childbirth together until now.

To love our enemies, we need to have compassion for their brokenness. This does not mean we excuse their evil toward us. But it does mean that God sees the evil in them and sent Jesus to redeem them in spite of themselves, just like He sent him to redeem us in spite of ourselves. Jesus died for them the way he died for us, and this is the wonderful hope the world has: to be set free from its slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, those who have been called by Jesus here and now.

2 Corinthians 5:18-19: 18 Now all these things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, 19 namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and He has committed to us the word of reconciliation.

Does this mean God is not counting their trespasses against them? Is He giving them a free ride? No! He is saying He will forgive—Jesus died for our sins in Adam, and then in the ministry of reconciliation, mankind will be given the chance to make right their sins. How many times did Jesus say every man will give an account for their actions and their words? This gives people an opportunity to have to deal with and make right the evils that they did. There will be no human being who can get away with the evil they have done in this world without having to deal with it later!

There will be consequences, but there will also be a path forward to righteousness. That is the point of a consequence—to correct and present a path forward. This is why Jesus loved his enemies the way he loved them. He gave his life for them so that they may have a chance and a path forward to righteousness, free from Adamic weakness and satanic influence.

Loving our enemies is hard, but there is nothing more worthwhile if we apply the principles that Jesus showed us. Remember, this is the kind of love that is benevolent, not vengeful. It looks at those enemies and says, I want what is best for you. When consequences are appropriate, love says to let those consequences happen in a way that can bring that person back toward God.

Love your enemies. Be like Jesus.

So, do I really have to love my enemies?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
