## Episode 1384 — Can I Find Balance When Overwhelmed With Anxiety? (Part II)
Published: 2025-05-12
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/anxious-part-ii/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/09121151/CQ_Rewind_5-12-25_Can_I_Find_Balance_When_Overwhelmed_With_Anxiety_Part_II.pdf

1 Peter 5:6-7: 6 Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you at the proper time, 7 casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.

Anxiety is an enemy of the heart. When left unchecked, it can take normally functioning human beings and turn them into a second-guessing, insecure and trembling mess. In Part I of our series, we talked about how Jesus showed us the depths of damage that anxiety can bring. He also taught us how to process the solutions for this challenge. As we continue this conversation, we will continue with Jesus’ teachings from the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 6. We will then concentrate on how and when anxiety can be a good thing! That’s right, the Bible shows us how to use anxiety in a focused way to bring honor and praise to God.

We are NOT medical professionals, and we have not been professionally trained to handle anxiety or depression disorders. Often Christians may need professional help, including medication, to handle these kinds of challenges. We fully advocate for such treatment where and when it is appropriate.

We also know anxiety isn’t cured just by reading a few scriptures. Having anxiety doesn’t make us a bad Christian, but we might have to work a little harder to keep scriptural principles in the forefront.

In Part I, we suggested four steps to use as an anxiety-coping mechanism:

Learn to gain a conscious awareness of our mind being overtaken by anxiety. This recognition is, Wait a minute. I know what is happening to me. I’m not in a good place.

Apply that awareness and pause the natural anxiety cycle of thinking and feeling. Make the conscious decision to stop and not go any further. I’m driving down the wrong road. I have to put the brakes on. I need to stop here!

Build towards feeding our hearts and minds with positive and productive ways of managing our anxiety-inducing circumstances. We have to reframe, or look at the problem differently, and then do something about it. Then rehearse how to see it differently.

Intentionally reboot our thoughts and emotions so we can see the circumstances through a lens of true faith, trust and peace.

We can understand “restarting by rebooting” when our computer gets wonky. The first way to troubleshoot is to shut it down and turn it back on so that all the programs and updates can reload properly. To reboot is to get a new start with the updates in place.

These steps are not some miracle cure. They are what we work on to establish the process. We may not go through the four steps right in a row during an experience. We will fall and then get up and start again and again. The whole point of this is to acknowledge that anxiety is real. We all have it. What do we do about it?

When Jesus taught about coping with anxiety in Matthew 6, he broke the process down into four parts, three of which were covered in Part I.

Matthew 6:25: (NASB77) For this reason I say to you, do not be anxious <3309> for your life…

Anxious: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3309 merimnao; from #3308; to be anxious about

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to be anxious 1a) to be troubled with cares

ANXIETY’S OBSESSION: I am nervous and restless about my life and have an impending sense of doom!

We discussed how we sometimes elevate our feelings into perceived facts, and how we tend to “catastrophize,” assuming the worst is always going to happen. Good anxiety provokes us towards good works, but when anxiety becomes obsessive, it can be destructive.

ANXIETY’S SOLUTION: Recognize what is happening and methodically ACT upon that realization.

In Part I, we read 2 Corinthians 4:7-9 that talked about us having treasure in earthen vessels. The vessels are these inferior, broken-down human bodies we drag around—but that’s where God puts His treasure! The greatness of God is what’s important, not ourselves. We can take comfort in this. He will protect us through the experience.

2 Corinthians 4:7-9: 7 But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power will be of God and not from ourselves; 8 we are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not despairing; 9 persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.

The Apostle Paul certainly understood anxiety, but he is telling us not to worry. There is always the next step, and God’s always got us. If we are experiencing a high level of anxiety about life in general, we need to take a breath and try to realize God really does have our lives in order. We can methodically act upon that realization.

Jesus gave us a second anxiety example:

Matthew 6:27: (NASB77) And which of you by being anxious <3309> can add a single cubit to his life's span?

ANXIETY’S OBESSION: I am worried that my life will not amount to much of anything. I’m a failure!

The first obsession was “everything about my life is wrong.” The second one is saying we can’t move forward because we just aren’t good enough.

Many of us struggle with finding what value we can personally bring before God, and this results in doubts and fears. We discussed how focusing so much on ourselves can be a type of humility that ironically leads to pride and even idolatry.

ANXIETY’S SOLUTION: Find the factual value of what I can bring before God. (But I don’t have anything!) Ah! But it’s about what I can bring before God from HIS perspective of me.

We want to see our value through God’s eyes and words instead of through our emotions.

Psalms 139:9-10: 9 If I take the wings of the dawn, if I dwell in the remotest part of the sea, 10 even there Your hand will lead me, and Your right hand will lay hold of me.

David poetically described that no matter where he went—even to impossible places, even in the darkest places—God would be there with him. It is so important to look at the Scriptures to find the inspiration to say, I’m not alone. This type of anxiety is about feeling irrelevant.

David, described as a man after God’s own heart, felt the same way. Knowing this helps us to gain perspective on why these four steps can be helpful.

The third example of Jesus asking about anxiety:

Matthew 6:28: (NASB77) And why are you anxious <3309> about clothing…

ANXIETY’S OBSESSION: I’m not only a failure; I don’t even look the part! I’m troubled internally with self-conscious anxiety. I believe that I look inferior to others.

We start comparing ourselves to others in our natural life and in our spiritual life.

This goes way beyond just the clothes we put on in the morning. It’s about our “image.” At no time more in history has image been more a source of anxiety than it is now, with social media demanding we all look and live a certain way. We also talked about how the aging and dying process can be scary.

One of the big concerns here is Satan taking our doubts and turning them into paralyzing fear. We continually minimize our worth and become our own worst enemy.

ANXIETY’S SOLUTION: Find the factual value of what I look like before God from HIS perspective, not mine! Our life’s focus is being presentable before God, NOT looking good to others.

Our theme text again:

1 Peter 5:5-7: 5 …all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, for GOD IS OPPOSED TO THE PROUD, BUT GIVES GRACE TO THE HUMBLE. 6 Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you at the proper time, 7 casting all your anxiety <3308> on Him, because He cares <3199> for you.

Anxiety: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3308 merimna; from #3307 (through the idea of distraction); solicitude

Cares: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3199 melo; a primary verb; to be of interest to, i.e. to concern (only third person singular present indicative used impersonally, it matters): care, take care

Casting all your anxiety on Him is casting our obsessiveness and anxiousness in His lap. He cares for you shows us His profound, deep concern for our anxiety.

These scriptures were so relevant to me this afternoon. I had a conversation with someone who was overwhelmed by anxiety, and rightfully so. The circumstance was enormous. They broke down and cried as they explained what was going on. I went to these verses and said, “Let’s look at this. You are looking at the future, but you cannot determine the future—that is in God’s hands.” We talked about anxiety and how God’s profound care and concern means He takes care of the future.

Knowing God has genuine concern for us helps us to face this next challenge with far less anxiety:

1 Peter 5:8-9: 8 Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. 9 But resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same experiences of suffering are being accomplished by your brethren who are in the world.

Be of sober spirit because your adversary, the devil, wants to use our anxiety to break us and trip us up. However, we are NOT alone. Let us cling to others who are also clothed with humility and faith.

This has been a recap of the kinds of anxiety Jesus taught us about in Part I.

Reexamining Our Anxiety: Anxiety can paralyze. So far, Jesus has shown us that for some, anxiety seems like a giant mountain that is in the way of every aspect of their lives. For some it can be about perceiving themselves as failures. With others it can explode into a fear of looking inferior. In every case, Jesus has shown us that our anxiety is always based on our broken human perceptions, and the solution is always based on God’s truths regarding our lives.

Jesus has given us a lot to think about and a lot to do. While working at reducing our anxiety can bring hope, it can be scary as well!

So far, we have examined three out of the four anxiety examples Jesus gave us in the Sermon on the Mount. What is his final example?

Jesus will conclude his teaching on anxiety management by using food as an example. As with so many of his teachings, he uses a physical part of our lives to show us a deeper part of our discipleship. We understand his last anxiety-causing example to have a deeper and more broad-based meaning regarding the “stability insecurity” of our lives.

ANXIETY’S OBSESSION: I truly cannot see any way to be able to stand firm, healthy and cared for.

Matthew 6:31: (NASB77) Do not be anxious <3309> then, saying, What shall we eat? or What shall we drink?

There’s a lot of room for anxiety in this category. Not only do we have to provide literal, daily food for ourselves and our families, which in some parts of the world can be a very real struggle, but not having overall financial security is stressful. We need a place to sleep. We need a place to live. We all have bills. Even new technology is stressful. Everything is changing so fast that we can quickly get left behind, or get scammed in ways we couldn’t possibly have considered. There are a LOT of reasons to be anxious.

There are so many reasons. I want to share a personal story of my development through anxiety, and it took a long time. When Christian Questions started almost 27 years ago, we essentially walked into something we had no idea how to do. When I say no idea, I REALLY mean NO idea!

From the beginning, part of my responsibility was putting together the content. I just didn’t know how to do it! Week after week this opportunity came up. I was running a business and now had this extra burden. I was having a really hard time balancing the two. It was overwhelming, but we knew it was clearly God’s will. God opened the door for us to walk through. We just had to be willing. I’ll unfold the story as we continue.

ANXIETY’S SOLUTION: The resounding and repeated truth that God knows and cares, needs to take root.

There is great power in faith. We need more than just an intellectual belief that overall God has things in control. Our faith must be bigger than what we obsess over.

Let’s go to the four steps using the focus of the power of faith.

Learn. The power of faith is first revealed in the power of RECOGNITION:

Matthew 6:32: (NASB77) For all these things the Gentiles eagerly seek; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.

Sounds simple—I have anxiety. God knows what I’m worried about. He knows what I obsess over at 3 am when I can’t get these things out of my head.

In my experience, the realization that I had this great anxiety but didn’t know what to do about it, took a while before I could recognize it and say, “Okay, it’s here; what am I supposed to do?”

God knows and therefore is well-equipped to handle our anxiety. Why doesn’t He just take care of it right away? Because He is just waiting to direct us:

Romans 8:15-16: (NLT) 15 So you have not received a spirit that makes you fearful slaves.

Instead, you received God’s spirit when he adopted you as His own children. Now we call Him, Abba, Father. 16 For His spirit joins with our spirit to affirm that we are God’s children.

Do we think He’s going to be an absent Father, or a loving, caring Father that does everything for our best spiritual benefit? Maintain that image of God as our loving, caring Father as we begin to recognize our anxiety. Recognizing the discrepancy between obsessive worry and God’s care should make us pause as we realize we need help.

We don’t all experience feeling anxious or worried in the same way.

All I have seen teaches me to trust the Creator for all I have not seen. – Ralph Waldo Emerson

Count your many blessings, name them one by one, and it will surprise you what the Lord hath done. – “Count Your Blessings” hymn

We need to pay attention to how the Lord leads us. That is the recognition step—we recognize something is happening to us.

Apply. The power of faith is next revealed in the power of DISCIPLINE.

Seek new direction:

Matthew 6:33: (NASB77) But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness; and all these things shall be added to you.

What a promise!

That promise ended up being the centerpiece of my anxiety experience as I went through week after week trying to figure things out. I finally settled into looking at this particular scripture. I worked in an office by myself and would pray out loud when I was overwhelmed.

It got to the point where I started to quote this scripture out loud, saying, “Lord, You’ve given us this opportunity of Christian Questions, and I have to also support my family. I’ve got both these things to do, and I am stuck.” I would quote the scripture and say, “Okay, I’m going to work on this first and then work really hard on everything right after that. I just need Your help to focus because I’m afraid.”

This particular scripture gave me the assurance, allowing me to refrain from my anxiety—to pause, back up and send my anxiety in a different direction.

If we Seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, we are assured our direction will be guided by Him.

When we remind ourselves of all the scriptural promises, we build an indestructible structure of stability on which to mentally stand.

Yet another promise:

Romans 8:28-29: (NLT) 28 And we know that God causes everything to work together for the good of those who love God and are called according to His purpose for them. 29 For God knew His people in advance, and He chose them to become like His son, so that His son would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.

My anxiety did not allow me to see how God arranged this for my good. All I saw was trouble. This was a problem. It was too much with too little! It took time to be able to reframe this whole circumstance so that I could see it differently.

Build. The power of faith is next revealed in the power of CHANGE.

Matthew 6:34: (NASB77) Therefore do not be anxious <3309> for tomorrow; for tomorrow will care for itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.

Jesus’ message is for us to live in the present—the future is not our jurisdiction! Doing just what’s in front of us can bring tremendous calm. Rick often says, “Do the next right thing.” It’s easy to say but not always easy to put into practice!

This verse commands us do not be anxious for tomorrow. We work on “today.” What is the next right thing, right here, right now? This is how we reframe, deciding to just do the next right thing, doing what we are supposed to be doing. Our anxiety diminishes a little because we are productively working, step-by-step.

For me, it was learning how to reframe and step forward, and it was scary. But I was learning how to put all of it in place.

This doesn’t mean we don’t have any regard for our future, that we don’t plan at all. It just means we don’t need to be anxious about it.

This makes us think of the Israelites getting manna to eat in the wilderness. They had to eat each day’s portion without saving any extra, or else it spoiled. They had to gather it every morning, or else it would melt. They had to pay attention to God’s rules and rely on Him. This required a daily faith that God would provide for their needs. We have to have that same daily faith that God will provide for our needs.

Understanding our insecurity over stability:

1 Corinthians 10:12-14: 12 Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed that he does not fall. 13 No temptation has overtaken you but such as is common to man; and God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape also, so that you will be able to endure it. 14 Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.

Yes, God gives us testings but nothing beyond our capacity. That is encouraging when we are feeling like we’re being overrun and overwhelmed. We are given the experience because He knows we can handle it and grow from it.

In my experience, I was learning to accept that He knows I can do this. Otherwise, He wouldn’t have put it on my plate. I just have to put my head down and try to separate myself from my anxiety and look to His providence rather than my problems. This way I could see the problem more clearly.

When I focused on it as a problem, it was essentially an idolatrous thought. Our obsessive anxiety IS a form of idolatry, as we are putting our perceptions above God’s truths! That was a hard lesson to learn, going through it again and again. This went on for months and months.

Intentionally reboot. The power of faith is next revealed in the power of deep and appropriate HUMILITY. God knows every state of our mind and heart.

This is the solid foundation for our restarting:

Psalms 139:21-24: 21 Do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD? And do I not loathe those who rise up against You? 22 I hate them with the utmost hatred; they have become my enemies. 23 Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me and know my anxious thoughts; 24 and see if there be any hurtful way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.

This is a great “rebooting” passage. Not only are we trying to calm our anxiety in the big things of life, but here we are looking into our innermost heart. What a prayer—we want God to search for the smallest spark of a thought that would take us off a godly perspective. Allow our updates of faith, trust and memories of how God has led us thus far to take effect.

Reflecting on our past experiences where God protected and provided for us can help reduce our anxieties about current circumstances.

We broadcasted Christian Questions on the radio every single week, every single year, without fail. After 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 weeks, we got the idea that God had delivered us! It helps to just look back to realize there is more to it than just getting through. We have to simply look back and see the providence of God. “All I have seen teaches me to trust the Creator for all I have not seen.”

Getting through stability and security issues requires patient endurance. It is a necessary yet difficult aspect of this battle to overcome self:

James 1:2-4: 2 Consider it all joy, my brethren, when you encounter various trials (including obsessive anxiety!), 3 knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance <5281>. 4 And let endurance <5281> have its perfect result, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

Our anxiety is one of our trials, and to face it we need endurance, just staying with it, because God’s providence is bigger than our perceptions.

Endurance here means the ability to withstand a difficult trial with hope. We persevere by moving forward through the difficulty.

Endurance: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5281 hupomone; from #5278; cheerful (or hopeful) endurance, constancy

Endurance: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5278 hupomeno; to stay under (behind), i.e. remain; figuratively, to undergo, i.e. bear (trials), have fortitude, persevere

Jesus tells us to seek first the kingdom of God when we struggle with our stability and security, then these things will be added—not miraculously—but through our honest and mature efforts. We have a pattern and a pathway to cope with our anxiety.

Reexamining our Anxiety: When our anxiety focuses on stability insecurity, it attacks our belief that we are being cared for by God in His way. As with other anxiety obsessions, this stability insecurity needs to be met squarely with the clarity of an active faith that can grow under pressure. This requires a development of discipline. We need to do the work and then do the work some more.

Our faith and spiritually-focused action bring glory to God.

The challenge is clear, and the battle lines have been drawn. The question is, what will I choose to do with my obsessive anxieties?

With Jesus’ teachings on managing anxiety laid out before us, one question we have not yet answered is, can anxiety ever be good?

Yes, there is such a thing as good anxiety! However, as you might have thought, it operates from a different perspective. For Christians, it’s based upon a spiritually-minded sense of wanting to profoundly contribute to others. It is truly based on selfless love and not on any self-protective thoughts or emotions.

Summing up what we have learned so far, we can see that obsessive anxiety is an earthly process of thinking and feeling that rehearses and reinforces negative and disappointing outcomes, without making room for sound, godly-driven, factual evidence.

Let’s quickly review one last consideration before we review scriptural examples of when anxiety is good for us. In addition to Matthew 6, Jesus taught us about anxiety in the Parable of the Sower with its analogy of the seed of the gospel falling onto four different kinds of soils, and how well it could grow in each.

Some seeds fell on thorny ground:

Mark 4:18-19: (KJV) 18 And these are they which are sown among thorns; such as hear the word, 19 And the cares <3308> of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful.

There wasn’t enough room for both the seeds and the thorns to grow in the same space. This is why the gospel message becomes unfruitful.

While hearing God’s word inherently affords us the opportunity for spiritual growth, our obession over the attachments and enticements of this world can easily choke out the seeds of the gospel even before they have a chance to start growing. The lesson here is that anxiety is everywhere, in everybody and in all kinds of circumstances. We need to recognize it and rise above it.

So, how does “good” anxiety work? How do we turn obsessive anxiety into something more spiritually productive? The Bible has many positive examples for us.

Our “good anxiety” is shown when Paul is describing the body of Christ which is formed and needs to work together to be fruitful:

1 Corinthians 12:21-22, 24-26: 21 And the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. 22 On the contrary, it is much truer that the members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary; 24 …But God has so composed the body, giving more abundant honor to that member which lacked, 25 so that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have <3309> the same care <3309> for one another. 26 And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

Have…care is the same Greek word for anxiety we’ve been talking about to this point in a negative way meaning worry and anxiousness, but in this context it is positive. It reflects sincere, heartfelt concern rather than distress.

Have care: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3309 merimnao; from #3308; to be anxious about

The King James Version translates this as “take thought” 11 times, “care” 5 times, “be careful” 2 times, “have care” 1 time

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to be anxious 1a) to be troubled with cares 2) to care for, look out for (a thing) 2a) to seek to promote one’s interests 2b) caring or providing for

How do we use the emotions of our obsessive anxieties for something positive?

The Apostle Paul is emphatic that the body of Christ is designed as a relationship that is both:

and

It is mutually strengthening by giving or contributing to others—our actions. Passionately caring comes from the inside, from the heart.

We are shown how to pour ourselves out for the sake of our brotherhood. We don’t do it because we have to; rather, it should be done with spiritually-driven passion. This is “productive anxiousness.” Anxiety can be a postive action when focused outside of ourselves.

Productive anxiousness can help us stay alert to the needs of others. It keeps us mentally sharp, actually triggering the release of brain chemicals that help with motivation and focus. As we said in Part I, nervousness and excitement feel roughly the same physically. If you can flip your brain to thinking it’s actually a positive feeling, the sense of anxiety can vanish.

The Apostle Paul had been stoned and left for dead by a mob of angry Jews. Right there he could have quit and said, “Enough is enough. I’m not going to go around preaching this “Jesus” message anymore—it’s too dangerous!”

Here’s how he actually reacted:

Acts 14:20-23: 20 But while the disciples stood around him, he got up and entered the city. The next day he went away with Barnabas to Derbe. 21 After they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, 22 strengthening <1991> the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying, Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. 23 When they had appointed elders for them in every church, having prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed.

Strengthening here means to support further, that is, to re-establish. Not only could Paul have just given up and gone back to being a pampered and respected Pharisee, but he could have just established these churches and then walked away. Moved on to other things. Safer pursuits. But he continually strengthened them, encouraged them and helped them to establish faithful leaders so they could, in turn, spread the gospel message effectively.

Strenthening the souls of the disciples—he was strengthening who they were. He was establishing and re-establishing the basis of their faith and the structure of their relationships because he knew they were in for a tough journey. He was there to strengthen and build them up before he had to move on.

Strengthen: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1991 episterizo; to support further, i.e. reestablish

The King James Version translates this as “confirm” 3 times, “strengthen” 1 time

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to establish besides, strengthen more

2) to render more firm, confirm

One of the positive results of anxiety is that it can help us detect potential dangers, allowing us to make safer decisions. It can signal when something requires attention, such as an unresolved issue in a relationship or workplace.

Paul had a wonderful way of recognizing and getting to the bottom of issues the early church faced, whether it was enemies from outside or moral/personality issues on the inside. He didn’t gloss over problems. He used his words like a surgeon’s knife to extract the diseased parts so they could heal stronger. We will get into those examples of passionate caring shortly.

After the elders meeting at Jerusalem, where they handled the issues and difficulties between Jewish and Gentile followers, many were sent out to spread the news of their conclusions:

Acts 15:30-33: 30 So when they were sent away, they went down to Antioch; and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. 31 When they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. 32 Judas and Silas, also being prophets themselves, encouraged and strengthened <1991> the brethren with a lengthy message. 33 After they had spent time there, they were sent away from the brethren in peace to those who had sent them out.

They go out after this meeting to encourage, strengthen and re-establish. They strengthened the brethren. In the first example of Paul continuing to teach even after being stoned, it was strengthening who they were. In this second illustration, the brethren were strengthened in what they needed to do by receiving encouragement and instruction. The productive anxiousness of Judas and Silas motivated the brethren to become stronger in Christ. They could stand up firmly, bind themselves together and move forward.

After Paul and Barnabas went separate ways:

Acts 15:40-41: 40 But Paul chose Silas and left, being committed by the brethren to the grace of the Lord. 41 And he was traveling through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening <1991> the churches.

Paul’s passion was to strengthen the various churches and small groups of Christians wherever he went. His productive anxiousness built up every aspect of their Christianity. It built up who they were, what they needed to do, and strengthened them as a group. When we are focused on building each other up and pouring ourselves out for one another, we have less time for our own anxiety.

Reexamining our Anxiety: The key to productive Christian anxiousness is focus. Rather than being anxious about things that might (or might not) happen to us or others, our anxiousness can zero in on contributing to what can happen through us and others relating to Christlikeness and contribution. Our natural anxiety can focus on others’ well-being, direction and collective strength.

This certainly gives a different look at anxiety with the big difference centered on choosing to be productive instead of just being worried!

Productive anxiousness focused on strengthening others is one thing. How can we be productively anxious about fellow disciples in a passionately caring way?

The whole concept of productive concern for our fellow disciples may not be a natural response. The fact that we are called to Christ from dramatically different walks of life means we need to develop a passionate caring toward those with whom we may have little in common. This is an important challenge to meet!

Let’s go back to those first productive anxiousness texts as a reminder:

1 Corinthians 12:25-26: 25 So that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have <3309> the same care <3309> for one another. 26 And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

Our engagement, our productive anxiety for one another, is expressed by our entering into, and passionately caring for, the experiences of our fellow disciples.

This redirects our natural anxieties into something more spiritually profitable. How do we do this on a practical basis?

We decide what is the next most important thing. If we’re called to be a disciple of Jesus, it is to do what he did. Remember when he was traveling toward the house of the little girl who was sick and was interrupted by the woman with the hemorrhage of blood? (Matthew 9:20-22) What did he do? He stopped to take care of her. This is our template. This is what we want to become. We can’t heal others, but we can show compassion, especially to those within our Chrisitan fellowship. It is not about our life. It is not about our relevance. It is not about our looking the part, or our security. It is about our building up the body of Christ. It is a choice to think and act like this. This is an intentional perspective.

Paul himself was a great example of this very specific passionate caring:

2 Corinthians 11:26-29: 26 I have been on frequent journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my countrymen, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers on the sea, dangers among false brethren; 27 I have been in labor and hardship, through many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure. 28 Apart from such external things, there is the daily pressure on me of concern <3308> for all the churches.

Wow, Brother Paul, is that all?

Verse 28 from The Message Bible: And that’s not the half of it, when you throw in the daily pressures and anxieties of all the churches.

Paul’s suffering wasn’t just physical (beatings, shipwrecks, imprisonment), but also mental and emotional. He was deeply invested in the churches, feeling their struggles as his own.

When we look closely at the specific Greek words in this text, Paul describes this emotional and spiritual weight as a pressing burden, almost like a crowd rushing upon him, overwhelming him with concerns. This wasn’t just a passing thought—it was a deep, ongoing anxiety for the spiritual health of believers.

ἐπίστασις (epistasis)—translated as pressure, burden or rush. It conveys the idea of something pressing upon Paul constantly, like an overwhelming responsibility.

μέριμνα (merimna)—meaning care, concern or anxiety. It is often used in the New Testament to describe deep worry or responsibility, particularly in a pastoral or protective sense.

καθ’ ἡμέραν (kath’ hēmeran)—meaning “day-by-day,” emphasizing the continuous nature of Paul's concern.

It is profound how he lists difficult physical hardships, but then says he has great anxiety over those who have come to the faith. He knew what they were being called to do was not natural for them. He knew they needed help and encouragement, constant reminders and building up. This was the most important thing and what drove him through and helped him cope with the anxiety of all the physical dangers he faced. It was the care of those other individuals who were following Christ, many as a result of Paul’s witnessing to them.

29 Who is weak without my being weak? Who is led into sin without my intense concern?

Verse 29 from The Message Bible: When someone gets to the end of his rope, I feel the desperation in my bones. When someone is duped into sin, an angry fire burns in my gut.

Again, when we look closely at the Greek words used, Paul is expressing deep empathy for the struggles of these new Christians. He doesn’t merely observe their weaknesses—he feels them personally. When someone falls into sin, he burns with concern, grief, indignation and a passionate desire to help. He carries the burdens of others as his own.

His concern for the churches was just as intense as his physical trials.

ἀσθενεῖ (asthenei)—meaning “is weak” and refers to physical, emotional, or spiritual weakness. Paul is saying that when others are weak, he feels their weakness as if it were his own.

σκανδαλίζεται (skandalizetai)—meaning “is led into sin” or “stumbles.” It conveys the idea of someone falling into temptation or being spiritually troubled.

πυροῦμαι (pyroumai)—meaning “to burn inwardly” and can indicate intense emotional distress, indignation or passionate concern. Some scholars interpret this as Paul feeling deep sorrow or righteous anger when others stumble.

This is a powerful message. If you have ever had the experience of walking alongside someone with a very heavy burden, you get a sense of what this means. If we truly enter into someone’s experience, we can feel the weight. We do not want to take the weight from them, but we want to help them carry it by working alongside them.

We need to reframe our anxiety so that it is the weight of a scripturally-sound, passionate care for all true disciples of Christ, rather than a focus on ourselves.

Timothy was a good example of this passionate caring:

Philippians 2:19-22: 19 But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, so that I also may be encouraged when I learn of your condition. 20 For I have no one else of kindred spirit who will genuinely be concerned <3309> for your welfare. 21 For they all seek after their own interests, not those of Christ Jesus. 22 But you know of his proven worth, that he served with me in the furtherance of the gospel like a child serving his father.

Paul is highlighting Timothy’s deep, sincere care for the Philippians, contrasting him with others who may have been more self-serving. The Greek word for concerned here doesn’t mean anxious worry, but rather a devoted, pastoral concern—the same kind of burden, the same kind of spiritual weight Paul described in 2 Corinthians 11:28 regarding his care for all the churches.

μεριμνάω (merimnaó)—verb meaning “to be anxious, to care for, to be deeply concerned.” It can imply worry, but in this context, it reflects sincere, heartfelt concern rather than distress.

γνησίως (gnēsios)—meaning “genuinely, sincerely.” Paul emphasizes that Timothy’s concern is authentic, not superficial.

ἰσόψυχον (isopsychon)—meaning “like-minded, of the same soul.” Paul is saying Timothy shares his heart and priorities in caring for the Philippians.

This was a deep engagement that went beyond just feeling bad for the person. This was walking alongside them, helping them bear their burdens.

If we are committed to standing by someone through thick and thin, we assure others they are not alone in their troubles. This is what Paul says Timothy has been like for the Philippians.

If we don’t have a genuine concern, we want to work at developing it by focusing on and entering into someone else’s trials, traumas and difficulties.

This is why passionate caring is such an effective anxiety eraser. You can’t focus on yourself so much when you are focused this intensely on the needs of others. Ask any hard-working mom focused too much on everybody else and not herself! Then she needs someone to help her. It is a balance.

We want to get outside of ourselves for the cause of Christ.

Paul described the Corinthian church as being passionately cared for by others, in light of their gifts to help those others in times of need.

Paul emphasizes both the practical and spiritual impact of generous giving:

2 Corinthians 9:12-15: (NLT) 12 So two good things will result from this ministry of giving— the needs of the believers in Jerusalem will be met, and they will joyfully express their thanks to God. 13 As a result of your ministry, they will give glory to God. For your generosity to them and to all believers will prove that you are obedient to the good news of Christ. 14 And they will pray for you with deep affection because of the overflowing grace God has given to you. 15 Thank God for this gift too wonderful for words!

We have been given an indescribable gift! Is it too much for us to passionately care about others? Let what we received pass through us so it can go to others. The Corinthian brethren helped these other brethren in Jerusalem in their time of need. As a result, the Jerusalem brethren had great gratitude for the Corinthian brethren because they so profoundly appreciated the love and concern. This give-and-take strengthened their relationship.

Wherever possible, let us be aware, be willing and be active in passionate caring:

Galatians 6:1-2: 1 Brethren, even if anyone is caught in any trespass (this suggests someone is sinning, perhaps even unintentionally), you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; each one looking to yourself, so that you too will not be tempted. 2 Bear one another's burdens and thereby fulfill the law of Christ.

Restore…in a spirit of gentleness has the goal of healing with kindness and patience, not punishment, judgment and gossip about what’s going on. Gentle correction might be all that’s needed. Be present for others in order to determine what is needed. To be present is to assure them they are not alone. Simply condemning them isn’t helpful. Be gentle, be driven and be spiritually-sound in our reactions.

As we begin reframing our anxiety, let us do so based on what God has already done for us:

Romans 8:31-32: 31 What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? 32 He who did not spare His own son, but delivered him over for us all, how will He not also with him freely give us all things?

Based on all we have been given, the least we can do is stand ready to be mutually strengthening and passionately caring. This helps us to reframe our anxiety into something positive and productive.

Because of this connection, we can truly face any and every challenge that comes our way:

Romans 8:35-39: 35 Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? 36 Just as it is written, FOR YOUR SAKE WE ARE BEING PUT TO DEATH ALL DAY LONG; WE WERE CONSIDERED AS SHEEP TO BE SLAUGHTERED. 37 But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through Him who loved us.

We can challenge our obsessive anxiety by firmly restating our clear convictions in Christ. Again, it comes down to the rehearsal: firmly restating this conviction because we believe it, and then working toward actually taking the steps.

38 For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, 39 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing (even my own anxious heart or mind!), will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

For I am convinced—the Greek word for convinced here is the “perfect passive indicative form,” meaning, “I have been fully persuaded and remain convinced.” There’s a completed action with ongoing results—Paul is saying his conviction is firm and enduring. Paul is absolutely certain that nothing can separate us from the love of God. This emphasis in the Greek shows this completed action is deeply rooted and unshakable.

The Greek word used in Romans 8:38 for “convinced” or “persuaded” is πέπεισμαι (pepeismai), which is the perfect passive form of πείθω (peithō).

πείθω (peithō)—verb meaning “to persuade, to convince, to trust, or to have confidence.” It conveys the idea of being fully assured or having unwavering certainty.

πέπεισμαι (pepeismai)—the perfect passive indicative form, meaning “I have been fully persuaded and remain convinced.” The perfect tense indicates a completed action with ongoing results—Paul is saying his conviction is firm and enduring.

Reexamining our Anxiety: Anxiety is real, and it can absolutely derail our Christian growth if we let it go unchallenged. Let us faithfully work at putting the teachings of Jesus in place to help us minimize and potentially remove that obsessiveness. Further, let us realize that the Scriptures teach us to direct our anxious energy towards the productive anxiety of mutual strengthening and passionate caring for the body of Christ.

Anxiety has a role to play. It is natural, and we all have it. We have to learn to deal with it by putting these steps in place, working on them, falling and getting up again and again. The energy of worry can be refocused toward something that honors God. We can take that energy, and by God’s grace, pour it into serving God through Christ.

This puts our anxiety to work for the betterment of God’s people in God’s way.

So, can I find balance when overwhelmed with anxiety?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Many of our topics are compiled with a Word Study using several concordances and other Bible helps. We see how a particular word is used in both the Old and New Testaments. Understanding how the words are used not only tells us what they mean, but it gives us the nuances of the original Hebrew or Greek when comparing how the writers of the Bible use them in different contexts. We can also learn more by seeing the origins of a particular word, providing a depth of understanding just reading scriptures in English cannot provide.

Anxiety: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3309 merimnao; from #3308; to be anxious about

The King James Version translates this as “take thought” 11 times, “care” 5, “be careful” 2 times, “have care” 1 time

All uses in the King James Version:

Matthew 6:25: Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought <3309> for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?

Matthew 6:27: Which of you by taking thought <3309> can add one cubit unto his stature?

Matthew 6:28: And why take ye thought <3309> for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:

Matthew 6:31: Therefore take no thought <3309>, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?

Matthew 6:34: Take <3309> therefore no thought <3309> for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought <3309> for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.

Matthew 10:19: But when they deliver you up, take <3309> no thought <3309> how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak.

Luke 10:41: And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful <3309> and troubled about many things.

Luke 12:11: And when they bring you unto the synagogues, and unto magistrates, and powers, take <3309> ye no thought <3309> how or what thing ye shall answer, or what ye shall say:

## Episode 1385 — Who Was Deborah and Why Should We Care?
Published: 2025-05-19
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1385-deborah/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/16085137/CQ_Rewind_05-19-2025_Who_Was_Deborah_and_Why_Should_We_Care.pdf

Judges 4:14: (NIV) Then Deborah said to Barak, Go! This is the day the Lord has given Sisera into your hands. Has not the Lord gone ahead of you?

Deborah stands out as one of the inspiring figures in biblical history. As a prophetess, judge and courageous leader, she rose above all expectations in a society driven by patriarchal influence. Her story, recorded in Judges 4 and 5, recounts her reliance on divine wisdom, as well as her decisive leadership and unwavering faith in God’s promises, as she rallied Israel to victory against their oppressors. Studying these chapters not only reveals the power of faith and obedience but also highlights timeless themes of justice, leadership and the importance of relying on God’s guidance in challenging times. Deborah’s story serves as a reminder that spiritual and moral courage can lead to extraordinary triumphs.

The letters “B” and “V” are the same in Hebrew.

The Hebrew name Deborah is pronounced “Devorah” and means “bee.” We have left the English spelling in the quoted scripture passages, but are spelling it as “Devorah” in our commentary.

In Jewish tradition, bees are celebrated for their industrious nature, their ability to work collectively, and for producing sweetness from humble beginnings. Even something small or seemingly unassuming can have a significant impact. We will see how these qualities are reflected in the biblical Devorah.

The account takes place during the time when Israel was ruled under judges, before they had kings.

Judges 4:1–2: 1 After Ehud’s (one of Israel’s judges) death, the Israelites again did evil in the LORD’s sight. 2 So the LORD turned them over to King Jabin of Hazor, a Canaanite king…

The Canaanites were bitter adversaries of ancient Israel, practicing many forms of immorality including idolatry and child sacrifice. For Israel, being ruled by this enemy was terrible.

Nevertheless, once Ehud died, Israel reverted to a time of idolatry. They were drawn into the practices of the Canaanites, worshipping other gods:

Judges 4:2–3: 2 …The commander of his army was Sisera… 3 Sisera, who had 900 iron chariots (advanced military technology for the time!), ruthlessly oppressed <3905> the Israelites for twenty years. Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help.

Oppressed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3905 lâchats; properly, to press, i.e. (figuratively) to distress:—afflict, crush, force, hold fast, oppress(-or), thrust self

This is the same form of the word used to describe their years of slavery in Egypt (Exodus 3:9).

Why did the Israelites wait 20 years before finally asking God to intervene?

Their stubbornness, even in this early time before the kings, was legendary. Judges 3 reveals a disturbing pattern of Israel being delivered, then forgetting God and becoming idolatrous. See Bonus Material for more.

- They forgot God and were punished by serving another nation for eight years.
- They were delivered and in peace for many years, forgot God and then served another nation for 18 years.
- They were delivered and in peace for many more years, forgot God and now served yet another nation, this time the Canaanites, for 20 years.

Why wait to cry out for deliverance? Likely it was generational. They would start down a bad road, thinking it wasn’t that bad, until the next generation grew up and realized this way of life apart from God wasn’t right. Some would wake up and call out to God. It was a pattern of idolatry then deliverance, idolatry then deliverance.

The Israelites had grown so accustomed to a way of life that strayed from God’s covenant that it took a full two decades of hardship before they recognized the necessity of turning back to God.

This is a good lesson for us. We can get too comfortable with all the wrong things, step- by-slippery step, until we wake up and realize we are under the oppression of sin. This is not good. It’s time to get out of this situation.

Israel’s previous two deliverances were led by their judges Othniel and Ehud. Now many years later, their deliverance would be led by another judge, Devorah:

Judges 4:4–5: 4 Deborah, the wife of Lappidoth, was a prophet who was judging Israel at that time 5 She would sit under the Palm of Deborah, between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites would go to her for judgment.

In spite of the fact that the roles of women in Jewish society at that time centered around care of the family and household, Devorah served as a prophetess, judge and military counselor, settling disputes and providing spiritual guidance. She was singled out as the only female for this work, suggesting her wisdom and skills were extraordinary.

While Devorah was the only female Judge of Israel, she was also a prophetess. Only four other Old Testament women were ever called prophets: Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Huldah (2 Kings 22:14), Noadiah who was evil (Nehemiah 6:14) and an unnamed prophetess (Isaiah 8:3).

Devorah’s primary function was to be a representative of God to the people. She was essentially the way the word of God came to the people. We will see how important and powerful her influence would become.

Wisdom and Humility.

While Israel wallowed under the ruthless oppression of the Canaanites, godly wisdom and humility were right there in their midst all along. Devorah positioned herself where God wanted her to be, and she humbly did the work He wanted her to do.

As the cries of the people towards God grew, she would be there to guide them.

She is doing what she is supposed to do. She is being faithful, even though many of the people around her—perhaps for years—were not. She is in position, waiting until God’s word comes. Then she will rise up and do something different and extraordinary.

Unfortunately, imperfect human nature is very predictable. Give us godly blessings and protection and then watch as we eventually wander away from them.

The stage has been set. After 20 years of hardship, Israel sees their need for God. How would Devorah respond with God’s direction?

The whole purpose of having judges in the land was to give the people a way to work out the issues between themselves in a wise and humble way. The purpose of prophets was to give the people clear instruction from God Himself. As Devorah filled both positions, her humble wisdom would now expand into courageous leadership and a stabilizing influence.

In the very next verse, Devorah collaborates with Barak to battle Sisera:

Judges 4:6–7: 6 One day she sent for Barak son of Abinoam, who lived in Kedesh in the land of Naphtali. She said to him, This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, commands you: (Enough! It’s time to go to war!) Call out 10,000 warriors from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor. 7 And I will call out Sisera, commander of Jabin’s army, along with his chariots and warriors, to the Kishon River. There I will give you victory over him.

This was not merely a suggestion. This was a command she received directly from the Lord. They were to gather the soldiers and the Lord would make sure Sisera and his soldiers were in the place where He needed them to be.

Devorah received instruction from God and instructed Barak to gather an army of 10,000 men from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun to confront Sisera at Mount Tabor. What a dramatic command! What a dramatic proclamation!

She fulfilled what God told her to do. She heard and responded like a prophet. After 20 years of not seeking God, Israel was finally ready to return to Him.

Faithful responses to God’s commands sometimes require our faith to be reinforced as we pursue God’s instructions:

Judges 4:8–10: 8 Barak told her, I will go, but only if you go with me. 9 Very well, she replied, I will go with you. But you will receive no honor in this venture, for the LORD’s victory over Sisera will be at the hands of a woman. So Deborah went with Barak to Kedesh. 10 At Kedesh, Barak called together the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali and 10,000 warriors went up with him. Deborah also went with him.

Barak would go, but only if Devorah (a woman!) would come with him. He needed the prophet of God, the judge of Israel, to come with him. With the reinforcement of God’s prophet assured, Barak now has the faith and courage to do exactly as commanded.

Devorah has provided not only God’s direction, but she has also provided the courage to follow it by her unhesitating willingness to go to the battle herself. She is 100 percent sure of victory. What great faith!

For the Lord’s victory (not Devorah’s victory or Barak’s victory) over Sisera will be at the hands of a woman—remember this prophecy because we will soon see how it was shockingly fulfilled!

The chief honor goes to him who conquers the chief; therefore, Barak would win the battle but not the full honor accorded the victor. —James Parkinson, Bible scholar

God’s battle plan will be revealed in the strategic use of the geography of Mount Tabor:

- Nine hundred iron chariots would not be effective in hurting the men 1,800 feet up on Mount Tabor.
- The Kishon River lies beneath Tabor and runs out to sea. Normally it is a dry riverbed, but it becomes a torrent during the rainy season.

Mount Tabor, Israel ©Itsik Marom| Dreamstime.com

Next is a key (yet seemingly insignificant) detail regarding this coming battle between the Israelites led by Barak, and the Canaanite army under Sisera:

Judges 4:11: Now Heber the Kenite, a descendant of Moses’ brother-in-law (some translations say father-in-law, as the names of these relationships are closely related) Hobab, had moved away from the other members of his tribe and pitched his tent by the oak of Zaanannim near Kedesh.

That’s a strange detail to drop in, isn’t it?

What does this mean? The Kenites were the nomadic people who lived nearby. They were at peace with both the Canaanites and the Israelites. They weren’t troublemakers; they knew how to live with tolerance among different peoples. For some reason, Heber had separated himself from the other Kenites and was living near Kedesh, close to the events of the battle. His tent was set up in an unusual place, and we don’t hear more about this until later.

Here is Sisera's response to Barak’s military movements:

Judges 4:12–13: 12 When Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor, 13 he called for all 900 of his iron chariots and all of his warriors, and they marched from Harosheth-haggoyim to the Kishon River.

We remember from Devorah’s prophecy that God would call Sisera out to the Kishon River area. God did not make him do that, but He knew the mind of Sisera, and that he would be provoked by Barak and his 10,000 men going up to Mount Tabor.

Sisera’s immediate response was a desire to crush them using his superior weaponry. As the oppressor, Sisera had the upper hand—he had the technology and the trained army. It looks like Sisera’s army will crush Barak’s.

Courage and Stability.

Devorah’s influence and direction as a prophet of God had caused Israel to obey and prepare for battle. This sudden and complete obedience to God’s commands rests squarely upon the shoulders of Devorah’s courage. She would lead them there, and in so doing, she would bring confident stability to those who followed her.

While she is not going to fight in the battle, Devorah is the one who brought the word of God to them. She will bring them to where God told them to go.

Barak would only go into this battle if Devorah went with him. She will bring confident stability and courage as appropriate of a prophet of the Lord. This is a lesson for us—if we are walking in accordance with the word of God, we can have confidence to move forward.

The drama is now growing as the inevitable clash between God’s people and those who were oppressing them is now being prepared!

The armies are assembled, and the battle lines are drawn!

How will God deliver His people from the might of this Canaanite army?

God’s deliverance of Israel had previously come in many ways before this particular battle, but the key ingredients in every fight are always the same:

- faith to follow, - courage to stand, and - confidence to follow through with whatever God directs.

Devorah’s wisdom, humility, courage and stability would now give Israel great confidence in God’s promised deliverance. She supplied that intangible faith and confidence not shown in a shield or spear; rather, in her leadership in following God’s command.

Devorah was in position to be used of God. This is another lesson for us—are we in position so God can use us in however He needs us to be used?

Think about what people would normally carry into battle—weapons, flags, maybe food— she was carrying confidence in what the Lord said was His will for them.

God's intervention and the Israelites' victory:

Judges 4:14–16: 14 Then Deborah said to Barak, Get ready! This is the day the LORD will give you victory over Sisera, for the LORD is marching ahead of you.

Think of this point of view! What confidence would you have making decisions in your life if you knew 100 percent that the Lord was marching ahead of you?

So Barak led his 10,000 warriors down the slopes of Mount Tabor into battle. 15 When Barak attacked, the LORD threw Sisera and all his chariots and warriors into a panic. Sisera leaped down from his chariot and escaped on foot. 16 Then Barak chased the chariots and the enemy army all the way to Harosheth–haggoyim, killing all of Sisera’s warriors. Not a single one was left alive.

As this battle unfolds, we see it is not much of a battle; it is a rout (a state of wild confusion or disorderly retreat). Israel’s army descended on the Canaanites, and somehow God sent Sisera’s army into a panic.

For the Lord is marching ahead of you—if we put the word of God before us as we face the trials and traumas of our lives (our own battles), we can have the confidence we are going in the right direction.

Devorah encourages Barak to attack, assuring him that God has delivered Sisera into his hands. It was essentially a done deal; Barak just had to do the work. This reflects Devorah's faith, confidence and leadership. She is the motivation behind the general, but the general leads them into battle. She played an incredible role without picking up a weapon. This is how God’s victories are won—our humility with His word and wisdom showing us the way.

The Lord confuses Sisera’s army, leading to their defeat.

Notice though, what the cycle was NOT. It was NOT that the people were oppressed and God just wiped out the enemy, and the people could go along doing what they did. They had to realize the depth of their distance from God, actively cry out to Him, have faith in Devorah’s commands, physically go to battle against a terrible enemy with a trained army and superior weapons, and THEN the Lord gave them victory. There was a lot for them to do in order to effect this deliverance, finally standing up to the oppression of the Canaanites with the Lord’s help.

Back to the account: Sisera abandons his chariot and flees on foot, while Barak pursues the fleeing troops and destroys them completely.

What did God do to panic an entire army that was militarily so superior to Israel? The details are in Judges 5, called The Song of Devorah and Barak.

Not only was she a prophetess, judge and a courageous leader, but we can add “songwriter” to her impressive resume!

This is a triumphant and poetic hymn celebrating Israel's victory over the Canaanites under Devorah's guidance.

It praises God’s intervention in Israel’s victory over the Canaanites under Devorah’s guidance, and recounts the bravery of the tribes who fought:

Judges 5:1–4: (NASB) 1 Then Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam sang on that day, saying, 2 That the leaders led in Israel, that the people volunteered, bless the LORD! 3 Hear, O kings; give ear, O rulers! I—to the LORD, I will sing, I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel. 4 LORD, when You went out from Seir, when You marched from the field of Edom, the earth quaked, the heavens also dripped, even the clouds dripped water.

The earth quaked, the heavens also dripped is a big hint of how God panicked Sisera’s army. Remember, God brought them to this specific place at a specific time to have this specific battle with the promise of deliverance.

Later in the song, we get further details:

Judges 5:19–21: 19 The kings came and fought; then fought the kings of Canaan at Taanach near the waters of Megiddo; they took no plunder in silver. 20 The stars fought from heaven; from their courses they fought against Sisera. 21 The torrent of Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. O my soul, march on with strength.

A torrent is a large amount of water moving quickly, like a flash flood.

(Source: Bible Commentary by David Guzik) The stars fought from heaven: The battle was fought from the heavens in the sense that God sent rain that made the Canaanite chariots of no use (the torrent of Kishon swept them away).

During this battle, God intervened by sending a sudden and heavy rainstorm. The downpour caused the Kishon River to swell and flood, turning the battlefield into a muddy quagmire. Sisera’s chariots, which were his greatest advantage, became stuck in the mud, rendering them useless. God is stronger than all the latest technology!

In our day, the greatest technological breakthrough of all time is AI, Artificial Intelligence. God is stronger and bigger than any of the latest technology! Artificial Intelligence is just that: artificial. God’s intelligence is eternal and higher. Whatever the technology, God is above it.

With its torrent of water, this big storm allowed the Israelite forces to gain the upper hand and achieve a decisive victory. The Kishon River is described as “sweeping away” the enemy forces.

While Mount Tabor is not directly next to the Kishon River, the Jezreel Valley, where the battle took place, has multiple tributaries that feed into the Kishon. When heavy rains occur, water from the surrounding hills—including Mount Tabor—rushes down into the Kishon, causing it to swell dramatically. This would have turned the normally calm river into a raging flood, sweeping away Sisera’s chariots and soldiers.

No one survived—except Sisera. As Judges 4:15 stated, Sisera leaped down from his chariot and escaped on foot.

Confidence in God’s deliverance.

Devorah’s words to Barak to, Get ready…for the Lord is marching before you, were a manifestation of overwhelming confidence in God’s promise, even when its fulfillment was not in plain sight and would seem impossible. When a leader such as Devorah shows unequivocal confidence, others line up to follow.

Devorah gave Israel the confidence to follow because she was willing to lead them. She heard the word of the Lord and believed in it with such confidence so as to create confidence in Barak and his men.

The turn of events here is remarkable; that is, unless you already grasp the power of God and the surety of His words!

Why would God allow Sisera to escape the utter defeat of his army?

Doesn’t that seem inconsistent with the way the battle was prophesied to go?

It is inconsistent and that is why we need to continue to read and understand the complete account of this battle. When it came to the protection of God’s people against oppression in the Old Testament, God always clearly stated His sovereignty. In every instance where God delivers Israel, His sovereignty is one of the biggest lessons stated in those decisive victories. As God’s messenger, Devorah proclaimed complete victory over Sisera, and it would come to pass.

Remember the weird detail of the introduction of Heber the Kenite back in Judges 4:11? He set up his tent in a strange place where no one else seemed to be. When Sisera’s chariot was stuck in the mud, he escaped. Where did he go? He ran several miles to his “ally,” Heber.

Sisera appeals to Heber’s wife Yael (Jael in English) to hide him:

Judges 4:17–20: 17 Meanwhile, Sisera ran to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because Heber’s family was on friendly terms with King Jabin of Hazor. 18 Jael went out to meet Sisera and said to him, Come into my tent, sir. Come in. Don’t be afraid. So he went into her tent, and she covered him with a blanket. 19 Please give me some water, he said. I’m thirsty. So she gave him some milk from a leather bag and covered him again. 20 Stand at the door of the tent, he told her. If anybody comes and asks you if there is anyone here, say no.

This is an exhausted man, fearful for his life—his entire army has been wiped out, and he needs to rest. He goes to his ally and now feels safe from his enemies. He tells Yael to watch and tell no one where he is.

Yael is a name of Hebrew origin that means “wild mountain goat,” specifically the Nubian Ibex. The Nubian Ibex is mostly found in the Middle East and the African countries of Sudan and Egypt. The name carries connotations of strength, agility and resilience. It is a popular name in modern-day Israel.

A more poetic meaning that has been given to the name is “strength of God.” Ja, pronounced “Ya,” is a shortened form of the divine name YHWH. “El” means “God” or “mighty one.”

And here’s why you never heard this story in Bible class:

Judges 4:21: But when Sisera fell asleep from exhaustion, Jael quietly crept up to him with a hammer and tent peg in her hand. Then she drove the tent peg through his temple and into the ground, and so he died.

Gory! This was a very decisive act, and he died.

The dramatic oppression that Sisera spent years perpetrating was over. His life for the many lives he destroyed:

Judges 4:22: When Barak came looking for Sisera, Jael went out to meet him. She said, Come, and I will show you the man you are looking for. So he followed her into the tent and found Sisera lying there dead, with the tent peg through his temple.

Barak’s active faith was well-rewarded with victory, though not with the victor’s glory. Remember, the chief honor goes to him who conquers the chief; therefore Barak would win the battle but not the full honor that would be accorded the victor. Devorah’s prophecy came true: The Lord’s victory over Sisera will be at the hands of a woman—at first the reader thinks that woman would be Devorah, but that woman was Yael!

Perhaps when we first heard the story, we thought Devorah meant herself and was just being humble. But she was not involved in the fight—she relayed God’s will to Israel by bringing Barak to the fight against the oppression of Sisera.

Jael ended up with the victory of defeating the commander of the opposing army.

Why did God allow Sisera to survive, only to die hours later by Yael?

Perhaps this accentuated the power of God over evil. You can run but you can’t hide! In the Old Testament, there was a price to pay for persecuting God’s people. God’s will is always done and His justice is always fulfilled, even if it happens in an unpredictable way.

Why did Yael kill Sisera if the Kenites were allies?

The Kenites were friendly with both Israel and the Canaanites. The Kenites were kind of in-between the two.

Remember Rahab (Joshua 2)? She was a Canaanite who lived on the wall of the city of Jericho, and yet she knew of and respected God’s sovereignty. She hid the Jewish spies and got them safely away from the city.

Also consider that just because you had a tribal allegiance didn’t mean you had a personal one. She acted independently of her tribe and with divine inspiration to fulfill prophecy. Our personal commitment to God is bigger than our political leanings.

It is a good lesson for us, that God can work using unexpected people or methods. We have to be “in position” to receive whatever God has planned.

Why is Barak mentioned in the list of “heroes of faith” in Hebrews 11 and not Devorah or even Yael?

Hebrews 11 is a wonderful chapter that lists by name many faithful ones from ancient times, even though everyone God relied on is not listed.

The explanation reveals itself:

Hebrews 11:32–34: (NASB) 32 And what more shall I say? For time will fail me if I tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets, 33 who by faith conquered kingdoms, performed acts of righteousness, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions, 34 quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, from weakness were made strong, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.

This section of the chapter credits warriors like Gideon, Barak, Samson... and then Samuel and the prophets. We think Devorah was included as a prophet. Here we read of those who fought literal battles for God, and then it includes the many prophets who spoke the words of God that in many instances inspired Israel to fight.

For the audience familiar with these historical cultural events, the mention of Barak would bring to mind Devorah, Yael, Jabin and Sisera.

What about Yael? She was neither a warrior nor a prophet.

She did not bring the army to the fight or encourage them. She wasn’t a soldier in the army. She played a role in God’s overall plan. She wasn’t from Israel, and we have no indication she ever became an Israelite (like Rahab). She was more a “hero of circumstance” than a “hero of faith.”

So great was the triumph of Israel over Sisera and his army that King David would later remember it in one of his psalms:

Psalm 83:9: (NASB1995) Deal with them as with Midian (the Midianites, an enemy of Israel) as with Sisera and Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.

We have another mention of the torrent. This flood was a key part in God confusing the army, bringing victory to Israel. David’s psalm recalls Israel’s ability to overcome enemies through divine intervention. It wasn’t because they were better soldiers. God chose to deliver them because He heard their cries of oppression.

Why should we care about Devorah? Well, I care as a woman because of her quiet, steady, dependable leadership. Her obvious good temperament, character and faith made her an important instrument of God’s. I don’t have to be a prophet to want to emulate these qualities so that the Lord can use me, too, in whatever way He deems my privilege.

Messenger of God’s will.

Devorah’s example, influence and actions were the lynchpin of the turning-point victory that delivered Israel from the oppression of the Canaanites. This “mother in Israel” indicating authority (Judges 5:7 KJV) boldly spoke God’s commands and honored and praised God in a song of victory (Judges 5). She lived up to the meaning of her name—bee—busy, patient, industrious and useful.

The account of Devorah helps us to see the importance of recognizing God’s word and choosing to follow God’s will with wisdom and humility.

Let us follow her example and make sound decisions and wise choices. Let us emulate her courage and faith in the overruling providence of God, as we show a concern for the needs of others. This is who Devorah was and why we should care!

So, who was Deborah (Devorah!) and why should we care?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the New Living Translation unless otherwise noted.
