### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1385-deborah/

1. What was the situation in Israel after the judge, Ehud, died? (Judges 3:7-12, 4:1-3)

a. What was the repeated pattern in ancient Israel?

b. Why did Israel wait 20 years to call out to God this time? Where is there danger like this for us?

2. What were the various responsibilities Deborah handled? (Judges 4:4-5)

a. Why was this unusual in her time?

b. How did Deborah show wisdom and humility during this time of oppression by the Canaanites?

3. What was the message Deborah gave to Barak? (Judges 4:5-9)

a. What was his response?

b. How did Deborah react to Barak’s request? What does this tell us about her faith and her leadership?

4. How did the battle go between Barak, Sisera and their armies? (Judges 4:10-16, 5:5, 19-22)

a. Did the Lord “trick” Sisera? Explain.

b. How did Deborah bring courage and stability to the situation?

c. Do you feel as confident moving forward in your spiritual life? Why or why not?

d. Do you fear technological advancements like AI? Why or why not?

5. Why does Sisera flee to Heber’s tent? Who was Jael? How did she fulfill God’s prophecy? (Judges 4:11,17-22)

6. What qualities made Deborah an effective leader in legal, spiritual and military arenas? (Judges 4 and 5)

a. What do you most admire about her? How can you apply her example to your life?

b. How can you “be in position” like Deborah to be used by God for His purposes? (2 Timothy 2:21, Isaiah 6:8)

7. What role does trust in God’s promises play in your life in overcoming life’s challenges? (Romans 8:31)

a. Describe what the phrase, “The Lord has already gone out ahead of you!” (Judges 4:14), means to you.

b. How will it affect your approach to troubled situations?

8. What in Deborah’s story is relevant to you today? What does it teach about faith, courage and obedience?

## Episode 1386 — I Am a Christian, So Who Am I?
Published: 2025-05-26
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1386-true-christian/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/23152047/CQ_Rewind_05-26-2025_I-Am_a_Christian_So_Who_Am_I.pdf
OCR pages from the Rewind PDF: 18

2 Corinthians 5:17: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things passed away; behold, new things have come.

We have all experienced or heard the conversational question that sometimes gets asked when one person is getting to know another: “So, are you religious?” The response can be a myriad of differing replies, one of which is, “Yeah, I’m a Christian.” That answer usually puts the respondent into the broad and vague category of Christianity in the 21st century. The real question is, what does it mean to be a true Christian according to the original biblical meaning? If we put aside all of the tradition, all of the preconceived notions and all of the countless denominations, what does the Bible say it means to be a genuine and sincere disciple of Jesus?

Why this specific topic? We were in a Bible study with one of our beloved brethren, who said she had been thinking about what it means to be a Christian. She told us, “This is who I am,” and read several scriptures. It was an eye-opening set of texts with different definitions that clarified what being a Christian is all about.

According to Wikipedia, Christianity is the world's largest and most widespread religion with over 2.4 billion followers, comprising around 31.2 percent of the world’s population.

It seems obvious, but a Christian is one who follows the teachings of Jesus Christ, so any and all understanding of being a Christian must begin with Jesus.

Some of the most well-known texts:

John 3:16-17: 16 For God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish, but have eternal life. 17 For God did not send the son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.

Being a Christian means being reliant on Jesus. He is the centerpiece. The salvation of the world through Jesus was God’s plan from the beginning.

He knew sin would enter His creation through Satan first and would be spread to humanity through Adam’s fall:

1 Peter 1:18-21: 18 Knowing that you were not redeemed with perishable things like silver or gold from your futile way of life inherited from your forefathers, 19 but with precious blood, as of a lamb unblemished and spotless, the blood of Christ. 20 For he was foreknown before the foundation of the world, but has appeared in these last times for the sake of you 21 who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.

Usually if there is a ransom to be paid, it involves money—perishable things like silver or gold—but here it’s different. We are redeemed with precious blood because of the sacrifice of Jesus.

This precious blood is more incredibly powerful than any amount of silver or gold. Moreover, the need for this blood was foreknown by God before the foundation of the world. Before the world was created, this plan was in place.

Jesus DID come to save the world, and in the process called out some to closely follow him:

Luke 9:23: And he was saying to them all, If anyone wishes to come after me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow me.

Most people would not be attracted to such a life of denial and cross-bearing. Jesus is calling out those who are willing to follow.

Like Jesus was the lamb slain before the foundation of the world, God’s plan also had a place for these “called out ones” long before humanity existed as well:

Ephesians 1:3-6: 3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, 4 just as He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and blameless before Him. In love 5 He predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the kind intention of His will, 6 to the praise of the glory of His grace, which He freely bestowed on us in the beloved.

This gets profound quickly. Not only was it God’s plan to rescue mankind even before mankind existed, but now this is saying a class of faithful Christians was planned from before the foundation of the world as well! God isn’t scrambling in a reactionary way to sin and suffering; there was a plan in place all along, with no “Plan B.”

There was no need for a Plan B because God’s (successful) Plan A was in place before anything started! The foreknowledge and power of God’s mind are beyond our comprehension.

Consider those 2.4 billion Christians. Are all of them thinking about their Christian life with this kind of seriousness and importance? Are some perhaps just “fans” of Jesus rather than true followers?

Being a follower of Jesus means where he goes, you go. What he does, you do. The way he thinks, you think. The way he responds, you respond. We have this incredible, magnificent calling available to us that the Scriptures indicate was in place for eons of time.

Jesus and his followers were also foreshadowed early in human history. Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice Isaac was one of many Old Testament accounts that surprisingly helps us see how the path of Christ and Christianity would later unfold.

This was the promise to Abraham because of his obedience to God:

Genesis 22:15-18: 15 Then the angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven, 16 and said, By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, Because you have done this thing and have not withheld your son, your only son, 17 indeed I will greatly bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heavens and as the sand which is on the seashore; and your seed shall possess the gate of their enemies. 18 In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice.

We call this the Abrahamic Covenant. It was repeated to Abraham and then his descendants several times in Genesis. It was about the everlasting blessing of the entire human race, and that blessing was to come through a specific lineage.

This plan set up from the beginning continued to unfold, but what is the connection between these Old Testament texts and the Christian? The Apostle Paul clearly connects this Old Testament event with the New Testament call to Christian discipleship.

First, the role of Jesus himself drawn from the Abraham and Isaac experience:

Galatians 3:16: Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, And to seeds, as referring to many, but rather to one, and to your seed, that is, Christ.

Jesus is THE “seed of Abraham” that blesses ALL the nations of the earth.

Paul’s reasoning continues as he adds the dimension of true discipleship to the equation:

Galatians 3:27-29: 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. 28 There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29 And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's descendants, heirs according to promise.

To be “clothed with Christ” is to be covered by his sacrifice, and therefore to be a part of him.

When you are an heir, you inherit something. Here the heirs inherit the promise made to Abraham, to be in a position to bless all the families of the earth. That certainly hasn’t happened yet, so we know it’s in a future time, specifically in God’s kingdom after everyone has been resurrected.

These are important questions! Who am I as a Christian? This is how being a follower of Christ is described in the Bible. Putting aside denominations, traditions and feelings, let’s go just to the Scriptures to understand what “being a Christian” means.

We’re just getting started, and already understanding what being a Christian means has entered the category of being a mind-blowing revelation!

Now that we have the inspiring and historical foundation for the call to Christianity in place, where do we go from here?

Our next major point in identifying who we are as Christians has to do with the things that set all true disciples apart from the rest of the world. Turns out there are many things that make this separation real. However, the most significant aspect of the defining differences has nothing to do with us and everything to do with God’s grace.

But how can we know for sure that we have been clothed with Christ and if we belong to Christ? Is it automatic if you’re claiming to be a Christian?

It involves receiving God’s holy spirit. Let’s explain.

God’s spirit plays a role in establishing who we are as Christians. As usual, it all began with Jesus:

Matthew 3:16-17: 16 After being baptized, Jesus came up immediately from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the spirit of God descending as a dove and lighting on him, 17 and behold, a voice out of the heavens said, This is My beloved son, in whom I am well-pleased.

The holy spirit is God’s invisible power and influence. Jesus was the first to be given God’s spirit as described here at the beginning of his ministry. He was outwardly identified as having God’s spirit.

We also know the holy spirit was given in a limited way during Old Testament times. But before Jesus’ baptism, its function was more “mechanical” for a specific task like inspiring craftsmen working on the Tabernacle, or to supernaturally guide and direct His prophets and other individuals by inspiring them to write or speak words they generally did not understand.

It operated through some people, but it wasn’t the same as this new way it worked within Jesus. The begettal of God’s spirit within the man Christ Jesus was something completely unique that had never before happened in the human realm.

The power and influence of God’s spirit within Jesus would now be used in an unprecedented way to further His plan. It was still the same power and influence of God but now operating differently.

Before Jesus was crucified, he told his followers that God’s spirit was coming to them. The magnitude of what Jesus meant was expressed in Ephesians:

Ephesians 1:13-14: (WEY) 13 And in him (Jesus) you Gentiles also, after listening to the message of the truth, the good news of your salvation—having believed in him (Jesus)—were sealed with the promised holy spirit; 14 that spirit being a pledge and foretaste of our inheritance, in anticipation of its full redemption—the inheritance which he has purchased to be specially his for the extolling of his glory.

Christians are sealed with the promised holy spirit; in other words, that’s the identifying mark, a stamp that authenticates the promise of a future heavenly inheritance. It’s a little like how an engagement ring promises a future wedding.

This gift of the holy spirit is God’s assurance to every true Christian that they are called to a remarkable new life. To be sealed with the promise of the holy spirit is not how the spirit was given in the Old Testament.

God’s spirit gives Christians a new way of living:

2 Corinthians 5:16-17: 16 Therefore from now on we recognize no one according to the flesh; even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him in this way no longer. 17 Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new <2537> creature <2937>; the old things passed away; behold, new things have come.

The new creature is unprecedented; an original formation never before been seen. Paul had known about Jesus before his conversion on the road to Emmaus, but after that experience, he knew Jesus in a completely different way—through the awakening of the holy spirit.

New: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2537 kainos; of uncertain affinity; new (especially in freshness)

Creature: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2937 ktisis; original formation (properly, the act; by implication, the thing, literally or figuratively)

When Jesus was baptized, the holy spirit caused something new to happen within his mind. After Pentecost, his followers receive the holy spirit to a lesser degree than Jesus. Did. This holy spirit drives the life of a true Christian from within.

As a result of receiving the holy spirit, Jesus gave himself as a ransom for the whole world. We can’t do that! What are we supposed to do with it? Paul shows us what we are supposed to be doing as a result of this complete change brought about by the indwelling of the holy spirit in the Christian.

What is the purpose of this gift to us?

2 Corinthians 5:18-19: 18 Now all these things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, 19 namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and He has committed to us the word of reconciliation.

The “work” of the new creature is to bring the world to God through Christ through the word of reconciliation. The word of reconciliation is the gospel message. Those who are “new creatures” are reconciled to God through Christ first. They in turn help the rest of the world to be reconciled back to God through Christ in the future kingdom.

2 Corinthians 5:20-21: 20 Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making an appeal through us; we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God. 21 He made him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.

An ambassador doesn’t get personally involved in the political wrangling of the host country they are visiting because that’s not their job. They are to be respectful of the laws of the land but act in such a way that shows their citizenship is elsewhere.

To be an ambassador for Christ, one must first be “in” Christ. This involves being a new creature. In essence, an ambassador for Christ is a faithful follower of Jesus who has been reconciled to God and is now tasked with representing God and Christ to the world, carrying the gospel message and ministry of reconciliation and living as a representative of their heavenly citizenship.

Can we expect to reconcile the entire world now?

No. We remember how in John 5:20,29, Jesus said there will come a time during the Day of Judgment (not a 24-hour day; rather, a period of time), when every man will hear the voice of the Son of Man and come from their graves; some to a resurrection of life (those are the ones who have been following Christ), and some to a resurrection of judgment (the “everybody else”).

This is when the reconciliation between God and the rest of the world will take place. Many Old Testament prophecies point to this day. Isaiah 35, for example, promises that resurrected mankind will walk up a highway of holiness. At that time, everyone will know the Lord (Hebrews 8:11).

One of the keys to aid in the future work of the reconciliation of mankind with God is the development in this age of the “ministers of reconciliation,” the true followers of Jesus, so they are prepared to help reconcile mankind with God in the future kingdom.

Being a follower of Christ does not mean we are magically endowed with power and wisdom that is far above our natural gifts. It requires us to develop maturity and spirituality in Christ.

This spiritual status every true Christian has been given requires them to walk, talk, think, act and live in a manner that reflects Christlikeness. This is a new life.

If we are living our old life while claiming to be a Christian, we are essentially “clapping for Jesus.” We are a fan, loving Jesus, which is good—but we are not closely following him.

The Apostle Peter explains that the true results of such a life lived now are not yet revealed but will be in the future:

1 Peter 1:3-5: (YLT) 3 Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, according to the abundance of His kindness did beget us again to a living hope, through the rising again of Jesus Christ out of the dead, 4 to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and unfading, reserved in the heavens for you, 5 who, in the power of God are being guarded, through faith, unto salvation, ready to be revealed in the last time.

An inheritance incorruptible—another “inheritance” promise—ready to be revealed in the last time. We aren’t rewarded with earthly treasures. We are promised heavenly treasures that will be given in the next life.

It’s not about what we get today; it’s about pouring our heart and soul into following Jesus that will lead to blessings when we work with him later to reconcile the world back to God.

Let’s take an honest look at our mind and heart as we go through the priorities of each day.

The loftiness of this newly created life within each true Christian is hard to grasp. All we can do is live according to the grace we’ve been given.

We have seen the profound prophetic background behind Christianity and the newness of life that comes with it. How do these things translate in a practical way?

As dramatic and overwhelming as these things are, our everyday application of them is where we see the proving ground of what being a true Christian means begin to unfold. We have reviewed what we are given; we now need to clarify what we are to give. and to be, as a result of those gifts.

We are just touching lightly on these concepts, many of which we have gone into great scriptural detail in other episodes. See the Bonus Material at the end of this Rewind for additional study recommendations. Write us at inspiration@christianquestions.com with any questions.

Let’s begin with something everyone knows but few have mastered—selfless love:

John 15:12-14: 12 This is my commandment, that you love one another, just as I have loved you. 13 Greater love has no one than this, that one lay down his life for his friends. 14 You are my friends if you do what I command you.

Jesus tells us to watch what he does so we can learn to live as he lived. Through this we gain an appreciation of the incredible value of laying down our lives for the brotherhood.

True disciples of Christ will always be seeking to fulfill this “new commandment,” but it’s not easy. It’s actually very difficult! As a matter of fact, it takes a lifetime to get there!

When we think about love, we might first think about 1 Corinthians 13, known as the “love chapter” because it’s often read at weddings.

Let’s start with the last verse and then go to the beginning of the chapter:

1 Corinthians 13:13: But now faith, hope, love, abide these three; but the greatest of these is love.

1 Corinthians 13:1-3: 1 If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. 2 If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. 3 And if I give all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I surrender my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.

The Pharisees were good at putting on a show, like a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal, without actually having selfless, benevolent love for those they were supposed to be teaching.

This selfless, benevolent love is not attention-getting—it is attentiveness in giving. It is about pouring ourselves out for others. Jesus leads the way at demonstrating selfless love. Love one another as I have loved you.

What have I uprooted inside my heart to make space to plant the seeds of this selfless love? In a normal, natural human heart, there is not enough room for everything else. We have to make space.

The “who am I” of Christianity is broadly described by the Apostle Peter:

1 Peter 2:9-10: 9 But you are A CHOSEN RACE, A royal PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION, A PEOPLE FOR God's OWN POSSESSION, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light; 10 for you once were NOT A PEOPLE, but now you are THE PEOPLE OF GOD; you had NOT RECEIVED MERCY, but now you have RECEIVED MERCY.

We are defined by all of these descriptions to help us grasp our privileged responsibilities. This is what God requires of us through Christ. These are commitments, not accolades:

- A chosen race/holy nation meaning we are the spiritual seed of Abraham.
- A royal priesthood meaning we serve others as representatives of God Himself.
- A people for God’s own possession meaning we are His children, His family. The King James Version says a peculiar people, indicating being different and displaying Christianity in its purest form.

These are not medals of honor, nor should we brag about our specialness in being chosen. We are not to be the clanging cymbal, drawing attention to ourselves in that way. Instead, we learn to follow the will of God through Christ, maturing into these roles and responsibilities. This is what defines a “Christian.”

Maybe I just love Jesus, and it’s enough for me to appreciate him from a distance. Living a good life is nice, but the call of true Christianity is deeper, more profound and costly.

These might be new concepts to our listeners. We want to put aside denominational ideas and emotions to scripturally ask: What am I supposed to be? Who am I supposed to be? What am I supposed to do? How am I supposed to do it? It is all written for us in Scripture.

The Apostle Paul revealed another “who am I” description of true Christianity— the bride of Christ:

Ephesians 5:22-27: 22 Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord. 23 For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the church <1577>, he himself being the savior of the body. 24 But as the church <1577> is subject to Christ, so also the wives ought to be to their husbands in everything. 25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church <1577> and gave himself up for her, 26 so that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, 27 that he might present to himself the church <1577> in all her glory, having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that she would be holy and blameless.

What is this church? It is the people—not the physical building with a steeple or a certain denominational affiliation. The true church means the community, the congregation made up of dedicated individual Christians. It is an individual calling.

Church: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1577 ekklesia; a calling out, i.e. (concretely) a popular meeting, especially a religious congregation (Jewish synagogue, or Christian community of members on earth or saints in heaven or both)

The book of Revelation helps us see that we are tasked with preparing ourselves now for our spiritual union with Jesus. A big part of our responsibility is to prepare for what is to come.

We should be preparing now for who the Lord will need us to be in the future work of the kingdom:

Revelation 19:7-8: 7 Let us rejoice and be glad and give the glory to Him, for the marriage of the lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready. 8 It was given to her to clothe herself in fine linen, bright and clean; for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.

Remember we read in Galatians 3:27 how we are to be clothed with Christ. He is our covering. That’s the initial transformation. Here the bride of Christ is clothed in fine linen, representing the righteous conduct and good deeds of the faithful Christians, preparing them for their union with Christ and their future role in blessing all the families of the earth. This is a progression of faith shown here. We are first clothed with Christ as the foundation. Then the victory of overcoming is shown as a bride being clothed in fine linen — the fulfillment of a faithful life.

The life of a Christian is a life of progression, a life of worth, a life of focus and a life of sacrifice.

These are serious “mirror” questions. Am I a fan or follower? Will I be clothed with linen as part of the bride of Christ? Matthew 22:14 (KJV) assures us that many are called, but few are chosen. All 2.4 billion Christians won’t receive this heavenly reward. If we truly desire to follow Christ, we need to make sure we are one of those chosen.

Being part of a chosen race, a holy priesthood, a holy nation, God’s family and the spiritual bride of Christ—there is so much privilege, yet so little time!

So far what we have seen makes being a true Christian a lot of work! What else is there and what kind of blessings should we expect?

There is always more. Once we briefly examine who the “saints” really are and what it means to be God’s temple, we will wrap up with the meaning of being part of the body of Christ. And the blessings we receive? They are transformational, they are spiritual, they are godly and they are eternal. What better blessings could anyone ever possibly hope for?

To reiterate, these are spiritual blessings and not earthly. We can’t take the physical blessings promised to the ancient Israelites for their obedience and apply them to us. For the spiritual Israelite—the new creature in Christ—we should expect trials and troubles, but they take on a different significance for us than the rest of the world.

Adversity was the blessing Jesus went through, and he was exalted to the right hand of God.

The Apostle Paul helps us understand the “who am I” of being saints and God’s temple:

Ephesians 2:19-22: 19 So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints <40>, and are of God's household, 20 having been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the corner stone, 21 in whom the whole building, being fitted together, is growing into a holy <40> temple in the Lord, 22 in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling of God in the spirit.

Holy: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #40 hagios; sacred (physically, pure, morally blameless or religious, ceremonially, consecrated)

The King James Version translates this as “holy” 161 times, “saints” 61 times, “Holy One” 4 times

Saints and holy here mean sacred, pure, morally blameless, consecrated. To consecrate is to declare something as sacred.

A consecrated person transforms their life, trying to follow the way Jesus lived his life. They resist their natural sinful tendencies and instead try to obey God’s will in every decision of life. We talked about receiving the holy spirit—becoming “spirit begotten” (1 John 5:1). A spirit-begotten person sees, thinks, speaks and acts differently than they did before (2 Corinthians 5:17). Their loyalty and allegiance as an ambassador are first to God and His son. They are committed to the higher purpose of doing things God’s way instead of their own way. It is not a natural tendency.

This “holy temple in the Lord” defines us as a dwelling place for God’s spirit:

1 Corinthians 3:16-17: 16 Do you not know that you are a temple of God and that the spirit of God dwells in you? 17 If any man destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him, for the temple of God is holy <40>, and that is what you are.

Faithful Christians are themselves considered a sacred place because the holy spirit of God dwells within them. This means we have a big responsibility to make sure we are glorifying God in our bodies and minds. Romans 12:1 (KJV) admonishes us to …present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

In addition to our individual bodies being temples, we just read Ephesians 2:19-22 how the saints are growing into a “holy building” where Jesus is the cornerstone and everyone fits together perfectly. The church—the collective body of faithful followers—is a holy temple or dwelling of God in that bigger sense. The responsibility is both individual and collective. We are part of the temple together.

Being part of this temple, this church, means being very different than those around us:

2 Corinthians 6:14-16: 14 Do not be bound together with unbelievers; for what partnership have righteousness and lawlessness, or what fellowship has light with darkness? 15 Or what harmony has Christ with Belial, or what has a believer in common with an unbeliever? 16 Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God…

This is a powerful responsibility and privilege at the same time. We want to take the responsibility part with immense seriousness.

This requires being different from the world around us, as there is no partnership between the temple of God and idols. It seems that everything is an idol today, taking us away from godly focus!

Our last “who am I” example from Paul as he describes the equally important aspects of the body of Christ:

1 Corinthians 12:14-16: 14 For the body is not one member, but many. 15 If the foot says, Because I am not a hand, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body. 16 And if the ear says, Because I am not an eye, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body.

The idea is that while there are many individuals, they collectively form one unified body in Christ. Just like a physical body has different parts (feet, hands, eyes, ears, spleen), the body of Christ has many integrated members with different gifts, talents, abilities and functions.

Sometimes, being human, we wrangle about who is more important.

This illustration helps us see the importance of what we are called to do, regardless of our abilities:

1 Corinthians 12:17-20: 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body, just as He desired. 19 If they were all one member, where would the body be? 20 But now there are many members, but one body.

These differences are by God's design, and He places the members in the body just as He desired. If your role is to be the little toe, be the best little toe you can be in order to help the whole body function in a healthy way!

There has to be give and take, mutual support and the recognition of the functions others fulfill. It is a remarkable, beautiful privilege and responsibility of what being a Christian really means.

Paul continues by explaining that each member of the body is vital in order to be a complete, self-sustaining, mutually-supportive unit, all under the head who is Christ.

Why is it set up this way? Because it is how Jesus lived and taught us to live:

1 Corinthians 12:26: And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

This places the responsibility on us to pay attention to each other’s needs. The interconnectedness of the members means they should have mutual care. If one member suffers, all suffer with it; if one is honored, all rejoice. We are to support and encourage one another. We cannot do that unless we know and love one another. Remember the clanging cymbals? The attention-getting? The body of Christ does not work on getting attention; it works on getting the work done, rejoicing as a unit.

Paul further brings out there is no division because there is no pecking order. All have equal value because all contribute. We’re called to be a part of a whole:

Ephesians 4:11-13: 11 And He gave some as apostles, and some as prophets, and some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, 12 for the equipping of the saints for the work of service, to the building up of the body of Christ; 13 until we all attain to the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the son of God, to a mature man, to the measure of the stature which belongs to the fullness of Christ.

Some have microphones like we on CQ are blessed to have, some have folded hands and can do the work by praying for those who might have more public roles; some have both. There are different functions of the body because the true church is a collection of diverse individuals, each essential and interconnected, working together in unity under Christ as the head. It’s about mutual dependence, honor and collective purpose.

Let ME do my part. Let me support YOU in doing your part, and let US rejoice together that we can do OUR part and help others do THEIRS. This is what being a true Christian is.

We have such a privilege and opportunity:

1 Corinthians 2:9 (NLT): No eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no mind has imagined what God has prepared for those who love Him.

We want to follow the many scriptural examples we have been given.

If you are not up for that intensity but still love Jesus—it’s okay. There is a blessing for all in the kingdom, and already loving Jesus will place you in line for those blessings. But for those who are true followers of Christ now, true Christians now, the responsibilities here are difficult but also blessed. Not with earthly riches, but with the privilege of being part of something that will play a role in the reconciliation of the entire world later on. What could be better than that?

When we think about what a Christian is and say, “Who am I?” The answer should be, “I am a footstep follower of Jesus Christ, taking up my cross daily and following him!”

So, I am a Christian, so who am I?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

1. How did sin enter the human race? What is the remedy for this? When did God start planning for this

remedy? Who is involved in this remedy? (John 3:16-17, 1 Peter 1:18-21, Ephesians 1:3-6)

2. Who am I? How can I be sure I appreciate the magnitude of the role in which I have the privilege to

participate?

3. Who am I? How does the Old Testament connect with my inheritance in Christ? How does the

Abrahamic Covenant apply to me? How can I know if I have been “clothed with Christ” and if I “belong to Christ”? (Genesis 22:15-18, Galatians 3:16,27-29)

4. Who am I? Am I truly reflecting my newly created life in Christ? Are my interactions with others a

testament to God’s spirit and His justice, wisdom, power and love? What are my expectations of the future? (1 Peter 1:3-5)

5. Who am I? How do I exhibit to others (and in my heart) clear evidence of a self-sacrificing love?

(John 15:12-14, 1 Corinthians 13:1-3,13)

6. Who am I? Do I have a deep and profound connection in accomplishing God’s purposes for me?

How does 1 Peter 2:9-10 describe the role I am to fulfill?

7. Who am I? Am I excited yet humble in my anticipation of being with Jesus in heaven?

(Ephesians 5:22-27, Revelation 19:7-8)

8. Who am I? How do I know if I am being transformed? How do I truly represent God’s holiness in an

unholy world? (Ephesians 2:19-22, 1 John 5:1, 1 Corinthians 3:16-17, 2 Corinthians 5:17, 6:14-16, Romans 12:1)

9. Who am I? How am I living in unity with other disciples of Jesus? How am I contributing and graciously

accepting help from others? (1 Corinthians 12:14-19, 26, Ephesians 4:11-13)

## Episode 1387 — Can I Really Love Someone I Don’t Like?
Published: 2025-06-02
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1387-selfless-love/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/30084759/CQ_Rewind_06-02-2025_Can_I_Really_Love_Someone_I_Dont_Like.pdf

1 Corinthians 13:4–6: 4 Love is patient, love is kind and is not jealous; love does not brag and is not arrogant, 5 does not act unbecomingly; it does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not take into account a wrong suffered, 6 does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth.

We all know God IS love, and because He loves His human creation, He sent Jesus to redeem us all from sin and death. We also know Jesus taught us to love our enemies and pray for those people who despitefully take advantage of us. According to the gospel, love is a clear centerpiece of how God’s plan works and how we are to emulate Jesus in relation to our enemies. But what about those people we just may not like? You know who we’re talking about—those individuals who are just irritating, who might see the world differently than we do and who always seem to be on the other side of issues. Can we just tolerate them—just “go along to get along”—or do we have to “love” them? If we do have to love them, what does that even look like?

Most of us don’t have mortal enemies, but we probably have a few people who irritate us or who we just don’t like to be around. Please note, we are talking about everyday life in general, not abusive, dangerous relationships. Let’s all take a moment to zero in on that one person (or several people!) in our lives who might fit into this category of, “I don’t really like you all that much.”

The first few verses of 1 Corinthians 13 review how we may be presenting ourselves and coming across to others, while showing us that we are nothing without this selfless love.

1 Corinthians 13:1–3: 1 If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love <26>, I have become a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. 2 If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have love <26>, I am nothing. 3 And if I give all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I surrender my body to be burned, but do not have love <26>, it profits me nothing.

Love: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #26 agape; from #25; love, i.e. affection or benevolence; specially (plural) a love-feast

Love: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #25: agapao; perhaps from agan (much) [or compare Hebrew #5689]; to love (in a social or moral sense)

I can do all these great things on the outside, but if I don’t have selfless, benevolent love on the inside, the Apostle Paul says it is worthless. We are wasting our time.

We can pretend—we can do nice things—but are we being that selfless person?

With this simple lesson in mind, let’s continue with the next few verses and focus on how to apply “selfless love” to those we don’t get along with and maybe don’t want to make time for.

1 Corinthians 13:4–6: 4 Love <26> is patient, love <26> is kind and is not jealous; love <26> does not brag and is not arrogant, 5 does not act unbecomingly; it does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not take into account a wrong suffered, 6 does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;

Positive: Love is patient, kind and rejoices with the truth.

Negative: Love is NOT jealous, it does NOT brag, it’s NOT arrogant, does NOT act unbecomingly, does NOT seek its own, is NOT provoked and does NOT take into account a wrong suffered.

We have more what love is “not” than what love “is.” There are three positives and many negatives.

My wife, Trish, reminds me often that every life matters. These three little words put everything into a much larger perspective.

Let’s take these texts apart and apply them to those people we may not like so much.

We often think of patience as being willing to calmly wait without complaining or being annoyed. But there’s more to this word: it means to have forbearance—to have self-restraint; self-control—not taking immediate action.

It is interesting that Paul lists this first. Apparently, we can’t practice selfless love without forbearance. This means we restrain our own preferences in the interest of respecting others.

Being a Christian is to be sanctified, to be “set apart for a holy purpose.”

- Am I applying sanctified and godly self-restraint?

Ephesians 4:1–2: 1 Therefore I, the prisoner of the Lord, implore you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling with which you have been called, 2 with all humility and gentleness, with patience (forbearance), showing tolerance for one another in (selfless) love.

Love is patient—full of self-restraint. This is where selfless love can begin. As footstep followers of Jesus, we first put forbearance in place.

- How forbearing am I with those I have a hard time tolerating?
- Do I hold myself back from reacting? (Generally, no!)

Selfless love instructs godly, Christian love to be built upon the foundation of forbearance, sanctified self-restraint.

We generally think of kindness as being generous and compassionate, but there’s also a nuance to this Greek word. It means to be useful. This isn’t just being passively nice. It involves deliberate acts of generosity and care.

Ephesians 4:31–32: 31 Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. 32 Be kind (employed, useful) to one another, tender- hearted, forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has forgiven you.

To be kind is more than just being nice. It is to be active and helpful.

- With those with whom we have a hard time, are we holding back our reactive responses and replacing them with useful actions?

Kindness isn’t about whether they deserve it; it’s about reflecting God and Jesus. Maybe we hold the door open for this person. Maybe we give them a referral to our doctor, our plumber, or someone who can help them in the moment.

- If nothing else, are they valuable enough to be in our prayers? How about praying, “Lord, help me to recognize an opportunity to be kind to this person.”

Self-restraint opens the door to being useful, to being a positive influence around them in some way.

Now that we have seen two of the three positive ways to apply love to others through patience and kindness, let’s see how it reflects in our characters by what it is NOT.

We all know what jealousy is, but the Greek word here can also mean “to be zealous”—to earnestly desire.

This jealous/zealous word can be positive or negative—to have warmth of feeling for or against; to burn with zeal.

Here is a negative use of the word:

Acts 7:9: The patriarchs became jealous of Joseph and sold him into Egypt. Yet God was with him.

Zeal and passion are important qualities to have, as long as they are properly focused and not used against others in a negative manner.

Here is a positive use of the word:

2 Corinthians 11:2: For I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy.

These are two different applications of the same Greek word. In the first example, Joseph’s brothers were jealous of him. That darkness drove them to sell him into slavery.

Conversely, it was light that drove the Apostle Paul to be jealous over the brotherhood with godly jealousy, so they would be sanctified, following after Christ.

Love is not that negative sense of jealousy. It does not want darkness for others.

- Is our selfless love for those we may not naturally like being expressed through selfless, strong and yet kind actions that are not passionate in a hurtful way?

We can start with something small—be active. Let the person know they matter, as every life matters. Love is not jealous and doesn’t produce that passionate, negative feeling against someone else. Being useful to them is one way to counteract this feeling.

To boast; self–display, self-promotion

Galatians 5:24–26: 24 Now those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. 25 If we live by the spirit, let us also walk by the spirit. 26 Let us not become boastful, challenging one another, envying one another.

Those who are boastful seek attention and recognition. It causes us to elevate ourselves even at the expense of others. It’s an external expression of pride. Love is the opposite; it does not put itself on display.

- With all of the self-restraint and giving in place for those we may not naturally like, are we EVER engaging in any kind of boastful confirmation of our “stepping up” and being attentive to them? Are we making sure they know we are rising above our little spat, seeing ourselves as the “better” person?

Thinking about the person (or people) we don’t like very much, we might have the tendency to show off in front of them. We feel better about ourselves knowing we are just a little superior in this area or that.

If I’m better than you, I don’t have to admit to myself I’m actually a little jealous of you.

But enough about me. Let’s talk about you. What do you think of me? —Bette Midler in the 1989 movie, Beaches

To inflate, puff up, make proud

1 Corinthians 8:1: Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge makes arrogant, but love edifies.

To edify means to build up, strengthen or encourage.

While being boastful is more outward, arrogance is more of an internal attitude of superiority—thinking too highly of ourselves. This is where the challenge gets deep and difficult because if it is internal, others can’t necessarily see it.

- Do we in any way adopt an arrogant attitude while being respectful towards difficult people? If we are boastful in any way, it is a sure outward sign of arrogance, which is an inward problem.

If we have such an “inward arrogance” issue, we need to find it and bring it to the Lord in prayer. Being arrogant is a big deterrent to being Christlike.

Behaving inappropriately, dishonorably or disgracefully; not up to accepted standards

Paul describes love as thoughtful, courteous and mindful of others, ensuring that actions align with kindness and integrity rather than selfishness or arrogance. Selfless love is never rude or inconsiderate.

James 1:14–15: 14 But each one is tempted when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust. 15 Then when lust has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin is accomplished, it brings forth death.

Here the word lust means a strong desire or longing for something self-indulgent or sinful. Lust leads to sin which ultimately has destructive consequences.

This is an important aspect of looking inward and assessing ourselves.

- What do our outward actions show everybody around us? Are we acting inappropriately in any way?
- Selfless love thrives in an environment of appropriate behavior. Do we as Christians see those who challenge us as deserving our highest level of acceptable, godly behavior? They do deserve it because every life matters. If Jesus died for them, then I, by rights, must treat them with that same kind of respect.

Not after its own self-interests or desires. After all, it’s not about ME; it’s about Christ.

1 Peter 2:11–12: (NLT) 11 Dear friends, I warn you as temporary residents and foreigners to keep away from worldly desires that wage war against your very souls. 12 Be careful to live properly among your unbelieving neighbors. Then even if they accuse you of doing wrong, they will see your honorable behavior, and they will give honor to God when He judges the world.

Peter tells us to be careful to present ourselves as Christlike in front of unbelievers. This doesn’t mean to put on an act or a façade. We are to actually BE Christlike. This will be a witness to them. They may not respond to it now, but they will later, even if it is after they are resurrected in the kingdom. They will be able to look back and think, I remember that person who always irritated me. I see now that there was something different about they way he/she conducted his/her life.

- Do we realize our internal battle to appropriately represent Christ is accentuated by those we have challenges with, as they likely define Christianity by observing our actions?

We may be the only Christian example they ever see! How do they interpret our Christian example? They deserve to see Christlike behavior, a more elevated model of conduct than they have experienced in the world. This is a huge responsibility for us.

Every life matters.

To make sharp, to stimulate or irritate

To provoke can also be positive or negative. In the negative sense, it means to incite anger, to purposely stir up, as in, “to provoke a fight.” Perhaps this is most likely a problem when we know the person really well, like a spouse or close family member. We know what buttons to push. We know that by just a look or word, we can cause the circumstance to quickly escalate.

Acts 17:16,22: 16 Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was being provoked within him as he was observing the city full of idols. 22 So Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, Men of Athens, I observe that you are very religious in all respects.

Paul took something that really frustrated him (the idol worship around him) and found a way past the irritation by seeing the people as those Jesus died for. He found a way to show them a better path. The Acts account goes on to explain how he used an idol dedicated to the Unknown God to open a dialogue about the real God. Paul met them where they were in order to help them see something different.

This is a classic example of using what could have been negative provocation as a positive witness. He loved them more than he hated what they were doing out of ignorance.

- Especially when dealing with those with whom we have challenges, are we truly remaining unprovoked by not being focused on our own agenda, and instead only pursuing only God’s agenda?

Paul showed us how to have selfless love in a difficult, ungodly circumstance and turn it into something godly. Selfless love is not provoked—especially with people who irritate us!

The Greek word used here has the thought of taking an inventory. In other words, don’t keep score.

We bring this point up a lot on our marriage episodes. Strong emotions imprint memories—for good or bad. When someone hurts us or betrays us or disappoints us or makes us mad, our brain can naturally hold on to that for a long time. Think about how a scab covers a wound. If we continually pick at it, it bleeds and won’t heal.

Matthew 5:39: But I say to you, do not resist an evil person; but whoever slaps you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also.

We can’t keep score! It is so easy to remember and focus on the negative, keeping it in the forefront of our minds. But selfless love does exactly the opposite.

- It is too easy to remember the wrongs done to us, especially by those we don’t trust. Are we focused on simply loving them as human beings Jesus died for?

Every life matters.

Since WE do not serve God perfectly, we can’t demand perfection from others or hold negative feelings by keeping score of their failures against us. God is not doing this to us! God knows all our faults, and yet sees us through the covering of Christ. We, too, want to see others through Christlike selfless love. Don’t keep score!

Not calmly happy with injustice or wrongfulness

Romans 6:13: and do not go on presenting the members of your body to sin as instruments of unrighteousness; but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God.

- Are we quietly and privately smiling when those we are challenged with run into difficulties due to the hard experiences of life? If so, we have essentially left selfless love at the door.

Think again, because every life matters!

We’re not supposed to be secretly full of glee when something goes wrong for the person we don’t like very much. While some of these reactions are easy to see in public, much of this has to do with our secret faults. It might be that no one catches that tiny gleam in our eye when we hear bad news about this person, but of course, God knows.

We need to be careful not to pile on to that person’s troubles by gossiping about them. By doing so, we have committed two sins.

It is not showing selfless love when we are secretly “happy” when something goes wrong for the person we don’t like.

To sympathize in gladness with truth

John 8:32: and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.

Selfless love sympathizes. When we sympathize with someone, we can enter into their experience because we have been through it ourselves. When we empathize, we feel bad for them and can pray for them and encourage them, but we haven’t personally experienced that situation.

Selfless love sympathizes with truth; it enters into it. We have been made free by the truth of the gospel, and that truth changes us. It enables us to treat others in a more Christlike way, especially with those we may not like so much.

- We know we are on the right track when we can respond to those difficult people in our lives, to let them know we are entering into their positive life experiences. Am I living this now?

On one hand, we love the people we love. On the other, we know Jesus told us to love our enemies. This is about the people in-between that we might have thought it was okay to treat or think of a certain way. We need to “rethink how we think” about these people. They are the ones who often get overlooked while we are working on trying to love everybody else.

Why? Jesus died for them—EVERY LIFE MATTERS. We want to apply what Jesus lived and died for in our everyday lives.

So, can I love someone I really don’t like?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
