### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1387-selfless-love/

Based on 1 Corinthians 13:1-6, what does the Apostle Paul say is one thing God requires of us?

1.

Love is PATIENT: What is the meaning of this word? (also, Ephesians 4:1-2)

⮚ How am I applying godly self-restraint in being forbearing with those I have a hard time tolerating?

2. Love is KIND: In what way is being kind more than just being nice? (also, Ephesians 4:31-32)

⮚ How am I replacing my reactive responses with useful actions towards those who annoy me?

3. Love is NOT JEALOUS: What are the two meanings of this word? (also, Acts 7:9, 2 Corinthians 11:2)

⮚ What small actions can I use to show someone I struggle with that their life matters?

4. Love DOES NOT BRAG: Why do we boast? (also, Galatians 5:24-26)

⮚ When am I boastful of my being the “better” person in a dispute?

5. Love is NOT ARROGANT: What is the difference between arrogance and edifying? (also, 1 Corinthians 8:1)

⮚ Am I secretly arrogant while pretending to be respectful towards difficult people?

6. Love DOES NOT ACT UNBECOMINGLY: What does this mean? (also, James 1:14-15)

⮚ Do I truly believe that those who challenge me deserve my highest level of godly behavior?

7. Love DOES NOT SEEK ITS OWN: What does this mean? (also, 1 Peter 2:11-12)

⮚ How are we a witness to unbelievers now and after the resurrection? Why is this particularly important?

8. Love is NOT PROVOKED: How do we provoke others positively and/or negatively? (also, Acts 17:16,22)

⮚ How can I let go of my own agenda, remain unprovoked, and pursue God’s agenda?

9. Love DOES NOT TAKE INTO ACCOUNT A WRONG SUFFERED: Keeping score! (also, Matthew 5:39)

⮚ How can I focus on loving those I don’t trust as Jesus loves them? Do I hold old wrongs against them?

10. Love DOES NOT REJOICE IN UNRIGHTEOUSNESS: Secretly full of glee! (also, Romans 6:13)

⮚ When have I privately smiled when those who have wronged me run into difficulties in their lives?

11. Love REJOICES WITH THE TRUTH: How do we sympathize with the difficult people? (also, John 8:3)

⮚ How can I enter happily into a challenging person’s joy?

## Episode 1388 — How Can I Best Share the Gospel With Others?
Published: 2025-06-09
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1388-witness/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/06152540/CQ_Rewind_06-09-2025_How_Can_I_Best_Share_the_Gospel_With_Others.pdf

1 Corinthians 9:19: For though I am free from all men, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I may win more.

Forty days after his resurrection, when Jesus was about to ascend to the Father, he gave his disciples their great commission. In Matthew 28:18-20, he said, …All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit, teaching them to observe all that I commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. The message here was simple and yet daunting. Preach the gospel everywhere. Find disciples throughout the world and then teach them how to truly follow Christ. To accomplish this massive task, we need God’s spirit and biblical examples of how to present ourselves. So, what are the foundational principles of effectively sharing the gospel?

In the book Fearfully and Wonderfully: The Marvel of Bearing God’s Image by Dr. Paul Brand and Philip Yancey, they talk about the term “compliancy” as it relates to this important topic of witnessing. We’ll read a few quotes during our conversation today, starting with, “Bioengineers use the word compliancy to describe a material’s capacity to mold to the shape of another surface, and skin exhibits this quality remarkably well.” Their explanation goes on to describe how in areas of stress, such as on the palm of the hand, there is a special cluster of fat calls and firm collagen fibers working together in a unique way. It’s described under the microscope as looking like fine Belgian lace. More on this soon!

To find these principles, let’s first look at the drive the Apostle Paul had to preach to others:

1 Corinthians 9:19: For though I am free from all men, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I may win more.

I am a slave to all so that I can do the job we were given to preach the gospel.

In these next verses, there are three specific categories of people to whom he was drawn to preach.

First, those appreciative of the Jewish nation, and in our case, those who may also appreciate Christianity:

1 Corinthians 9:20: To the Jews I became as a Jew, so that I might win Jews; to those who are under the Law, as under the Law though not being myself under the Law, so that I might win those who are under the Law.

Second, those who are non-Christians, who have rejected all of what God’s favored people were given:

1 Corinthians 9:21: To those who are without law, as without law, though not being without the law of God but under the law of Christ, so that I might win those who are without law.

Third, those who are weak and struggling, no matter what their background is:

1 Corinthians 9:22: To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak; I have become all things to all men, so that I may by all means save some.

The Message Bible paraphrases these verses beautifully:

1 Corinthians 9:19-23: (Message Bible) Even though I am free of the demands and expectations of everyone, I have voluntarily become a servant to any and all in order to reach a wide range of people: religious, nonreligious, meticulous moralists, loose-living immoralists, the defeated, the demoralized—whoever. I didn’t take on their way of life. I kept my bearings in Christ—but I entered their world and tried to experience things from their point of view. I’ve become just about every sort of servant there is in my attempts to lead those I meet into a God-saved life. I did all this because of the Message. I didn’t just want to talk about it; I wanted to be in on it!

Paul did not just say, “Let me tell you about the gospel!” Instead, he sought to enter into the lives of those he was communicating with—"Let me, as a human being, connect with you as a human being. Let me show you something of great value to both of us.” This serves as our basis as we review biblical examples of how to effectively share the gospel with others.

Each of these examples share a few general principles:

1. RECOGNIZE: Seek to understand who it is that you are speaking to. Know your audience! This means recognizing the values, background, expectations and level of understanding of the people you’re addressing. When we tailor our message to suit our listeners, we’re more likely to engage them, build trust and ensure our ideas are clearly understood.

2. RESPECT: Establish a common ground of respect, even if it has to be very basic.

This might include using relatable language or appropriate examples for our audience’s experiences. It will often lead to a more productive and meaningful dialogue.

3. LISTEN: For us to be heard, we should be willing to listen with attentive conviction. The Apostle Paul shows this in 1 Corinthians 9:19-23. We need to listen attentively with the conviction that these individuals are important.

4. AWAKEN: Try and awaken the listener from their normal pattern to an interest in the gospel. Surprising your listener with something they didn’t expect can be a powerful way to engage them. When someone is caught off guard in a good way, it forces them to pause, pay closer attention and process the message more deeply. It often signals that there’s something important or unique worth noticing.

5. TEACH, PREACH, REASON AND ENCOURAGE: Deliver the Good News with heart! We won’t necessarily do all four of these things in the same witnessing conversation, but we should think about delivering at least one of them. We are lights in a dark world, and our message of real hope is comforting.

Further about compliancy, Fearfully and Wonderfully: The Marvel of Bearing God’s Image describes about how the fat and collagen in your palm redistribute to conform to the objects it grasps—“firm enough to hold a hammer without discomfort, yet gentle enough to cradle delicate items like a crystal goblet or a kitten. Engineers nearly shout in awe when they analyze this amazing property, for they cannot design a material that so perfectly balances strength and pliability.”

In Acts 23, a plot to assassinate Paul is uncovered, and Roman authorities transfer him to Caesarea for safety.

Acts 24 sees Paul standing trial before Governor Felix, where he refutes accusations from Jewish leaders and speaks about righteousness and judgment. Felix keeps Paul imprisoned for two years.

In Acts 25, Paul is brought before Governor Festus, who wants to send him back to Jerusalem, but Paul asks for an appeal to Caesar who is in Rome. King Agrippa, a Jewish king under Roman rule, is visiting Caesarea at the time and wants to listen to Paul’s case. Paul is unwavering in his commitment to spread the gospel despite opposition.

Next in Acts 26, he is granted an audience with King Agrippa about the accusations against him and is given permission to defend himself. This is self-defense, but it becomes a planned witness by the Apostle Paul after being imprisoned for two years. Most people would want to say what they have to say and leave as soon as possible, but that's not what Paul does.

Paul begins by applying the first two principles, opening the door for his great witness.

1. RECOGNIZE: Seek to understand who it is that you are speaking to.

2. RESPECT: Establish a common ground of respect, even if it has to be very basic.

Acts 26:2-3: 2 In regard to all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, I consider myself fortunate, King Agrippa, that I am about to make my defense before you today; 3 especially because you are an expert in all customs and questions among the Jews; therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.

Paul humbly asks for permission to explain. He RECOGNIZED King Agrippa as a fellow Jew who shared the same cultural understanding as Paul did. He will tell his dramatic story from his early life as a Pharisee and then his conversion. He RESPECTED his audience in King Agrippa, which would enhance the gospel message he was about to explain.

Incidentally, there were two rulers named Herod Agrippa who were closely tied to Roman politics. This one is Herod Agrippa II (AD 27 to around AD 100), who was the last ruler of the Herodian dynasty.

Agrippa was a “client king,” meaning the ruler of an independent area but that operated under the influence and protection of Rome.

These kings were recognized as “amicus populi Romani” (friend of the Roman people) and were expected to maintain stability in their regions, support Roman interests and provide military assistance when needed. Rome used client kings as a way to govern distant territories without direct administration, allowing local rulers to handle internal affairs while Rome controlled foreign policy and defense.

3. LISTEN: For us to be heard, we should be willing to listen with attentive conviction.

Paul had been in prison for two years, so he was not here in Caesarea to listen, he was here to talk! Paul would continue his defense, which would inevitably be a witness to the gospel by citing his past. In so doing, he was identifying with his accusers, showing them that he had been one of them.

Paul already knew their perspective from his own life experience. He had already listened to his accusers:

Acts 26:4-7: 4 So then, all Jews know my manner of life from my youth up, which from the beginning was spent among my own nation and at Jerusalem; 5 since they have known about me for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that I lived as a Pharisee according to the strictest sect of our religion. 6 And now I am standing trial for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers; 7 the promise to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly serve God night and day. And for this hope, O King, I am being accused by Jews.

Paul is making a legal and theological argument before King Agrippa. He begins by establishing his credibility—reminding Agrippa that he (Paul) has lived as a devout Jew from his youth, well-known among his people. This serves as evidence that his faith and actions are not new or radical but rooted in Jewish tradition.

He then shifts to the hope of the promise made by God to Israel, referring to the resurrection (Acts 26:8). By framing his trial around this shared belief, he argues that his faith in Christ aligns with Jewish teachings rather than contradicting them. This is a strategic approach appealing to Agrippa’s knowledge of Jewish customs while subtly challenging the legitimacy of the accusations against him.

By identifying with his accusers, Paul brought the important realities of his history and motivation before the king.

Paul established before King Agrippa that he shared common history with his accusers. Since they believed in the same things, why were they putting him on trial?

Finding that commonality to build upon can open the door for witnessing.

It is remarkable to think about the privilege we are given to know about Jesus and to represent him as well. Let’s pay attention.

As we further uncover Paul’s preaching approach, the question is, how willing are we to follow his example?

On the surface, we may look at this and think it’s all pretty basic: You make a connection with your audience and then tell them what you are going to tell them. The key point here is how focused we are on actually proclaiming the precious word of God versus saying something good that also focuses on us looking good! It should ALWAYS be all about the gospel!

Continuing with the Apostle Paul speaking before King Agrippa:

4. AWAKEN: Try and awaken the listener from their normal pattern to an interest in the gospel.

Paul goes on to awaken the king to the reality of the power of the gospel. Listen as we hear how Paul’s going to be very blunt about who he was and what he did. We appreciate how the Bible shows the flaws and failures of the faithful, setting it apart from other historical records.

Acts 26:9-11: 9 So then, I thought to myself that I had to do many things hostile to the name of Jesus of Nazareth. 10 And this is just what I did in Jerusalem; not only did I lock up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, but also when they were being put to death I cast my vote against them. 11 And as I punished them often in all the synagogues, I tried to force them to blaspheme; and being furiously enraged at them, I kept pursuing them even to foreign cities.

We can imagine King Agrippa hearing Paul, who has been in prison for two years, speaking as a representative of Jesus, listening in amazement as Paul is recounts his persecution of Christians!

By confessing his own negative past, Paul is “awakening” King Agrippa. By hearing the story of Paul’s history unfold, he could better understand the magnitude of the absolute transformation of the apostle’s life, making him want to hear more!

We want to form authentic connections with those who are searching. We want to share how God’s grace has transformed us. People relate to real stories rather than abstract theological concepts.

Sometimes when we make mistakes or bad decisions, talking about them as we witness in the context of God’s grace can be an important way of awakening others.

5. TEACH, PREACH, REASON AND ENCOURAGE: Deliver the Good News with heart!

Paul went on to teach, beginning with his own transformational experience:

Acts 26:12-16: 12 While so engaged as I was journeying to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests, 13 at midday, O King, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining all around me and those who were journeying with me. 14 And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew dialect, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?... 15 And I said, Who are you, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. 16 But get up and stand on your feet; for this purpose I have appeared to you, to appoint you a minister and a witness not only to the things which you have seen, but also to the things in which I will appear to you.

This was an appearance of the resurrected Jesus as a spirit being—an eyewitness proof he had been raised from the dead. This was important because the original twelve apostles were appointed by Jesus, but Jesus was killed before Paul could physically meet him. (This lends credibility to Paul being the apostle to replace Judas.)

Such a story of events! Paul tells King Agrippa how opposed he was to Christianity and details some of the terrible things he did to Christians. He then tells Agrippa of the dramatic turnaround when he was literally stopped in his tracks while on the way to persecute Christians. Jesus himself told Paul to STOP persecuting Jesus’ followers, and to now do the work Jesus would give him to do.

Paul did not hide any of his misguided past so he could reveal his Christ-guided present! Paul was not afraid to present the drama of the tremendous change of his life and character.

He continued explaining his transformation, revealing the mission of his new life:

Acts 26:19-20: 19 So, King Agrippa, I did not prove disobedient to the heavenly vision, 20 but kept declaring both to those of Damascus first, and also at Jerusalem and then throughout all the region of Judea, and even to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds appropriate to repentance.

- Before his conversion, Paul was full of activity, actively persecuting Christians. He chased them down, punished them and imprisoned them—even getting permission from the priests to zealously continue. - After his conversion, Paul was full of activity, actively preaching Christianity. He did what the heavenly vision of Jesus told him to do—he kept declaring the message of Jesus to Damascus, Jerusalem and all through Judea, even unto the Gentiles. He wouldn’t stay quiet!

Through Christ, God took Paul’s natural abilities and turned them into godliness. King Agrippa was seeing how that darkness turned into incredible light.

Paul then brought everything back to the present circumstances of having to defend himself:

Acts 26:21-23: 21 For this reason some Jews seized me in the temple and tried to put me to death. 22 So, having obtained help from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great, stating nothing but what the prophets and Moses said was going to take place; 23 that the Christ was to suffer, and that by reason of his resurrection from the dead he would be the first to proclaim light both to the Jewish people and to the Gentiles.

Paul was defending his life but also able to tell a gripping true story that showed God’s leadings and God’s plan all at once.

If we are aware of what we were and where we came from, we can use our own fallibility and bad decisions to say that glory can come to God when we learn to walk away from such things. This was an effective way for Paul to present the gospel to King Agrippa.

Paul continues to brilliantly defend himself:

Acts 26:27-29: 27 King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you do.

This is a strategic question—remember, Herod Agrippa II is Jewish. If Agrippa answers yes, then he has to also consider the possibility that Jesus fulfills those prophecies and Paul is right.

28 Agrippa replied to Paul, In a short time you will persuade me to become a Christian. 29 And Paul said, I would wish to God, that whether in a short or long time, not only you, but also all who hear me this day, might become such as I am, except for these chains.

What a beautiful response! Paul was quick. He wanted Agrippa—and everyone—to be like him and embrace his faith in Christ, except for the being a prisoner part, of course!

Paul masterfully showed us how to TEACH, PREACH, REASON AND ENCOURAGE.

Matthew 5:14-16: 14 You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; 15 nor does anyone light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on the lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house. 16 Let your light shine before men in such a way that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

We are to let our light shine in such a way so as to draw others to who we are and what we stand for.

Fearfully and Wonderfully: The Marvel of Bearing God’s Image: “Compliancy, a word with special meaning to my engineering colleagues, is a meaningful word for both the physical body and the spiritual Body. Compliant tissues covering my bones assume the shape— awkward or smooth—of whatever I am grasping. I do not demand that the object fit the shape of my hand; my hand adapts, distributing the pressures. The art of Christian living, I believe, can be glimpsed in this concept of compliancy. As my shape moves into contact with other, foreign shapes, how does my skin respond? Whose personality adapts? Do I, as does my grasping hand, become square to those things that are square, round to those things that are round?”

This is 1 Corinthians 9:19-23 right in the palm of our hand! To the Jew, Paul was Jewish. To those not under the Law, he wasn’t under the Law. To the weak, he was weak. He became all things to all men for the sake of the gospel. He demonstrated compliancy in his witnessing. We need to learn to become the shape necessary to get the job done.

It is remarkable to read, think about and apply all that we are given so we can be better representatives of God’s plan.

We have just walked through a great example of preaching to those who may have a similar basis as our own. What about those who are totally opposite?

As we move forward, it is important to note that the same five steps we saw unfold will still apply, but now they will be built in a very different way. In our next example, our efforts to expand another’s thinking without offending them will require a large measure of self-restraint and wisdom.

Our second example of a non-Christian audience—both Gentiles and former Jews who has rejected all of what God’s favored people were given:

1 Corinthians 9:21: To those who are without law, as without law, though not being without the law of God but under the law of Christ, so that I might win those who are without law.

Here we see compliancy again. He was going to seek common ground in order for the gospel message to be heard. It’s important to note he would do this without violating his conscience.

If we’re going to witness to a drug dealer, we’re not going to do drugs with her in order to get her to identify with us. Paul didn’t worship idols in order to get the lifelong idol worshippers to listen to him. We do not become so compliant to the point of becoming that individual; instead we become compliant to the point of being able to reason with that individual.

As Paul traveled and preached, he came to the city of Athens, which happened to be a focal point of deep and abiding idolatry. How would he meet this massive and serious challenge?

1. RECOGNIZE: Seek to understand who it is that you are speaking to. Know your audience.

Apostle Paul and his experience leading up to and at Mars Hill:

Acts 17:16-17: 16 Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was being provoked within him as he was observing the city full of idols. 17 So he was reasoning in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearing Gentiles, and in the market place every day with those who happened to be present.

Paul’s spirit was provoked as he was observing this pagan city full of idols. The passion for truth burned within Paul as he talked in the synagogue and in the marketplace, speaking about Jesus and the resurrection to those who would listen.

Some who heard invited him to more broadly present the spiritual doctrine he was teaching on Mars Hill. Mars Hill is also known as the Areopagus. It is a rocky hill in Athens, Greece, that today is a popular tourist site but historically served as a court and meeting place for legal and philosophical discussions. To be invited to this area to speak to everyone was a big opportunity for Paul. The ancient Greeks loved a good debate and discussion!

2. RESPECT: Establish a common ground of respect, even if it has to be very basic.

Acts 17:22-23: 22 So Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, Men of Athens, I observe that you are very religious in all respects. 23 For while I was passing through and examining the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription, TO AN UNKNOWN GOD...

The Apostle Paul didn’t start by saying, “You are all fools because your idols are all nonsense!” Instead, he said, I observe that you are very religious in all respects. I see that you take your objects of worship very seriously. I also found an altar with this inscription, TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. He shows respect for their beliefs without endorsing them.

3. LISTEN: For us to be heard, we should be willing to listen with attentive conviction.

Here Paul shows his ability to listen: …Therefore what you worship in ignorance, this I proclaim to you.

Paul connects the dots: You’re religious. You have all these objects of worship, and one is set up as AN UNKNOWN GOD. Clearly, they aren’t sure about this one!

He found a way in, but the space between respect and perceived insult can be small. Wisdom and grace must be applied.

It would have been easy to insult them, but he phrased it in such a way that he showed RESPECT even as he was about to expand their thinking.

This is something to keep in mind for us today when sharing comments online. Christians should be the MOST respectful and the MOST kind, but sadly, this isn’t always the case.

4. AWAKEN: Try and awaken the listener from their normal pattern to an interest in the gospel.

Acts 17:24-31: 24 The God who made the world and all things in it, since He is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands; 25 nor is He served by human hands, as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives to all people life and breath and all things.

In explaining this UNKNOWN GOD, Paul was gently stretching their spiritual intellect, all while respecting their beliefs.

Why did Paul say God does not dwell in temples made with hands? Jehovah God WAS dwelling in the Temple in Jerusalem. He WAS served by human hands through the priest and high priest arrangement. What did Paul mean?

He was speaking to a Greek audience who worshipped gods and idols confined to physical temples. Paul emphasized that the true God is sovereign over all creation, not limited to a single location or dependent on human rituals. The Temple in Jerusalem was a symbol of God’s presence among the people. Worship of God isn’t restricted to a physical structure.

5. TEACH, PREACH, REASON AND ENCOURAGE: Deliver the Good News with heart: 26 And He made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth… 27 that they would seek God, if perhaps they might grope for Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us; 28 for in Him we live and move and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, For we also are His children.

Paul is expanding their understanding of God. He keeps their attention by throwing in a quote from one of their own writers while he weaves a beautiful tapestry of truth. Here is this unknown God. This is what you worship in ignorance. I’m explaining the magnitude of this God.

29 Being then the children of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of man. 30 Therefore having overlooked the times of ignorance, God is now declaring to men that all people everywhere should repent, 31 because He has fixed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness through a man whom He has appointed, having furnished proof to all men by raising him from the dead.

Now he gives this dramatic conclusion: this UNKNOWN GOD put His plan into place and proved it through the resurrection of Jesus. Paul has introduced a concept of God way beyond what they had ever before considered. Paul’s conclusions put the fundamental truths of the gospel right before them.

This serves as an important lesson for us. We want to start by getting the fundamentals out like Paul did. What are some of the fundamental truths of the gospel we want to share?

God’s plan was always in place:

Revelation 13:8: All who dwell on the earth will worship him, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the lamb who has been slain.

Jesus died for all:

1 John 2:2: And he himself is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world.

God’s kingdom will come to earth:

Isaiah 11:9: They will not hurt or destroy in all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

The gospel needs to be preached:

2 Timothy 4:2: Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with great patience and instruction.

If it’s convenient, be ready. If it’s inconvenient, be ready! It doesn’t matter—this is our job.

These are sound scriptural teachings. If nothing else, we want to ensure that we convey some of these fundamental truths to others when we are sharing the good news.

But we can’t get them to hear unless they are in a position to want to hear. How can we help with that? We go through the steps of RECOGNIZING who they are, RESPECTING them and their beliefs, and then surprising them, which AWAKENS them to hear a new truth and be drawn to it.

Paul is absolutely inspiring, to say the least. Reviewing what he did and how he did it is a great exercise to sharpen our awareness and skills.

In both of our examples so far, Paul’s tenacity was key in delivering the needed good news. How should we respond when our hearers are weak and struggling?

This still requires tenacity, but it here needs to be applied in a very different way. At Mars Hill, it was all about being respectful and giving a truthful presentation. When dealing with those who are weak and struggling, it’s all about having a base of deep compassion and patience upon which we can give a truthful presentation. We use the same steps, but applied in a different way.

Let’s continue with our third example of audiences to preach to.

Those who are weak and struggling, no matter their background:

1 Corinthians 9:22: To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak; I have become all things to all men, so that I may by all means save some.

Again, Paul was compliant and adaptable, but never compromising. He was willing to meet people where they were in order to be more effective, but he did not need to get down into the slime with them.

Sometimes the gospel needs to be revived in those who already believe. This was the case with Jesus reviving the faith of the two disciples on the Road to Emmaus, on the day of his resurrection.

How did Jesus share the gospel with those who already knew the gospel? They did know the gospel but were confused and afraid. They did not know what to do, where to go or how to act because their beloved Jesus had been crucified. They had been thrown into a whirlwind of doubt and bewilderment. So, Jesus witnessed the gospel to them, using the same principles and approach that works with those who do not yet have the gospel.

1. RECOGNIZE: Seek to understand who it is that you are speaking to. Know your audience.

Here we have two disciples discussing the events surrounding Jesus’ crucifixion:

Luke 24:13-17: 13 And behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was about seven miles from Jerusalem. 14 And they were talking with each other about all these things which had taken place. 15 While they were talking and discussing, Jesus himself approached and began traveling with them. 16 But their eyes were prevented from recognizing him.

Though they did not initially recognize Jesus, he came to them and made himself available. He RECOGNIZED who they were and where they were emotionally.

2. RESPECT: Establish a common ground of respect, even if it has to be very basic.

17 And he said to them, What are these words that you are exchanging with one another as you are walking?...

Jesus asked a simple question. He opened the door for them to vent their confusion and frustration. They were probably talking amongst themselves with no conclusion, no answer, certainly with no direction. And here, this stranger comes up and asks what they are talking about. Asking this question gave Jesus the opportunity to LISTEN.

3. LISTEN: For us to be heard, we should be willing to listen with attentive conviction.

Think about how he listened and absorbed all their frustration:

Luke 24:17-21: 17 …And they stood still, looking sad. 18 One of them, named Cleopas, answered and said to him, Are you the only one visiting Jerusalem and unaware of the things which have happened here in these days? 19 And he said to them, What things? And they said to him, The things about Jesus the Nazarene, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word in the sight of God and all the people, 20 and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him to the sentence of death, and crucified him. 21 But we were hoping that it was he who was going to redeem Israel...

They were heartbroken. They thought he was the Messiah they had been waiting for, the one who would lead them into a glorious new kingdom for Israel. And now it was all over—or so they thought. They had no explanation.

They poured their hearts out and further explained what the women had said about his being raised and the empty tomb. They were utterly confused.

4. AWAKEN: Try to awaken the listener from their normal pattern to an interest in the gospel.

At this point, the men were in a pattern of disbelief, confusion and fear:

Luke 24:25-26: 25 And he said to them, O foolish men and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! 26 Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?

He rebukes them gently for not believing the testimony of Scripture. Once they were done, Jesus got their attention with a dramatic statement and question. “Don’t you remember what has been written for ages and ages and generations?” Now they are awake—now the door is open, and he can teach them, preach to them and reason with them.

5. TEACH, PREACH, REASON AND ENCOURAGE: Deliver the Good News with heart!

Luke 24:27-33: 27 Then beginning with Moses and with all the prophets, he explained to them the things concerning himself in all the Scriptures. 28 And they approached the village where they were going, and he acted as though he were going farther. 29 But they urged him, saying, Stay with us, for it is getting toward evening, and the day is now nearly over. So he went in to stay with them. 30 When he had reclined at the table with them, he took the bread and blessed it, and breaking it, he began giving it to them. 31 Then their eyes were opened and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight. 32 They said to one another, Were not our hearts burning within us while he was speaking to us on the road, while he was explaining the Scriptures to us? 33 And they got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem…

It was getting late. The men want this stranger to stay and eat with them because there is something about this man that is feeding the healing of their emotional wounds. As soon as they recognize him, he vanishes!

They are so excited that they immediately turn around and walk the seven miles back to Jerusalem!

Can we imagine, just for a second, how amazing it would be for Jesus himself to teach us all the connections of Scripture?

Fearfully and Wonderfully: The Marvel of Bearing God’s Image. “Though we live among others who may not share our beliefs and values, we have the clear example of Jesus, who found acceptance among physical and moral outcasts as well as despised minorities and Roman officers. Somehow he moved compliantly among diverse groups without compromising his good-news message of love and forgiveness.”

We can see this in action. Sharing the gospel with those who are already believers, using these same principles, is just as effective with those who are not believers. Enter into their

difficulty, struggle, strife and trauma. Then, walk with them and become trustworthy, giving them something to rely upon. The power of the gospel truth to reset our troubled minds is immeasurable!

The truth, encouragement and hope of the gospel needs to be shared:

Matthew 9:35-38: 35 Jesus was going through all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every kind of disease and every kind of sickness. 36 Seeing the people, he felt compassion for them, because they were distressed and dispirited like sheep without a shepherd. 37 Then he said to his disciples, The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. 38 Therefore beseech the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.

Send out workers into his harvest—share the gospel. Not only are we told to go share the gospel, we are told how to do it.

We are told about the concept of compliancy, of gathering ourselves into a position where we can be molded toward the individuals we are witnessing to. We find common ground to build upon, so that we can show them something utterly remarkable.

We are truly fearfully and wonderfully made! (Psalm 139:14) We are an amazing design— now, every time we look at the palm of our hands, think of this “sharing the gospel” lesson. It’s that combination of strength and pliability. Conforming without strength is weak. Strength without conforming destroys.

When we ask the question, How do we share the gospel with others? What do we do? How do we act? How do we think? Where do we go? It comes down to these simple five principles:

- RECOGNIZE who it is you have the opportunity to speak to.
- RESPECT them. Find some common ground to relate to them.
- LISTEN with the attentiveness that says, “I want to know who you are and where you are coming from.”
- AWAKEN them to something they may never have thought of.
- TEACH, PREACH, REASON AND ENCOURAGE. Open their hearts and minds because the gospel news is for everyone.

This is good news for all people because Jesus died for every human being. Share the message!

So, how can I best share the gospel with others?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!
