## Episode 1397 — What Does It Mean to Have Faith as a Mustard Seed?
Published: 2025-08-11
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1397-mustard-seed/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/08150603/CQ_Rewind_08-11-2025_What_Does_It_Mean_to_Have_Faith_as_a_Mustard_Seed.pdf

Luke 17:5–6: 5 The apostles said to the Lord, Increase our faith! 6 And the Lord said, If you had faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, Be uprooted and be planted in the sea; and it would obey you.

As Christians who are to walk by faith and not by sight, the statements Jesus made about having faith as a mustard seed sure are appealing. In Luke, Jesus says having faith like a mustard seed can uproot a tree and toss it into the sea! In Matthew, he said mustard seed faith can move a mountain and make nothing impossible for us. So, what did Jesus mean? Obviously he was using picture language, but he was still showing us that mustard seed faith can dramatically change our lives. Why a mustard seed and how does this work? What do we need to do to have such a strong and foundational faith that the obstacles of our lives will be diminished before us?’

Most Christians will say this means we can do great things with just a tiny amount of faith. It’s all about how small the seed is, just like how the gospel itself grew from a tiny beginning. Jesus referenced a mustard seed, after all, not an acorn. What more is there to say?

Quite a bit! It really isn’t all about how small the mustard seed is—that’s part of it, but as we will see, it’s not the main point. Let’s look closer.

Jesus uses this faith like a mustard seed phrase in two different places.

Let’s begin with context:

Luke 17:1–4: 1 He said to his disciples, It is inevitable that stumbling blocks come, but woe to him through whom they come! 2 It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea, than that he would cause one of these little ones to stumble. 3 Be on your guard! If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. 4 And if he sins against you seven times a day, and returns to you seven times, saying, I repent, forgive him.

This would have been alarming for his disciples to hear!

We have to be self-aware, not a stumbling block for others or the source of someone’s temptation. And we are to forgive abundantly, as Jesus explains (if your brother sins against you seven times a day… forgive him). It’s not easy following Jesus!

Jesus was showing them the hard realities of the responsibilities and actions their discipleship would require. He was teaching them hard things, and it was unsettling.

Their response? They directly asked Jesus to increase their faith:

Luke 17:5–6: 5 The apostles said to the Lord, Increase our faith! 6 And the Lord said, If you had faith ...as small as a mustard seed… WAIT! That’s not what he said, but it’s what a lot of us seem to remember.

He actually said: If you had faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, Be uprooted and be planted in the sea; and it would obey you.

Jesus’ analogy compares faith like or as a mustard seed; not “as small as” a mustard seed. It’s all about what it can do despite its size.

The seed’s size is not the main lesson. Rather, faith has the potential to grow, just like the mustard seed has the potential to grow into a mustard plant.

Let’s consider the mulberry tree in the analogy. Mulberry trees are known for their extensive root systems, making them notoriously hard to remove. And of course, trees don’t grow in saltwater, so being planted in the sea is absurd and obviously picture language.

To pull up a mulberry tree would be very difficult. Jesus is using this mustard seed analogy for something dramatic.

In another parable, Jesus reveals WHY this mustard seed illustration is so powerful. It is not about just the size; it is about what the seed can do:

Matthew 13:31–32: 31 He presented another parable to them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field; 32 and this is smaller than all other seeds, but when it is full grown, it is larger than the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.

The mustard seed was the tiniest of seeds planted in Jesus’ day, and some mustard plants can reach 6 to 20 feet tall. When the apostles asked Jesus to increase our faith, he responded with the mustard seed analogy, implying that even a tiny measure of true faith can accomplish great things.

So perhaps a good, foundational mustard seed thought is:

It’s not about the size of our faith but the substance of what our faith can produce— the quality and potential for growth.

This is faith with the potential of—not “as small as.” Jesus used the mustard seed in this example because of its dramatic potential for growth.

Jesus also used the example of a mustard seed in Matthew 17 when he removed the mental health malady from a boy whose desperate father begged for help. We covered this in great detail in Episode 1356: “Are There Different Kinds of Evil Spirits?” The account is in Matthew 17, Mark 9 and Luke 9.

Here are a few excerpts to put the context in place:

Luke 9:40: I begged your disciples to cast it out… Matthew 17:16: …and they could not cure him. Mark 9:19: And he answered them and said, O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I put up with you? Bring him to me! Luke 9:41: …bring your son here.

Jesus walked into this very volatile situation. This father was beside himself with grief, and nobody could help.

They brought the boy to Jesus, and he gathered more background and personal information:

Mark 9:22–24: 22 It has often thrown him both into the fire and into the water to destroy him. But if you can do anything, take pity on us and help us! 23 And Jesus said to him, IF you can? All things are possible to him who believes. 24 Immediately the boy’s father cried out and said, I do believe; help my unbelief.

The father believes enough to bring the boy to Jesus, but he doubts anything can be done, especially after the disciples have failed to heal him. We could say his faith at this point was incomplete.

Jesus was opening the door for him to understand that there’s something broader in which this faith can begin to develop. He uses this incident to introduce the idea that great trauma can cause the growth of great faith.

The account concludes with a lesson on the power of faith and prayer. Jesus heals the boy:

Matthew 17:20: And he said to them, Because of the littleness of your faith; for truly I say to you, if you have faith the size <2848> of a mustard seed <4615>, you will say to this mountain, Move from here to there, and it will move; and nothing will be impossible to you. Mark 9:29: This kind cannot come out by anything but prayer.

Mustard Seed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4615 sínapi; perhaps from sínomai (to hurt, i.e. sting); mustard (the plant):—mustard

With the first mustard seed of faith reference, we could symbolically uproot a mulberry tree and plant it in the sea. With this second mustard seed reference—if you have faith the size of a mustard seed—we can move a mountain! This is a powerful seed! But is the main point about the size of as stated here in Matthew 17:20, or is it the potential for growth, as we have been saying?

Here is the problem: several translations (like the NASB95 above) use size for the Greek word kókkos.

Size: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2848 kókkos; apparently a primary word; a kernel of seed:—corn, grain

But the word translated size here means a kernel or grain.

For example, the King James Version we believe correctly translates this as faith as a grain of mustard seed. A single grain of mustard seed IS the seed. So, it is not only about the size, even though size does play a part.

Think about this. How many grains of sand are there in the world? Hundreds of trillions? A mustard seed is about the size of a grain of sand. Jesus did not say, if you have faith as a grain of sand… though that could be a very dramatic picture of tiny faith. Instead he said, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed.

Why? Because that tiny little seed has potential. A grain of sand is not going to grow into anything else and will remain as a grain of sand. Faith as a grain of mustard seed can grow into something much different. This is the lesson! We miss its depth if we limit the meaning to the size of the mustard seed only. The lesson is really about a small faith with great potential.

We do not want faith as a grain of sand. We want faith as a grain of mustard seed because that is where the potential is.

The whole point here is that our faith should not be the same today as it was yesterday. It needs to grow, change and mature!

The frantic cry for help of the mentally ill child’s father speaks volumes. What can we learn from Lord I believe, help my unbelief?

Our lessons here are many, and they apply to several different aspects of how our faith works. As we open up the growth lessons of “mustard seed faith,” we need to accept that it always begins as little faith. We must realize that our little faith needs to grow into a mature and life-altering foundation upon which we can build a powerful, guiding and implicit trust in God through Jesus.

When we say little faith, we think of how Jesus used the phrase, you of little faith (ye of little faith in the King James Version) four times. This is comprised of two Greek words together meaning “lacking confidence,” “trusting too little.”

Little faith: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3640 oligopistos; from #3641 and #4102; incredulous, i.e. lacking confidence

#3641 olígos (puny) + #4102 pistis (persuasion, i.e. credence; moral conviction)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: of little faith, trusting too little

But it’s all about putting our faith in the right things. Mustard seed faith may not be entirely sure of itself but can expand in the right direction. Believing in the wrong things won’t bring us in the right direction.

Think about Elijah going against the 450 priests of Baal in 1 Kings 18. Those priests had great faith, but in a false god. They made a big show of faith in something that wasn’t real. Elijah stood alone and allowed the one true God to act.

In the four times Jesus used this phrase, you of little faith, we can trace the experiences necessary for us to develop a mustard seed faith upon which a Christlike life can be built. We will find a fascinating progressive lesson of faith growing and expanding in chronological order.

REALIZE THE MAGNITUDE OF WHAT OUR “MUSTARD SEED FAITH” IS BASED ON.

Jesus first said men of little faith when calming the stormy sea. The account of this is found in Matthew 8:23–27, Mark 4:36–41 and Luke 8:22–25.

Up to this experience, Jesus had taught and healed as his Father had directed him.

This event would break new ground, as Jesus was about to show them the power of God’s spirit in a whole new way:

Matthew 8:24–26: 24 And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being covered with the waves; but Jesus himself was asleep. 25 And they came to him and woke him, saying, Save us, Lord; we are perishing! 26 He said to them, Why are you afraid, you men of little faith <3640>?...

Again, this is faith that lacks confidence, but it has potential—it’s aimed in the right direction.

Jesus is essentially saying, I’m in the boat! What could you possibly be worried about?

It is interesting when we combine all three accounts in the gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke. Jesus talks about faith twice; before he calms the storm and then after. This is the “before”:

He asks, Why are you afraid, you men of little faith? He puts them into a place of thought in the middle of all of this before he does a single thing about the storm raging around them.

In the depths of the storm, Jesus challenged his disciples regarding their faith. Why? They were frightened for their lives, and the only one who could possibly protect them was asleep! They cried out, Save us, Lord; we are perishing! They turned to Jesus to save them. They were afraid. But he was in the boat! Why were they so worried? It’s easy for us to say!

MAGNITUDE: Little faith sees the magnitude of the experience and knows but does not yet trust the solution. It’s like the father in Mark 9:24 who said, I do believe; help my unbelief.

The disciples knew who to turn to: Lord, save us lest we perish. They knew the answer was Jesus, but while caught in the violent storm, they were not yet ready to trust in the sea. That is mustard seed faith.

Mark 4:39–41: (KJV) 39 And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. 40 And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? How is it that ye have no faith? 41 And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

It sounds like they were still learning the extent of the power God gave Jesus. They didn’t yet understand its magnitude—how limitless and comprehensive it is.

Jesus had demonstrated the magnitude of his power through God. The disciples had just witnessed it, but the meaning had not yet sunk in. Jesus’ lesson was clear: in his presence, there was nothing to fear, even from the arising of a great storm.

Before he calmed the storm, his message was to rise above fear: Why are you afraid, you men of little faith?

After calming the storm, Jesus’ message was, Why are ye so fearful? How is it that ye have no faith? He provided physical verification that they were in the company of God’s chosen one. They personally experienced the wind ceasing and a great calm. They realized they were in the company of the one who, by God’s grace, COULD calm the storm!

In other words, “God’s got this” through His son Jesus. Their faith was aimed in the right direction. They went to the right place by waking Jesus. It’s not like they were praying to idols for deliverance! They just did not yet know how to develop that faith.

Jesus’ message for them and us: realize the magnitude of who and what we believe in! You of little faith was a big, introductory message for them and us.

Jesus himself had to feel and believe in the magnitude of God’s providence for his own experiences. He had to learn a type of faith he would not have needed when he was still in heaven with the Father, before he came to earth.

This is a wonderful and powerful example of Jesus leaning on the magnitude of God’s power and deliverance for him:

Matthew 26:38–39: 38 Then he said to them, My soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death; remain here and keep watch with me. 39 And he went a little beyond them, and fell on his face and prayed, saying, my Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as You will.

Jesus himself had to claim the magnitude of what he had faith in—God’s overruling power on his behalf. When he asks, Let this cup pass from me, God’s answer was no. This is where Jesus’ magnitude of faith came in, and he marched forward in spite of the answer.

In four different examples, Jesus unfolds the lesson of you of little faith. He learned these lessons, put them into his heart and understood the necessity of growth.

Our Christian faith has an established standard of action for us to acknowledge and follow in our daily experiences:

Jude 1:3: Beloved, while I was making every effort to write you about our common salvation, I felt the necessity to write to you appealing that you contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all handed down to the saints.

Jude wants to write a letter of encouragement, but he feels like he can’t do that because too many difficult things are going on. So, he writes about earnestly contending for the faith that was originally delivered to the saints. This is a struggle, and Jude wants them to contend with (fight to overcome) it.

This struggle implies a GREAT obstacle or challenge that requires a GREAT core effort right from the heart with GREAT resiliency. Life’s storms give us the opportunity to develop the magnitude of our mustard seed faith! Our experiences reveal that potential.

Jesus allowed his disciples to feel the fear of the storm’s destruction and then to see their deliverance. Their faith in Jesus and the heavenly Father is building this faith structure in their hearts and minds. He could have stopped the storm before it started, but that would not have helped the disciples grow in faith.

Our little mustard seed faith has the potential for massive growth because it is based on the right things. It is not based on something foolish or silly. It is based on the foundation of God and His son Jesus. The utter magnitude of what our mustard seed faith is based upon is overwhelming. We are called to follow Jesus to do the will of the Creator of the universe!

The drama of Jesus calming the storm is breathtaking. In what other areas of our lives does Jesus show us how mustard seed faith develops?

As we would expect, Jesus’ teachings about the growth of mustard seed faith are comprehensive. With the magnitude of calming a stormy and life-threatening sea as a backdrop, we will now look at the second time Jesus talked about his followers as those of little faith.

This next example is VERY different but no less vital.

REALIZE THE PERSONAL PRACTICALITY OUR MUSTARD SEED FAITH IS BASED ON.

Let’s talk about the teaching about anxiety in the Sermon on the Mount (also quoted in Luke 12):

Matthew 6:27–33: 27 And who of you by being worried can add a single hour to his life? 28 And why are you worried about clothing? Observe how the lilies of the field grow; they do not toil nor do they spin, 29 yet I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory clothed himself like one of these. 30 But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is alive today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, will He not much more clothe you? You of little faith <3640>!

Again, little faith—having faith but lacking confidence.

31 Do not worry then, saying, What will we eat? or What will we drink? or What will we wear for clothing? 32 For the Gentiles eagerly seek all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. 33 But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

The lessons from Matthew 6 in the Sermon on the Mount about anxiety remind us how life is filled with it. Any aspect of our lives can, at some point, cause anxiety.

Jesus says we must realize our mustard seed faith’s potential and let it sprout and grow based on the most important things:

Matthew 6:33: …Seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

Our personal, practical and daily experiences can readily cause us internal anxiety. Even though these verses tell us, Do not worry, we worry anyway. Our mustard seed faith cannot be built upon the ever–shifting circumstances of life; rather, it must be built upon the personal and practical knowledge of God’s providence on our behalf.

We are his children. He is our Father. We can have faith He will provide for us because that is what a good father does.

Faith with confidence instead of anxiety reminds us of the Apostle Paul in Philippians 4:12: (NLT) I know how to live on almost nothing or with everything. I have learned the secret of living in every situation, whether it is with a full stomach or empty, with plenty or little. His circumstances didn’t matter; he stayed afloat no matter what storm of stress was around him.

We are assured God provides exactly what is needed for our highest spiritual welfare. But, do we believe it? I believe; help my unbelief.

The key is that we believe, and our belief (because it is based on the right foundation) carries the magnitude of what we believe in. Our personal practicality, dealing with our practical everyday lessons, grows from our faith in the magnitude of God’s power and His care for us.

James shows us the practicality of mustard seed faith when we are being tested:

James 1:2–6: 2 Consider it all joy, my brethren, when you encounter various trials, 3 knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance. 4 And let endurance have its perfect result, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

Faith can and should be tested. Testing is necessary because faith must become our foundation. Meeting those tests is the basis from which the practicality of our faith grows—like a mustard seed.

5 But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

Asking for wisdom is another practical method of developing mustard seed faith. Notice the scripture does not say to go to the local bookstore for books on knowledge and wisdom. It says to ask of God. Go to the source that provides the foundation on which our mustard seed faith’s potential can grow.

6 But he must ask in faith without any doubting, for the one who doubts is like the surf of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.

Isn’t this an interesting use of words, after we have already seen Jesus literally calm the wind and storm!

Here we see the struggle of applying our personal practicality. This is a battle between self and spirituality. We can think we are pretty strong and smart, and maybe we can figure out this problem. This is not so good—our mustard seed faith is NOT based on our own potential. It is based on Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:27). This is something much bigger than us. We have to put “self” aside.

“Drain the anxiety out of the tub” is an expression that reminds us of the disciples’ boat about to sink—it’s the same message of safety. We can have assurance because of what our faith is based on—faith aimed in the right direction, rather than fearing the water will drown us.

Mirror lesson: How has the MAGNITUDE of what I see driving my faith taken on PERSONAL PRACTICALITY into changing my life? Our faith in God through Christ is what brings us to life-changing circumstances.

REALIZE THE COMPASSIONATE PERSONAL DELIVERANCE THAT OUR MUSTARD SEED FAITH BRINGS US.

This third illustration brings us again to a practical, everyday lesson, but with “deliverance” attached. When we are delivered from something, we are taken out of or lifted up from the experience.

The third example of you of little faith has to do with an experience Peter had.

It was night. The disciples were in the boat being battered by the wind and waves when they saw Jesus walking on the water:

Matthew 14:26–29: 26 When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, It is a ghost! And they cried out in fear. 27 But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, Take courage, it is I; do not be afraid. 28 Peter said to him, Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water. 29 And he said, Come! And Peter got out of the boat, and walked on the water and came toward Jesus.

How dramatic! But at least Peter stepped up and stepped out in faith to do what should have been impossible—kind of like planting a mulberry tree in the ocean or moving a mountain. None of the others are said to have even considered this.

Let us appreciate Peter’s growth from the first time they were battling wind and waves when Jesus slept. He was willing to step out of the boat and trust Jesus because he had learned that lesson from the first storm.

Peter knew the magnitude of Jesus’ position and God’s power!

Matthew 14:30–33: 30 But seeing the wind, he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, Lord, save me! 31 Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and took hold of him, and said to him, You of little faith <3640>, why did you doubt?

Doubt is a tool used by Satan to hinder our progress and growth in Christ.

Other than having momentary doubt and a subsequent sinking, Peter’s initial faith was strong enough to attempt the impossible, but he momentarily lost his focus.

Was Jesus disappointed in Peter, chastising his small faith, or was he actually encouraging Peter?

We don’t see this as a chastisement at all; he did get out of the boat. We understand Jesus to be saying:

o You came so far, then you allowed the distraction of what you were coming through to get in front of you.

o What was in front of you when you stepped out of the boat? Just me.

o What got in front of you? The wind and the waves.

o You will grow bigger and stronger in faith; just keep your eyes on me.

This was a lesson in potential!

32 When they got into the boat, the wind stopped. 33 And those who were in the boat worshiped him, saying, You are certainly God’s son!

The disciples unequivocally knew Jesus was God’s son at this point!

Peter DID have faith as he DID walk on water. His faith HAD grown; it just needed to grow even stronger. This is the process. That is why Jesus says you of little faith four different times. He is showing us the process, the steps we need to take so our faith can grow higher and stronger.

Peter’s faith was being tested in a very individual way here, so he would begin to appreciate the compassionate personal deliverance of mustard seed faith. If Jesus had wanted to chastise him, he could have thought, Well, let him take a few mouthfuls of water. But he didn’t. He reached out his hand and pulled Peter up because it was a compassionate personal deliverance—a reward for stepping out and working on developing his faith.

Our compassionate personal deliverances are also tested by our figuratively leaving the boat to walk to Jesus:

Philippians 3:7–9: 7 But whatever things were gain to me, those things I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. 8 More than that, I count all things to be loss in view of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them but rubbish so that I may gain Christ, 9 and may be found in him, not having a

righteousness of my own derived from the Law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which comes from God on the basis of faith.

Let’s compare this to the mustard seed. Both challenge us to trust beyond appearances. This is a matter of size versus substance: small faith has potential to grow into much greater spirituality, and here in Philippians, the Apostle Paul assures us that great loss has the potential to lead to great gain.

It is not faith as a grain of sand; it is faith as a grain of mustard seed, with potential for great growth because it is focused on the right things.

Sometimes we are pulled through that experience with a LOT of help. But it encourages us to develop our existing faith into something much larger and unwavering. It is because of the potential within the seed. God’s spirit is working in us, and therefore, the potential for growth is within that seed.

The concept of mustard seed faith is becoming clearer. It shows us that we are provided for in every area of our Christian lives!

Jesus has thus far taught us about the magnificent foundation of our faith as well as the practicality and deliverance it brings. What’s next?

Jesus’ final use of you of little faith comes in what appears to be a much simpler and far less dramatic context. However, looks can be deceiving! As we will see, this last application of mustard seed faith is the one that essentially carries us all the way home! It may not look as dramatic, but it is very significant.

REALIZE THE SPIRITUAL NURTURING AND GUIDANCE OUR MUSTARD SEED FAITH BRINGS US.

Jesus’ final you of little faith lesson comes from the disciples’ frequent misunderstanding of what Jesus was saying.

He uses their lack of comprehension to teach them many times:

Matthew 16:5–8: 5 And the disciples came to the other side of the sea, but they had forgotten to bring any bread. 6 And Jesus said to them, Watch out and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. 7 They began to discuss this among themselves, saying, He said that because we did not bring any bread.

Leaven is the rising agent (like yeast) in bread. These poor disciples, always thinking about food! Here is the disconnect—Jesus says, Watch out and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees (avoid the false teachings and just stay with my teachings). The disciples reply with, Ugh, he’s right! We forgot the bread!

They didn’t have that spiritual discernment he expected them to have by this point.

Well, let’s see how Jesus answered them: 8 But Jesus, aware of this, said, You men of little faith <3640>, why do you discuss among yourselves that you have no bread?

Jesus was elevating their thoughts—bringing them to the most important things. He was bringing them up to a level where their faith could be developed—not to fill their stomachs, but to fill their hearts and minds with the development of a true faith.

The lesson was simple: Stop dwelling on your physical life and needs and learn to dwell first and foremost on the narrow, spiritual path before you. You follow me. You must walk where I walk.

As we follow Jesus, we learn to develop that mustard seed faith and see and grasp the spiritual nurturing and guidance that comes to us as we follow in his footsteps.

Matthew 16:9–12: 9 Do you not yet understand or remember the five loaves of the five thousand, and how many baskets full you picked up? 10 Or the seven loaves of the four thousand, and how many large baskets full you picked up? 11 How is it that you do not understand that I did not speak to you concerning bread? But beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. 12 Then they understood that he did not say to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

So, Jesus didn’t mean literal bread. Leaven in the Bible often symbolizes sin. Jesus clarified that he was referring to the teachings of these religious groups.

Therefore, the leaven of the Pharisees symbolizes their corrupt or misguided teachings and, by extension, their hypocritical and unrighteous influence.

This was spiritual, nurturing guidance, right before them. That was what they were there to develop—not to fill their stomachs! He had done that for them already by feeding them and the multitudes. Do you not…remember the five loaves…or the seven loaves..? Plus all the leftovers!

But the most important thing is to walk in the footsteps of Jesus and be spiritually nurtured and spiritually guided every step of the way. This is what mustard seed faith is there for. That is the potential mustard seed faith has. This spiritual nurturing and guidance is, once again, a very personal lesson to help us grow our mustard seed faith.

After studying this topic, I now have started to think habitually of mustard seed faith. It helps remind me of the great potential waiting to be watered and cultivated so it can grow.

Based on his own experiences and the leading of God’s spirit, Peter helps us see this spiritual nurturing and guidance more clearly. It’s wonderful to see Peter as the voice of reason after he’s spiritually grown and matured, since he had denied Jesus three times in the recent past.

2 Peter 1:2–4: 2 Grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord; 3 seeing that His divine power has granted to us everything pertaining to life and godliness, through the true knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. 4 For by these He has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises, so that by them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world by lust.

These precious and magnificent promises are the plant food and the water necessary to reach the full potential of the seed. Mustard seed faith is fed by God’s grace, peace and promises.

With this feeding, it is expected to blossom into a fruitful Christian life:

2 Peter 1:5–9: 5 Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love. 8 For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they render you neither useless nor unfruitful in the true knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 For he who lacks these qualities is blind or short-sighted, having forgotten his purification from his former sins.

We see the growth process here, in your faith supply moral excellence…knowledge…self- control…perseverance…godliness…brotherly kindness…love. It goes up and up.

Our job is to grow up in Christ, and this is how we achieve that growth.

The spiritual nurturing and guidance of our mustard seed faith grows in increments, step- by-step. It’s not just claiming the name of Jesus and being saved. No, claiming the name of Jesus is only the beginning of the growth and transformation of this mustard seed faith in our lives.

Originally when putting this study together, we thought these next texts would be good to end with. After looking closer, we realized they clearly mirror our four you of little faith lessons.

Each part of the scripture brings us to another piece of the lesson:

Philippians 4:4–9: 4 Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice! 5 Let your gentle spirit be known to all men. The Lord is near.

Jesus is near, just like he was in the boat.

REALIZE THE MAGNITUDE OF WHAT OUR MUSTARD SEED FAITH IS BASED ON.

We don’t have to be afraid because our Lord is near. Remember when Jesus ascended to the Father, he said to his disciples, Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. The magnitude of the basis of our faith is always right there.

6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.

We talked about managing our daily anxieties. We want faith with confidence. Drain the anxiety out of the tub!

REALIZE THE PERSONAL PRACTICALITY OUR MUSTARD SEED FAITH IS BASED ON.

Feel the personal practicality of God providing for you each and every step! It takes away our anxiety, which can then be put aside—it ceases to be the centerpiece of our lives as we grow in Christ.

7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Jesus reached into the water to pull Peter out, saying, O, you of little faith. He encouraged him that there was no reason to doubt. He just needed to stay focused on Jesus.

The peace of God surpasses all comprehension. Peter is going under, and the peace of God through Christ pulls him up and rescues him.

REALIZE THE COMPASSIONATE PERSONAL DELIVERANCE THAT OUR MUSTARD SEED FAITH BRINGS US.

We need to grab hold of it, remember it and live through it when we go from experience to experience.

8 Finally, brethren, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is of good repute, if there is any excellence and if anything worthy of praise, dwell on these things. 9 The things you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.

The disciples didn’t immediately understand what Jesus meant about the leaven of the Pharisees. In fact, they had a lot to figure out, but they didn’t give up or give in. They completely transformed their lives by the grace of God and the power of the holy spirit.

REALIZE THE SPIRITUAL NURTURING AND GUIDANCE OUR MUSTARD SEED FAITH BRINGS US.

Again, these verses show us the building process: whatever is true…honorable…right…pure …lovely…good repute, if there is any excellence and if anything worthy of praise, dwell on these things. This is what our mustard seed faith develops. This is the spiritual nurturing and guidance that puts us in a position to be able to grow.

Spiritual nurturing and guidance transforms us from what we were and makes us what we can be. That is what this experience of mustard seed faith is all about.

What does it mean to have faith as a mustard seed? It is not about being tiny; it is about having potential that comes from what we believe in. It grows through the practicality of dealing with our life experiences. It grows through the compassionate personal deliverances that God, through Christ, brings us. And it grows consistently through our lives through the spiritual nurturing and guidance that comes our way so we can walk in Jesus’ footsteps and be faithful unto death.

So, what does it mean to have faith as a mustard seed?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

More about faith Faith throughout the entire New Testament is always from the same Greek word:

Faith: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4102 pistis; persuasion, credence, conviction. Reliance (especially upon Christ for salvation) constancy (in such profession). (By extension the system of religious) truth.

Persuasion, credence, conviction and reliance are internal decisions we make when we observe the evidence needed to commit ourselves to an approach or cause. This is an internal process and is an absolute Christian necessity!

Christian faith requires much more than an intellectual and emotional recognition of something; it requires action:

Hebrews 11:6: (KJV) But without faith <4102> it is impossible to please Him: for he that cometh to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him.

Christian faith has an established standard of action for us to acknowledge and follow:

Jude 1:3: (KJV) Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith <4102> which was once delivered unto the saints.

We have a clear heritage of the true gospel and those who were tasked with its care and expansion.

In the following examples of the faithful in Hebrews 11, we focus on the way these people lived, how they acted or did not act as an expression of faith:

Abel:

Hebrews 11:4: By faith <4102> Abel offered to God a better sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained the testimony that he was righteous, God testifying about his gifts, and through faith <4102>, though he is dead, he still speaks.

Abel loved God and lived in righteousness.

This was shown by God’s own testimony and his appropriate sacrifice which was modeled after God’s sacrifice to clothe his parents after their sin:

Genesis 3:20–21: 20 Now the man called his wife’s name Eve, because she was the mother of all the living. 21 The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.

We know very little about Abel:

Genesis 4:1–4: 1 Now the man had relations with his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain, and she said, I have gotten a manchild with the help of the LORD. 2 Again, she gave birth to his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of flocks, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. 3 So it came about in the course of time that Cain brought an offering to the LORD of the fruit of the ground. 4 Abel, on his part also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD had regard for Abel and for his offering;

Both Genesis and Hebrews point to Abel’s “life of faith” as the result of his righteous dedication to God. NO drama, just righteous obedience.

Enoch:

Hebrews 11:5: By faith <4102> Enoch was taken up so that he would not see death; AND HE WAS NOT FOUND BECAUSE GOD TOOK HIM UP; for he obtained the witness that before his being taken up he was pleasing to God.

Not see death could mean he either never saw anyone die, or that he (in his young age of 365 years) did not see any signs of death coming to him. Either way, we see God’s grace in his life and the plain fact that he was pleasing to God.

Noah:

Hebrews 11:7: By faith <4102> Noah, being warned by God about things not yet seen, in reverence prepared an ark for the salvation of his household, by which he condemned the world, and became an heir of the righteousness which is according to faith.

Noah was already faithful! The reverence of his conviction that God was guiding him gave him the strength and focus to build the ark.

Abraham:

Hebrews 11:8–10: 8 By faith <4102> Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going. 9 By faith <4102> he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise; 10 for he was looking for the city which has foundations, whose architect and builder is God.

Abraham’s life of faith was exemplified by his willingness to leave his father’s heathen household and follow an unseen God to an unknown location.

Abraham’s works of faith were built upon his life of faith:

James 2:21–24: 21 Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up Isaac his son on the altar? 22 You see that faith <4102> was working with his works, and as a result of the works, faith <4102> was perfected; 23 and the Scripture was fulfilled which says, AND ABRAHAM BELIEVED GOD, AND IT WAS RECKONED TO HIM AS RIGHTEOUSNESS, and he was called the friend of God. 24 You see that a man is justified by works and not by faith <4102> alone.

Again, we see the need to believe in God here and now and also as One who will act in the future.

b. recognize the PERSONAL PRACTICALITY of dealing with our growth experiences?

## Episode 1398 — How Do We Genuinely Appreciate Those Who Guide Us? (Christian Conduct Series)
Published: 2025-08-18
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1398-spiritual-leaders/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/16175559/CQ_Rewind_08-18-2025_How_Do_We_Genuinely_Appreciate_Those_Who_Guide_Us-1.pdf

How Do We Genuinely Appreciate Those Who Guide Us? (Christian Conduct Series)

1 Thessalonians 5:12: But we request of you, brethren, that you appreciate those who diligently labor among you, and have charge over you in the Lord and give you instruction.

Christians are supposed to live lives that reflect godliness every day and in every way. This is not only difficult, but also frankly looked down upon. Because our world is driven by technology and social media, we are daily saturated with images, commentary, suggestions and pressure to stand for ourselves with pride and conviction. To stand as one subservient to God through Christ and to be guided by the Bible (which to many is misguided, ancient and outdated) is seen as a useless and even dangerous way of life. So, what do we do? How do we stand firmly and confidently as disciples of Christ? It begins with the biblical principles we claim to hold as sound and true.

This episode will be the first of a multiple-part series that examines what our Christian conduct should be, as explained by the Apostle Paul in his first letter to the Thessalonian church.

To answer how we can genuinely appreciate those who guide us:

1. We will define what true leaders in God’s true church look like and what they are responsible for.

2. We will look at Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians and trace his own behavior as a model for how our spiritual guides should be acting so we can learn how to appreciate them.

First and foremost, Christian leadership is to be humble:

John 13:14: If I then, the Lord and the teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet.

It is simple—we are to serve.

Secondly, Christian leadership is to be founded on good character and integrity in all areas of life, all the time:

Titus 1:5-9: (Paul writes) 5 …appoint elders in every city as I directed you, 6 namely, if any man is above reproach, the husband of one wife, having children who believe, not accused of dissipation or rebellion. 7 For the overseer must be above reproach as God's steward, not self- willed, not quick-tempered, not addicted to wine, not pugnacious, not fond of sordid gain, 8 but hospitable, loving what is good, sensible, just, devout, self-controlled, 9 holding fast the faithful word which is in accordance with the teaching, so that he will be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict.

What a comprehensive list! It touches every aspect of an individual’s life.

These character requirements are essential in a Christian leader, as is fidelity to the gospel. So that he will be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict— it’s not just about being good and standing with high integrity. It is about doing these in the context of knowing God’s word.

What did leadership in the early church look like?

The early church did not have an organization to assign or train a hierarchy of elders, bishops/overseers or pastors/shepherds.

These titles are various ways of describing any individual who is given responsibility for Jesus’ flock. The leaders came from within the congregations of small groups of believers in the early church. There were no job interviews or salary discussions; those never existed. This was a voluntary and unpaid service.

Some Christian denominations today appoint an individual for each responsibility within the church; elder, bishop, overseer, pastor or shepherd. In the early church, elders served in all capacities.

Let's examine how it worked in Scripture:

1 Peter 5:1-3: 1 Therefore, I exhort the elders <4245> among you, as your fellow elder <4245> (this is how the Apostle Peter refers to himself) and witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a partaker also of the glory that is to be revealed, 2 shepherd <4165> the flock of God among you, exercising oversight <1983> not under compulsion, but voluntarily, according to the will of God; and not for sordid gain, but with eagerness; 3 nor yet as lording it over those allotted to your charge, but proving to be examples to the flock.

Some Christian denominations think the Apostle Peter stood above the others, but he didn’t. He was a fellow elder.

Those who lead must:

- Serve, not because you must, but out of a willing heart that drives you to do so. - Serve, not for money, but out of sheer eagerness to serve God through Christ. - Serve, not in a dominating way, but as a living example of Christlikeness.

Elder: Describes the care for the flock of Jesus in a way that exhibits his spiritual maturity. Chronological age is not necessarily relevant.

Elder: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4245 presbuteros; …older; as noun, a senior; specifically, an Israelite Sanhedrist

Bishop/Overseer: Describes the care for the flock of Jesus in terms of oversight, watching the details of the things that happen in the group. Watching over and focusing on the flock’s functionality.

Bishop: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1985 episkopos; from #1909 and #4649 (in the sense of #1983); a superintendent

Bishop: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1984 episkope; from #1980; inspection (for relief); by implication, superintendence

Pastor/Shepherd: Describes personal care for the flock in their varied and challenging life experiences. These words describe the responsibility to provide practical, life- giving help and counsel.

Shepherd: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4165 poimaino; from #4166; to tend as a shepherd of (figuratively, superviser)

Pastors: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4156 poimen; a shepherd (literally or figuratively):-shepherd pastor

Those in a position of spiritual leadership are responsible for three different areas: elder, bishop and pastor.

Acts 20:28: (KJV) Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost (more accurately, holy spirit) hath made you overseers (bishops) <1985>, to feed (shepherd) <4165> the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.

Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock—the overseer role takes care of the functionality of the flock.

To feed the church of God—this role handles the practical needs.

These are separate reponsibilities that could be fulfilled by one person; this does not describe a hierarchy. These are the responsibilities given to leaders whose characters match the requirements listed in Titus 1:5-9.

Ephesians 4:11: And he gave some as apostles, and some as prophets, and some as evangelists, and some as pastors <4166> and teachers <1320>.

Teachers: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1320 didaskalos; an instructor (generally or specifically):—doctor, master teacher

Leaders have different talents and abilities. Therefore, having more than one elder in an ecclesia (assembly, congregation) can bless the church as a whole.

The Greek word ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia) appears 115 times in the New Testament and is most commonly translated as church, though its original meaning is “assembly” or “gathering.”

For example, some are better at leading Bible studies, and others are better at giving sermons. Some may be better counselors, and some may have a talent for evangelizing.

Ephesians 4 lists different areas of stronger focus or talent. This does not mean those in positions of leadership have only one thing they can do, but we want to maximize their abilities for the highest spiritual well-being of the flock.

We can see from these descriptions what mature Christian leadership looks like, with its character traits, integrity and humility. This is serious!

Next, Christian leadership is to be the first line of defense against wolves in sheep’s clothing:

Acts 20:28-30: 28 Be on guard for yourselves and for all the flock, among which the holy spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God which he purchased with his own blood. 29 I know that after my departure savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; 30 and from among your own selves men will arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them.

The Apostle Paul warns that “wolves” will attack, perhaps wanting to take advantage of the brethren's kindness. We need to be on our guard.

Jonathan and I have been elected by our local congregations to be shepherds. We have been put in a position of great responsibility, and we regularly talk about how ominous it is! We attempt to approach it with great fear and trembling to just do it the right way.

As long as we seek the Lord’s help and guidance over all our services, we are on the right track. If we are seeking a position for selfish reasons or in our own way, we are going down the wrong road.

Elections in our different churches are held annually. The choice of elders is not about personal preference, family kinship or selfish ambition. The choice is made based on who the congregants believe is capable of guiding the flock in a way that helps all to walk in Jesus' footsteps.

Both Rick and Jonathan’s separate congregations choose their servants by an annual vote taken by the raising of hands, after sincere prayer for the Lord’s guidance and for His will to be done. We believe in an upaid ministry, and each individual congregation decides as a group how donations (all unsolicited) will be used.

Those who step into the role of shepherding Jesus’ flock step into a profound and difficult privilege. Let’s think about that!

With all of these responsibilities laid out before us, how do we determine what accomplishing them really looks like?

A surefire way to find true church leadership in action is to closely examine one who was present in the early church when all of these things came into being. Through the power of God’s spirit working in him, the Apostle Paul played a big part in not only writing down what church leadership is supposed to look like, but also showing us by his personal example how it works.

I'd rather see a sermon than hear one any day. —Edgar A. Guest

That's essentially what we want to do as we go through this episode—we want to see the Apostle Paul's sermon in action.

Paul’s request to the Thessalonians:

1 Thessalonians 5:12: But we request of you, brethren, that you appreciate (see) those who diligently labor (work hard) among you, and have charge over you in the Lord and give you instruction.

Paul wanted the Thessalonians to take time to appreciate those who worked hard for their spiritual benefit. This is an interesting perspective because it is not mentioned too often in Scripture.

Before we get into the lesson, let's introduce the context of the Apostle Paul's experience with the brotherhood in Thessalonica. It wasn't the typical experience when he founded a new church.

We will quote periodically from gotquestions.org, which wrote a succinct description of several aspects of Paul and Silas' mission in Thessalonica.

(Source: gotquestions.org) Paul and Silas traveled to Thessalonica from Phillipi on Paul’s second missionary journey to preach... He spent three weeks teaching in the Jewish synagogue, but most of the Thessalonian Jews became indignant and formed a mob to drive the men out of the city. However, “some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few prominent women” (Acts 17:4). That was the beginning of the church at Thessalonica.

The beginning stages of this church were full of difficulty. Notice Paul and Silas were only there for three weeks. We will expand on this later.

Watch with an open heart to let what you see take root.

We’re going to go through most of 1 Thessalonians up to chapter five, verse 12 and unfold Paul’s teachings as he pours his heart out about appreciating those who diligently lead.

Paul shows us what the work of shepherds looks like:

1 Thessalonians 1:2-6: 2 We give thanks to God always for all of you, making mention of you in our prayers;

Appreciate their prayerful handling of our lives.

3 constantly bearing in mind your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ in the presence of our God and Father,

Appreciate their thoughtful and specific understanding of who we are.

4 knowing, brethren beloved by God, His choice of you; 5 for our gospel did not come to you in word only, but also in power and in the holy spirit and with full conviction…

Appreciate their clarity in observing God’s spirit and providence in our lives. Appreciate those who are observing us in our own attempts at spiritual growth and maturity.

6 You also became imitators of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much tribulation with the joy of the holy spirit.

(Source: gotquestions) In Thessalonica, Paul and Silas stayed with a man named Jason, and when the Thessalonian mob decided to get rid of the missionaries (Paul and Silas), they rushed Jason’s house and dragged him into the streets. After a hasty consultation with city officials, they made Jason post bond, and they released him.

The city officials made Jason promise he was going to take Paul and Silas out of the city or there would be consequences.

You also became imitators of us and the Lord, having received the word in much tribulation—we start to get a sense of what that tribulation looked like!

Appreciate our shepherds’ observation of our heartfelt application of discipleship. You also became imitators of us and the Lord. Paul loved them and saw growth in them.

1 Thessalonians 1:7-8: 7 so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia. 8 For the word of the Lord has sounded forth from you…in every place your faith toward God has gone forth, so that we have no need to say anything.

They had become examples to Christians all over the place.

Appreciate THEIR appreciation of our work of growth and maturity in Christ.

We have received this beautiful template of what shepherding looks like, from God, through Christ, through the pen of the apostle. We are thankful for the principles we have been given.

9 For they themselves report about us what kind of a reception we had with you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God.

Appreciate their remembering the powerful transformation from our former lives. Appreciate how they are paying close attention.

Now to chapter 2:

1 Thessalonians 2:1-2: 1 For you yourselves know, brethren, that our coming to you was not in vain, 2 but after we had already suffered and been mistreated in Philippi, as you know, we had the boldness in our God to speak to you the gospel of God amid much opposition.

(Source: gotquestions.com) Meanwhile, the new Thessalonian believers hid Paul and company until dark and then sent them on to Berea, a city about 45 miles to the southwest (Acts 17:10). Even though Paul and Silas had left their city, the unbelieving Thessalonian Jews were not satisfied. They followed the missionaries to Berea and tried to stir up the crowd against them there as they had done in their own city (Acts 17:13). The Berean believers smuggled Paul to the coast where he boarded a ship for Athens. Silas and Timothy remained in Berea to teach and strengthen the new church there.

We had boldness in our God to speak to you the gospel amid much opposition—this is the opposition. They had to hide Paul twice from people who wanted vengeance. Berea was a day’s journey away, and yet the Thessolonian Jews were still intent on destroying Paul. He continued to shepherd, preach and teach without allowing anything to stand in the way.

Appreciate our shepherds’ continuous, unrelenting and often fearless efforts for the sake of the gospel. We want to thank them for being that kind of an example.

1 Thessalonians 2:3-6: 3 For our exhortation does not come from error or impurity or by way of deceit; 4 but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not as pleasing men, but God who examines our hearts. 5 For we never came with flattering speech, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed… 6 nor did we seek glory from men…

Appreciate our shepherds’ clearly distinguishable humility in the service of God and the gospel. It’s not about pleasing people.

I was at a Bible conference several months ago, and I saw this brother sitting by himself, and he’s several years older than I am. He has this work ethic in the gospel work that is just remarkable. He travels all over the place. And I looked at him from a few rows away and thought, I need to tell him I appreciate him. So, I just plopped myself down and said, “Brother, how are you? I just want to let you know how much your work inspires me.” We had this wonderful conversation. It’s important to recognize what others do. Even though someone may be a shepherd, it doesn’t mean they don’t need that deep, profound inspiration and appreciation they get from others.

1 Thessalonians 2:7-9: 7 But we proved to be gentle among you, as a nursing mother tenderly cares for her own children. 8 Having so fond an affection for you, we were well-pleased to impart to you not only the gospel of God but also our own lives, because you had become very dear to us. 9 For you recall, brethren, our labor and hardship, how working night and day so as not to be a burden to any of you, we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.

Verse 7—Appreciate their tender care for us as children in Christ, like a mother cares for her infant.

Verse 8—Appreciate their giving us the word and the wholehearted giving of themselves. It's not just imparting the word; it's imparting their very lives to us.

Verse 9—Appreciate their selflessness on every level without seeking temporal, physical support in return.

The Apostle Paul was a tent maker, which allowed him to earn a living to support himself. He is our pattern for elders today. The elders in the early church did not serve for financial gain. Their focus was about the spreading of the gospel and the building up of others.

The work of shepherding Jesus’ flock is a full-time commitment to daily building up and protecting the lives of those who are called of God.

It’s hard to fathom all that we are given by those who are truly in positions to lead us! How do we genuinely show REAL appreciation?

To observe and appreciate the love, zeal, wisdom, fearlessness and tireless efforts of those who effectively lead us is to open our hearts and minds to fully receive what they have to give. However, this is only the beginning. True appreciation cannot be genuinely achieved until we learn to internalize what we have seen, felt and learned. This internalization opens us to being able to transform what we have been given into what we are now capable of giving. The receiver, in turn, becomes the giver.

We have been noticing WHAT to appreciate; now let’s look at ways to SHOW that appreciation.

We will now begin to observe ways we can and should show the appreciation we have been noticing:

1 Thessalonians 2:13-14: 13 For this reason we also constantly thank God that when you received the word of God which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men, but for what it really is, the word of God, which also performs its work in you who believe. 14 For you, brethren, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea, for you also endured the same sufferings at the hands of your own countrymen, even as they did from the Jews.

For you, brethren, became imitators…you also endured what you’ve seen others endure. They were learning to reciprocate, to give back what they had been given.

RECIPROCATE—Daily strive to live according to (and to be strong in) the high standard of God’s word and not the words of men.

It is God’s word, therefore I stand in it and will give back what I have been given.

There was no sectarianism, as they were all of one body and one faith. Paul also encouraged these new converts to imitate the brethren in Judea. They had similar trials. There is no difference in Christ; they were all equal. It didn’t matter who was more or less mature, who was brand new, who had been there for years and years—they were all equal in Christ. There is a power in that. This is where reciprocation can work so well, with each supporting each other.

Supporting texts:

Ephesians 6:10-12: 10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of His might. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you will be able to stand firm against the schemes of the devil. 12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the powers, against the world forces of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

Be strong in the Lord and in the strength of His might—it is not about how strong we think we are. it is about standing in the strength of His might. That is where reciprocation comes in. Everyone draws strength from the same source. By reciprocating, we can show our appreciation of those called to guide the true church.

How else we can show this appreciation?

1 Thessalonians 2:17-20: 17 But we, brethren, having been taken away from you for a short while—in person, not in spirit—were all the more eager with great desire to see your face. 18 For we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, more than once—and yet Satan hindered us. 19 For who is our hope or joy or crown of exultation? Is it not even you, in the presence of our Lord Jesus at his coming? 20 For you are our glory and joy.

Paul only knew them for three weeks, and those three weeks weren’t easy! He loved them instantly, and he certainly built them up. They were his hope or joy or crown of exultation because they were in Christ. It is amazing the connection Paul had with these individuals after such a short time. They were so close. His heart was being poured out in this epistle.

RECIPROCATE—Absorb the depth of dedication given to us and, in turn, give it back to others. If we’ve been given such powerful dedication, we want to pour it back out, because it’s not given to us just to sit. It’s given to us so we can expand it.

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is...

We can't have that spiritual level of reciprocation without the transformation of the mind.

If our shepherds are starting to go down different roads and not following Christ, we need to seriously consider what is happening.

We recently had several people write in from around the world concerned about their ministers and not knowing what to do about it. For example:

I'm in a church where the pastor controls everything. He doesn't allow anyone to make suggestions or contribute to church matters. No one has any idea how the church ﬁnances are managed. The pastor makes all the decisions and won't allow anyone to question him. Is this biblical?

No! Jesus allowed his disciples to question him, and he had others handle the financial matters. If we are in such a situation, we have to ask ourselves, Am I in a situation where the shepherding is Christlike? What is it teaching me? Are the “sheep” treated as the shepherd’s joy or crown of exaltation? This is what we look for. If we want to be Christlike, we need to follow those who are showing us the steps of Christlikeness. We have to be careful.

Now to chapter 3:

1 Thessalonians 3:1-5: 1 Therefore when we could endure it no longer, we thought it best to be left behind at Athens alone, 2 and we sent Timothy… to strengthen and encourage you as to your faith, 3 so that no one would be disturbed by these afflictions; for you yourselves know that we have been destined for this. 4 For indeed when we were with you, we kept telling you in advance that we were going to suffer affliction; and so it came to pass, as you know. 5 For this reason, when I could endure it no longer, I also sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the tempter might have tempted you…

Paul here reassures the Thessolonian church that he told them in advance he needed to suffer afflictions, and now he was suffering them. But I was so concerned for you that I started to have this internal anxiety that maybe Satan was going to tempt you. So, I had to send a messenger, Timothy, to see if you were standing strong.

Earlier, we discussed reciprocating to show our appreciation. This example here is straightforward appreciation.

APPRECIATE—Recognize the depth of trial and testing we are ALL subject to and steel our hearts and minds to truly stand together.

Notice the Apostle Paul couldn’t stand fully until he knew his brethren were okay. He sent his right-hand man, Timothy, to make sure they were covered. That’s what shepherding is. We need to show our appreciation for such actions by putting ourselves in the position of having that same concern for others.

1 Peter 5:6-9: 6 Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you at the proper time, 7 casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. 8 Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. 9 But resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same experiences of suffering are being accomplished by your brethren who are in the world.

Do we see the connection? We’re supposed to be tied together, not just with those in our local group, but with those of “like faith,” wherever they may be. Casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. Satan is looking to derail the true church, so we need to be able to stand together in this appreciation in order to build one another up. This is the example true shepherds give us.

1 Thessalonians 3:6-8: 6 But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us good news of your faith and love, and that you always think kindly of us, longing to see us just as we also long to see you, 7 for this reason, brethren, in all our distress and affliction we were comforted about you through your faith; 8 for now we really live, if you stand firm in the Lord.

Now that's a true shepherd! For now we really live, if you stand firm in the Lord. What an intimate relationship!

For those of us who are called to the responsibility of shepherding, this is the standard. For those of us who are being shepherded, this is the character we look for in our leaders. We want to be able to sincerely imitate.

3. SINCERELY IMITATE—Learn by receiving and then live by giving.

Recognize the interconnectedness the body of Christ must have to be functional.

1 Corinthians 12:12-13,26: 12 For even as the body is one and yet has many members, and all the members of the body, though they are many, are one body, so also is Christ. 13 For by one spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, and we were all made to drink of one spirit. 26 And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

We want to appreciate that the unity of the church starts with its leadership of Christ and is demonstrated by our shepherds..

As an elder, I want to share the support I receive from other elders in our church. They are always willing to substitute responsibilities if sickness or unexpected travel plans come up, and they do so in a spirit of helpfulness and love. I'm grateful for their examples in my life.

There are so many ways to show appreciation and all of them are centered on building one another up spiritually.

There are obviously many ways we can show our deep appreciation for those who lead us. Where does this bring us?

As we shall see, the end result of applying this appreciation in our lives is the completion of the body of Christ. Think about the foundation Paul has laid. He has taught us to stand firm in God’s strength, live according to a spiritually transformed mind, stand our ground against all challenges and build the interconnectivity of the body of Christ.

Again, we’re going through the book of 1 Thessalonians to see how Paul explains what shepherding looks like and how to appreciate it. Our question from verse 12 is, how do we appreciate their diligent labor on our part?

1 Thessalonians 3:11-13: 11 Now may our God and Father Himself and Jesus our Lord direct our way to you; 12 and may the Lord cause you to increase and abound in love for one another, and for all people, just as we also do for you; 13 so that He may establish your hearts without blame in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

4. ELEVATE—We can show our appreciation by working to elevate our own standards and interactions to the highest form of love (agape, selfless love) wherever and whenever appropriate.

Paul’s standard of selfless love had the church’s best interests at heart.

A good companion set of verses is the “love chapter”:

1 Corinthians 13:4-7: 4 Love is patient, love is kind and is not jealous; love does not brag and is not arrogant, 5 does not act unbecomingly; it does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not take into account a wrong suffered, 6 does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; 7 bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

That's exactly what Jesus said. Love one another even as I have loved you, and love your neighbor as yourself. Paul certainly was following Christ.

We follow our shepherds only as they follow Christ. We keep repeating this because that’s the foundation. If they leave the foundation, if the shepherds we follow are starting to go in different directions, we have to ask ourselves why we are following them. That’s not the guidance we’re supposed to be following.

Our appreciation of our shepherds’ care is powerfully reflected in our selfless love towards them and others. If we receive that selfless love, we appreciate it by giving it back to them and others.

Chapter 4:

1 Thessalonians 4:1, 3-6: 1 Finally then, brethren, we request and exhort you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us instruction as to how you ought to walk and please God (just as you actually do walk), that you excel still more… 3 For this is the will of God, your sanctification; that is, that you abstain from sexual immorality; 4 that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, 5 not in lustful passion, like the Gentiles who do not know God; 6 and that no man transgress and defraud his brother in the matter because the Lord is the avenger in all these things

We just talked about elevating our actions to the standard of selfless love. To do this, we need to learn to subjugate, meaning certain things in our lives need to be subject to others.

SUBJUGATE—By resisting and removing our fleshly desires, we not only appreciate our examples, but we also become examples for others.

We cannot elevate to a higher selfless love if we bring all the fleshly junk along with it. We have to subjugate (bring under control) all those desires; put them aside, put them down, because those are not the important things.

Again, we want to appreciate the example we’ve been given in the lives of those shepherding us:

Ephesians 6:13-17: 13 Therefore, take up the full armor of God, so that you will be able to resist in the evil day, and having done everything, to stand firm. 14 Stand firm therefore, HAVING GIRDED YOUR LOINS WITH TRUTH, and HAVING PUT ON THE BREASTPLATE OF RIGHTEOUSNESS, 15 and having shod YOUR FEET WITH THE PREPARATION OF THE GOSPEL OF PEACE; 16 in addition to all, taking up the shield of faith with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. 17 And take THE HELMET OF SALVATION, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God.

The very next verse says pray for one another. The armor is not complete without prayer.

Notice that the victory comes not because we’re so strong but because we’re so well armed with the spirituality of standing in the strength of the Lord and the power of His might. We are shown this great example of how to do this through those who shepherd us. The Apostle Paul said, follow me as I follow Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1).

We follow our shepherds only as they follow Christ. There is no other qualification, and if they are not following Christ, we must go in a different direction.

In 1 Thessalonians, the apostle lays out a powerful connection between the shepherding aspects of the leadership and appreciation shown in the flock for that sherpherding.

Chapter 5:

1 Thessalonians 5:1-2,5-6: 1 Now as to the times and the epochs, brethren, you have no need of anything to be written to you. 2 For you yourselves know full well that the day of the Lord will come just like a thief in the night. 5 for you are all sons of light and sons of day. We are not of night nor of darkness; 6 so then let us not sleep as others do, but let us be alert and sober.

So far, we've learned to:

1. RECIPROCATE

2. APPRECIATE

3. SINCERELY IMITATE

4. ELEVATE

5. SUBJUGATE

6. INVESTIGATE—Our appreciation can be plainly expressed by our making the proving of God’s truth through Scripture our own. Not just hearing it, but proving it to ourselves.

2 Timothy 2:15-16: 15 Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth. 16 But avoid worldly and empty chatter, for it will lead to further ungodliness.

It's interesting the Apostle Paul is telling Timothy to be diligent to present yourself approved to God. Timothy followed Paul everywhere and was spiritual fed by him. Yet here Paul instructs Timothy to prove everything himself.

We can show our appreciatiation by doing our own investigation; and then by saying to those who guide us, “We’ve seen it in you; we’ve learned it, and now we have investigated and proved it for ourselves.”

Their job is to begin the work. Our job is to pick it up and run with it. In this way, we show appreciation.

1 Thessalonians 5:11: Therefore encourage one another and build up one another, just as you also are doing.

This is the verse before our theme scripture about appreciating those who lead us. It’s interesting what Paul ends with before he asks for that appreciation— he says, encourage one another and build up one another, just as you also are doing.

He’s essentially putting the answer right in front of us, telling us how to appreciate what drives those called to guide the church.

One of my experiences is the privilege of working with the brotherhood through challenges, trials and difficulties. Often that person will say, “Rick, thank you. What can I do?” And the answer is always the same. “Do what you’ve received for someone else.” Because there’s no better way to put things in perspective than to do for others what we’ve been given. This is what Jesus was all about. He showed us how to do that.

Again, let’s read our theme scripture:

1 Thessalonians 5:12: But we request of you, brethren, that you appreciate those who diligently labor among you, and have charge over you in the Lord and give you instruction.

Diligently seek to follow their guidance.

In Paul’s letter to the Thessalonians, he sums up our appreciation for those who lead as follows:

Appreciate by standing firm in God’s strength.

Appreciate by living according to a spiritually transformed mind.

Appreciate by standing our ground against all challenges.

Appreciate by building the interconnectivity of the body of Christ. Appreciate by carefully reflecting selfless love towards others.

Appreciate by proving all things and grow in truth.

Appreciate by passing on what we have received to others.

The Apostle Paul showed us the path; we just need to follow it.

So, how do we genuinely appreciate those who guide us?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!
