Bonus Material and Study Questions

Recommended additional study:

Ep.1140: Does My Church Leadership Have It Right?

Uncovering what biblical church organization and leadership look like https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/church-leaders/

For children, parents and Bible class teachers, continue your studies on this topic with these short, animated videos for kids at ChristianQuestions.com/YouTube:

- What makes a good Christian leader? https://christianquestions.com/cq-videos/videos-cq-kids/what-makes-a-good-christian-leader/
- What are some wisdom lessons for children from the Apostle Paul? https://christianquestions.com/cq-videos/videos-cq-kids/wisdom-lessons-from-apostle-paul/
- What is humility? https://christianquestions.com/cq-videos/videos-cq-kids/what-is-humility/

(Source: gotquestions.org): Thessalonica was a prominent city in Macedonia (in modern-day Greece) due to its location: it had a seaport on the Aegean Sea and was a principal stop on the Egnatian Way, a major Roman road. Paul and Silas traveled to Thessalonica from Phillipi on Paul’s second missionary journey to preach the news about Jesus. He spent three weeks teaching in the Jewish synagogue, but most of the Thessalonian Jews became indignant and formed a mob to drive the men out of the city. However, “some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few prominent women” (Acts 17:4). That was the beginning of the church at Thessalonica. In Thessalonica, Paul and Silas stayed with a man named Jason, and when the Thessalonian mob decided to get rid of the missionaries, they rushed Jason’s house and dragged him into the streets. After a hasty consultation with city officials, they made Jason post bond and released him. Meanwhile, the new Thessalonian believers hid Paul and company until dark and then sent them on to Berea, a city about 45 miles to the southwest (Acts 17:10). In Berea, Paul found a much more receptive audience (verses 11 and 12).The Bereans considered Paul’s words and compared them with the Scriptures instead of taking offense and resisting the gospel as the Thessalonians had.

Even though Paul and Silas had left their city, the unbelieving Thessalonian Jews were not satisfied. They followed the missionaries to Berea and tried to stir up the crowd against them there as they had done in their own city (Acts 17:13). The Berean believers smuggled Paul to the coast where he boarded a ship for Athens. Silas and Timothy remained in Berea to teach and strengthen the new church there.

Not long after his initial visit to Thessalonica, Paul was in Corinth, where he wrote two letters that we now call 1 and 2 Thessalonians, addressed to the newfound church in Thessalonica. First Thessalonians is one of the first of Paul’s letters, or epistles, to churches. Despite the hostile environment the new believers experienced in Thessalonica, they were holding fast to the word that was preached to them, and news of their devotion to Christ was becoming well-known throughout Macedonia (1 Thessalonians 1:7–8).

Paul’s stay in Thessalonica had most likely been difficult for him. In his first letter to the church there, Paul mentions that he had to work during his time in that city, in addition to teaching and preaching, in order not to be a burden to his hosts (1 Thessalonians 2:9). Although Paul does not state what kind of work he did, it was most likely tent-making, which was a trade he was experienced in (Acts 18:1–3).

Due to the short time he had been able to spend in Thessalonica, Paul was concerned about the church there. He tried to return to them “again and again—but Satan blocked our way” (1 Thessalonians 2:18). So Paul sent Timothy to check on them and encourage them in their faith (1 Thessalonians 3:1–5). Paul “was afraid that in some way the tempter had tempted [them]” and that his labors among them had “been in vain” (verse 5). But Timothy returned to Paul bearing good news about the thriving church in Thessalonica, and Paul wrote the book of 1 Thessalonians to encourage them and to explain the “day of the Lord” more clearly.

It seems that, later, some people began teaching the Thessalonian church that the Lord had already come and that Judgment Day was upon them (2 Thessalonians 2:1–2). Worse yet, these false teachers were alleging that their message came from Paul. The apostle wrote 2 Thessalonians to allay their fears and teach them more fully about “the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered to him” (verse 1). They had not missed the coming of the Lord.

The church at Thessalonica, located as it was in a prominent city of Macedonia, had an ideal opportunity to share the gospel with the whole region. And that’s what they did, as “the Lord’s message rang out” from the Thessalonian church (1 Thessalonians 1:8). Just like the church in Thessalonica, many churches today are planted in areas hostile to the gospel. Paul’s exhortations and encouragement to the Thessalonians are also encouragements for those today who “have longed for His appearing” (2 Timothy 4:8). Paul’s words to his friends at the church in Thessalonica are timeless promises to us all.

We are excited that this Episode #1398 starts our Christian Conduct Series, methodically going through 1 Thessalonians 5:12-24:

1 Thessalonians 5:12-24: 12 But we request of you, brethren, that you appreciate those who diligently labor among you, and have charge over you in the Lord and give you instruction, 13 and that you esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Live in peace with one another. 14 We urge you, brethren, admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with everyone. 15 See that no one repays another with evil for evil, but always seek after that which is good for one another and for all people. 16 Rejoice always; 17 pray without ceasing; 18 in everything give thanks; for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus. 19 Do not quench the spirit; 20 do not despise prophetic utterances. 21 But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; 22 abstain from every form of evil. 23 Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. 24 Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

We will break each part into specific themes, continuing with:

#1399: “How Can We Each Contribute to the Health of Our Church?”

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1398-spiritual-leaders/

1. Explain what the leaders’ characters in God’s true church look like. What are the responsibilities of these leaders? Define the areas a leader might need to cover as an elder, bishop, overseer, pastor, shepherd and teacher. (John 13:14, Titus 1:5-9, 1 Peter 5:1-3, Acts 20:28-30, Ephesians 4:11)

2. What is Paul’s question of the Thessalonians in 1 Thessalonians 5:12? How do the following verses show what we should appreciate about the work of our shepherds?

a. (1 Thessalonians 1:2-8) List the eight references in these verses as to what we should appreciate.

b. (1 Thessalonians 2:1-9) List the additional five references in these verses.

3. How can we show this appreciation? Expand on each item:

a. Reciprocate: Stand in God’s word and give it back. (1 Thessalonians 2:13-14, Ephesians 6:10-12)

b. Reciprocate: Absorb the dedication given us and give it back. (1 Thessalonians 2:17-20, Romans 12:2)

c. Appreciate: All are subject to trials and need to stand together. (1 Thessalonians 3:1-5, 1 Peter 5:6-9)

d. Sincerely Imitate: Receive, give, connect with the body of Christ. (1 Thessalonians 3:6-8,

1 Corinthians 12:12-13,26)

e. Elevate: Lift our standards, interactions to agape love. (1 Thessalonians 3:11-13, 1 Corinthians 13:4-7)

f. Subjugate: Remove our fleshly desires, become examples. (1 Thessalonians 4:1-6, Ephesians 6:13-17)

g. Investigate: Prove God’s truth for ourselves. (1 Thessalonians 5:1-6, 2 Timothy 2:15-16)

4. Each of us need to consider. Are we:

a. standing firm in God’s strength?

b. living according to a spiritually transformed mind?

c. standing our ground against all challenges?

d. Helping build the interconnectivity of the body of Christ?

e. reflecting selfless love towards others? f. proving all things and growing in truth?

g. passing on what we have received to others?

5. Which of these do you have the most trouble with? What do you need to work on first and how will you start?

## Episode 1399 — How Can We Each Contribute to the Health of Our Church? (Christian Conduct Series)
Published: 2025-08-25
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1399-healthy-church/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/22101907/CQ_Rewind_08-25-2025_How_Can_We_Each_Contribute_to_the_Health_of_Our_Church.pdf

How Can We Each Contribute to the Health of Our Church? (Christian Conduct Series)

1 Thessalonians 5:14–15: 14 We urge you, brethren, admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with everyone. 15 See that no one repays another with evil for evil, but always seek after that which is good for one another and for all people.

According to the New Testament, Christians are instructed to work together as a community. Even more than that, we are taught to care for one another as a family, humbly serve one another and protect one another as soldiers in battle, even to the point of being willing to sacrifice ourselves. All of this is to be put in place while we each are dedicated to following the clear and godly teachings of Jesus in Scripture. So, how do we go about making all of this happen? In Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians, he lists practical ways we should care for one another. While this list is not comprehensive, it alerts us to several foundational principles of sound Christian conduct.

This episode is the second in our Christian Conduct Series, where we are carefully examining God’s instructions to us given by the Apostle Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5:12-24.

Let’s do a quick recap from our previous episode. The two verses before our theme text in 1 Thessalonians 5 are the foundation for Paul’s practical and powerful teachings regarding how we are to care for one another.

Paul began with a request:

1 Thessalonians 5:12: But we request of you, brethren, that you appreciate those who diligently labor among you, and have charge over you in the Lord and give you instruction,

Throughout the New Testament, Paul and others showed what those who shepherd the flock do and how we can consistently appreciate them.

Summing up his teaching, we appreciate those who shepherd us by:

Standing firm in God’s strength Living according to a spiritually transformed mind Standing our ground against all challenges Building the interconnectivity of the body of Christ Carefully reflecting selfless love toward others Proving all things to ourselves and growing in truth Passing on what we have received to others

These are what led up to the request to appreciate those who diligently labor among us.

Paul concluded this request with the following:

1 Thessalonians 5:13: and that you esteem them very highly in love because of their work.

Live in peace with one another.

Live in peace with one another—we can see this thought as both a conclusion to Paul’s previous request as well as an introduction to his next teaching. By collectively working at having appropriate appreciation, we essentially bind ourselves to one another. This unity can provide a solid foundation for the next step so that each of us can mutually contribute to the health of our fellowship.

The thought is, if we are in a mindset of appreciating our leaders, we are more apt to humbly and respectfully serve each other, making for a healthy church family.

(Source: The Daily Study Bible Series by William Barclay) Live in peace with one another— it is impossible that the gospel of love should be preached in an atmosphere poisoned by hate.

We could add to that concept by including other negative emotions or thoughts such as jealousy or having personal agendas.

Let’s go on to our next lesson:

1 Thessalonians 5:14–15: 14 We urge you, brethren, admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with everyone. 15 See that no one repays another with evil for evil, but always seek after that which is good for one another and for all people.

admonish the unruly... encourage the fainthearted... help the weak... be patient with everyone...

See that no one repays another with evil for evil... but always seek after that which is good for one another and for all people...

William Barclay’s commentary calls these a “chain of jewels of good advice.” Let’s break this down one “jewel” at a time.

admonish the unruly...

1 Thessalonians 5:14: We urge you, brethren, admonish <3960> the unruly <813>…

Admonish: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3560 noutheteo; to put in mind, i.e. (by implication) to caution or reprove gently: warn, admonish

Unruly: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #813 ataktos; from 1 (as a negative particle) and a derivative of 5021; unarranged, i.e. (by implication) insubordinate (religiously): --unruly

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) disorderly, out of ranks (often so of soldiers)

2) irregular, inordinate, immoderate pleasures 3) deviating from the prescribed order or rule.

The key word here is ADMONISH, meaning to caution, warn or correct. This isn’t a harsh rebuke; it’s meant to restore the person and not put them down.

Admonish the unruly—some translations say, warn the lazy, the idle or the undisciplined. This gentle correction shows disapproval of someone’s actions.

This Greek word for unruly was used in Greek society to describe those who didn’t show up for work, like a soldier who “breaks rank.” Paul uses this word to describe believers who were living irresponsibly—some of whom had stopped working.

Notice Paul is making a heartfelt appeal not just to the leaders but to the whole church community. This is a shared responsibility.

Paul’s paraphrased instruction: We call on you to caution, to gently and appropriately reprove, those among you who are struggling with being out of order with the Christian principles we have been given to follow.

Is it strange that the first thing Paul starts with in this list for brotherly unity is correcting those who are doing something wrong?

Usually when approaching a difficult situation, people start with fluffy, nice things. But this is the Apostle Paul. This is not about being fluffy and nice; it is about making something work!

The fact that Paul begins his instructions to mutually strengthen and care for the brotherhood with what can be viewed as an awkward and difficult challenge is telling. His message is to truly care in all areas of life.

This specific challenge of some being “lazy” regarding their obligations to themselves and others was apparently an ongoing issue, as described by Paul later:

2 Thessalonians 3:10–15: 10 For even when we were with you, we used to give you this order: if anyone is not willing to work, then he is not to eat, either. 11 For we hear that some among you are leading an undisciplined life, doing no work at all, but acting like busybodies. 12 Now such persons we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ to work in quiet fashion and eat their own bread. 13 But as for you, brethren, do not grow weary of doing good. 14 If anyone does not obey our instruction in this letter, take special note of that person and do not associate with him, so that he will be put to shame. 15 Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish <3560> him as a brother.

Take special note of that person—publicly and consciously identify someone who is persistently disobedient—not in a shaming way, but to make the issue visible.

Do not associate with him—this Greek phrase implies not mixing closely in fellowship. It doesn’t mean total rejection or cruelty, but rather a pause in normal fellowship in order to encourage reflection and change.

So that he will be put to shame—the goal is restoration, not punishment. The shame here is meant to awaken the person to their error and encourage repentance.

Admonish him as a brother—there’s that ADMONISH key word again—gently reprove and correct.

This isn’t about avoiding someone who’s struggling. It’s about lovingly confronting someone who refuses correction and persists in behavior that harms himself or herself and the community. It’s a form of gentle discipline meant to protect the integrity of the church and guide the person back to responsible living.

Though it is meant to be a form of gentle correction, that correction has to be clear. The necessary actions are done with love and compassion. This is the baseline for our actions. It is not to cut the person off from the community but to firmly and gently draw attention to upholding the principles of self-support. This can be difficult.

The apostle was speaking of some who were evidently being supported by others and were leading an undisciplined life, acting as busybodies and not working to help themselves or others in the church community. Some Bible commentaries suggest certain ones stopped working, believing the end of the world was at hand.

I’m aware of a circumstance where someone was living with a family from church because they had been through a hardship and needed help. Even though they had a job, this situation continued even once they were more financially stable. The brethren suggested the person needed to get back on their feet, move on with their life and move out. This did not happen despite several reminders. Finally, it came down to saying, “Look, you are working and can support yourself. We are giving you a timeframe, and then you will have to be on your own because that is the appropriate thing to do.”

The admonishing had to come again and again. Once the timeframe was up, the person still was not moving out! The brethren had to say, “It’s time for you to go!” Eventually the person moved out and everything worked out.

This kind of admonishing has to be consistent because allowing these situations to exist doesn’t help the person or the spiritual community.

It is an interesting place for Paul to start. How do we mutually build each other up? We keep after those who need keeping after. We gently and lovingly guide them, showing them how to move forward until they find a way to stand on their own.

This is the way to move them forward, not to embarrass them. The Apostle Paul is starting with this strong message about mutual support.

We are just getting started and already we can see that our contributions to others are not always easy, but they are always necessary.

Contributing can be challenging! What does the attitude we are to display with the hard things teach us about our attitude with other things?

Because the Apostle Paul began with an uncomfortable example, he’s setting up an attitude foundation for the rest of our opportunities. As we now investigate the further opportunities he is revealing, we can understand the importance of beginning each experience with the attitude of humble obedience and selfless love.

encourage the fainthearted...

1 Thessalonians 5:14: We urge you, brethren, admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted <3642>.

Our key word is to ENCOURAGE, meaning comfort. Comfort the fainthearted. This is sometimes translated as “comfort the fearful.”

Encourage: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3888 paramutheomai; to relate near, i.e. (by implication) encourage, console

Fainthearted: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3642 oligopsuchos; little-spirited, i.e. faint-hearted: feebleminded

The Greek oligopsychos directly translates as “those whose souls are small.”

(Source: Bible Commentary by David Guzik) The fainthearted are those who, literally, are small- souled. By nature or experience, they tend to be timid and lack courage. These need comfort— in the sense of assisting strength—to be brought to them.

These are people who feel overwhelmed, discouraged or timid. Paul calls for gentle encouragement, not pressure. There's enough pressure in this world!

Paul went from talking about those who are just not applying themselves to those we need to walk alongside to support their struggles of “not being able to,” as they face certain experiences in their lives. These two scenarios are different, but they both can be difficult.

Those who struggle with “not being able to,” with discouragement or timidity, get stuck. We ALL need to be encouraged because we ALL experience this challenge at some point in our lives and become fainthearted.

We have the opportunity to support them by observing and then sharing in their hard experiences.

This Greek word for ENCOURAGE isn’t used in the New Testament very often. Here are two examples:

John 11:19: (KJV) And many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary, to comfort <3888> them concerning their brother.

Martha and Mary are grieving over the death of their brother Lazarus. We are encouraged to do likewise, to comfort those in the brotherhood who have suffered loss.

1 Thessalonians 2:11: (KJV) As ye know how we exhorted and comforted <3888> and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children,

A good father doesn’t just say, “Oh, it’s okay.” A father comforts his child by saying, “Oh, it’s okay. Now let’s get up, brush ourselves off and grow through this.”

Two kinds of comfort are demonstrated here:

Those who live with the sense of “not being able to” often have anxiety. Let’s look at the challenge of anxiety and how we can support those living with it:

Matthew 6:31–32: (NASB77) 31 Do not be anxious <3309> then, saying, What shall we eat? or What shall we drink?… 32 …for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.

Anxious: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3309 merimnao; to be anxious about

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) to be anxious… 2) to care for, look out for (a thing)

It is easy to say, Do not be anxious…for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. Of course, we intellectually know this. But sometimes worry and anxiety goes round and round in our heart and mind to the point where we cannot get past it.

Many of us have anxiety. Many of us are just wired to be anxious! We can encourage others to take their anxiety and form it into “productive anxiety.”

We discussed productive anxiety in Episode 1384: “Can I Find Balance When Overwhelmed With Anxiety? (Part II).” This is the process of training our anxious thoughts and energy towards mutual strengthening and passionate caring for others. It is a matter of turning the energy of being anxious into a different direction.

1 Corinthians 12:25–26: 25 so that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have <3309> the same care <3309> (the same word as anxious) for one another. 26 And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

These verses speak about having anxiety in a positive way because we are working at building each other up. It is not worrying unproductively; it is engaging with our anxiety in a positive process.

In our previous example, there was a person who was able to work but wasn’t moving out and living on their own like they should have. They needed clear and firm direction.

Our next example is someone who was on a fixed income but was still financially capable of living on their own. However, they, too, were living with one of the brethren from church. They just didn’t know how to change to a different living arrangement. It was overwhelming, so they hibernated.

Some of the brethren realized they needed help in this decision. They got together and figured out logistically how to get the person the kind of housing appropriate for their budget. The brethren did all the work and physically helped the person move out and on with their lives.

This was years ago, and the individual has flourished ever since! But they were stuck, and then they were hiding. The brotherhood took an active role in building them up, showing them how and then walking them through the process because the individual had doubts, thinking, I don’t think I can. I don’t think I’m able to. This is another example of us supporting one another in our faith.

help the weak...

Alongside giving encouragement to the fainthearted, Paul further focuses us on contributing:

1 Thessalonians 5:14: …help <472> the weak<772>

Help: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #472 antéchomai; to hold oneself opposite to, i.e. (by implication) adhere to; by extension to care for:—hold fast, hold to, support

Weak: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #772 asthenēs; strengthless (in various applications, literal, figurative and moral)

Our key word is HELP, meaning “to adhere to,” “to cling to.” It suggests holding onto someone with strength and loyalty, not letting go even when it’s inconvenient or difficult.

We just discussed the fainthearted—those who might be overwhelmed by circumstances, fear or grief. They need encouragement—gentle words, reassurance and emotional support to lift their spirits and some practical help to restore their confidence.

The weak, on the other hand, are those who lack strength—they might be struggling with a spiritual or moral weakness. They need help in a more active and sustained way—someone to come alongside them, bear their burdens and offer practical support.

It comes down to sticking by them. When somebody can’t do something because they are “strengthless” in whatever circumstance, it is so important for us to be aware and be able to walk alongside them if we want to contribute not only to them but also to the health of our church.

From a practical standpoint, help the weak could include those who are literally lacking capability. The Greek word asthenēs is broad and flexible, as it can refer to physical frailty, illness or general incapacity.

In the context of the early church, this would have included hands-on support and practical aid for: Elderly members needing help with daily functions Widows or orphans without support Those with disabilities or chronic illness Anyone unable to contribute in the same way as others

I think of how many times late at night have I had to call on our friend Kris to help when my computer has gone wonky. I am “weak” (incapable)—in that I have no idea how to fix my computer, but he stays with me until it’s working again.

Sometimes the weakness is obvious, such as an elderly person needing physical help. Sometimes we are weak in that we are not capable to perform the task, as in the case of the computer repair.

We all can have areas of weakness. When this is the case, others can support us, walk alongside us and help us fill the gaps. We contribute to the health of our church by helping those who are in situations they can’t handle alone for whatever reason.

Adhering to, and caring for the “weak” according to Scripture, should be an expected responsibility for all:

1 Corinthians 1:27–29: 27 but God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God has chosen the weak things <772> of the world to shame the things which are strong, 28 and the base things of the world and the despised God has chosen, the things that are not, so that He may nullify the things that are, 29 so that no man may boast before God.

This was a radical concept! In Greece and Rome at this time, strength, honor and self- sufficiency were highly prized. Weakness—whether physical, emotional or social—was often seen as shameful or inferior. Instead of shaming the weak, Paul calls on the church to honor them through active support so they can be essential members of the body of Christ. The strong serve the weak, which of course reminds us of the attitude of Jesus. Blessed are the poor in spirit… (Matthew 5:3 KJV). Blessed are the meek… (Matthew 5:5 KJV).

This shows us that nobody is out of place in the body of Christ. We are called to work together. This may be why Jesus sent out his disciples in pairs. If one was discouraged or tired, the other could lift him up. They could gently correct each other when necessary. It’s a lesson in companionship and interdependence in the body of Christ. We aren’t walking alone!

Mark 6:7: (KJV) And he called unto him the twelve, and began to send them forth by two and two; and gave them power over unclean spirits.

Luke 10:1: (KJV) After these things the Lord appointed other seventy also, and sent them two and two before his face into every city and place, whither he himself would come.

Our response to those with little strength is to identify with them and be a part of their lives. This is what the Apostle Paul did personally:

1 Corinthians 9:22–23: 22 To the weak <772> I became weak <772>, that I might win the weak <772>; I have become all things to all men, so that I may by all means save some. 23 I do all things for the sake of the gospel, so that I may become a fellow partaker of it.

Paul’s willingness to become all things to all people included helping the weak, adapting himself to their needs and walking alongside them. Paul wasn’t just preaching the gospel; he’s a fellow partaker, sharing not only in the joys and benefits but also the trials and sufferings. It pained him when these churches were having issues.

He was transparent about his challenges so that they could identify with him.

Our place is by the side of those who struggle. Why? Because they are VITAL to us!

1 Corinthians 12:21–22: 21 And the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. 22 On the contrary, it is much truer that the members of the body which seem to be weaker <772> are necessary;

Again, this is directly in contrast with the culture of the day, which celebrated strength. Here the Apostle Paul celebrates weakness, saying it is a part of us, the body of the church. By God’s grace, we can all share in this, work together and build one another up.

Not everyone needs the same kind of care. Some need comfort; others need strength. Paul tells us to discern the specific needs of our church and respond accordingly, always with patience and love. Sometimes we will be the needy, and sometimes we will be the needed.

Seeing these very heavy burdens in the light of mutual contribution really helps us see just how important our spiritual focus is.

We have been shown the vital importance of being present in the lives of the brotherhood through their difficulties. What comes next?

As we have already observed, the Apostle Paul is showing us how to mutually contribute by first revealing some of the more intense challenges. His next teaching will take one of the fundamental lessons from these experiences and apply it across the board. This next lesson can literally be applied to our contributions to every member of the brotherhood!

be patient with everyone...

1 Thessalonians 5:14: …be patient <3114> with everyone.

We must develop several different types of biblical “patience.” It most often describes endurance.

For example:

Luke 21:19: (KJV) In your patience <5281> possess ye your souls.

Patience: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5281 hupomone; cheerful (or hopeful) endurance, constancy

Jesus teaches us that this kind of patience is broad and absolutely necessary for discipleship.

However, in 1 Thessalonians 5:14, this is NOT the patience the Apostle Paul is telling us to have regarding our brotherhood. It is from a completely different Greek word, focusing on appropriately handling what requires internal restraint. This particular patience means “forbearance.”

Patience: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3114 makrothumeo; to be long-spirited, i.e. (objectively) forbearing or (subjectively) patient

Forbearance means you have self-restraint by holding back from getting what you are rightfully owed. Be patient with everyone—our key word here is the FORBEARANCE kind of patience.

Here’s a practical example that became popular during the COVID-19 pandemic. When a loan is in forbearance it means there’s a temporary pause or reduction in loan payments. It’s meant to prevent default or foreclosure while giving the borrower time to recover financially. The loan holds back on its legal and required payment schedule. But you still owe the money and often the interest owed continues to accumulate.

The apostle is saying to have this kind of patience—forbearance—with everyone.

Forbearance is a willingness to be non-reactive and appropriate. It is willing to wait for a situation to completely unfold—to be disciplined in holding back our own reactions.

This “patience” (forbearance) gives the benefit of the doubt and can only be displayed by humanity through a humble spirit:

Galatians 5:22–23: 22 But the fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, patience <3115>, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.

Patience: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3115 makrothumia; longanimity, i.e. (objectively) forbearance or (subjectively) fortitude:—longsuffering, patience

The fruit of the spirit is having God’s spirit develop these special character qualities in us. The fruit of patience here is from a form of the same Greek word meaning forbearance.

The fruitage of forbearance is a newly-developed discipline based on selfless love. Paul’s lesson here is broad and inclusive. To truly engage in mutual contributions to our brotherhood, we need to hold back our reactions to make room for God’s spirit to guide us instead!

Why is this a “newly-developed discipline”?

Patience (forbearance) does not come naturally. God’s spirit works within us to develop the fruit of selfless love, joy, peace, forbearance, etc. It is newly developed by God’s spirit, and we want to rely on that level of forbearance rather than our own natural tendencies.

In other words, don’t give up on those who are unruly, fainthearted or weak. Extend them time, space and support.

I frequently pray for the heavenly Father to help me be sensitive to the needs of others. Often, I get caught up in what I’m doing and forget to do something for others in need, and I miss opportunities.

If we learn to hold our natural inclinations back, we give ourselves the opportunity to allow God’s spirit to provoke us to something beyond what we would normally see and feel. It is really remarkable! Be patient with everyone. Have forbearance with everyone.

The Ephesians also needed this lesson.

While imprisoned, Paul wrote to them about their experiences with some core belief issues challenging Jewish and Gentile Christian fellowship:

Ephesians 4:1–6: 1 Therefore I, the prisoner of the Lord, implore you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling with which you have been called,.

Walk like a disciple of Christ walks! Make sure to follow in his footsteps.

2 with all humility and gentleness, with patience <3115> (forbearance), showing tolerance for one another in love <26> (agape, selfless love) 3 being diligent to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace.

Putting all these elements together, forbearance is right in the middle. Paul is saying: Have humility and gentleness be your basis as you restrain yourself in selfless love from reactive behavior towards those with whom issues may arise.

Having forbearance with all isn’t just being tolerant. It is holding “self” back so that God’s spirit can work through us.

Forbear—use self-restraint—and stand firm in Christ and for Christ: 4 There is one body and one spirit, just as also you were called in one hope of your calling; 5 one Lord, one faith, one baptism, 6 one God and Father of all who is over all and through all and in all.

Forbear with everyone. Especially when there is tension, forbearance is required with selfless love. We must have this with all the brotherhood in order to build one another up.

Forbearance is a defining characteristic of discipleship and selfless love:

1 Corinthians 13:4–7: 4 Love is patient <3114> (forbearance), love is kind and is not jealous; love does not brag and is not arrogant, 5 does not act unbecomingly; it does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not take into account a wrong suffered, 6 does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; 7 bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

Notice the first characteristic is patience (forbearance). When we practice forbearance, we are kind, we lack jealousy, we refrain from bragging or arrogance, among other virtues. This self-restraint serves as the baseline of our selfless love. That is how we support the body of Christ. This is what Paul is teaching us in 1 Thessalonians.

We need to hold ourselves back so we can appropriately contribute, and then build others up.

Applying forbearance to our contribution equation adds depth, creates clarity and gives us an even higher objective to strive for.

With admonishing, encouraging, helping and forbearing all in place, what’s left to be added?

While no specific word jumps out of Paul’s next teaching, there is a powerful theme: Live like Jesus lived! Considering each theme we have discussed in light of this simple phrase, the example of Jesus becomes plain and evident. Considering this theme as Paul concludes his teaching will tie everything together:

See that no one repays another with evil for evil...

1 Thessalonians 5:15: See that no one repays another with evil for evil…

Jesus never did this! He suffered great evil and did not react in any evil way. His example shows tremendous forbearance and selfless love. He showed so many spiritually-driven characteristics.

This is well summed up in a prophecy about Jesus:

Isaiah 53:7: He was oppressed and he was afflicted, yet he did not open his mouth; like a lamb that is led to slaughter, and like a sheep that is silent before its shearers, so he did not open his mouth.

Revenge is personal and emotional. It is about getting even and is often fueled by anger or resentment. Retaliation can be a little more calculated response. Sometimes we frame it as justice or self-protection.

Regardless of motive, the Christian response is to choose mercy and trust God for justice:

1 Corinthians 6:7–8: 7 Actually, then, it is already a defeat for you, that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded? 8 On the contrary, you yourselves wrong and defraud. You do this even to your brethren.

This seems harsh. People are inclined to sue others for money or over what is rightfully theirs, such as property or a privilege. Paul is questioning whether this demand should occur amongst the brotherhood. If it’s rightfully ours, shouldn’t we be able to demand that right? Doesn’t that let the other person get away with taking what is ours? Paul is helping us see that we need to rise to a higher level.

Jesus was wrongfully put to death, yet he did not open his mouth.

Would lawsuits among the brotherhood be an example of repaying evil for evil? This is a dramatic but important example.

What if our manager at work criticizes us? Do we withhold our efforts on the next project we work on? Do we say a few unkind words and gossip about that manager to get back at them in some way? If a family member gets angry and yells at us, are we going to respond sarcastically or with harsh language? Do we rehearse potential evil responses in our minds, even if we never take action?

Romans 12:14–19: 14 Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. 15 Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. 16 Be of the same mind toward one another; do not be haughty in mind, but associate with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own estimation. 17 Never pay back evil for evil to anyone. Respect what is right in the sight of all men. 18 If possible, so far as it depends on you, be at peace with all men. 19 Never take your own revenge, beloved, but leave room for the wrath of God, for it is written, VENGEANCE IS MINE, I WILL REPAY, says the Lord.

These texts are straightforward. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. Rejoice. Make sure that you have the same mind toward one another, that you are always looking at the good side of one another.

ADMONISH | ENCOURAGE | HELP | FORBEAR | LIVE AS JESUS LIVED

God’s judgment is just AND merciful! Let us completely rest in His wisdom. Do we think God is unaware, or not paying attention to our circumstances so that we need take matters into our own hands? Leave vengeance where it belongs!

but always seek after that which is good for one another and for all people...

1 Thessalonians 5:15: …but always seek after that which is good for one another and for all people.

This is exactly what Jesus did! He sought good for ALL by following God’s will and paying the ransom price.

A prophecy describing Jesus:

Isaiah 53:11–12: (NIV2011) 11 After he has suffered, he will see the light of life and be satisfied; by his knowledge my righteous servant will justify many, and he will bear their iniquities. 12 Therefore I will give him a portion among the great, and he will divide the spoils with the strong, because he poured out his life unto death, and was numbered with the transgressors. For he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

Jesus always handled the harshness of others with an eye towards the greater good. In that moment of space between the stimulus and our response, we can consider and choose the reaction that will benefit our highest spiritual welfare, as well as the highest spiritual welfare of the person who is making us so mad.

This takes forbearance. In that space, we apply forbearance and selfless love, and then we try as best we can to live like Jesus lived!

Live like Jesus lived! Live intentionally, not by just reacting. Live by seeking good for ALL by following God’s will. We can’t do what Jesus did, but we can follow in his footsteps and do our best to act with selfless love.

1 Peter 3:8–9: 8 To sum up, all of you be harmonious, sympathetic, brotherly, kindhearted, and humble in spirit; 9 not returning evil for evil or insult for insult, but giving a blessing instead; for you were called for the very purpose that you might inherit a blessing.

Jesus never returned evil for evil. He was always looking to plant seeds of growth and hope. We must see that no one in the church repays evil for evil, but only seeks that which is good for one another and for all people.

It was obviously a problem in the early church because this is the third time we are being told not to repay evil for evil. It’s still a problem today because human nature is reactive. Human nature is about “me.” Spiritual nature is about God. We need to change ourselves to be part of that new creation so that we are about godly things. Live like Jesus lived!

Even when we are challenged, slandered or persecuted, follow in Jesus’ footsteps and seek good for all by being faithful to what we are called:

1 Peter 3:15–17: 15 but sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts, always being ready to make a defense to everyone who asks you to give an account for the hope that is in you…

What is that hope? The good news of great joy that will be for ALL the people (Luke 2:10).

...yet with gentleness and reverence; 16 and keep a good conscience so that in the thing in which you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ will be put to shame. 17 For it is better, if God should will it so, that you suffer for doing what is right rather than for doing what is wrong.

Our Christian lives will include suffering. Do I want to suffer for the sake of God and God’s righteousness and Christlikeness, or do I want to suffer because I was angry and lashed out? There is going to be suffering either way. If we choose the godly path and follow in Jesus’ footsteps, our contribution to those around us is to never repay evil for evil, but always put something good, something blessed, something hopeful in place of that evil.

We can never build a relationship on evil for evil. But we can build bridges and tremendous fortresses of peace and love on the basis of sowing seeds of goodness and righteousness, kindness, love and compassion.

This is what the Apostle Paul is teaching us. It is about giving to all of the body of Christ, all of the church, so that we can build each other up.

Paul is teaching us about not just contributing to the brotherhood, but mutually contributing. All of us together, working from wherever we may be in our experiences, in our lives, in our trials, in our tribulations, and so forth, and finding ways to be giving, to be contributing, to building others up.

It comes down to admonishing when admonishing is needed, encouraging when encouraging is needed, helping when somebody just can’t, and holding “self” back so that we can instead give something godly. We put all of these together and walk in Jesus’ footsteps.

Live like he lived, contribute to the body of Christ, and make the environment in which you worship something beautiful and special.

So, how can we each contribute to the health of our church?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

## Episode 1400 — What Does It Mean to Rejoice Always? (Christian Conduct Series)
Published: 2025-09-01
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1400-rejoice-always/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/31170200/CQ_Rewind_09-01-2025_What_Does_It_Mean_To_Rejoice_Always.pdf

What Does It Mean to Rejoice Always? (Christian Conduct Series)

1 Thessalonians 5:16: Rejoice always.

A Christian life is supposed to be an energized and fulfilled life. It is supposed to be this way because we have been called to follow in Jesus’ footsteps. This means our lives are to be centered around following God’s word and will, regardless of what circumstances may lie before us. So, when things are going smoothly and difficulties seem to be at a minimum, we can rejoice and thank God for His providence. By the same reasoning, when things are unstable, disastrous and traumatic, we can rejoice and thank God for His providence! Wait, what? How do we do that? How do we find and embrace true rejoicing in our lives when our external circumstances and internal emotional state are breaking down?

This episode is the third in our Christian Conduct Series, where we are carefully examining God’s instructions to us given by the Apostle Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5:12-24.

Let’s do a quick recap from our previous two episodes. In the few instructions before this admonition, the Apostle Paul instructed us in two specific aspects of our Christian life.

The first aspect is all about showing appreciation for those who shepherd us:

1 Thessalonians 5:12-13: 12 But we request of you, brethren, that you appreciate those who diligently labor among you, and have charge over you in the Lord and give you instruction, 13 and that you esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Live in peace with one another.

Live in peace with one another is a solid foundation for the second aspect— learning to mutually and consistently contribute to the health of our fellowship:

1 Thessalonians 5:14-15: 14 We urge you, brethren, admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with everyone. 15 See that no one repays another with evil for evil, but always seek after that which is good for one another and for all people.

These two aspects of our lives are about our relationship with our brotherhood, first with those who lead and then with all who follow. Paul seems to be saying, Now that you have seen what you are supposed to look like and how you are supposed to act towards all, I will encourage you to grow from the inside out.

Paul next introduced six, powerful internal growth lessons:

Rejoice always

Pray without ceasing

In everything give thanks

Quench not the spirit

Despise not prophesyings; prove all things

Abstain from all appearance of evil

One of our brothers in Christ, Carl, pointed out how in 1 Thessalonians 5, the Apostle Paul effectively used the “staccato” technique—short, impactful phrases that stand out. Paul made this series of admonitions short and to the point, making them powerful and memorable.

Paul says few words here, but they all have powerful meaning.

In this episode, we will examine the first impactful lesson on the list:

1 Thessalonians 5:16: Rejoice <5463> always <3842>.

Rejoice: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5463 chairo; a primary verb; to be cheerful, i.e. calmly happy or well-off; impersonally, especially as a salutation (on meeting or parting), be well

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to rejoice, be glad 2) to rejoice exceedingly 3) to be well, thrive

Always: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3842 pantote; every when, i.e. at all times

Based on these definitions, the meaning of rejoice always is “be calmly happy and thrive at all times.” The other five stacatto admonitions follow this one. Because we see these six lessons of our internal growth in Christ as interconnected, we will look at rejoice always as a foundation.

Let’s begin with the obvious questions regarding rejoice always:

What about trials, loss or grieving? When things are going wrong and there is trauma all around, how do we rejoice? It sounds unreasonable.

There are some beautiful lessons in developing this perspective. We suggest this rejoicing fits the definitions of “calmly happy” and/or “thriving.” Here’s why:

First, we look at Jesus’ actions and responses as he underwent pain and suffering:

Hebrews 12:2-3: 2 Fixing our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy <5479> set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. 3 For consider him who has endured such hostility by sinners against himself, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.

Joy is the noun form of the word rejoice we previously defined.

Joy: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5479 chara; noun from 5463; cheerfulness, i.e. calm delight

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) joy, gladness 1a) the joy received from you 1b) the cause or occasion of joy 1b1) of persons who are one’s joy

Who for the joy set before him endured the cross—Jesus had a calm and internal gladness as he underwent unspeakable shame, pain, injustice and dishonor. He thrived on his Father’s will, and in so doing, showed us how to thrive even when things aren’t going the way we would like them to.

Before Jesus came to earth, he experienced joy by helping his heavenly Father create all things. Paying the ransom price on the cross for Adam ensured the resurrection of the entire human creation—everyone who has ever lived.

The joy set before him was the promise of God’s future kingdom and helping mankind come into harmony with God. Jesus’ joy was a state of being as he honored his Father’s plan and will.

The joy we’re talking about is not about feelings and emotions. Even when Jesus was going through very difficult times, he was able to mainain an internal joy based on what was set before him. This was the base he relied upon because it meant the accomplishment of the Father’s will.

We can’t find a higher example than Jesus, but let’s look at the apostles who also teach us how to rejoice always:

In Acts 5, very soon after Pentecost, the apostles got into a lot of trouble with the Jewish leaders for preaching.

The leaders did NOT want to hear the gospel and the name of Jesus. The apostles were thrown into prison (the Bible does not say which of the apostles), escaped with the help of an angel, went back to preaching and then were in danger of being killed. Gamaliel, the respected Pharisee who taught Saul of Tarsus, advised that these apostles should not be killed.

Here’s what happened—this is where the rejoicing comes into play:

Acts 5:40-42: 40 They took his (Gamaliel’s) advice; and after calling the apostles in, they flogged them and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and then released them. 41 So they (the apostles) went on their way from the presence of the Council, rejoicing <5463> that they had been considered worthy to suffer shame for his name.

Verse 40 refers to the apostles collectively, without naming individuals. However, earlier in Acts 5:29, Peter and the other apostles are mentioned as being arrested and questioned by the Sanhedrin. So while Peter was certainly among them, the exact list of who was beaten isn’t detailed.

They were just beaten, and yet they were rejoicing! They were hurting, but they were rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer shame for his name. They had a sense of focus, clarity and gratitude to be a part of God’s mission for them. Rejoicing doesn’t have to be an outward celebration; it is an inner strength and focus.

42 And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they kept right on teaching and preaching Jesus as the Christ.

Nothing could stop their focus on following in Jesus’ footsteps. What wonderful examples!

They were beaten and firmly instructed not to do it again. Yet they continued to preach every day in the temple and from house to house. They didn’t hide because they were rejoicing in doing the Father’s will.

The apostles were “thriving” in the call to follow Jesus, no matter how much they were threatened and hurt! This is not about feeling euphoric; it is about being centered and calm in ALL circumstances!

Let’s go back to Jesus for a moment.

His teachings added the more emotional response that is built upon our calm rejoicing:

Matthew 5:11-12: 11 Blessed are you when people insult you and persecute you, and falsely say all kinds of evil against you because of me. 12 Rejoice <5463> and be glad <21>, for your reward in heaven is great; for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were before you.

Glad: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #21 agalliao; from agan (much) and 242; properly, to jump for joy, i.e. exult

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: to glorify, exult in, rejoice exceedingly, be exceedingly glad

Now, here’s the excitement and emotion. The word for glad literally means “to jump for joy” or “exult.” It’s that adrenaline-filled rush with a sense of glory, wonder and energy. This is very different from rejoicing.

Notice how the addition of be glad is directly related to our future reward— Rejoice and be glad for your reward in heaven is great. Rejoicing (thriving) is to be an “all the time thing” for us now. However, the exultation kind of joy is added at appropriate times. It’s not always there. The scripture doesn’t say “rejoice and be glad always.” It says rejoice always. Be glad comes into play at certain times under certain circumstances.

If we are found faithful, what is the future reward? Glory, honor and immortality. As spiritual sons of God, we will help to bless all the families of the earth and work side-by- side with Jesus. Now that’s exciting and motivating!

That YES! feeling is exultation. Rejoicing is that calm centeredness inside our being that thrives on doing God’s will.

We’ve looked at Jesus and his example, the apostles and their example. Now let’s look at ourselves:

It is fitting that the Apostle Peter is the one to show us what our present “thriving and rejoicing” should look like. He observed it in Jesus and was among the very first to experience it himself—remember his experiences in Acts 5 when they rejoiced under such difficult circumstances.

Here is what Peter tells us:

1 Peter 4:12-14: 12 Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal among you, which comes upon you for your testing, as though some strange thing were happening to you; 13 but to the degree that you share the sufferings of Christ, keep on rejoicing <5463>...

What did the apostles do after they were beaten? They rejoiced. Peter is not telling us this to make himself look good. He is telling us this because this is what works in a spiritually- oriented life and heart. We want that sense of rejoicing, even in the face of our trials.

...So that also at the revelation of his glory you may rejoice <5463> with exultation <21> (that’s the “jump for joy” word). 14 If you are reviled for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the spirit of glory and of God rests on you.

Peter is reminding us of the mindset to keep going. He tells us that the exultation is not necessarily present while we are experiencing difficulty, but it is to come.

Again, Rejoice always is that calm centeredness, thriving on doing the will of God, whatever the circumstances, so we can move forward and move up.

Keep on rejoicing; keep on thriving as you stay centered on your ultimate goal in life. When it is achieved, you can rejoice with great joy! That is excitement—and that is appropriate.

Exultation will not be there every day of our lives. There are too many uncertainties and ups and downs, but the rejoicing can always remain in place.

Two words come to mind: peace and trust. We need peace and trust that God will overrule in our lives so we can keep rejoicing, come what may.

Come what may—that touches me because it reminds me of a very difficult time in our lives as a family. Several times on this podcast, we have shared that our youngest daughter was assaulted when she was 15. It was a very traumatic, difficult time for several years. There was a lot of rebuilding that had to go on.

My task was to be her dad, to be that steady firmness that helped her hold onto something stable, so she could move forward and do everything else in life.

Rejoicing is not something you would think would fit into times like that, but here is how God overruled with me personally.

Christian Questions was a two-hour radio broadcast at that time. No matter what was happening outside, that had to be done. Focusing on that every single week kept me sane, kept me straight and able to focus on the next day because I was pressed to be in the Scriptures. Being in the Scriptures reminded me that God has got this. He is the God of eternity. He could certainly walk our family (and me) through this period of trial. So, for a couple of years of very uncertain life circumstances, my rejoicing came through the challenge of showing up every week. By God’s grace, this gave me strength so I could give her strength.

Looking back, I realize that is what “thriving” in doing God’s will looks like, even if it is uncomfortable. That is a “rejoice always” scenario.

Our “rejoice always” state of being needs selfless love driven by truth to feed its growth:

1 Corinthians 13:4-7: 4 Love is patient (forbearing), love is kind and is not jealous; love does not brag and is not arrogant, 5 does not act unbecomingly; it does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not take into account a wrong suffered, 6 does not rejoice <5463> in unrighteousness...

There is no “calm happiness” in unrighteousness.

...but rejoices <4796> with the truth; 7 bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

Love rejoices with the truth. It has that calm, firm clarity—the state of being that keeps us moving forward. That’s what selfless love is. Our rejoice always is fed by our development of this selfless love, which is not looking for anything in return. It is benevolent, always just looking to give.

It’s a powerful combination. Be stable, strong and calmly happy because it’s not about fleeting emotion. It’s about having our heart and mind focused on doing God’s will each and every day with the sense that it is God who carries us.

As we continue developing this internal state of being (living in a state of always rejoicing), Paul shows us a way to expand it to others:

Philippians 2:14-18: 14 Do all things without grumbling or disputing; 15 so that you will prove yourselves to be blameless and innocent, children of God above reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you appear as lights in the world, 16 holding fast the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I will have reason to glory because I did not run in vain nor toil in vain.

Paul is talking about their faithfulness. In many ways, his well-being depended on the faithfulness of his brethren because he had invested so much into them. Their faithfulness “fed” him.

17 But even if I am being poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice <5463> and share <4796> my joy with <4796> you all. 18 You too, I urge you, rejoice <5463> in the same way and share <4796> your joy with <4796> me.

Share joy with: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4796 sugchairo; from 4862 and 5463; to sympathize in gladness, congratulate

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to rejoice with, take part in another’s joy

2) to rejoice together, to congratulate

The words share and joy with mean we sympathize in gladness. We take part in another’s joy. This personal connection is so important.

Paul is saying, “Even though I am being poured out as a drink offering (when pouring out a drink offering, there is nothing left in the pitcher), even though my life is being poured out to its end, I rejoice and share my joy with you. I have that calm happiness and thriving within myself, and I am sending it to you. I want you to have that as well, and to send it back to me.

Our rejoice always state of mind is not meant for merely keeping ourselves calm, happy and thriving. Its greater purpose is to be shared with others to remind, encourage and uplift! We need to let each other know of our rejoicing, and we need to share in the rejoicing because that gives others a stronger basis upon which to thrive.

As we share our rejoice always state of being with others, we are reminded to “go beyond” our normal life circumstances because our lives are to be sacrificed daily, as Jesus’ life was.

These verses sound a little harsh, but we are going to look at them in the context of rejoicing:

1 Corinthians 7:29-30: 29 But this I say, brethren, the time has been shortened, so that from now on those who have wives should be as though they had none;

Paul is NOT saying to ignore your spouse. He is saying those married have that godly covenant between them. With that as the basis, they are able to reach beyond that relationship to give more to others. The marriage relationship is good, but it is only the beginning of our “stretching.”

30 And those who weep, as though they did not weep...

Paul is not saying, “Stop crying and pull yourself together!” He is saying that even through our trials and difficulties, we can learn to reach beyond our sadness and give more to others. We have watched those who are are going through difficult trials or great loss still reach out to others and touch them with grace and encouragement. We should not be stuck in our sadness and weeping. We can thrive because God is with us. We can then reach out to touch others, understanding their grief, to bless and build them up.

...and those who rejoice <5463>, as though they did not rejoice <5463>…

Paul is not saying to stop rejoicing. He is saying that rejoicing has to be expanded. Reach beyond just our own thriving to give more to others. When we talk about rejoice always, it is not just about us and how we feel. It is about our certainty of the privileges this rejoicing within us brings.

All of this points to the ultimate faithfulness that will be celebrated in heaven and on earth.

This is a voice in heaven, rejoicing as well:

Revelation 19:7-8: 7 Let us rejoice <5463> and be glad <21> and give the glory to him, for the marriage of the Lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready. 8 It was given to her to clothe herself in fine linen, bright and clean; for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.

Rejoice and be glad. Again, be glad is the “YES!” exultation that the hard work of development has been done, and the bride of Christ has made herself ready. Being clothed in fine linen, the righteous acts of the saints, has everything to do with rejoice always and living in that daily thriving in the Lord’s service. It contributes to the heavenly rejoicing and the heavenly exultation at the recognition of ultimate faithfulness.

Heaven rejoices in our faithfulness, just like Paul rejoiced in the faithfulness of the Philippians! Rejoice always.

The love of God that comes through Jesus should come into us and pass out of us to others. We thrive in the concept of simply being God’s children, doing God’s will, following His guidance, providence and spirit.

Let’s understand how important it is to rejoice always in Christ every day. Even if we are weeping, even if we are sad or confused, we can still rejoice because we are held in the palm of the hand of God through Jesus. Rejoice always!

So, what does it mean to rejoice always?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
