## Episode 1401 — What Does It Mean to Pray Without Ceasing? (Christian Conduct Series)
Published: 2025-09-08
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1401-pray-without-ceasing/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/05143623/CQ_Rewind_09-08-2025_What_Does_It_Mean_to_Pray_Without_Ceasing.pdf

What Does It Mean to Pray Without Ceasing? (Christian Conduct Series)

1 Thessalonians 5:17: Pray without ceasing.

To live a truly dedicated Christian life is to live a life that has a firm grasp on prayer. It is a life that strongly and regularly seeks out God’s will and blessing in all that we do. It also seeks to regularly ask for blessings and providence over the lives of our fellow disciples. Many scriptures teach us about how to pray and how not to pray. So, how does all of this fit into the life of a Christian living in the 21st century? Does the fact that our life experiences are so vastly different than the times of the apostles change or alter anything? We are taught to pray without ceasing. How can we practically accomplish this on top of managing all of life's other responsibilities?

This episode is the third in our Christian Conduct Series, where we are carefully examining God’s instructions to us given by the Apostle Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5:12-24.

Before we get into pray without ceasing, let’s do a quick recap of 1 Thessalonians 5:12-15 to see how Paul got us to this point. In these verses, Paul taught the Thessalonian brethren and us about respecting and appreciating our shepherds—our church leaders. He then taught us how to mutually care for each other and thereby contribute to the health of our church.

Paul next introduced six powerful, internal and interconnected growth lessons:

Rejoice always

Pray without ceasing

In everything give thanks

Quench not the spirit

Despise not prophesyings; prove all things

Abstain from all appearance of evil

The first of these lessons serves as a foundation for the rest of them.

1 Thessalonians 5:16: Rejoice always.

This is one of those we call the “staccato” texts— short, impactful phrases that stand out from the Apostle Paul’s usually longer sentences.

To rejoice always is to live with a thriving, calm and happy state of mind—not euphoria. This state of mind is nourished by focusing on the scriptural examples of Jesus and the brotherhood handling their trials, sufferings and testing.

The answer to HOW we rejoice always is in the next two staccato lessons:

This mindset of rejoicing always is a solid base for Paul’s next important lesson:

1 Thessalonians 5:17: Pray <4336> without ceasing <89>.

Pray: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4336 proseuchomai; from #4314 and #2172; to pray to God, i.e. supplicate, worship

Without ceasing: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #89: adialeiptos; adverb from #88; uninterruptedly, i.e. without omission (on an appropriate occasion)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) without intermission, incessantly, without ceasing

The Greek word for without ceasing means “constantly recurring,” “without intermission,” “incessantly.” It implies a continuity. Does this mean we are supposed to pray out loud, 24/7? No, pray without ceasing is the attitude of prayerfulness that should never be turned off.

Just like rejoice always, pray without ceasing is a state of being. It’s having a continual lifeline of sincere, trusting communication with our Father.

The broad-based word for pray includes a wide variety of prayer types. The message is to be regularly in a prayerful state of mind without omitting any part of our experience or opportunity!

Now we consider the practicality of HOW we can do this. Let’s examine some examples of the kinds of things Paul said he did without ceasing:

1 Thessalonians 1:2–3: 2 We give thanks to God always (at all times) for all of you, making mention of you in our prayers <4335> (noun form of #4336); 3 constantly <89> bearing in mind your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ in the presence of our God and Father.

Paul prayerfully and continually remembers the Thessalonians for WHO they were and WHAT they stood for. He is going back to bearing in mind your work of faith and labor of

love and steadfastness. He is remembering what he saw and who they were becoming, constantly bringing that before the Lord. This is one of his pray without ceasing examples.

Paul is praying constantly. He is showing them this was important to him, and therefore important to bring before the heavenly Father:

1 Thessalonians 2:13: For this reason we also constantly <89> thank God that when you received the word of God which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men, but for what it really is, the word of God, which also performs its work in you who believe.

Again, he is constantly praying. He is living pray without ceasing. Paul continually prayed in gratitude regarding HOW the Thessalonians wholeheartedly accepted God’s word under severe conditions.

The experience of the Thessalonians was very difficult. Paul was only able to be with them for a short time before he was forced to leave town. He is remembering how they received the word even though they risked persecution. He is going back to something that already happened, and yet he prays about it again and again. Why? Because he is so grateful. He is bringing this before God over and over, even though it already happened, because it motivates him.

This is an important principle, because this continued prayer of thanks shows us the apostle’s deep appreciation of God's calling being so genuinely and impactfully received by these brethren.

DON'T FORGET THE BLESSINGS! Bring them before God.

Let’s go a little further to another example of something Paul does without ceasing:

Romans 1:9: (KJV) For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of His son, that without ceasing <89> I make mention of you always in my prayers <4335>;

Without ceasing (incessantly) doesn’t mean Paul never ate or slept; it just means “continually.”

Here, his prayerful attitude is towards the brotherhood in general, not limited to the Thessalonians.

Paul’s prayerful attitude towards the brotherhood was regularly engaged because his gratitude for the brotherhood was regularly engaged. Paul’s prayers verified his gratitude. They made his gratitude even greater, because he brought that gratitude before the Father.

What might this look like?

Micro prayers or breath prayers: A few words you can say in a single breath, whispering thanks, asking for wisdom or expressing concern to God in real time.

Echo prayers: Reciting memorized scriptures back to God.

Flare prayers: Short and often in a state of distress, decision-making or even desperation. Think of an emergency flare sent up in darkness as a call to rescue.

Inner Dialogue: Keeping an open line of communication with God in our minds, like walking with someone whom we trust.

The point is to develop a spiritual reflex, where we instinctively turn to God regardless of whether things are going well, really bad, or somewhere in between.

These are good examples that give us permission to use these forms of prayer in our lives.

In my own experience, all of these forms of prayer are regularly present in my life, especially when I’m counseling those having troubles and difficulties. Those “flare prayers” go up like fireworks sometimes—Lord, I don’t know what to say. Lord, help them to be calm. Inevitably, there appears a pathway for me to follow. So, it’s important to have prayer as that ever-present experience, that ever-present state of mind that helps us get through things.

How do more specific types of prayers fit into our pray without ceasing mentality?

Philippians 4:6–7: 6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer <4335> and supplication <1162> with thanksgiving (grateful language…you can’t be thankful and resentful at the same time) let your requests be made known to God. 7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Supplication: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1162 deesis; a petition

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) need, indigence, want, privation, penury

2) a seeking, asking, entreating, entreaty to God or to man

Supplication comes from a Greek word meaning “petition,” which comes from another Greek word meaning “to beg” or “to plead.” This is a specific, earnest request. It’s not just general prayer—it’s asking God for something with deep need and humility.

Paul pairs the general act of communing with God (prayer) with the specific act of asking (supplication). In other words, he’s saying, Talk to God about everything, and don’t be afraid to ask Him for what you need.

Asking for what we need is often a very intense experience because sometimes our needs are very intense. This is what supplication or petition really means—This has been profoundly on my mind. These prayers of supplication are to be included in our regular prayer activities.

Notice how supplication is coupled with thanksgiving. This is no accident, as our deep entreaty to God is best offered in the context of an overwhelmingly thankful heart expressed with thankful words and pouring out your heart for what you need. Having thankfulness as the base helps us to appropriately express our deep needs. God gets it! But we want to show Him our gratitude for even listening and then wait for His providence to unfold.

There is a fine line between that and demanding something of God. This isn’t demanding.

We hear of people who follow the Prosperity Gospel say we are to “Decree and declare” and “Name it and claim it,” directing God what He needs to do or not do. Is that supplication? Is that how we claim the promises in the Bible?

Actually, we think “Decree and declare” is a form of idolatry. This is proclaiming and demanding what is going to happen. The person who decrees and declares is taking the place of God by demanding that God do something for him or her. That’s an idolatrous way to approach the humility of prayer: You shall have no other gods before Me.

Jesus himself prayed with supplication for what he needed. But he always prayed with the attitute of, Nevertheless, not my will, but Thy will be done. Incidentally, when he prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane to have the “cup” removed from him, God did not grant the request. Jesus needed to go through the full experience.

In summary, supplication is an intense request to have a need fulfilled, be it for ourselves or others. While this is not always how we pray, it is certainly an important part of our praying without ceasing.

In Ephesians, Paul reminds us to pray in the spirit, as we pray with supplication:

Ephesians 6:18: (KJV) praying <4336> always with all prayer <4335> and supplication <1162> in the spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication <1162> for all saints;

Before explaining praying in the spirit, the context is that the last seven verses were all about putting on the whole armor of God to be able to withstand evil. Now that you are all suited up, you do not go into battle without prayer!

And look around—we are to make supplication for all saints—we aren’t alone on that battlefield. We’re concerned for the safety of our fellow soldiers, too.

What does it mean to pray in the spirit?

In the spirit implies that we are focusing our prayers on seeing matters handled by God’s grace, by God’s spirit and in God’s way—not MY way!

In other words, I am going to say, “Lord, I want this to unfold in this way, if it is Your will.” We state our preference and then lay it before the Lord. Our requests should be in the attitude of rejoicing in whatever the answer is.

To pray in the spirit removes self from being the centerpiece and allows God’s spirit to be the conduit through which we can communicate. Therefore we receive what His will is. We have to be in the mindset of being able to give up self.

When we have these big petitions and supplications, we can easily get into the mindset of telling God what to do. We can tell Him how we feel, which is perfectly acceptable. But we need to be sure we are truly looking for His guidance and are willing to put our preferences completely aside.

Praying without ceasing is not about repetition; rather, it is about sincerity:

Matthew 6:7–8: 7 And when you are praying, do not use meaningless repetition as the Gentiles do, for they suppose that they will be heard for their many words. 8 So do not be like them; for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.

Sometimes if something big is happening in my life, I might pray the same prayer over and over as I’m going through the experience. Should I be worried that it’s wrong to repeat a prayer, or repeat scriptures out loud that I have memorized? Why pray this prayer at all if God already knows what I am going to say before I ask Him?

First, the repetition part: It is not wrong to repeat a prayer, but let’s make sure that it maintains its meaning as we do so.

When you are praying, do not use meaningless repetition as the Gentiles do. Meaningless repetition is just that—it is filling up space. Repetition with great intensity and great meaning is very different and acceptable.

Of course, repeating scriptures is always appropriate. For example, Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on Thee (Isaiah 26:3 KJV). Lord, my mind is trying to be stayed on You, but I don’t feel a perfect peace, and You said You will keep me in perfect peace when my mind is stayed on You. That kind of repetition is important because it is the sincere pouring out of the heart.

Many Christians pray the Lord’s Prayer (Our Father Who art in heaven…), a beautiful example of what prayer should look like. In repeating it, am I really dwelling on it or just repeating the words? We don’t want to just check the “I prayed” box. Prayer is not about just repeating the words; it's about sincere communication.

Why should I pray if God already knows what I need before I ask Him?

Because we need to put it in His hands, and He can answer us by letting us have our faith in Him solely and completely. He will uphold us with His righteous right hand, but we have to go there. This is where we have to live. Prayer brings us there. Yes, God already knows, but He needs us to know that He knows, to have faith in His knowing and to have faith in His providence.

Paul continues this thought of sincere, spiritually-sound prayers.

He asks for specific prayers, likely specific supplications/intercessions on his behalf for his own strength, clarity and fortitude:

Ephesians 6:18–20: (KJV) 18 Praying always with all prayer and supplication <1162> in the spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication <1162> for all saints; 19 and for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel, 20 for which I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.

Paul is asking for supplication on his own behalf. “I’m imprisoned and need your prayers for my encouragement to do what I am supposed to do. I am feeling weak; pray for me.” He is appropriately asking for others to make supplication on his behalf.

In addition to our continually prayerful attitude and action, we see the importance of supplication for God’s will in our own challenges as well as intercession for others with their challenges. Let us not be afraid to bring those in our brotherhood before God with their challenges and ask for His will to be done in their lives. We should also ask for mercy and grace and direction as to how we can be a blessing to them.

Jesus absolutely had a pray without ceasing attitude. He would seek solitude to be with his Father, he would sometimes pray all night, and he brought his deepest and most intense needs before God.

This scripture reveals a depth and intensity that is not elsewhere mentioned in Scripture:

Hebrews 5:7–9: 7 In the days of his flesh, he offered up both prayers <1162> and supplications <2428> with loud crying and tears to the One able to save him from <1537> death,* and he was heard because of his piety. 8 Although he was a son, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered. 9 And having been made perfect, he became to all those who obey him the source of eternal salvation,

From: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1537 ek is a primary preposition

denoting origin (the point whence action or motion proceeds), from, out

(of place, time, or cause); literal or figurative

*This is more accurately translated save him out of death.

Hebrews 5:7: (Darby) Who in the days of his flesh, having offered up both supplications and entreaties to him who was able to save him out of death, with strong crying and tears; (and having been heard because of his piety;)

This was really the ultimate prayer at the ultimate crisis. Jesus is fully identifying with human suffering. This word for supplications is a different Greek word used once in the Bible. In writing the book of Hebrews, Paul chose a word that would have been familiar to that culture:

Supplication: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2428 hiketeria; from a derivative of the base of #2425 (through the idea of approaching for a favor); intreaty

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) an olive branch 1a) for suppliants approached the one whose aid they would implore holding an olive branch entwined with white wool and fillets*, to signify that they came as suppliants 2) supplication

*In ancient Greek ritual, the word “fillets” referred to narrow bands or ribbons of cloth—typically wool or linen—used in sacred ceremonies. When a person approached a ruler seeking mercy or protection, they would carry an olive branch wrapped in white wool and fillets. This visual symbol marked their peaceful intent and humble posture. The fillets, often entwined with the branch, signified purity, sacredness and vulnerability. They signaled that the person came in reverence, not rebellion.

(Source: Bible Commentary by David Guzik) This word means “an olive branch wrapped in wool” because that is what the ancient Greek worshipper held and waved to express their desperate prayer and desire.

This was a visual symbol showing peaceful and humble intent, sacredness and vulnerability. In modern times, we know waving a white flag symbolizes surrender.

Notice the word prayers <1162> in Hebrews 5:7 is the Greek word for supplications. The special supplications <2428> word used only once is then added. Jesus offered up petitions and then this entreaty, which was incredibly deep.

Jesus’ prayers were raw, earnestly laid out before his Father, knowing the gravity of the situation in having to pay the ransom price for all of mankind.

The end result of his life and his prayers: he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him.

(Source: Bible Commentary by David Guzik) Significantly, this supplication of Jesus took place in a garden of olives—and he supplied the “wool,” being the Lamb of God.

The depth and intensity of Jesus’ prayers are an example for us to follow. God is willing to hear and answer our prayers. We need to put ourselves in the right attitude.

Psalm 62:8: Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before Him; God is a refuge for us. Selah.

Jesus’ attachment to his Father was so strong that he pleaded that his work and mission were acceptable, and that he would therefore be raised out of death. His mission had to be perfectly completed. While we don’t have the same mission, our pray without ceasing can also appropriately include intense pleading.

Our praying without ceasing also includes the necessity of praying based upon the words of Jesus and the word of God:

John 15:7–8: 7 If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. 8 My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit, and so prove to be my disciples.

My words abide in you—this goes well beyond just listening. Jesus’ words must abide in us; they take root and grow. Our Christianity is based on the word of God.

Spiritual fruitage is a result of spiritual growth and development nurtured by the Bible and not by our own ideas, preferences and desires. We make sure the words of Jesus and the word of God overall dwell within us so they direct us. That is part of praying in the spirit.

Our praying without ceasing needs to the best of our ability; in all cases have a solid basis of thanksgiving and praise:

Colossians 4:2–4: 2 Devote yourselves to prayer <4335>, keeping alert in it with an attitude of thanksgiving (grateful language); 3 praying <4336> at the same time for us as well, that God will open up to us a door for the word, so that we may speak forth the mystery of Christ, for which I have also been imprisoned; 4 that I may make it clear in the way I ought to speak.

The Apostle Paul is telling us to be devoted to praying and keeping alert with the attitude of thanksgiving and gratitude as our baseline.

Even if life is falling apart, we know we can be grateful that God is always there. His providence will rule. We can always be grateful in the worst times and then put everything else in place.

We need that basis of thanksgiving and then have a basis of praise as well:

Hebrews 13:15: Through him (Jesus) then, let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that give thanks to his name.

Sacrifice of praise—this frames praise as a replacement for the original Temple sacrifices. A sacrifice implies giving something valuable. Praise becomes sacrificial when it’s offered even during difficult times. Think of Job: The LORD gave and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (Job 1:21). That’s sacrificial praise. Paul and Silas sang while in prison (Acts 16:25). Sacrificial praise is sometimes difficult to offer, but it reframes our circumstances and declares that God is still worthy regardless of how we are feeling. He is looking out for our best spiritual welfare.

God is praiseworthy at all times and places because He is eternal and His plan was from before the beginning of time. He is absolutely worthy of our praise, no matter what!

Fruit of lips—spiritual produce! We said earlier that Paul’s prayer verified his gratitude. Fruit is the outward appearance of what’s happening on the inside. This would be what comes from our mouths when our heart is aligned with God—like words, songs, prayers—offered continually, and all through Jesus. Praise shouldn’t be a reaction; it should be part of the rhythm of our communion with God.

Constantly here means “through all time.”

This is something uninterrupted and permanent:

Psalm 34:1: (NKJV) I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise shall continually be in my mouth.

This is fruit of lips! Such fruitage demonstrates depth, sincerity, clarity and intention, not prayer as a mindless activity.

We have the example of pray without ceasing. The Apostle Paul has demonstrated what it means by his own words and actions.

We have looked at different kinds of prayer coming from within. It allows us to communicate through Jesus to the Father, who has the power of providence over our lives and the power of His spirit to work through us and with us. Are we using this privilege?

So, what does it mean to pray without ceasing?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

It is interesting to observe how supplication is used throughout the New Testament. Sometimes the word prayer is the same as supplication—a supplication type of prayer being offered. Reading these texts helps us understand its importance.

Prayer/Supplication: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1162 deesis; a petition: prayer, supplication, request

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) need, indigence, want, privation, penury;

2) a seeking, asking, entreating, entreaty to God or to man

All uses in the King James Version:

Luke 1:13: But the angel said unto him, Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer <1162> is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John.

scriptures below and then give an example of how we can do this in our modern lives:

b. 1 Thessalonians 2:13 – What does praying about past events reveal about gratitude?

(Matthew 6:7-8)

might you improve?

## Episode 1402 — Can We Really Be Thankful in Everything? (Christian Conduct Series)
Published: 2025-09-15
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1402-thankful-in-everything/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/12113545/CQ_Rewind_09-15-2025_Can_We_Really_Be_Thankful_in_Everything.pdf

Can We Really Be Thankful in Everything? (Christian Conduct Series)

1 Thessalonians 5:18: In everything give thanks; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

One of the hallmark attitudes of a focused Christian life is being thankful. The very foundation of our Christian belief is the fact that being redeemed from sin and death by the love and sacrifice of Jesus is a gift that is, in every case, beyond our ability to earn or deserve. We are freely given life in Christ, and therefore, we have great motivation to live in a state of gratefulness. That being said, how far should this grateful attitude go? Is it really supposed to encompass each and every experience we have? Does being thankful in everything mean we should never be sad or anxious?

This episode is the fifth in our Christian Conduct Series, where we carefully examine God’s instructions to us given by the Apostle Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5:12-24.

We will examine the third of six briefly stated and yet powerfully connected “inside out” Christian Conduct lessons in 1 Thessalonians 5. We call these “staccato” texts—short, impactful phrases that stand out from the Apostle Paul’s usual longer sentences.

Rejoice always

Pray without ceasing

In everything give thanks

Quench not the spirit

Despise not prophesyings; prove all things

Abstain from all appearance of evil

Let’s do a quick recap from our previous two episodes.

Our first lesson was: 1 Thessalonians 5:16: Rejoice <5463> always<3842>.

Rejoice: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5463 chairo; calmly happy

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to rejoice, be glad 2) to rejoice exceedingly 3) to be well, thrive

Always: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3842 pantote; every when, i.e. at all times

This rejoicing is not emotional euphoria; it is a state of being that is calmly happy or thriving. It exemplifies working through any and all challenges with God’s power and providence nourishing and driving us.

Rejoice always is a foundation upon which the other five Christian Conduct lessons are built.

Next, we looked at: 1 Thessalonians 5:17: Pray <4336> without ceasing <89>.

Pray: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4336 proseuchomai; from #4314 and #2172; to pray to God, i.e. supplicate, worship

Without ceasing: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #89: adialeiptos; adverb from #88; uninterruptedly, i.e. without omission (on an appropriate occasion)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) without intermission, incessantly, without ceasing

The more we calmly rejoice and thrive in God’s will, the wider the door to pray without ceasing opens.

The message is to be regularly in a prayerful state of mind without omitting any part of our experience or opportunity.

This continuously prayerful mentality includes prayers of praise, worship, supplication and thanksgiving—all kinds of prayers given in all different kinds of ways.

With the concept of rejoicing always and praying ceaselessly, Paul now brings us to our third Christian Conduct lesson:

1 Thessalonians 5:18: In everything give thanks <2168>; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

Thanks: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2168 eucharisteo; verb from #2170; to be grateful, i.e. (actively) to express gratitude (towards); specially, to say grace at a meal

Thayer’s Greek English Lexicon: 1) to be grateful, feel thankful 2) give thanks

Gratitude toward God through Christ should drive the perception and processing of our life experiences. Paul says this is God’s will for us. Why does he say that here? These three are linked together as a collective process.

A rejoicing or thriving state of being creates a solid environment for growth.

A prayerful state of mind keeps us tapped into our truest source of strength.

A thankful state of perception opens and reopens our ability to receive and apply God’s direction.

This is ALL God’s will for us!

Let’s take a look at one example of the connection between rejoice always and in everything give thanks.

The next set of verses follows Paul’s earnest prayers to have his thorn in the flesh removed.

While the Apostle Paul does not use the word “rejoice,” look at the “thriving” he expresses:

2 Corinthians 12:9-10: 9 And he has said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness. Most gladly, therefore, I will rather boast about my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. 10 Therefore I am well content (think well of) with weaknesses, with insults, with distresses, with persecutions, with difficulties, for Christ’s sake; for when I am weak, then I am strong.

This text combines being grateful and rejoicing in spite of suffering. Paul is saying, “Thank you for NOT healing me so that I can rely on the strength of Christ. Thank you for saying no. Thank you for taking what I believed was a solid argument, brought before You for all the right reasons, and yet You are telling me no.”

This is a powerful example of what this thanksgiving is all about. Paul is not only thankful, he is glad to have these weaknesses because he sees it is through them that what he was hoping for actually comes. Through Jesus, God gave Paul the end result in a way he could not have even imagined.

If we truly thrive in God’s sufficiency through Christ in us, then perceiving our weaknesses with true thankfulness is absolutely in order! Paul had that thankful state of perception. He was able to perceive difficult things, thankfully embrace them, and make them powerful tools for growth, witnessing, praise and honor. It was a beautiful paradigm shift for him.

Our previous episode’s theme—pray without ceasing—integrally connected all three Christian Conduct lessons. Paul shows us these connections in his letter to the Philippians.

When reading the book of Philippians, we often think of it as a source of incredible rejoicing:

Philippians 4:6-7: 6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving <2169> let your requests be made known to God. 7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Thanksgiving: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2169 eucharistia; noun from #2170; gratitude; actively, grateful language (to God, as an act of worship)

Thayer’s Greek English Lexicon: 1) thankfulness 2) the giving of thanks

If we are anxious for nothing, it means we are thriving. Being anxious is the opposite of thriving. Paul encourages us to let go of our anxiousness. Thrive, pray and be thankful. We need to put these three together. This three-part approach is the solid basis for Christian being. By following this, we will be brought to the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, that will guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus—this a huge promise!

Paul likely understood this because he did it himself. He prayed and was grateful and thankful. This all connects like a mathematical equation:

THRIVING PRAYERFUL THANKFUL THE PEACE OF GOD WHICH SURPASSES ALL COMPREHENSION

Even if we do not like math, this is good to memorize to help us find peace in the midst of trouble.

We admit this is a hard decision. What happens if we are in the middle of grieving the loss of a loved one? What happens when we can’t find a job? What about marriage problems?

Having this state of gratitude, of perceiving events around us through the lens of thankful eyes, is like saying, “In the midst of my deepest troubles, I look up knowing the heavenly Father has this in His hands. I can’t see the answer. I can’t even fathom where the answer is, but I can be grateful because God has it under control.”

We can cope with such difficult things by transferring our anxiety and lifting it up to Him, then having that thankfulness begin to have an effect on our lives. That doesn’t mean God’s answer comes quickly. It means we can more readily cope and have endurance along the way.

This is a smaller example. We live in Connecticut, which is not known for tornadoes, but occasionally, we get them. And, occasionally, they like to visit me!

Five years ago, the last tornado to come through Connecticut came to my office. I had seen the weather warning, so I went home because our dogs freak out when the storm is bad. Then I got a phone call 15 minutes later, and somebody from the office building said I had better get back there. He didn’t tell me why.

I drove back, and the seven-minute drive took 40 minutes because trees and debris were down on the roads. I wondered what had happened! When I got to the office, I saw what had happened. This tornado came through, and half the aluminum roof got ripped, rolled up and thrown into the street. My office is on the top floor, and the water completely destroyed two offices. Mine was one of them.

When I went up the stairs, I saw all the damage, and it was so wet that I splashed just walking across the carpet. My gut reaction was to look up, and I said out loud, “I am still the most blessed person I know.”

I had no idea how to handle the mess, but that came with time, and the blessing proved itself. It wasn’t easy—it took eight months for the building to be rebuilt— but I was thankful to have come through the experience alive. We want to try to be thankful, even when things are really difficult.

There are so many scriptures about thanking God in prayer. Is our “thankfulness in all things” only to be expressed to God in prayer?

Interestingly, these words for thanks and thanksgiving are almost always related to prayer, but that does not mean we only focus our expressions of thanks toward God.

Let’s look at an example:

Paul had cause for concern for the Thessalonian church, which received the gospel under hard conditions. We talked about this in more detail in Episode #1398: “How Do We Genuinely Appreciate Those Who Guide Us?” (Christian Conduct Series). Paul founded the Thessalonian church but spent very little time with them since the Jews in the area were out to kill him and he had to flee.

As a result, he had great cause for concern for their spiritual welfare since they were new to Christianity with so little time for their preparation. He sent Timothy to them.

Timothy returned and reported what happened:

1 Thessalonians 3:6: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us good news of your faith and love, and that you always think kindly of us, longing to see us just as we also long to see you.

Paul’s deep concern was relieved because Timothy firmly reestablished the connection with the Thessalonians.

The results of Timothy’s trip must have brought vital comfort to Paul. This comfort was life-invigorating:

1 Thessalonians 3:7-8: 7 For this reason, brethren, in all our distress and affliction we were comforted about you through your faith; 8 for now we really live, if you stand firm in the Lord.

For now we (Paul speaking of himself) really live, if you stand firm in the Lord. This is a powerful connection that changes the way Paul is able to handle his own experiences. It lifts him up. This is what their connectivity did for him. Their spiritually strong state of being gave Paul deep inspiration and determination.

This vital comfort also provoked a deeper conviction to attain and maintain his state of rejoicing, prayer and thankfulness. Those three things were provoked in a positive way. This was not a state of euphoria; it was a state of being, a state of perception that reaffirmed that the Thessalonians were in God’s hands. I see your strength and His strength and will move forward with everything I have.

Let’s go to the next verses to see what happens:

1 Thessalonians 3:9-10: 9 For what thanks <2169> can we render to God for you in return for all the joy with which we rejoice <5463> before our God on your account, 10 as we night and day keep praying most earnestly that we may see your face, and may complete what is lacking in your faith?

Paul wrote to the Thessalonians to express his deep thanksgiving for them. This helps us understand that our own thankfulness, most often expressed to God in prayer, is also necessary to express to one another.

Within our Christian fellowship, we might struggle with this because we’re so worried about not puffing one another up with pride. Where’s the balance?

Rick: The Scriptures clearly teach that we should show thankfulness and gratitude. We need to check ourselves. If I say Jonathan was so instrumental in this or that, but I don’t want to tell him because I don’t want to puff him up, who might have the pride issue? Maybe it is me! I might be deciding that Jonathan’s character is too weak to handle the praise.

We have to be careful about why we withhold deserved praise. We should trust in the Lord and encourage others by saying, “I appreciate you. Keep up the good work; let’s work together.”

While we must be careful, it is important to thank our brethren because the Apostle Paul showed us this template for our activity and communication with one another.

Earlier we said a thankful state of perception opens and reopens our ability to receive and apply God’s direction. We are able to see all things through the eyes of gratefulness because we know God has it all in control.

Let’s examine another example of the Apostle Paul’s gratitude for others:

Romans 16:3-4: 3 Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, 4 who for my life risked their own necks, to whom not only do I give thanks <2168>, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.

The Apostle Paul is telling us to be thankful in all things and to express it fully. Being thankful in all things results from intentional actions, not just a feeling. Our causes for concern should provoke stronger connectedness, providing vital comfort and resulting in deeper conviction.

It’s not just about thinking thankfully; it’s about living thankfulness, and making it an outward expression of who we truly are.

There are many things to be thankful for. Here are just three:

Be thankful for our call to follow Christ!

Colossians 2:6-7: 6 Therefore as you have received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, 7 having been firmly rooted and now being built up in him and established in your faith, just as you were instructed, and overflowing with gratitude <2169>.

Being called is all about God’s grace, which means undeserved favor. We received this privilege to walk in Christ. How can we not live with gratitude? This call is so far beyond anything any imperfect human being could ever do in a lifetime to deserve even a small bit of it.

If we are grieving or can’t find a job or all those difficulties we discussed before, this kind of thankfulness, gratitude or reasoning comes in to help us say, Let me be thankful that my life experiences are in hands that are bigger and stronger than mine. God sees the future in ways that I cannot.

Be thankful for our Lord Jesus!

2 Corinthians 9:15: Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!

Jesus is everything to us and the entire human race because there is no hope for the future without his ransom sacrifice that paid the price for all of mankind. Nothing needs to be added. It is all because of Jesus. Our call wouldn’t exist had it not been for Jesus.

We should be able to lean on this constantly as a motivation for living with gratitude. Being thankful for Jesus is so big and powerful that we can review it 10,000 times without it losing its potency.

Be thankful for our God!

Psalms 92:1-4: 1 It is good to give thanks to the LORD and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High; 2 To declare Your lovingkindness in the morning and Your faithfulness by night, 3 With the ten-stringed lute and with the harp, with resounding music upon the lyre. 4 For You, O LORD, have made me glad by what You have done, I will sing for joy at the works of Your hands.

This reminds us of a verse from the hymn, Endless Song, “How can I keep from singing?”

With resounding music—with this sense of greatness and wonder and the awesomeness of God.

Gratitude can be expressed anytime, day or night. Its appropriate expression can come through the creativity of music or singing it out loud. Gratitude is meant to not only be felt, but is also to be expressed!

Be thankful in all things. That means to live thankfully in all things. Don’t merely feel it. Feeling gratitude is just the introduction to a book of glorious beauty. We must open that book and let the chapters flow as we live the gratitude.

The Apostle Paul says, this is the will of God concerning you, because he is putting these all together and giving us a formula for being able to step forward to deal with and overcome all the difficult experiences in our lives.

When we read the scriptures that say—Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks—we often skim through them quickly and then move on, thinking, I need to remember that. However, we should take a moment to appreciate the depth of these messages: the significance of God’s providence, His power and grace, the strength we find in Him, and His spirit shining through us. This is what we need to see.

With these things in place, we will be well equipped to accomplish further what Paul had in mind in the next verses:

1 Thessalonians 5:19-24: 19 Do not quench the spirit; 20 do not despise prophetic utterances. 21 But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; 22 abstain from every form of evil. 23 Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. 24 Faithful is he who calls you, and he also will bring it to pass.

Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything. Together these are the foundation for our lives.

So, can we really be thankful in everything?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1402-thankful-in-everything/

1. How do these three “Christian Conduct principles”—"rejoice always,” “pray without ceasing” and “give

thanks in everything”—interconnect to form a foundation of spiritual resilience? (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18)

2. In what ways does Paul utilize his “thorn in the flesh” experiences? How does this show a thankful state

despite his suffering? (2 Corinthians 12:7-10)

3. Were you ever able to give thanks to God for a painful physical or emotional experience?

What helped you give thanks, or what held you back?

4. What enables us to find the “peace of God”? What does that peace look like in daily life?

(Philippians 4:6-7)

5. Share when you have felt the peace of God in your life. What led you to this kind of stability?

6. Besides God, to whom did Paul express thanks? Why?

7. Can it ever be harmful to praise someone? Please explain. Wherein lies the danger?

(1 Thessalonians 3:6-10, Romans 16:3-4)

8. Can you think about someone you could intentionally express gratitude to this week for what they mean

to you, or for something they have done for you, especially if they do not expect it? Will you act on this thought?

9. What are three things we can always look to with thankfulness? How can these help us reframe our

personal hardships into experiences for which we can give thanks? (Colossians 2:6-7, 2 Corinthians 9:15,

Psalms 92:1-4, Romans 8:28)

10. In 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18, Paul tells the Thessalonians (and us) to “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing,

in everything give thanks; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.” How do these three admonitions work together to make a strong Christian life? When we practice all three, especially in difficult times, why is this “God’s will for you in Christ Jesus”?

## Episode 1403 — What Does It Mean if I Quench the Spirit? (Christian Conduct Series)
Published: 2025-09-22
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1403-quench-the-spirit/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/19112824/CQ_Rewind_09-22-2025_What_Does_It_Mean_if_I_Quench_the_Spirit.pdf

(Christian Conduct Series)

1 Thessalonians 5:19: Do not quench the spirit.

God’s spirit, His power and influence, is a power we cannot even begin to comprehend. His spirit was introduced to us as the mighty power of His will in

Genesis 1:1-3 as His creative process began with Let there be light. This same power and influence is described in Ephesians 1:13 as taking root in us where it says we were sealed with God’s spirit through the salvation of Jesus. With all of the marvel of this mighty power of God working in us, how is it that we can quench it? Why would we ever even think of doing such a thing, and most importantly, what do the Scriptures tell us about handling this awesome privilege with reverence and humility?

We have been systematically going through the admonitions of the Apostle Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5, so you can listen to the episodes or read the Rewinds in chronological order as we look closer at each text. They also stand alone as individual lessons.

This is the fourth of six briefly stated yet powerfully connected “inside out” Christian Conduct lessons in 1 Thessalonians 5. We say “inside out” because the guidance Paul gives will help us develop our inner character, which reflects our outward selves.

The first three lessons presented a foundation for us to stand upon:

1 Thessalonians 5:16–18: 16 Rejoice always; 17 pray without ceasing; 18 in everything give thanks; for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus.

Paul provided these three powerful, internal admonitions for us as a basis for coping with whatever may come our way:

- Rejoice always—a rejoicing, thriving state of being creates a solid environment for growth. - Pray without ceasing—a prayerful state of mind keeps us tapped into our truest source of strength. - In everything give thanks, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus—this is a thankful state of perception. When we perceive everything through a thankful state of perception, it opens and reopens our ability to receive and apply God’s direction.

This is ALL God’s will for us! Together, these three build a spiritual resilience in us.

Applying these first three lessons in our daily lives will lay the foundation to help us handle the next three.

These next three are presented as negatives—what not to do:

1 Thessalonians 5:19–22: 19 Do not quench <4570> the spirit; 20 do not despise prophetic utterances. 21 But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; 22 abstain from every form of evil. (Do not do evil things.)

Let’s look at this first one: Do not quench the spirit. (King James Version: Quench not the spirit.) Quench means to extinguish or stifle. If I quench my thirst by drinking a big glass of water, I am no longer thirsty.

A firefighter tries to quench the flames, meaning put out the fire.

Quench: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4570 sbennumi; a prolonged form of an apparently primary verb; to extinguish (literally or figuratively): quench, go out

Do not quench the spirit; extinguish not the spirit.

One of the first and most important points to consider here is that Paul is warning us to intentionally avoid extinguishing God’s spirit in ourselves. He tells us we must make this a clear priority in our hearts and minds. This means that once we have come into God’s favor through His spirit, we can remove ourselves from the power of His favor working in our lives by our own thinking and actions. We can be given this amazing, glorious privilege, and we can actually remove ourselves from that privilege.

This is the warning that ties the previous three together. When we neglect the “fuel” of joy, prayer and gratitude, we risk extinguishing the spirit’s fire in us. To quench the spirit is like turning down or even turning off our power source. Eventually, we will run out and have nothing left.

Let’s set the baseline for where we are, where we are supposed to be, and then look at what can go wrong:

2 Corinthians 5:17: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things passed away; behold, new things have come.

We have this beautiful picture. We are a new creation through God’s spirit in Christ. Old things are behind us—we are basing our lives on the new. Quenching the spirit implies that we are replacing what is new with what is old! Weren’t we supposed to put the old ways and old thinking behind us? We would not want to return to our old habits.

The Apostle Paul understood the importance of making this a clear, intentional lesson.

We suggest two basic things to watch out for here:

1. Quenching the spirit implies we would be putting God’s spirit aside and ignoring its influence in our daily lives.

This might be amply described as we look at a portion of the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus touches on principles that help define “quenching the spirit”:

Matthew 5:14–16: 14 You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; 15 nor does anyone light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on the lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house. 16 Let your light shine before men in such a way that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

A city set on a hill—it can’t be hidden because it is out in the open.

Let your light shine before men—a lamp is a powerful example of God’s spirit in us. A lamp (in context, an oil lamp) is meant to bring light where there is darkness.

If we take the light of God’s influence within us and cover it over, we do two things:

We remove the lamp’s very reason for being. Why is it even there if we cover it with a basket?

We eventually may extinguish its flame by depriving it of the oxygen it needs for fuel. The oxygen will finally be used up if it is covered with a basket.

While this is a dramatic example, it cautions us to live up to our commitment of following in Jesus' footsteps.

In Scripture, God is described as light (1 John 1:5, Psalm 27:1, Isaiah 60:19, Ezekiel 10:4, Luke 2:9 and others). In the Tabernacle, His presence was symbolized by a brilliant glow above the mercy seat on the Ark of the Covenant. At Pentecost, God’s power and influence were revealed through tongues of fire resting on each believer. God’s word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path (Psalm 119:105 KJV).

Jesus, filled with the holy spirit, was called the true Light in John 1:9. Here in Matthew 5:14, even his followers are light (You are the light of the world). So, God, Jesus and faithful followers are all identified as light.

But that flame is fragile. It can be snuffed out by the winds of worldly influence, or dimmed when we hide it—cutting ourselves off from that necessary spiritual fuel.

We began this episode by referencing the creative power of God: …and the spirit of God was moving over the surface of the waters. Then God said, Let there be light; and there was light (Genesis 1:1-3). This metaphor of light is so important that Jesus warns us frail human beings to not cover or hide the glorious light we have been given!

We do not have the great light God and Jesus possess, but we have a precious gift of light that needs to be fed, not quenched. We should not ignore it or hide its influence.

2. We can DO things that set us on a spirit-minimizing path, or we can NOT do things to keep us on the right path.

These actions or inactions can minimize the power of God’s spirit in our experiences. We need to be careful about what we do:

Ephesians 4:29–32: 29 Let no unwholesome word proceed from your mouth, but only such a word as is good for edification according to the need of the moment, so that it will give grace to those who hear.

Once we receive the holy spirit, we have the responsibility to maintain it. We can quench it, but we can also grieve it.

30 Do not grieve <3076> the holy spirit of God, by which you were sealed for the day of redemption. 31 Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.

Grieve: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3076 lypeō; to distress; reflexively or passively, to be sad:—cause grief, grieve, be in heaviness, (be) sorrow(-ful), be (make) sorry

God’s power and influence can be “distressed” by what we do, say or think. This is why we are to let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. Don’t go backward to what you were; this is not who you are now. When we go back to how we were, we distress the power and influence of God working in our lives. We must work on putting those things aside and replacing them with something else.

32 Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has forgiven you.

We have the capacity to replace that which was with that which can bring us to a different level of spiritual maturity and an entirely different kind of life. Paul is saying, “Go in this new direction. Don’t go backward.”

Paul links grieving the spirit with things like gossip, unforgiveness and rage. Not only will we grieve the spirit, but we will stomp out our joy! We can’t “calmly thrive” in such an environment.

Rejoice always—that calm thriving in our experiences—depends on our giving God’s spirit permission to guide us. Once we stop giving it permission, that calm thriving will stop as well.

Grieving God’s spirit, while different than extinguishing it, is still a serious departure from our discipleship path. Make no mistake, grieving God’s spirit opens the door for the extinguishing process to potentially begin, because we are minimizing and replacing the guidance of the spirit with our own choices. In the simple words of our theme Scripture— Do not quench the spirit—the apostle is giving a clear, focused warning to not go down this road.

Let’s look at a scriptural example of grieving the spirit that can lead to quenching the spirit.

This comes down to not acting on what we see and know to be true:

James 1:22–24: 22 But prove yourselves doers of the word, and not merely hearers who delude themselves. 23 For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror; 24 for once he has looked at himself and gone away, he has immediately forgotten what kind of person he was.

This describes NOT acting on what we see and know to be true. We can think of at least two ways this can happen:

Through indifference: We neglect our spiritual priorities like prayer, Christian fellowship and study because we are bored or lazy that day or know that, eh, God will be there tomorrow. We’re disengaged, so no real or lasting character transformation is going to happen.

Through distraction: We let worldly concerns drown out spiritual sensitivity. Everything is competing for our attention these days. We can become so busy with life and leisure that God slips lower and lower down our list of priorities. Perhaps we turn on our “spiritual autopilot” and do just the bare minimum, like maybe zooming into church on Sunday while busy doing other things. Are we just checking a box?

I think of taking weekly piano lessons as a young girl. I would open my music book at the lesson, knowing the last time I opened it was at last week’s lesson. The entire week flew by, and I never once practiced. There was no faking with the teacher when I couldn’t play the piano.

Ask yourself, was the last time I opened my Bible last Sunday?

Last holiday? Last year? Spiritual knowledge and development require time, practice and discipline. And I still can’t play the piano!

We become so “busy” with leisure that it takes up all our time. We forget the most important things. If we see our true selves in the mirror and forget the kind of person we are, what good was looking?

When we think about it, our job is simple: walk where Jesus walked and how he walked.

We will not be attentive to our walk if we forget what we see in the mirror. A lack of attentiveness to our condition can easily lead to a lack of response when we stray from Jesus’ way of walking. When we lack response, we get into trouble.

This grievous state of mind can be the beginning of a spirit-quenching pattern. Let’s not avoid what we see in the mirror. Let’s see it and do something about it! Let’s “open the book” and practice during the week, like we are supposed to do, so we can move forward.

If we don’t, here’s what happens…

James next reveals a deeper issue that goes beyond a lack of attentiveness and on to self-deception:

James 1:25–26: 25 But one who looks intently at the perfect law, the law of liberty, and abides by it, not having become a forgetful hearer but an effectual doer, this man will be blessed in what he does.

The Greek word for doer here is not just someone who performs, but someone who creates or produces. And effectual implies fruitfulness—not just effort, but impact. This is having an active faith.

26 If anyone thinks himself to be religious, and yet does not bridle his tongue but deceives his own heart, this man’s religion is worthless.

There's a difference between not paying attention and deceiving oneself.

The Greek word here for worthless means no purpose or spiritual value. It’s the same word used elsewhere to describe idols and vain pursuits, things that look impressive but are empty.

In context, James is saying that if someone claims to be religious but can’t even control their own tongue, they are deceiving themselves and their religion is empty. This is serious.

This self-deception is a classic tool of spirit quenching. When we think of ourselves one way—I’m okay, this is good, this is the way we want to be—and act another way, we are displaying a spirit-quenching mentality. We are assuming we are in God’s grace but are in fact far from it.

We put ourselves in this position, then we make it okay. That is self-deception! Let’s not rationalize our behavior. We need to recognize it, name it for what it is, and step away.

This self-deception starts leading to areas of pride because maybe we’re clinging to bitterness or sin that we've grown really comfortable lugging around. Maybe we are dismissive of others whose opinions differ from ours. Maybe we read in our Bible, “Love your enemies,” “Avoid sexual immorality,” or “Forgive as the Lord forgave you,” and pretend it doesn’t apply to us.

Maybe we aren’t responding to the obvious direction the Lord wants us to walk—we suppress our convictions, that inner prompting that tells us deep down what we should be doing or not doing. We think of Jonah running as far as he could in the other direction to get away from the Lord, knowing what he was supposed to do and yet rebelling against it.

Like Jonah, this happened to me recently in a big way, a week and a half ago.

A dear friend of ours passed away. She was a fellow student of the Bible whom I’ve known since I was 10 years old. She was about 15 years older than I am and lived in a city that was too far to drive. The family was going to have a memorial service for her. Her children called and talked to my wife, Trish, and asked if I could do the service, which was going to be in nine days.

Here I was in the midst of a lot of moving parts. Trish called me at my office to give me the message. I was by myself, and as soon as I got off the phone, I said out loud, “I can’t do this. This is beyond my capacity. I can’t do it.” It was emotional. I’m starting to cry because I feel like I should, but I can’t. I kept saying, “I can’t do this, I can’t do this.” Then after 30 or 40 seconds, I thought, “Or can I?”

Why would the Lord put this tremendous privilege in front of me if He wasn’t going to give me the strength? I had to backtrack through all the “I can’t, I can’t do it, it’s too much,” to “Thank you for this beautiful privilege.”

We flew out there on Friday and returned home Saturday night because that was the only way to fit it in, but what a blessed experience! It was thoroughly exhausting, but afterwards, I was thoroughly blessed.

That was rationalizing. We all have that trouble. We all can get into that situation. So, we want to stop and focus and ask, “Okay, but what is the Lord guiding me toward?”

Other examples of ignoring our convictions might include:

- We rationalize a bad habit—it’s not that bad. It’s not hurting anyone. - We sense God telling us to forgive someone but instead we keep rehearsing what they did to us, and worse, telling everyone who will listen how wronged we were.

Suppressing says, “Not now, Lord; maybe later.”

Responding says, “Yes, Lord, even if it’s difficult.”

It comes down to working through the process. Just because we may have the wrong reaction originally doesn’t mean we have to continue in that wrong reaction. We can choose to change our response. Do not quench the spirit!

How do we keep far away from grieving or quenching God’s spirit in our lives?

Remember, before this warning to quench not the spirit, Paul provided three powerful internal admonitions for us to cope with whatever may come our way.

DO what we are supposed to do:

Rejoice always: Spiritual resilience—a rejoicing or thriving state of being creates a solid environment for growth.

Pray without ceasing: A prayerful state of mind keeps us tapped into our truest source of strength. We set the state of being to rejoicing, looking to God’s providence, and then we pray, pray and pray.

In everything give thanks: A thankful state of perception opens and reopens our ability to receive and apply God’s direction.

This is ALL God’s will for us!

Having the right state of being (rejoice always), state of mind (pray without ceasing) and state of perception (in everything give thanks) will help us to not quench the spirit.

Instead of quenching the spirit, let us learn to be armed with ALL of God’s armor (Ephesians 6: 10-18). The sword of the spirit (the word of God) is the only offensive weapon listed. If we are quenching the spirit, this sword is useless.

Standing armed as one of God’s people affords us unique protection against all enemies as we stand together.

In this context, attentive use of our shield of faith keeps us protected and turns the tables on what gets extinguished:

Ephesians 6:16: (KJV) Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench <4570> all the fiery darts of the wicked.

Paul told us not to quench the spirit. Here he tells us how to quench the attacks of Satan. Holding our shield of faith in front of us will intercept and extinguish the fiery darts (spirit- quenching influences) Satan throws at us, letting them fall harmlessly. This shield is a powerful tool.

But not even Satan can quench the spirit in us unless we, in some way, allow it. We must guard that flame both in our hearts and among our church fellowship. This reminds us of how a healthy church stands together against Satan, as we discussed at length in Episode #1399, “How Can We Each Contribute to the Health of Our Church?”

There is another kind of armor described in Romans 13:12. We are to put on the armor of light. This is a metaphor for living in Christ to protect us from the strong pull of evil.

We need to be aware and stand behind the shield of faith, shoulder-to-shoulder with the other soldiers, working together. This is how we avoid the quenching of the spirit.

Feeding the power of God’s spirit in our lives is part of our fundamental growth in Christ:

Ephesians 3:14–19: 14 For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, 15 from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name, 16 that He would grant you, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with power through His spirit in the inner man,

To be strengthened with power through His spirit—the spirit is not a small thing. This is a gift of tremendous power and influence through the strength and power of God Himself. This is what we are working with. What happens when we are strengthened with His power and spirit?

17 so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith...

This isn’t just a warm and fuzzy feeling; it is about a change of being. Christ can dwell within our hearts, transforming us into a more Christlike state.

...and that you, being rooted and grounded in love, 18 may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,

We now have the spirit—this power that brings Christ to dwell in our hearts—and we are rooted and grounded in love and are now able to better comprehend spiritual things. By doing all these things, we are feeding the spirit.

19 and to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled up to all the fullness of God.

This is feeding the spirit, not quenching the spirit.

Building on the three “do’s” helps us continually work at putting away any spirit extinguishing habits:

Philippians 2:3–4: 3 Do nothing from selfishness or empty conceit, but with humility of mind regard one another as more important than yourselves; 4 do not merely look out for your own personal interests, but also for the interests of others.

This tells us not to quench someone else’s spirit. We can do that if we are critical instead of encouraging. Do we make them second-guess their service in the Lord or the Lord’s dealings with them? It is like Judas chastising the apostles, saying that this money could have been better spent on the poor (John 12:4-5). It might have made the apostles second- guess themselves.

We are all very fragile. We cannot influence others by reducing or minimizing God’s capacity to work with them. Let us always work at building one another up.

Working with God’s spirit, we must realize that we have been granted a tremendous privilege and that this is a daily growth process.

Finally, we must always remember that God’s mercy and love will not quench our feeble efforts to rise above our challenges. Remember, we can cause the spirit to be quenched. We can leave ourselves unprotected and vulnerable to Satan’s fiery darts. Or, we can take the shield of faith and say to Satan, “No, not here; not now.”

God’s perspective of us is one of nurturing and upbuilding:

Matthew 12:20: (KJV) A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he <4570> not quench <4570>, till he send forth judgment unto victory.

This quench lesson is important! We do NOT quench the spirit, but we DO quench or extinguish Satan’s attacks by putting on the full armor of God and having that shield of faith ready at all times. In turn, God and Jesus will be merciful and generous with us, fanning our pathetic little ember into a warming, light-producing fire. Even those barely hanging on with just a flicker aren’t discarded.

With the potency of God’s spirit, even if it is just a flicker and the desire to honor God, He will take care of the rest. He can take that little pathetic flame and say, “This is precious to Me.”

Understanding God’s mercy, grace, power, providence and strength working in and through us can help us avoid quenching the spirit.

Not quenching the spirit is a very important lesson. It is the first “don’t” on the list Paul gives us about Christian conduct. Be aware, be attentive, recognize the warning and take steps in the right direction.

So, what does it mean if I quench the spirit?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
