### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1404-teachings-and-prophecies/ See:

1. 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18: What is the foundation we can stand on as a basis for coping with life? Verses 19-22: What might “quenching the spirit” look like in our Christian lives?

2. How would you rephrase “do not despise prophetic utterances”? How does this admonition change the focus from “do not quench the spirit”? Why is this an important transition? (1 Thessalonians 5:20)

3. 1 Corinthians 12:4-31, 13:1-2: If we are all one body in Christ, should we not all work and think the same way? If we are all individuals with different talents and different circumstances, does God’s spirit work with us differently? What is our goal as the collective body of Christ? How can we possibly achieve this with all of us so different? What gave the early church the connection with each other to grow a viable church?

4. How are you responsibly listening and testing against Scripture the teachings you are given?

5. What does “prophesying” encompass in the New Testament? How does this differ from the Old Testament? (1 Corinthians 14:1-5, Ephesians 4:11)

6. Jesus, the living example for the believers, had died. Why was the miraculous spiritual gift of prophesying needed so much in the early church? Explain how 1 Thessalonians 5:20-22 helps in these situations:

a. Acts 8:9,18-20

b. Galatians 2:11-14

c. Acts 15:1-2

7. Influencers with self-serving agendas abounded in the early church. Why was the miraculous spiritual gift of prophesying needed for these circumstances? Connect 1 Thessalonians 5:20-22 in your answers:

a. 2 Peter 2:1-3—how do we avoid following false prophets and teachers?

b. 2 Timothy 3:1-7—do we fall into any of these categories? Are we growing in acting like Jesus?

c. Galatians 6:7-10—how do we judge the true value of the input we are receiving?

8. Why do we need to “hold fast”? Explain the examples of holding fast in Luke 8:14-15 and Hebrews 3:5-6.

9. How do we know what is “good”? (2 Timothy 3:15-17) Why is it not enough to just say you believe it? (2 Timothy 2:14-15) What is our mission now that we have the understanding and have received the warning? How do you feel a “full assurance of faith”? (Hebrews 10:22-24)

10. What do I need to do to examine all I hear from my leaders, and others, and from my studies in the light of God’s word? How am I holding fast to that which is good without wavering? (Hebrews 10:22-24)

11. How do I sift out any and all things contrary to God’s teachings, abstaining from all evil?

## Episode 1405 — How Do We Keep Ourselves Separate from the World? (Christian Conduct Series)
Published: 2025-10-06
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1405-sanctify/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/03154556/CQ_Rewind_10-06-2025_How_Do_We_Keep_Ourselves_Separate_from_the_World.pdf

How Do We Keep Ourselves Separate from the World? (Christian Conduct Series)

1 Thessalonians 5:23–24: 23 Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. 24 Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

If we are serious about our Christianity, then we know the bottom line of everything in our lives is to be more like Jesus. If we call ourselves disciples of Christ, if we call ourselves his footstep followers, then any and every other objective in life must, by definition, become secondary. Our last seven episodes have examined several of the Apostle Paul’s pointed statements regarding our separateness from the world in

1 Thessalonians 5:12–24. Having God “sanctify us entirely” is the dramatic conclusion of this powerful set of teachings. So, how does it work? What are the secrets of Jesus’ true followers living their daily lives in a truly holy fashion? Does God just set us apart? What standards must we adhere to, and how do we know we are on the right track?

Our recap of the previous episodes in this series will fully unfold as we lay out the conclusion to the Apostle Paul’s pointed teachings in these verses:

1 Thessalonians 5:23: Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify <37> you entirely <3651>; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

May the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely—who is the you in this verse? Who does Paul want entirely sanctified?

It is not an individual. It is the collective body of Jesus’ true disciples. In writing to the Thessalonians as a group, Paul is writing to all of us as a group. More on this soon.

May the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely—what does sanctify mean?

Sanctify: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #37 hagiazo; to make holy, i.e. (ceremonially) purify or consecrate; (mentally) to venerate

This is a powerful statement. Quite simply, sanctification is the process of becoming holy.

It means setting apart for a holy purpose; to consecrate. To be “sanctified” is to be considered as holy or to be made holy.

May the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely—what does entirely mean?

Entirely: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3651 holoteles; complete to the end, i.e. absolutely perfect

This is the only time this Greek word appears in the Bible. It means complete to the end, or completion with a purpose—a sanctification that reaches its intended goal, making every part of us whole. We are made “wholly holy!”

The sanctification process begins when we are being drawn to God—even before we are justified—and accelerates after. God Himself—Creator of all things, Father of our Lord Jesus and our Father as well—is the one who can and will make us fully, completely and eternally holy!

Sanctification starts when God draws an individual to Him. The word also means to consecrate. The person sees the difference between what is sinful versus God-honoring and makes a conscious effort to live righteously, trying to follow God’s will in every decision of life.

It begins with God’s word:

John 17:15–17: 15 I do not ask You to take them out of the world, but to keep them from the evil one. 16 They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. 17 Sanctify <37> them in the truth; Your word is truth.

Sanctify them. Set them apart. Consecrate them. Make them holy by Your word. Your word is truth. God’s word is a tool in this process of setting apart for a holy purpose.

But there is much more to it.

The blood of Jesus sanctifies, as it was the price paid to truly justify anyone before God:

Hebrews 10:9–10: 9 Then he said, BEHOLD, I HAVE COME TO DO YOUR WILL. He takes away the first in order to establish the second. 10 By this will we have been sanctified <37> through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

It is important to recognize that we are sanctified by God’s word—and we may think: Okay, now I’m good! But that’s only part of it. We are sanctified by the blood of Jesus— okay, now I’m good! Yes, but there is still more to it. These are things that come from the outside that have a sanctifying effect. But some things have to come from the inside as well.

We must also sanctify OURSELVES. Our holiness is both a gift (from God through His word and through the blood of Jesus) AND a developmental responsibility:

1 Thessalonians 4:3–7: 3 For this is the will of God, your sanctification <38>; that is, that you abstain from sexual immorality; 4 that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification <38> and honor, 5 not in lustful passion, like the Gentiles who do not know God;

6 and that no man transgress and defraud his brother in the matter because the Lord is the avenger in all these things, just as we also told you before and solemnly warned you.7 For God has not called us for the purpose of impurity, but in sanctification <38>.

Sanctification: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #38 hagiasmos; from #37; properly, purification, i.e. (the state) purity; concretely (by Hebraism) a purifier

We need to know how to possess our person in sanctification, in a holy way. Setting ourselves apart for God’s holy purpose involves a developmental process.

Sanctification and justification are technical terms. We discussed these in detail in Episode #1108: “What Three Steps Will Get Us To Heaven? (Part I).”

Justification is God’s act of acquitting a person from the condemnation of Adamic sin through the ransom of Jesus, which we receive by faith.

Sanctification is the lifelong process of growth in holiness, where the Christian believer, aided by God’s word and spirit, works to conform their life to God's will, becoming a “new creature” fit for His purpose. This process is symbolized by baptism, representing a death to the old self and the start of a new life.

Some Christians look at the acquittal—being brought back by Jesus’ blood—and they stop there. Yes, we have been saved! Are we good now? No, we have only been introduced to the beginning of the process. The door has now been opened so we can live a sanctified life. It is not “once in grace, always in grace.” It is “once in grace, now it is time to do the work of actually following Jesus—setting ourselves apart, consecrating ourselves to God’s will.”

This is truly a great responsibility. May the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely is an announcement of grand proportions. It is a privilege, and with great privilege comes the responsibility of working to live up to it.

We are just beginning, and keeping ourselves separate from the world is already no easy task. It’s a good thing the Bible shows us how to do it!

God fully sets us apart for His purposes, but we have to dig in and do our part. Where do we start?

Obviously, we begin with being called by God and coming to Him through Christ. God accepts our imperfection and justifies us through Jesus’ blood, and now we begin to walk the walk. This is exactly the position the Thessalonian church was in when the Apostle Paul had to leave them after just a few weeks. What he wrote to them in this first letter gave them AND gives us the pathway to follow!

We are looking at the pathway Paul laid out for us.

The next phrase of our theme scripture continues this unfolding process:

1 Thessalonians 5:23: Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify <37> you entirely <3651>; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming (presence) of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Church: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1577 ekklēsia; a calling out, i.e. (concretely) a popular meeting, especially a religious congregation (Jewish synagogue, or Christian community of members on earth or saints in heaven or both):—assembly, church

Back in 1 Thessalonians 1:1, Paul addressed this letter to the church of the Thessalonians. In Greek, the word for church here is ekklēsia (in English, “ecclesia”), meaning an assembly.

The Greek word ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia) appears 115 times in the New Testament and is most commonly translated as church, though its original meaning is “assembly” or “gathering.”

We said earlier that Paul was referring to the whole group of the Thessalonian ecclesia, and by extension, all faithful Christians as the whole body of Christ, not as individuals.

How do we know this is not addressed to individuals?

First, the letter is addressed to the group. If a letter was addressed, “Dear Jonathan and Julie, as my co-workers on Christian Questions…” they would know the letter is for both of them.

Further, let’s look closer at may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete. What does Paul mean by this? How do we know this is intended as a group admonition and not just to individuals?

What is meant by the “spirit” of the church?

Your spirit reflects the unity of the spirit within the Thessalonian church and, by extension, the needed unity of the spirit within all of the true churches (ecclesias) who believe in Jesus.

Let’s look at companion texts:

Ephesians 4:1–6: 1 Therefore I, the prisoner of the Lord, implore you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling with which you have been called, 2 with all humility and gentleness, with patience, showing tolerance for one another in love, 3 being diligent to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. 4 There is one body and one spirit, just as also you were called in one hope of your calling; 5 one Lord, one faith, one baptism, 6 one God and Father of all who is over all and through all and in all.

In 1 Thessalonians 5:23, the phrase may your spirit...be preserved complete refers to the presence of God’s spirit within us. Here in Ephesians 4:4-5, we read about one hope of your calling, which comes through the one spirit, along with one faith and one baptism. This emphasizes the one spirit coming from the one God, indicating the spirit originates from Him—reflecting His power and influence.

To preserve the unity of the spirit—to collectively have the spirit work to actively fulfill God’s sanctification in us as a group—requires us to give God’s spirit a position of dominant influence in our thoughts and decisions as the group. Normally, we think about the spirit working in us in individual terms, but the ecclesia, the church, has the same responsibility as the individual to have God’s spirit be the driving force.

Romans 15:13–14: 13 Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you will abound in hope by the power of the holy spirit. 14 And concerning you, my brethren, I myself also am convinced that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able also to admonish one another.

How does God fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you will abound in hope?

- Because you focus your attention? NO! - By your own discipline? NO!
- By the power of the holy spirit? YES! May your spirit as a group, as a church, as the ecclesia, look to God’s spirit, not your own opinions. It is not about “me,” it is about “us” as we look at our circumstances through God’s spirit.

What is meant by the “soul” of the church? Why would the church have a soul?

It was their collectively unified stance upon the one foundation of Christ, which was their “being” and mission statement.

Another example of this phrase was from the very early stages of the church, shortly after Pentecost:

Acts 4:32–33: 32 And the congregation of those who believed were of one heart and soul; and not one of them claimed that anything belonging to him was his own, but all things were common property to them. 33 And with great power the apostles were giving testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and abundant grace was upon them all.

Those who believed were of one heart and soul—they had spiritual and emotional unity with a shared purpose and intention. This was a unique time in the early church because for a short time, they voluntarily shared their possessions in a communal way.

We have to give them credit for having such an incredibly high standard. They modeled what the soul of the ecclesia should be—a unified group of individuals acting as one.

To have the soul of our church be an active fulfillment of God’s sanctification in us requires us to be a collective example (not just an individual example) to those around us.

The early church was built on holy teamwork:

Philippians 2:13–15: 13 for it is God who is at work in you, both to will and to work for His good pleasure. 14 Do all things without grumbling or disputing; 15 so that you will prove yourselves (referring to ecclesia at Philippi collectively) to be blameless and innocent, children of God above reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you appear as lights in the world.

When we combine many individual lights, a brighter, more powerful light is visible. May your spirit, God’s spirit in all of us, and your soul, the collective group of individuals, all work together.

What is meant by the “body” of the church?

It follows the same pattern. It is a reflection of how each individual who is called to Christ is to be seamlessly melded into working with the rest of the body in such a way that WE as the body members can see and appreciate one another. It is not just about what other people see. It is about us actually working in a coordinated fashion.

It is similar to a new learning experience where we feel uncoordinated and unenthusiastic. But after much practice, it becomes something we don’t even have to think about. We want to be “coordinated” with each other in that way.

1 Corinthians 12:22–26: 22 …It is much truer that the members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary; 23 and those members of the body which we deem less honorable, on these we bestow more abundant honor, and our less presentable members become much more presentable, 24 whereas our more presentable members have no need of it. But God has so composed the body, giving more abundant honor to that member which lacked.

Even the parts of Christ’s body that seem weak are actually essential. The ones we might overlook or consider less honorable are given special attention and respect. God designed the church so that those who appear to lack status or beauty are lifted up with greater honor—ensuring that every member is valued and cared for.

25 so that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. 26 And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

This shows the members seamlessly coordinated as one unit. Your spirit and soul and body—the collective church.

These three pieces have to work together in order for us to be living witnesses of Christlikeness.

It is obvious that our Christian responsibilities extend far beyond our own personal lives. We truly are very connected to each other.

God sets us apart as holy; in that sanctification, we are to act and live in unity. How do we personally contribute to all of this?

Obviously, our part in this arrangement has so much to do with how we not only handle one another in our Christian fellowship, but also everyone and everything else around us. The only way to be able to handle so much responsibility appropriately is to be prepared from the “inside out.” What we will find is that the end of this particular teaching of the Apostle Paul will circle right back to the beginning of his teachings.

So far, we talked about the God of peace sanctifying us entirely, and what the spirit, soul and body are. Now let’s move on to the end of 1 Thessalonians 5:23 with some quick thoughts regarding the end of this verse:

may your spirit and soul and body be preserved (intentional care that something remains intact and uncorrupted) complete, without blame (entirely faultless, protected from moral failure) at the coming (again, the word here means “presence;” be preserved until Jesus is again present) of our Lord Jesus Christ

In summary: As a body of believers, we need to be fully faithful so that we can be faultless before the world. We must maintain our spiritual integrity.

The apostle is laying out this tremendous process of sanctification. One of the ways he tells us to stay separate from the world is to be so preoccupied with our fellow Christians that we don’t have time to get stuck in all the attractions of the world.

Paul urges his beloved brethren to stay strong in their spirituality and fight off any and all potential contaminations from the world.

Paul prayed for this congregation at Thessalonica that the spirit of the church, the soul of the church and the body of the church would be sanctified and preserved. The actual church at Thessalonica did not survive as a continuous, traceable entity through the centuries, but Paul’s letters have endured and helped Christians throughout the centuries to remain faithful.

We want to have a legacy of unity; that is what the apostle is trying to teach us. This wasn’t just a challenge for the Thessalonians; it was an issue throughout the early church and has continued to this day.

This challenge was also stated to the Ephesian ecclesia:

Ephesians 5:25–27: 25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave himself up for her, 26 so that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, 27 that he might present to himself the church in all her glory, having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that she would be holy and blameless.

We read in the Thessalonians scripture, that your spirit and soul and body of the church be preserved, complete, without blame. Here in Ephesians, Paul talks about the purity of the bride of Christ. We can see this is one of the reasons we need to stay apart from the world—we are representing the bride of Christ. This is a beautiful privilege but an awesome, overwhelming responsibility as well, to stay away from all defilement and work on being sanctified, set apart, consecrated for God’s holy purposes.

With this final admonition, Paul will now conclude this specific teaching regarding Christian conduct:

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

What a powerful statement! God is faithful. He will make it happen. But how?

God accomplishes all of this by giving us His sanctifying spirit and His undefiled words in Scripture as instructions. We are given everything we need; we just need to do our part! How do we do that?

Let’s go back to the beginning of this group of teachings:

In Episode #1398, we began this Christian Conduct Series by recognizing and appreciating our Christian leaders who shepherd us:

1 Thessalonians 5:12: But we request of you, brethren, that you appreciate those who diligently labor among you, and have charge over you in the Lord and give you instruction.

Summing up Paul’s teaching, we appreciate those who shepherd us by:

Standing firm in God’s strength while living according to a spiritually transformed mind.

Standing our ground against all challenges while building the interconnectivity of the body of Christ.

Carefully reflecting selfless love towards others.

Proving all things and growing in truth and passing on what we have received to others.

Paul concluded this request:

1 Thessalonians 5:13: and that you esteem them very highly in love because of their work.

Live in peace with one another.

This introductory lesson tells us to appreciate those who are guiding us, and he gives us ways to appreciate them. We appreciate how these pieces were laid out in order!

By collectively working at appropriate mutual appreciation, we bind ourselves to one another. This unity provides a solid foundation for each of us to mutually contribute to the health of our fellowship. How does God accomplish this? He gives us the responsibility of following through on the admonitions of 1 Thessalonians 5.

If we appreciate our leaders, we are more likely to humbly and respectfully serve each other, which makes for a healthy church family.

It is not as much about God changing us as it is about God giving us the capacity, through His spirit, through His word and our experiences, to make the change He is leading us to.

Paul’s final conclusion in verse 24 applies to each of the pieces we studied in this Christian Conduct Series:

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

God’s faithfulness is proven by His care in giving us diligent, spirit-driven and humble shepherds.

In Episode #1399, we learned to mutually and consistently contribute to the health of our fellowship:

1 Thessalonians 5:14–15: 14 We urge you, brethren, admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with everyone. 15 See that no one repays another with evil for evil, but always seek after that which is good for one another and for all people.

This is the next step. We appreciate those who guide us, but we are also told to take care of each other. We are bound together, with and for each other in unity. With our appreciation of spiritual shepherding and our mutually caring for one another, Paul is saying, “Now that we have these two pieces and have seen what we are supposed to look like and how we are supposed to act towards all, I will next illustrate how to grow from the inside out to accomplish all of this.”

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

God’s faithfulness is proven by His care in setting up His church in a mutually upbuilding way.

I really appreciated going through the difference between “encouraging the fainthearted” and “helping the weak.” The fainthearted, sometimes translated as “fearful,” are those who feel overwhelmed, discouraged or timid. They need our gentle encouragement. The weak literally lack capability. They need help, which means we cling to them because they lack strength either physically, morally or spiritually. We stick by them and offer aid.

Interestingly, God calls the weak on purpose. He calls many of us who are broken. In this way, His power, spirit, guidance and word can work through us, bringing Him glory. But we need to be mutually engaged in appreciating our leaders and building up one another.

Paul then introduced six powerful, internal and interconnected growth lessons. We called these “staccato lessons,” because they are so short.

Rejoice always.

Pray without ceasing.

In everything give thanks.

Quench not the spirit.

Despise not prophesyings; prove all things.

Abstain from all appearance of evil.

The first lesson was discussed in Episode #1400:

1 Thessalonians 5:16: Rejoice always.

This rejoicing is not emotional euphoria; it is a state of being that is calmly happy and/or thriving. It exemplifies working through our challenges with God’s power and providence nourishing and driving us.

Rejoice always is a foundation upon which the other five Christian Conduct lessons are built.

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

God’s faithfulness is proven by His care in providing a spirit-driven environment that invites a thriving state of being.

In our episode on rejoicing, I really appreciated the example of how the apostles were “thriving” in the call to follow Jesus, no matter how much they were threatened and hurt! They didn’t hide because they were rejoicing in doing the Father’s will.

They were in trouble, under challenge and difficulty, but they didn’t hide. This is where the thriving took place. Rejoicing is not euphoria; it is a sense of calm happiness and clarity with the belief that what is happening is supposed to happen, ready to go in whatever direction the Lord would have us go.

The second lesson in Episode #1401 is another staccato verse:

1 Thessalonians 5:17: Pray without ceasing.

The more we calmly rejoice and thrive in God’s will, the wider the door to Pray without ceasing opens! Be regularly in a prayerful state of mind without omitting any part of our experience or opportunity. We pray about everything. This continuous prayerful mentality includes prayers of praise, worship, supplication and thanksgiving.

We talked about different kinds of prayers like those you can say in a single breath, like whispering thanks as we go about our day. And my favorite, “flare prayers,” short and often in a state of distress, decision-making or even desperation. Think of an emergency flare sent up in darkness as a call to rescue. The point is to develop a spiritual reflex, where we instinctively turn to God regardless of whether things are going really well, really bad, or somewhere in between.

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

God’s faithfulness is proven by His care in setting up his church with a continuous line of communication through prayer.

As we put all of these lessons together, we should be beginning to feel an overwhelming sense of awe at how discipleship really works.

Obviously, this series of lessons Paul taught the Thessalonians is VERY important to us as well. What should be our main takeaway?

As we continue putting all of the moving parts together, we really need to focus on the big picture of our Christian conduct. Each and every aspect of these lessons is modeling what our conduct as true Christians should look like to our shepherds, our fellow Christians and to all who observe us on a daily basis.

In Episode #1402, we went deep into verse 18 for our third lesson:

1 Thessalonians 5:18: in everything give thanks; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

Gratitude toward God through Christ should bring us to a thankful state of perception regarding the processing of our life experiences—a thankful state of all we see in our lives. Paul is saying all of these things together are God’s will for us.

No matter how difficult the situation or trial, we have abundant reasons for gratitude. We learned to:

- Rejoice always—a rejoicing, thriving state of being creates a solid environment for growth. - Pray without ceasing—a prayerful state of mind keeps us tapped into our truest source of strength. - In everything give thanks—a thankful state of perception opens and reopens our ability to receive and apply God’s direction.

One of my special takeaways was how the Apostle Paul intertwined gratitude and joy despite suffering from his thorn in the flesh. He turned his infirmity into a powerful tool for growth.

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

God’s faithfulness is proven by His care in providing us with abundant reasons for daily gratitude.

The apostle’s next three teachings can be appropriately handled once the previous three things are already at work in our lives. We covered these in Episode #1403:

1 Thessalonians 5:19–22: 19 Do not quench the spirit; 20 do not despise prophetic utterances. 21 But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; 22 abstain from every form of evil.

We began with:

1 Thessalonians 5:19: Do not quench the spirit;

Paul warns us to intentionally avoid extinguishing God’s spirit in us. Once we have come into God’s favor, we can, by our own thinking and actions, remove ourselves from the power of His favor working in our lives.

That’s a big problem. Instead of quenching the spirit, let us learn to be armed with ALL of God’s armor (Ephesians 6), using our shield of faith to keep us protected and turn the tables on what gets extinguished.

Ephesians 6:16: (KJV) Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.

I loved the juxtaposition. Paul told us to NOT quench the spirit of God in 1 Thessalonians, but here in Ephesians he turns it around and says we ARE to quench the attacks of Satan. Holding our metaphorical shield of faith in front of us will intercept and extinguish the fiery darts (spirit-quenching influences) Satan throws at us, letting them fall harmlessly at our feet. But not even Satan can quench the spirit in us unless we, in some way, allow it. We must guard that flame both in our hearts and among our church fellowship.

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

God’s faithfulness is proven by His care in giving us His spirit and giving us ways to feed its influence.

The opposite of quenching the spirit is feeding it. He has given us many ways to feed it, which is why this whole lesson is built around working together. If we want God’s spirit to flourish within us, we need to be around others of like mind who are walking in the same way. God’s spirit will not flourish in me as a solo act. It was never built that way. We need to be together.

With this serious potential challenge in mind, we now move to our next negative in this list:

1 Thessalonians 5:20–22: 20 do not despise prophetic utterances. 21 But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; 22 abstain from every form of evil.

Rephrasing verse 20: Don’t emphatically and without strong consideration, toss away what some have formally spoken to you regarding applying God’s word. Don’t just arbitrarily throw away what you have been taught. Consider those things.

Prophesying in this verse does not mean giving future prophecies like in the Old Testament. To prophesy is described elsewhere as being a speaker who edifies, builds up and promotes Christian growth, exhorts, provides a calling near to bring comfort, and consoles, persuades, stimulates or calms others.

In the early church, the ability to do these things was a spiritual gift, meaning it was miraculously bestowed upon some instead of being the natural result of a long time of study, prayer, meditation and experience.

We talked about the need for miraculous spiritual gifts in the early church. Jesus had been killed, so he wasn’t around to clarify teachings or settle disagreements—and there were a lot of disagreements when Christianity was still a new idea. Even the apostles didn’t always see eye-to-eye.

Today, we still want to respectfully listen to what our fellow Christians have to say, but we need to critically examine everything and prove it against the Scriptures to be genuine.

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

God’s faithfulness is proven by His care in setting up His church in a mutually upbuilding way.

Our final negative is a powerful and necessary conclusion:

1 Thessalonians 5:21–22: 21 But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; 22 abstain from every form of evil.

Based on what we have seen, the method by which we “do not despise prophesying” is to examine with great care all things taught, testing for genuineness. Just because somebody may know more than we do doesn’t mean we just take what they say at face value. We need to understand the source and foundation of the teaching. What is the basis of their thought? Is it edifying? If not, it is to be discarded.

WHAT ARE WE LOOKING TO AVOID—TO ABSTAIN FROM?

- False teachers: Ego and greed are dangerous elements to allow ourselves to follow. We must examine—test—to see what is genuine. Error can be disguised in beautiful ways.
- Complacency and human rationalization: These are natural human issues that can easily creep in and mislead us with the passage of time. Some Christians may start out zealously and sound genuine, but end up leading with human thinking.
- Anything that may result in our receiving error instead of biblical truth: We have to study to know what is scripturally sound doctrine.

How do we truly know what we are to hold fast to? How do we know it is good? We should recognize that our highest authority is the Bible and be diligent in handling that recognition. It is great to listen to someone we really respect, and that respect may be well-placed.

However, the Bible is the final authority:

2 Timothy 2:15: Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth.

The Apostle Paul is writing to Timothy, entrusting him with great responsibility. This is Paul’s last letter, and he is telling Timothy he must assume this burden and work with it, accurately handling the word of truth. Part of that handling is for him to prophesy, exhort, comfort, build others up and teach them to accurately handle the word of truth.

1 Thessalonians 5:24: Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

God’s faithfulness is proven by His care in giving us divine tools to help us abstain from all evil.

We have been looking at how to keep ourselves separate from the world. The Apostle Paul provided the Thessalonians—and us—with a detailed and well-defined process of conduct.

We are called as individuals to be a part of something bigger. We are not just called as individuals to stay individuals; we are called to be a part of this body of Christ. To be a part of this working together and this growing together and this sharing and this following God’s spirit and His providences together; helping each other and building one another up in this most holy faith.

Rejoicing always, praying without ceasing and in everything giving thanks. Making sure we do not quench the spirit: this is what Christian conduct truly looks like!

Revelation 2:10: …Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.

The Apostle Paul has given us the recipe for being faithful unto death. What are we going to do now that we see it?

So, how do we keep ourselves separate from the world?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

## Episode 1406 — Was Paul an Imposter Apostle or Appointed by Jesus?
Published: 2025-10-13
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1406-apostle-paul/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/10214632/CQ_Rewind_10-13-2025_Was_Paul_an_Imposter_or_Appointed_by_Jesus.pdf

1 Timothy 1:1: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus according to the commandment of God our Savior, and of Christ Jesus, who is our hope.

The Apostle Paul wrote a significant portion of the New Testament. There are 27 different “books” in the New Testament, and Paul is credited with writing about half of them. For the vast majority of Christians, his writings provide extremely practical teachings and examples for us to build upon the single and solid foundation of Jesus Christ. With all of this being said, there are some Christians who believe that Paul was an imposter, a self-appointed apostle who was actually diminishing the power of the gospel of Jesus. What would make someone question the validity of Paul’s writings? Turns out there are several varied reasons for this perspective. Are they legitimate, and what do they imply?

We have observed that a number of Christians question the legitimacy of Paul’s apostleship. Much of the suspicion has to do with Paul’s perceived contradictions of Jesus’ teachings. For some, his writings seem to overshadow the words of Christ. These concerns often stem from a deep desire to remain faithful to Jesus’ original message.

Recently, a very sincere Christian posted nine thoughtful objections on our website blog at ChristianQuestions.com, and we want to take the time to respond to each of these individually, with the same respectful tone in which they were presented to us.

1. “PAUL NEVER MENTIONS THE TEN COMMANDMENTS IN THEIR ENTIRETY.”

This is a common argument that Paul’s gospel is somehow disconnected from the Mosaic Law or that he redefined moral boundaries.

RESPONSE: This can be interpreted as correct, as he never listed them. It’s important to recognize that Jesus never listed the Ten Commandments either, though he DID teach his followers about their value on a higher level.

Jesus didn’t use the Ten Commandments as a checklist. In fact, Jesus never directly quoted the Third Commandment—Do not take the Lord’s name in vain—or the Tenth Commandment—Do not covet—though they were both absolutely implied.

The Apostle Paul actually followed suit with Jesus’ approach. Let’s look at how he dealt with the Commandments.

The first three Commandments—no other gods, no idols and not taking God’s name in vain were covered at Mars Hill:

Acts 17:23,29: 23 For while I was passing through and examining the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription, TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship in ignorance, this I proclaim to you. 29 Being then the children of God, we ought not to think that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of man.

Paul critiques idolatry and affirms the worship of the one true God while talking to these pagan worshipers. He doesn’t specifically mention not taking God’s name in vain, but neither did Jesus. It is implied in the tone and tenor of what Paul is teaching these idol worshipers, as it was implied in the absolute respect Jesus showed God when he spoke of Him.

Paul observed the Sabbath as a day to honor and learn about God through Christ, just as Jesus did:

Acts 18:1-4: 1 …(Paul) left Athens and went to Corinth. 2 And he found a Jew named Aquila… with his wife Priscilla... 3 and… he stayed with them… for by trade they were tent-makers. 4 And he was reasoning in the synagogue every Sabbath and trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.

The phrase every Sabbath suggests a habitual practice. Paul didn’t just drop in occasionally—he was going every week to the synagogue to engage people with Scripture. While it’s true that Paul in his letters never commanded Gentile believers to keep the Sabbath, his actions here show he didn’t discard the practice either.

In fact, he had great respect for the Sabbath. It was a wonderful place and time to go to the synagogue to draw people into talking about heavenly things—spiritual things—to honor and praise God. This is the reason for the Sabbath to this day—to rest from our other responsibilities and consider the things of God.

Paul actually quoted the Fifth Commandment:

Ephesians 6:1-3: 1 Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. 2 HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER (which is the first commandment with a promise), 3 SO THAT IT MAY BE WELL WITH YOU, AND THAT YOU MAY LIVE LONG ON THE EARTH.

While we agree that Paul never mentions the entire Ten Commandments at one time, we can see how he goes through them within the context of his teaching, just as Jesus did.

In the Book of Romans, Paul directly quoted four more: the Sixth, Seventh, Eighth and Tenth Commandments.

Romans 13:8-9: 8 Owe nothing to anyone except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. 9 For this, YOU SHALL NOT COMMIT ADULTERY, YOU SHALL NOT MURDER, YOU SHALL NOT STEAL, YOU SHALL NOT COVET, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.

That sounds like Jesus, doesn’t it? This is how Jesus treated the Ten Commandments. He summed them up within the context of love. The Apostle Paul followed Jesus’ example.

What about the Ninth Commandment, which instructs us not to bear false witness? This commandment was not included in the previous group in Romans.

Paul’s teaching on the Ninth Commandment is clear, although it doesn’t use those words:

Ephesians 4:25: Therefore, laying aside falsehood, SPEAK TRUTH EACH ONE of you WITH HIS NEIGHBOR, for we are members of one another.

Speak truth each one of you with his neighbor is a blanket statement. Do not speak improperly or wrongly in any way. The Apostle Paul was dealing with Gentiles, and they had a different set of morals than did the Jewish people. Paul had much to teach the Gentiles about morality; he wanted to make sure they were clear and truthful with everyone and about everyone.

When we look at all these concepts and how he dealt with them, Paul’s teachings, just like Jesus’, were focused on transforming the heart by following Jesus and his precepts. Paul followed up with what Jesus set in motion.

Here is what Paul said about the transformation of the heart through Christ:

Romans 13:10: Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the Law.

This sounds very familiar because Paul learned this from his teacher, Jesus.

Let’s compare it with Jesus’ statement:

Matthew 22:36-40: 36 Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law? 37 And he said to him, YOU SHALL LOVE THE LORD YOUR GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART, AND WITH ALL YOUR SOUL, AND WITH ALL YOUR MIND. 38 This is the great and foremost commandment. 39 The second is like it, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF. 40 On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets.

To summarize, Paul’s emphasis was on the Law’s fulfillment through Christ, not in recapping each commandment of the Law. He taught that love is the fulfillment of the Law, aligning with Jesus’ summary here in Matthew 22:37-40.

In fact, the only commandment Paul did not explicitly mention was the Third Commandment—Do not take the Lord’s name in vain. Not explicitly quoting it doesn’t mean he rejected it; Jesus did not explicitly quote it either.

The apostle emphasized that the true fulfillment of the Law involved a higher, broader understanding and application than the Jews had practiced in the past. Neither Paul nor Jesus emphasized a checklist of commandments.

2. “CIRCUMCISION PUTS YOU BACK UNDER THE LAW AND FORFEITS SALVATION.”

How about when Paul said that if you are circumcised, you are put back under the Law and you lose the free gift of salvation? But would that contradict the fact that Jesus himself was under the Law?

RESPONSE: This conclusion is a misplaced assumption, as Paul never said that. Paul’s teaching in Galatians 5 is not anti-circumcision, but anti-legalism.

Paul was dealing with Judaizing Christians (Christians who were formerly Jews and believed in still practicing many Jewish customs).

Legalism refers to strict adherence to the letter of the Law at the expense of the spirit and intent of the Law. Early Jewish Christians brought their practices of the Law with them into their new belief and tried to force it upon all the followers of Jesus, including Gentile Christians.

Paul was teaching everyone (Jew and Gentile) they could not bring the Law with them because Christ had fulfilled it; he had nailed it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). They now had to follow Christ, not the Law.

This shows anti-legalism, not anti-circumcision. His warning was that if circumcision is pursued as a means of justification, then it nullifies grace. Circumcision (symbolic of keeping the old Law) will never lead to justification with God. This practice takes Jesus out of the center of our justification. To a Christian, the ONLY source of lasting justification is through the sacrifice of Jesus, not the Law.

Galatians 5:1-6: 1 It was for freedom that Christ set us free...

Notice who set us free—Christ, not the Law.

...therefore keep standing firm and do not be subject again to a yoke of slavery.

The yoke of slavery was the sacrifices, the rituals, the lock and key of the Law versus the spirituality and liberty opened up to the Christian followers of Jesus.

Here is the crux of the argument: 2 Behold I, Paul, say to you that if you receive circumcision, Christ will be of no benefit to you.

It sounds like he is saying circumcision puts them back under the Law, and it forfeits salvation. Circumcision, especially, was such a big part of the Jewish identity that they found it difficult to give up.

It’s critical to look at the context of the bigger teaching: 3 And I testify again to every man who receives circumcision, that he is under obligation to keep the whole Law. 4 You have been severed from Christ, you who are seeking to be justified by law; you have fallen from grace.

Paul’s message: You who seek to be justified by the works of the Law are therefore putting the grace of Christ aside. Don’t do that! Paul is addressing the erroneous belief, even among some Gentile Christians, that the rituals of the Law could lead to justification, instead of the truth that justification can only come through the blood of Christ.

This is strong language. We need to read further to get the full meaning: 5 For we through the spirit, by faith, are waiting for the hope of righteousness. 6 For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything, but faith working through love.

What Paul actually said was, if you are circumcised or not, it’s not relevant if we are under Christ. He does not say if you’re circumcised that you’ve gone away from Jesus. It didn’t

matter one way or another, as they could not use circumcision as a tool to bring them to justification. Being under Christ is the only path to justification.

In fact, Paul did have Timothy circumcised (Acts 16:3) so that he could preach the gospel, but it wasn’t to “save” him. Paul knew the Jewish Christians would be more willing to listen to Timothy (a Gentile) if he were circumcised. This showed flexibility, not contradiction.

Paul’s issue was with requiring circumcision for salvation, which the Jerusalem Council also rejected (Acts 15) when deciding if circumcision should be forced on Gentile converts. Peter and James spoke up and said that practice should not be forced on the new Gentile Christians.

So, if we have an objection against Paul for this, we also have to question Peter and James.

Before the Apostle Peter was sent to Cornelius (the first Gentile convert to Christianity), God gave him a vision. In the vision, he was told by God three times to eat what the Law had deemed as unclean. This taught him how the Gentiles, considered “unclean,” would now be a part of the call of the gospel. Peter was the first to explain how Gentile Christians should not be forced to follow Jewish Law practices.

3. “ALL CHURCH ASSEMBLIES IN ASIA REJECTED PAUL.”

2 Timothy 1:15: You are aware of the fact that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.

Response: Paul’s statement reflects the abandonment he felt by those who were ashamed to associate with him due to his imprisonment. It was not a universal rejection of him or his message.

The context of the next verse speaks of one who stood by him:

2 Timothy 1:16: The Lord grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains.

Here we see the reason for this rejection. Those in the previous verse were ashamed that this apostle was put in prison, but Onesiphorus and his house were not. This is not a rejection of him as an individual or as an apostle; it is rejecting the circumstance, the embarrassment of his imprisonment.

Paul’s extensive ministry in Asia (Ephesus, Colossae and others) is evident. His letters to these churches show his deep spiritual connection and mutual respect for them. There was no general rejection here, just tremendous respect.

Paul’s lament in 2 Timothy 1:15 describes his feelings of personal abandonment during imprisonment, a time of deep suffering. This wasn’t a universal rejection; rather, it was a reaction by some who distanced themselves from fear of being associated with a prisoner.

Paul had been arrested and imprisoned, and some apparently distanced themselves out of fear of being associated with him. We saw that same reaction after Jesus was crucified. Paul was preparing Timothy to face similar trials—don’t be discouraged when people aren’t loyal. God is always loyal.

Sometimes rejection comes out of fear; these brethren weren’t ready to stand up and support Paul. The apostle says Onesiphorus was willing to stand up with him even though it was difficult. However, all the church group assemblies in Asia did NOT reject Paul.

4. “REVELATION 2:2 PRAISES EPHESUS FOR EXPOSING FALSE APOSTLES —IMPLYING PAUL?”

In Revelation 2:2, the risen Messiah praises the assembly in Ephesus for exposing apostles who are not apostles, and their lies.

Revelation 2:2: I know your deeds and your toil and perseverance, and that you cannot tolerate evil men, and you put to the test those who call themselves apostles, and they are not, and you found them to be false.

Response:

1. Revelation 2:2 does not name Paul.

2. Paul is the one who brought the gospel to the Ephesians and built them up so they could receive this teaching in Revelation 2:2.

He spent years teaching there (Acts 19).

Paul taught them to test for false apostles:

Acts 20:29-31: 29 I know that after my departure savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; 30 and from among your own selves men will arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them. 31 Therefore be on the alert, remembering that night and day for a period of three years I did not cease to admonish each one with tears.

If Paul himself is warning them, who are the false apostles in the warning?

The same people Paul warned the Corinthians about:

2 Corinthians 11:13-14: 13 For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. 14 No wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

The Ephesian church did not later denounce the very apostle who founded their church.

KEY POINT: Revelation was written decades after Paul’s death, so it makes more sense that Revelation refers to later imposters who claimed authority. When we look at these later imposters, we must consider the vast number of Christian denominations and ask, why so many? The apostle firmly warned about a lot of deception. So no, Revelation 2:2 does not refer in any way to the Apostle Paul.

5. “Paul contradicts Jesus’ teachings on the Law.”

This is probably the most important objection because if true, we absolutely SHOULD reject Paul.

Response: Jesus said he came to FULFILL the Law (Matthew 5:17), NOT abolish it.

Paul agrees. He teaches that Christ is the “end” (Greek: telos, meaning goal or fulfillment) of the Law for righteousness. He's saying exactly the same thing Jesus did.

Romans 10:4: For Christ is the end (the fulfillment) of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

Paul taught that the Law was intended to be a tutor that leads to Christ for the Jew (Galatians 3:24). Once faith comes, the believer no longer needs the tutor. This is not a contradiction; it’s a progression. Jesus told his disciples to rise above what they were and to follow him. A new commandment I give to you (John 13:34). How dare he bring a new commandment! But wait! It was built upon the foundation of what the Law gave, expanding it. Paul reinforces this.

Tutor in Galatians 3:24 refers to a servant who walked boys to school each day. Today we might equate that to a bus driver.

The Law was given by God to the Jews to “drive” the students to the true source of life, Christ. The Apostle Paul is not contradicting Jesus’ teachings on the Law; he is enhancing them and explaining them to Gentile Christians who had never heard such things. He had to start at the beginning.

Jesus’ sacrifice was a FULFILLMENT of the ceremonial Law. (The moral part of the Law, like the Ten Commandments, will be in effect forever):

Hebrews 10:4-7,9: 4 For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Sin needs to be eradicated permanently. Bulls and goats could not do that, but Jesus could. 5Therefore, when he comes into the world, he says, Sacrifice and offering you have not desired,

but a body you have prepared for me; 6 in whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you have taken no pleasure (Psalm 40:6). 7 Then I said Behold, I have come (in the scroll of the book it is written of me) to do Your will, O God (Psalms 40:7,8). 9…He takes away the first in order to establish the second.

We can see the two worked together: Jesus laid the foundation during his ministry, and Paul followed and firmly built upon anything and everything Jesus taught.

6. “Paul’s gospel was not taught by Jesus to the Twelve.”

Before we get into the discussion, context is important. Jesus preached in a mostly Jewish, rural setting shaped by synagogue life, Torah observance and expectations of Israel’s restoration under Roman occupation. Jesus spoke to a people longing for messianic deliverance. His audience was steeped in Scripture and local religious customs. They were well-grounded.

Paul, by contrast, is translating the gospel across cultural and ideological boundaries. He is preaching in the urban, multicultural world of the Roman Empire. Cities were filled with diverse religious practices (Greek gods, Roman imperial cults, mystery religions), philosophical schools (Stoics, Epicureans) and different ethnic groups (Jews, Greeks, Romans, and others)—all living side-by-side. This made his message of one God AND one Lord (Jesus) both radical and deeply challenging, because it confronted a world where people were used to picking and mixing spiritual ideas like a food buffet.

Repeat: “Paul’s gospel was not taught by Jesus to the Twelve.”

Response: This is not true! The gospel Paul taught was the same gospel Jesus taught the twelve apostles. Paul didn’t teach a “different” gospel. The way he taught it, though, was to a different audience. Therefore, it had to have a different starting point. The same truth, same gospel, but teaching it to people learned in the scriptures of the Old Testament rather than to people who knew something else. If someone does not know the basics, they cannot understand. So the teacher must start in a different place.

Paul explicitly says his gospel came by revelation from Christ (Galatians 1:11–12). This doesn’t mean it contradicts Jesus’ gospel; it complements and expands it to the Gentiles. Acts 15 and Galatians 2 show the other apostles also affirmed Paul’s ministry.

This is critical. How do those who look at the Apostle Paul and say he is an imposter explain why other apostles affirmed him?

Why, then, does the Apostle Peter speak so highly of him?

2 Peter 3:15-16: 15 And regard the patience of our Lord as salvation; just as also our beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given him, wrote to you, 16 as also in all his letters, speaking in them of these things, in which are some things hard to understand, which the

untaught and unstable distort, as they do also the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.

Did Peter just call what the Apostle Paul wrote “Scripture”? If Paul were teaching a contradictory gospel, Peter would never equate Paul’s letters with Scripture.

Of course, Peter would challenge someone to their face if they needed him to. Yet he says, just as our beloved brother Paul...wrote to you…in which some things are hard to understand. Why were they hard to understand? Because they were written to the Gentiles.

Understand, when they were teaching the Jewish people of that time about Christianity, they were starting on a flat foundation. When they were teaching Gentiles about Christianity, it’s as if they were underwater. They were not even on or near the same level with each other. Paul had to bring them up, dry them off, set them up and say, Okay, here is where we are going. But what he was teaching is the same gospel. There needed to be a different method and approach because of a different audience with different backgrounds.

7. “Paul stifled Gentile spiritual growth by avoiding the Ten Commandments and Sabbath.”

We’ve already talked about these, but is there more to add?

Response: Paul powerfully taught moral principles rooted in the Law (e.g., love, holiness, integrity).

He also emphasized freedom from the ritual observance, from the legalism of the Law:

Colossians 2:16-17: 16 Therefore no one is to act as your judge in regard to food or drink or in respect to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath day— 17 things which are a mere shadow of what is to come; but the substance (literally body—the body of Christ, exemplified there in the Colossian church) belongs to Christ.

The Colossian church was primarily Gentiles. Paul taught them to rise above their background. He did not stifle growth; he contextualized the gospel for Gentiles, which had never been done before. He helped them renounce paganism, avoid Jewish legalism and embrace Christlike righteousness. That was what he was there for. That was the mission given to him by Christ.

In other words, he did teach the morality of the Ten Commandments, but he freed Gentiles from ceremonial obligations of the Law that were never their oblications to begin with.

The ceremonial laws were previews—a school bus driving to Christ, or a tutor to lead to Christ. Things like the burnt offerings, sin offerings, peace offerings, the day of atonement, Passover and the Tabernacle were all shadows of the reality to come.

(Search any of these terms on our website for detailed episodes.)

He reframed holiness around Christ, not the Law. His assignment was to preach this to the Gentiles. When we look at Paul’s teachings in context, we see him following Jesus very closely.

8. “Paul opened the door to pagan festivals like Christmas and Easter.”

The argument is that by preaching to the Gentiles, Paul opened the door to converts from various sun worship cults to bring in remnants of their pagan beliefs and festivals.

Response: When does he do this? How does he do this? By preaching to Gentiles? There is NO biblical or historical evidence that Paul endorsed pagan festivals at any time or under any circumstance.

These developments occurred centuries later. Paul warned against idolatry:

1 Corinthians 10:13-14: 13 No temptation has overtaken you but such as is common to man; and God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape also, so that you will be able to endure it. 14 Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.

This objection has two arguments: Paul didn’t do enough to require, and he didn’t do enough to condemn. Let’s explain:

1. Because Paul didn’t demand that Gentile Christians keep the Passover and other Jewish festivals, it allowed later church leaders to substitute them with culturally familiar festivals. He left a vacuum that was filled.

2. Paul preached in cities with rampant idolatry, such as Corinth, Ephesus and Rome. By not explicitly condemning all pagan customs, Gentile converts reinterpreted certain traditions that later became Christianized. For example, spring fertility rites were turned into Easter. This process is known as “syncretism,” where elements from two or more religions are combined into a new, hybrid system.

Neither of these argments should fault Paul! Paul brought Gentiles to Christ. Bringing them to Christ did not bring them to the rituals of the Law. Christ fulfilled (ended the rituals of) the Law. Christ himself said that.

What did Paul bring them to? The ritual of self-sacrifice to help others, the ritual of gathering together in worship of Jesus and God’s word, and the ritual of witnessing to this gospel of salvation that brings life to every human being in the resurrection. He brought them plenty to hold onto!

What happened centuries after him was not because he should have created other rituals! Had he done that, someone would have made the argument that Paul made up his gospel, and they would have been right. He picked up where Jesus left off, and he was able to spread the gospel to both the Jews as well as the Gentiles. He did not open the door to pagan festivals.

9. “Jesus warned of false teachers—does Paul fit the profile?”

Matthew 24:24: For false Christs and false prophets will arise and will show great signs and wonders, so as to mislead, if possible, even the elect.

Have we been deceived by Paul and HIS gospel, a gospel Jesus “forgot” to give to his twelve disciples, a gospel that contradicts the words of the Messiah himself?

Response: Jesus warned of false teachers, but Paul didn’t fit the criteria—he wasn’t self- centered. Can we mark how many places he went where he worked and supported others?

He wasn’t after gaining something; he was after giving something. His whole life was marked by suffering, sacrifice and unwavering devotion to Christ. Let’s look at how Paul got started.

There were eyewitnesses to the conversion of Saul of Tarsus. Let’s look at when Jesus appeared to Saul:

Acts 9:5-7: 5 And he (Saul) said, Who are you, Lord? And he said, I am Jesus whom you are persecuting, 6 but get up and enter the city, and it will be told you what you must do. 7 The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.

Hearing the voice—so others heard what was said. Incidentally, Luke wrote the Book of Acts, not Paul. Luke was another eyewitness.

Saul’s conversion was validated by Ananias, a disciple of Christ, and his sufferings were foretold to Ananias before anyone else:

Acts 9:13-17: 13 But Ananias answered, Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much harm he did to your saints at Jerusalem; 14 and here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name. 15 But the Lord said to him, Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine, to bear my name before the Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel; 16 for I will show him how much he must suffer for my name’s sake. 17 So Ananias departed and entered the house, and after laying his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you were coming, has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the holy spirit.

Ananias is a credible eyewitness who even tried to resist going to see Saul (Paul). When Ananias was told what great things Paul would suffer for the name of Jesus, he obeyed and went to Paul, addressing him as Brother Saul. So we have the verification right up front that the Apostle Paul was not going to be a false teacher but was drawn by Jesus himself.

Another big indication of Paul not being an imposter was his miraculous credentials (healing—Acts 28:8-9, resurrection of Eutychus—Acts 20:9-12, casting out demons—Acts 16:18, imparting gifts—Acts 19:6) and a consistent, Christ-centered message. There is also no debate on his effectiveness in including the Gentiles and expanding the gospel message. It’s pretty much how you and I are here! We owe a lot to our Brother Paul’s dedication and commitment.

On every issue, Paul was a witness to Jesus, not a rival.

We need to study the depth of his teachings because he is all about the simple, straightforward lessons he himself gave.

1 Corinthians 11:1: (KJV) Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.

That is the message, that is the life. Those are the writings of our beloved Apostle Paul, who brought us closer to Jesus by his words, actions, desires and teachings. Let’s keep that in perspective.

So, was Paul an imposter apostle or appointed by Jesus?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

1. Was the Apostle Paul’s gospel teaching disconnected from Mosaic Law, redefining the moral boundaries

of the Ten Commandments? Did this differ from Jesus’ approach to the Ten Commandments?

Ephesians 4:25,6:1-3, Romans 13:8-9)
