(Romans 13:10, Matthew 22:36-40)

2. How did Paul distinguish between the ritual observances of the Jewish Law (like circumcision which

physically defined the Jews from the Gentiles) and the gift of salvation through Jesus Christ? (Galatians 5:1-6)

a. Did this mean that Gentiles who chose to be circumcised (like Timothy) lost their free gift of

salvation?

b. What is the source of our justification (being made right) with God? Did the Law permanently justify

the Jews with God? (Colossians 2:11-13)

c. What did the legalistic Jewish Christians want to demand of new Gentile converts? Who backed Paul

against this practice? (Acts 15)

d. How do I make sure I don’t just use outward religious practices for my sense of righteousness?

3. How was Paul “rejected” in the Roman province of Asia? What was Paul referring to in 2 Timothy 1:15-16?

4. Why is it not likely Revelation 2:2 is referring to Paul when it warns against false apostles?

(Acts 20:29-31, 2 Corinthians 11:13-14)

5. Did Paul disagree with Jesus’ teaching on the Law?

a. Who was the end or fulfillment of the Law? (Matthew 5:17, Romans 10:4)

b. How did the Law help the Jews? (Galatians 3:24, John 13:34)

c. How does Paul explain Jesus’ role in fulfilling the ceremonial Law?

6. Why was Jesus’ ministry to the 12 apostles different from Paul’s ministry to the Gentiles (of the same

teachings) different? Again, who spoke highly of him? What was said? (Galatians 1:11-12, 2 Peter 3:15-16)

7. How did Paul contextualize the gospel for the Gentiles? (Colossians 2:16-17) How did he teach the moral

principles of the Law?

8. Would it have been right for Paul to develop his own festivals to make sure others would not fill the

vacuum of the old Jewish festivals with pagan customs? Was this his mission? What did Paul do? (1 Corinthians 10:13-14)

9. How was Paul the antithesis of a false prophet? How do we know he was truly called by God? (Matthew

24:24, Acts 9:5-7,13-17, 16:18, 19:6, 20:9-12, 28:8-9)

## Episode 1407 — Does Christian Liberty Give Us Freedom of Choice? (Part I)
Published: 2025-10-20
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1407-christian-liberty-part-i/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/17130500/CQ_Rewind_10-20-2025_Does_Christian_Liberty_Give_Us_Freedom_of_Choice_Part-I.pdf
OCR pages from the Rewind PDF: 15

Galatians 5:13: For you were called to freedom, brethren; only do not turn your freedom into an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.

The freedom, the liberty we obtain when we have been called to be disciples of Jesus is so much more than just a feeling of relief and joy. The fact is, having liberty in Christ actually defines a state of being as it describes our freedom from whatever previously held us captive in our lives. It’s no wonder we feel the thrill of liberation! Here are the practical questions: What does having this freedom so firmly set in our lives mean on a practical, daily level? What freedom of choice does it give? What freedom of choice does “liberty in Christ” take away? How are we supposed to know the difference?

Let’s begin by defining the most important terms regarding our liberty in Christ so we know exactly what we’re talking about:

This word has a wide range of meaning, from the power to do as one pleases to the enjoyment of various social, political or economic rights and privileges which hints there are “guardrails” on some of the freedoms enjoyed within a society.

The most common New Testament Greek word for liberty means freedom, especially in a moral or spiritual sense; being unrestrained, as in a citizen would have versus a slave. However, we will see that it does NOT mean unrestricted autonomy.

Liberty: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1658 eleutheros; ADJECTIVE unrestrained (to go at pleasure), i.e. (as a citizen) not a slave

Liberty: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1659 eleutheroo; VERB from #1658; to liberate, i.e.(figuratively) to exempt (from moral, ceremonial or mortal liability)

Liberty: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1657 eleutheria; NOUN from #1658; freedom (legitimate or licentious, chiefly moral or ceremonial)

Liberty: Merriam Webster Online Dictionary (other definitions not quoted)

1. the quality or state of being free:

a. the power to do as one pleases

b. freedom from physical restraint

c. freedom from arbitrary or despotic control

d. the positive enjoyment of various social, political, or economic rights and privileges

Hebrews 10:9–10: 9 Then he said, BEHOLD, I HAVE COME TO DO YOUR WILL. He takes away the first in order to establish the second. 10 By this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

Initially, the cost is not what WE had to pay; it’s what it cost Jesus. The reason we even have Christian liberty is because of Jesus. God calls certain individuals to follow in the footsteps of His son. Those who commit to doing God's will and are accepted by Him receive the gift of the holy spirit. This enables them to understand God's word and demonstrate holiness in their daily lives.

This is an important initial understanding: our Christian liberty isn’t because of us; it is because of Jesus. Our understanding and acceptance of Jesus’ sacrifice sets us apart and is the initial “cost” of our liberty.

Our liberty comes as a result of God’s spirit:

2 Corinthians 3:16–18: 16 But whenever a person turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. 17 Now the Lord is the spirit, and where the spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty <1657> (freedom). 18 But we all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as from the Lord, the spirit.

Where the spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty (freedom)—through the sacrifice of Jesus.

In the Old Testament, certain individuals like the prophets were given a small measure of God’s spirit in order to miraculously and temporarily accomplish His will.

In the New Testament, Christians are given a measure of God’s spirit to dwell within us. This was enabled through the sacrifice of Jesus.

God called us to follow in Jesus’ footsteps. By accepting that call—along with God accepting our acceptance—we receive God's spirit, which then dwells within us. This is how we find this incredible freedom.

In this example, Peter is speaking of false teachers that he prophesied would plague Christianity:

2 Peter 2:18–20: 18 For speaking out arrogant words of vanity they entice by fleshly desires, by sensuality, those who barely escape from the ones who live in error, 19 promising them freedom <1657> (liberty) while they themselves are slaves of corruption; for by what a man is overcome, by this he is enslaved. 20 For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world by the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and are overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.

The Apostle Peter exposes false teachers who offer a counterfeit version of Christian liberty. This describes misapplied liberty because what looks like freedom is actually bondage to sin. Followers are enslaved to whatever overcomes them, such as lust, pride or false doctrine.

We can be given this incredible Christian liberty, but have it contaminated by unscriptural teachings. We live in a time when false teachers clearly continue to have influence—just look at how many denominations of Christianity exist! But there is only one true, original gospel.

Jude helps us connect our true liberty with the HOW and WHY of corrupt liberty:

Jude 1:3–4: 3 Beloved, while I was making every effort to write you about our common salvation (essentially, our common liberty), I felt the necessity to write to you appealing that you contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all handed down to the saints. 4 For certain persons have crept in unnoticed, those who were long beforehand marked out for this condemnation, ungodly persons who turn the grace of our God into licentiousness <766> and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.

Licentiousness: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #766 aselgeia; from a compound of #1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed selgḗs (of uncertain derivation, but apparently meaning continent); licentiousness (sometimes including other vices):—filthy, lasciviousness, wantonness

(in other words, “no” + “continent” meaning self-restraint = a lack of self-restraint)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: unbridled lust, excess, licentiousness, lasciviousness, wantonness, outrageousness, shamelessness, insolence

Does this mean there are professed Christians among us, not even believing in the sacrifice of Jesus for salvation? Unfortunately, yes. They turn the grace of our God into

something that's convenient and perhaps exciting—licentiousness (lasciviousness in the King James Version).

Licentiousness means a lack of self-restraint; unrestrained indulgence, especially in sensual or immoral behavior. In the New Testament, this word reveals diabolical results of what misapplied interpretations of freedom in Christ can bring.

In English, it comes from the word “license,” in the sense that freedom is used irresponsibly in a perversion of liberty, a lack of holiness. It is the counterfeit of liberty. It says, “Because I’m forgiven, I can do whatever I want.”

Let’s look at the similarities and differences between licentiousness and liberty. A license is usually a good thing.

A driver’s license means we have earned the privilege to drive wherever we want by meeting specific requirements. But licentiousness is something much broader. It means a freedom, a lack of self-restraint, used irresponsibly.

Bending the rules just because we can is something a Christian should avoid. In this context, licentiousness is irresponsibly using freedom or liberty in Christ. How might we do this, and how can we avoid it?

The Greek root word for liberty is not the main focus for Christian liberty in the New Testament:

1 Corinthians 12:12–13: 12 For even as the body is one and yet has many members, and all the members of the body, though they are many, are one body, so also is Christ. 13 For by one spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free <1658>, and we were all made to drink of one spirit.

Liberty: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1658 eleutheros; ADJECTIVE unrestrained (to go at pleasure), i.e. (as a citizen) not a slave

The Apostle Paul is saying that no matter what walk of life we are coming from, we all come together under the spirit of God through Christ. Nothing about our heritage, gender or social status changes when we come to Christ—both Jews and Greeks were welcomed, male or female, slave or free.

Before stating the benefits of Christian liberty, it’s important to realize that this liberty is NOT in place to release us from our social status in this life. Whether we are slaves or free is not going to change. Coming into Christ will not change our position in society. When we look through the New Testament, this becomes obvious. Many Christians are bothered by this. If God is a God of love and justice, shouldn’t that be applied throughout the age of

Christianity? No, because now is not the time for social justice. This will happen in the future.

The verb form of liberty describes liberation, not just “not being a slave” but a higher liberation:

Romans 8:1–4: 1 Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. 2 For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free <1659> (in other words, has given you liberty) from the law of sin and of death. 3 For what the Law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did: sending His own son in the likeness of sinful flesh and as an offering for sin, He condemned sin in the flesh, 4 so that the requirement of the Law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit.

Liberty: #1659 eleutheroo; VERB from #1658; to liberate, i.e.(figuratively) to exempt (from moral, ceremonial or mortal liability)

Paul declares that what the Law couldn’t accomplish because human weakness made it ineffective, God accomplished by sending His son to provide a permanent remedy for sin. It’s a shift from external obligation to internal liberation—freedom—not to sin, but rather to walk in the spirit. Again, this was at an extreme cost to Jesus who sacrificed his high position in heaven to be made a man to suffer for the whole human race. He sacrificed his spiritual liberty for us. How thankful we should be!

This freedom in Christ gives us something we could never have had before. It liberates us from our old habits and thoughts that have held us captive in terms of our own personal experiences. We will expand on this soon.

Once the Old Testament Law was provided, it was the only way to have a relationship with God until Jesus came. Paul explains in Romans 8 that it was ineffective because humanity could not live up to it. Jewish religious leaders added to the Law, confusing and complicating it even further than needed. The Law did not let people down by not bringing them to God; people let the Law down. Through Christ, we are released from the “bondage” of failing to live up to the Law.

The noun form of liberty gives us a sense of living in that higher liberation—the practicality of how that higher liberation looks in action:

James 1:22–25: 22 But prove yourselves doers of the word, and not merely hearers who delude themselves. 23 For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror; 24 for once he has looked at himself and gone away, he has immediately forgotten what kind of person he was. 25 But one who looks intently at the perfect law, the law of liberty <1657>, and abides by it, not having become a forgetful hearer but an effectual doer, this man will be blessed in what he does.

Liberty: #1657 eleutheria; NOUN from #1658; freedom (legitimate or licentious, chiefly moral or ceremonial)

To recap, Christ died, giving his life in sacrifice. This was the initial cost of our Christian liberty. God made His holy spirit available to individuals, through which our Christian liberty comes. The next step is to prove yourselves doers of the word.

Are we going to be the person James talks about, who looks at ourselves in the mirror and sees our imperfections but walks away and forgets? Or are we going to see our faults and do something about them, working on living on a higher, more righteous plane? This is what it means to be a doer of the law of liberty.

It sounds strange, but being confined within Christian liberty brings God’s blessing, and what could be more important? By having guardrails, essentially walls around us, we experience the greatest freedom. How? This freedom is FROM the degradation of sin. It is freedom FROM that which causes grief and trouble in this life. So, let us have these guardrails, these restrictions, so we can have freedom from our sinful cravings. In this sense, restriction by not being able to do what we would normally want is freedom!

We have been talking about two personal benefits:

1. Being raised to a higher level of liberation.

2. Having the door open for God’s future blessings to come.

With these two significant personal benefits in place, we must remind ourselves about the cost. We have already established the price paid by Jesus; we now need to establish the cost that we as disciples of Jesus are required to pay.

Paul passionately urges us:

Romans 12:1: Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

Paul wants us to take what we have been given and stretch further. He urges us to be that living sacrifice, to truly walk in Jesus’ footsteps.

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

We may “come as we are” to Christ, but we cannot stay as we are. We cannot stay or remain as we came to him, because our lives are now all about living differently from the world around us. Christian liberty thrives in NOT being in the world and about the world’s business. It is being in the world, but not of the world, because we are transformed to a higher level of living. This is part of the cost of this incredibly beautiful and powerfully life-changing liberty.

Let’s go further, as there is more to this cost:

Romans 12:3–5: 3 For through the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think more highly of himself than he ought to think; but to think so as to have sound judgment, as God has allotted to each a measure of faith. 4 For just as we have many members in one body and all the members do not have the same function, 5 so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.

This takes it even further. We had the cost of giving and transforming; now we have the cost of applying. We have to apply what we have been given, what we have learned and what we have been shown so that this Christian liberty can flow through our lives, giving us direction, grace, strength and blessing.

The application of ourselves to all our external circumstances, if we are living in Christian liberty, must be different. It must be higher and spiritually oriented, which is difficult to do.

GIVE TRANSFORM APPLY

Godly liberty takes a lot of work! All this is at great personal cost but with unimaginable benefits. We are taking the time to understand the cost and that with it comes a benefit beyond our capacity to imagine, one that brings a sense of relief.

Rick: Jonathan, I know your past and the world you were stuck in and that you now live in Christian liberty. How do you feel about how your life was and how it is now?

Chaos in the past and peace in Christ in the here and now. Like night and day!

Remember the words "liberty” and “license” are similar. The word for “licentiousness” comes from the word “license.” Think about when we first get our driver’s license with the freedom to drive from point A to point B. We don’t have to check in with anyone; we just drive. But if we drive recklessly and get caught, we can have our license taken away. We lose the privilege of being able to drive where we want to go at our own discretion because we have stepped outside of the guidelines. It is a serious consequence.

Christian liberty is the same way. We have been given this “license” to drive our lives according to spiritual rules. We want to stay within the guardrails (the guidelines) so that we can keep our license.

We do not want the Lord Jesus to say we have to give him back that license because we were not following spiritual guidance!

Jesus and the apostles understood that this walk is about spiritual freedom, not personal freedom in the social sense. It is about rising above the world and its challenges in a spiritual sense. This is only possible because of the price Jesus paid.

In our next episode, we will look at several detailed examples of how applying true Christian liberty brings spiritual blessings and how applying licentiousness in Christian liberty brings nothing but trouble.

Let’s understand that liberty in Christ was a gift because God, through Christ, made it possible. We are given that gift through God’s holy spirit. That liberty, that freedom, is to follow everything God would have us do, but it has to be in His way according to the Bible.

So, does Christian liberty give us freedom of choice?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

## Episode 1408 — Does Christian Liberty Give Us Freedom of Choice? (Part II)
Published: 2025-10-27
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1408-christian-liberty-part-ii/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/24094441/CQ_Rewind_10-27-2025_Does_Christian_Liberty_Give_Us_Freedom_of_Choice_Part_II.pdf

Galatians 5:13: For you were called to freedom, brethren; only do not turn your freedom into an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.

In our last episode, we spent some time defining exactly what Christian liberty is and what it is not. We found that Christian liberty has little to do with the kinds of freedoms that are reflected in a social status kind of way and everything to do with being given spiritual freedom that is to be exercised with great humility and responsibility. We also uncovered how the gift of Christian liberty can be easily misrepresented and therefore misused. This is troubling, as the results of these misapplications add up to decisions and conclusions that are not Christ-based. How can we avoid these pitfalls?

As a quick recap from Part I, we discussed the New Testament word for liberty in its noun, verb and adjective forms. It means freedom, especially in a moral or spiritual sense; unrestrained.

However, we came to the conclusion that Christian liberty does not mean unrestricted autonomy. There are “guardrails” with Christian liberty—we don’t get to do whatever we feel like in the moment.

We also found that this kind of freedom is not “free.” It came at a great cost to Jesus and to each of us as his followers. Christian liberty is founded in Jesus’ sacrifice and comes through God’s holy spirit working in our lives.

Liberty applied in a damaging way can result in licentiousness, which is a lack of self- restraint or unrestrained indulgence, especially in sensual or immoral behavior. In the New Testament, this word reveals some diabolical results of what misapplied interpretations of freedom in Christ can bring.

Being licentious means we have used our liberty irresponsibly, outside the guardrails of Christlikeness.

Let’s move on to look at the practicality of how Christian liberty works:

Galatians 5:1: (KJV) Stand fast therefore in the liberty <1657> wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.

Liberty: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1657 eleutheria; from #1658; freedom (legitimate or licentious, chiefly moral or ceremonial) NOUN

In the immediate context of this letter, this yoke of bondage refers to the Jewish Law. However, as we shall see, the principle of standing in the liberty we have in Christ applies to all earthly circumstances.

Stand fast (be firm) in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free—do not turn back to what we have been drawn out of. Do not go back to the old ways. Stand firm in your liberty.

Jesus and the apostles were not deeply concerned with physical freedom and the equity of society. They understood servitude and social inequity to be temporary conditions to be resolved in the future, contrasted with the deeper, personal freedom to be spiritually gained in Christ.

What examples and experiences do we have that show us how and when Christian liberty can be misrepresented and therefore create inappropriate choices?

We are going to consider several examples of what might at first look like Christian liberty but are in fact Christian liabilities.

Example #1: How we act

The Apostle Paul sets a strong general standard for our personal behavior. Are we showing evidence of Christian liberty or evidence of irresponsibility?

Galatians 5:13–17: 13 For you were called to freedom <1657>, brethren; only do not turn your freedom <1657> into an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. 14 For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in the statement, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF. 15 But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another. 16 But I say, walk by the spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh. 17 For the flesh sets its desire against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are in opposition to one another, so that you may not do the things that you please.

Our flesh naturally seeks self-indulgence and gratification. Walking in God’s spirit, however, should instead lead to love, unity and true transformation.

These Galatians texts tell us we do not have freedom FROM responsibility; it is freedom FOR righteousness, FOR responsibility in Christ.

Our freedom in Christ is only in place for one purpose: to praise and honor God through Christ. How we act is an evidence of either living in Christian liberty or living in our own broken-down interpretations, which do not bring God glory.

So, our freedom in Christ isn’t to get what we want, which is contradictory to the so-called Prosperity Gospel. This isn’t about getting what we think we are entitled to. True Christianity is absolutely not all about ME.

If we are following the gospel because it is advantageous to us from an earthly perspective, we need to think again about what liberty we are actually pursuing.

In 1 Corinthians, the Apostle Paul addressed the specific debate among Christians about eating meat that had been offered to idols. His point was that all idols are meaningless; however, each individual’s PERCEPTION of the idol has a dramatic effect on the propriety of eating such meat.

Even though we know idols mean nothing, when we are dealing with someone who perceives them to be important, our Christian liberty allows us to be responsive to their understanding.

This affects how we should act and express our liberty in Christ:

1 Corinthians 8:7–12: 7 However not all men have this knowledge; but some, being accustomed to the idol until now, eat food as if it were sacrificed to an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled. 8 But food will not commend us to God; we are neither the worse if we do not eat, nor the better if we do eat. 9 But take care that this liberty <1849> of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. 10 For if someone sees you, who have knowledge, dining in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, if he is weak, be strengthened to eat things sacrificed to idols? 11 For through your knowledge he who is weak is ruined, the brother for whose sake Christ died. 12 And so, by sinning against the brethren and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.

Liberty: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1849 exousia; from #1832 (in the sense of ability); privilege, i.e. (subjectively) force, capacity, competency, freedom, or (objectively) mastery (concretely, magistrate, superhuman, potentate, token of control), delegated influence:—authority, jurisdiction, liberty, power, right, strength

We need to be sensitive to the needs of others. When we sin against our brethren by not taking into account his/her particular weakness, we sin against Christ. Our liberty does not allow us to say, “Well, they should just grow up!” We need to be attentive.

This is something we have to absorb, especially if we are having an adverse effect on those around us. Choose properly and apply TRUE Christian liberty!

It is critically important that we remain focused on what would be God-honoring and Christlike in the freedoms we express.

Inappropriate application of our liberty is ignoring Jesus and his example:

1 Peter 4:1,3: (KJV) 1 Forasmuch then as Christ hath suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves likewise with the same mind: for he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin; 3 For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness <766>, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:

Licentiousness: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #766 aselgeia; from a compound of #1 (as a negative particle) and a presumed selgḗs (of uncertain derivation, but apparently meaning continent); licentiousness (sometimes including other vices):—filthy, lasciviousness, wantonness

(in other words, “no” + “continent” meaning self-restraint = a lack of self-restraint)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: unbridled lust, excess, licentiousness, lasciviousness, wantonness, outrageousness, shamelessness, insolence

Arm yourselves likewise with the same mind—this is military language, a call to intentional readiness.

(Source: Bible commentary by David Guzik) Many of us are defeated in our battle against sin because we refuse to sacrifice anything in the battle. We only want victory if it comes easy to us.

Jesus called us to have the kind of attitude where we would sacrifice our own preferences or even legitimate wants in the battle against sin.

Just because I am a Christian doesn’t mean I have the right to (fill in the blank). We must be careful because we are representatives of Jesus Christ. For some people, the only Bible they will see is our example. Which translation of the Bible are they reading when they read our actions? Are they reading a godly translation or a corrupted version?

Our actions are real reflections of the kind of liberty we are living. How are we doing with this? Are we acting with Christlikeness or reflecting just ourselves?

Example #2: What we say and the freedom to follow truth

Let’s be careful to understand the vast difference between “MY truth” and “THE truth.”

THE truth:

John 8:31–32, 36: 31 So Jesus was saying to those Jews who had believed him, If you continue in my word, then you are truly disciples of mine; 32 and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free <1659>.… 36 So if the son makes you free <1659>, you will be free <1658> indeed.

Free/Liberty: #1659 eleutheroo; VERB from #1658; to liberate, i.e.(figuratively) to exempt (from moral, ceremonial or mortal liability)

Free/Liberty: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1658 eleutheros; ADJECTIVE unrestrained (to go at pleasure), i.e. (as a citizen) not a slave

We don’t like the phrase “MY truth.” It means we make our own standards and our own rules, and it doesn’t matter what anyone else thinks. It is much better to say, “This is my perception of truth,” or “This is my understanding of truth.”

Our truth must be entirely scripturally based, founded in Jesus’ teachings. Jesus said, You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free (John 8:32).

Knowing THE truth is a start, but being doers of that truth is where we need to live. It is one thing to be able to recite scriptures and another to act on them:

James 1:22–25: 22 But prove yourselves doers of the word, and not merely hearers who delude themselves. 23 For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror; 24 for once he has looked at himself and gone away, he has immediately forgotten what kind of person he was. 25 But one who looks intently at the perfect

law, the law of liberty <1657>, and abides by it, not having become a forgetful hearer but an effectual doer, this man will be blessed in what he does.

Being a doer of the word means there are many things we don’t do or say:

James 1:26–27: 26 If anyone thinks himself to be religious, and yet does not bridle his tongue but deceives his own heart, this man’s religion is worthless. 27 Pure and undefiled religion in the sight of our God and Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

The Greek word here for worthless means of no purpose or spiritual value. It is the same word used elsewhere to describe idols and vain pursuits—things that look impressive, but are empty. James says that if anyone thinks himself religious, and yet does not bridle (control) his tongue, he is deceiving himself and his religion is empty.

To visit orphans and widows reminds us that our focus is to be on serving others, not ourselves.

Notice how the focus on serving others should be especially trained on those in the background who may not be noticed. This is part of Christlikeness. Jesus didn’t try to attract the most popular people of his time; he went to those who were in greatest need. Those are the footsteps we are supposed to follow and is where our liberty comes from. This is how we can be doers of THE truth.

MY truth:

2 Peter 2:18–19: 18 For speaking out arrogant words of vanity they entice by fleshly desires, by sensuality <766>, (liberty misapplied!) those who barely escape from the ones who live in error, 19 promising them freedom <1657> while they themselves are slaves of corruption; for by what a man is overcome, by this he is enslaved.

For speaking out arrogant words of vanity, this describes “my truth.” When we write our own law of truth, it can become a form of idolatry, putting ourselves and our wants first instead of focusing on God. Instead of saying, “This is my truth,” we should qualify our words with “my opinion,” or “my perspective,” as in, “I’m asking you to recognize my perspective on this.” We want to make sure what we say brings glory to God and does not muddle His truth.

It is not about Christ fitting into me; it is about me fitting into Christ. That is freedom. To live in Christ is to dwell in his goodness, righteousness and wisdom.

Example #3: How we pursue the FULL application of God’s peace and joy in our lives

God’s peace is there! We just need to claim it:

Philippians 4:4–7: (KJV) 4 Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. 5 Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand. 6 Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. 7 And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.

Let’s be vulnerable and empty ourselves before our heavenly Father by bringing to Him all we struggle with that is not in harmony with Christlikeness.

We claim His peace not by demanding it, but by humbly bringing ourselves before Him in prayer:

Hebrews 4:15–16: (KJV) 15 For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. 16 Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.

While preparing for this podcast episode, Rick received a text from a dear brother in Christ that providentially fit exactly into our topic of how we embrace Christian liberty, witness its transformative power and set aside anything that competes with its purpose.

You know I have overcome, through God’s pure grace, a lifetime of near- death situations, alcohol and drug addictions, cheap dopamine addictions of all sorts. I am no longer in a critical health condition, no longer homeless, lonely and godless. I have gotten back control over most of my life. But, somehow, I cannot fully feel the JOY and the PEACE that I should be getting from my numerous trials.

It is good that he realizes trials can produce peace, even if he is not yet feeling it. The difficulties bring us to where we need to go.

There is obviously still a remnant of my old rebel/victimhood mindset that is keeping me from experiencing that peace. It is one thing to KNOW God is polishing you for the success of your sanctification process, but it’s another thing to fully grasp the whole teaching God intended for you to get through those trials. I have been stuck on a plateau.

He is recognizing that he is working at it, but he has leveled out.

There is ONE THING I had apparently never fully done. I had never FORMALLY ASKED FOR FORGIVENESS, for both my old ways and my hidden sins. Sure, I have asked a lot of times, but maybe never in a deep, deep way. I had never wanted to fully admit my deep-rooted flawed mindset that I didn’t even know I still had, until I started having to deal with “stuff” again and realized I was STILL not getting that promised JOY.

He realized he hadn’t been completely honest with himself. He had to dig in and go deeper.

So, here is my testimony: before even thinking of asking for help, grace and more holy spirit, we need to first truly repent, thus formally ask for His forgiveness for our shortcomings. There is no way out: we need to CLEAN HOUSE first!

We have to humble ourselves first, and let go of our own best understanding, our false expectations and our flawed self-indulgent coping mechanisms before God’s teachings have any chance to sink in. I’m NOT holding back this time! Asking for His forgiveness is the first step, even for the things we don’t even know are still there at the root of our sins. These things are often what is keeping us from TOTAL SUBMISSION to God’s will. “Search me, God, so that I can experience peace and give it back to You by witnessing Your work in me, by showing fruits of love toward You and my neighbor.”

Psalm 19:12: (KJV) Who can understand his errors? Cleanse Thou me from secret faults.

When we look at a testimony like this through the lens of Christian liberty, we realize such freedom is a tremendous, lofty privilege, but it doesn’t come without a cost.

However, it is freely available through Christ’s sacrifice. It is freely available through being given God’s spirit. It can thrive by us controlling our thoughts and actions, and in seeking God’s peace, joy, love and spirit above all else.

We all have dramatic choices to make. Recognize the guardrails God has put around us for our own protection. Follow God’s will and way through Christ to make good God- honoring choices.

Our ability to choose liberty in Christ pays great dividends for all!

Romans 8:18,20–22: 18 For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed to us...

There is something greater to come!

20 For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it,

The creation (those who are not followers of Christ) has futile lives. God allowed Satan to bring sin and death to reign over the world. Why?

…in hope 21 that the creation itself also will be set free <1659> from its slavery to corruption into the freedom <1657> of the glory of the children of God.

As children of God, what we learn and how we develop now will help the world in the future.

22 For we know that the whole creation groans and suffers the pains of childbirth together until now.

We are the example of learning Christian liberty in difficult and evil surroundings, yet we still honor God. Christian liberty is a privilege. Stay within the guardrails. Look up and honor your Father with the liberty He gives us in Christ!

So, does Christian liberty give us freedom of choice?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1408-christian-liberty-part-ii/ See:

1. What does Galatians 5:13-17 teach us about the battle we wage between our personal desires and Christian liberty? How does Paul’s warning shape our understanding of freedom in Christ?

2. How does Paul’s counsel in 1 Corinthians 8:7-12 guide us in using liberty responsibly? What does it reveal about the relational impact of our choices? (also 1 Peter 4:1,3)

3. How can you make sure your words don’t just reflect “my truth,” but “THE truth”?

4. Are you careful to speak with humility, clarity and scriptural backing? How can you better align your speech with integrity and humility? (John 8:31-21, 36, 2 Peter 2:18-19)

5. When we abide in the “law of liberty,” why is it necessary to be “effectual doers”? (James 1:25)

6. What is the connection between laying ALL before God (fully surrendering our anxieties in prayer to Him), and experiencing His peace? How is this peace connected to liberty in Christ? How do we claim this peace? (Philippians 4:4-7, Hebrews 4:15-16, Psalm 19:12)

7. How do you fully surrender your past and present struggles to God in prayer? What might be holding you back from His full peace and joy that is offered through your liberty in Christ?

8. How does Romans 8:18,20-22 describe the future hope of creation being set free from the sin and degradation they are experiencing now? What role do believers play in modeling this liberty amid present suffering?

9. Are there areas in your life where you are tempted to use liberty as an excuse for self-centered choices rather than Christ-centered service? How can you realign your liberties to be focused on what God expects of you?

## Episode 1409 — Do We Get What We Deserve? Karma vs the Gospel
Published: 2025-11-03
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1409-karma/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/24095013/CQ_Rewind_11-03-2025_Do_We_Get_What_We_Deserve_Karma_vs_the_Gospel.pdf

Galatians 6:7: Do not be deceived, God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, this he will also reap.

“People should get what they deserve.” I’m guessing most of us would see this as a general statement of fairness and equity. Of course, for this statement to ring true, we need to agree on who or what ultimately determines what people deserve. On a very basic level, this may sound like karma. So, what is karma? Basically, karma is the idea that what you do, especially your choices and intentions, shapes what happens to you later. If you act kindly and do good, good things are more likely to come your way. If you act selfishly or harm others, you may face negative consequences. In many Indian traditions, this isn’t just about this life; it can affect what kind of life you’re born into next. So, do Bible teachings support the idea of karma? Are the two in harmony?

This is a little like asking someone of the Hindu faith to summarize all of the sects and denominations of Christianity in 40 minutes. We only have time to make general statements about this very detailed topic.

Karma is understood in vastly different ways. People who believe in karma don’t all agree on how it works. Some think it’s a natural law that affects your future lives, while others believe it only applies to this life. Some focus on intentions and morals, while others include rituals or social customs. There’s also debate over whether karma is automatic or guided by gods, whether its effects happen right away or later, whether good or bad karma can be shared between people, and how it connects to free will, fate, and ways to break free—like prayer, repentance or spiritual practice.

If we were going to use the Bible to prove the existence of karma, what would our arguments be?

Argument 1: The Bible repeatedly teaches “you reap what you sow.”

This is classic karma:

Galatians 6:7-10: 7 Do not be deceived, God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, this he will also reap. 8 For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the spirit will from the spirit reap eternal life. 9 Let us not lose heart in doing good, for in due time we will reap if we do not grow weary. 10 So then, while we have opportunity, let us do good to all people, and especially to those who are of the household of the faith.

These verses certainly sound like karma with the sowing and reaping analogy. The apostle not only says it in passing, he explains it, getting deeper into why it’s important to sow to the spirit and not to the flesh, so that we can reap eternal life. Treat others well.

Job and Proverbs seem to support the concept as well:

Job 4:8: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity and those who sow trouble harvest it.

What goes around comes back around!

Proverbs 22:8-9: 8 He who sows iniquity will reap vanity, and the rod of his fury will perish. 9 He who is generous will be blessed, for he gives some of his food to the poor.

We gain a blessing if we give generously. We get what we give!

So, we have both Old and New Testament confirmation that we reap what we sow.

Argument 2: Reciprocity and moral accounting appear in Jesus’ teachings. This echoes the logic of karma.

Matthew 7:1-2,12: 1 Do not judge so that you will not be judged. 2 For in the way you judge, you will be judged; and by your standard of measure, it will be measured to you. 12 In everything, therefore, treat people the same way you want them to treat you, for this is the Law and the Prophets.

Jesus himself is saying when we set a standard, that same standard will be used to judge us. It’s the same concept as sowing and reaping. In everything… treat people the same way you want them to treat you.

Luke 6:38: (NLT) Give, and you will receive. Your gift will return to you in full—pressed down, shaken together to make room for more, running over, and poured into your lap. The amount you give will determine the amount you get back.

The teaching of reciprocity and moral accountability is clearly stated here in Jesus’ words. He is focused on the great power of being grace-motivated towards others, assuring us of blessings as a result. That essentially, from what we understand, is what karma is saying, supporting this second argument.

Argument 3: Individual biblical accounts show clear consequences for actions.

The Bible gives countless case studies where sin leads to consequences. Are these examples of divine justice or the cause-and-effect logic of karma?

- King David and his household suffering after his sin with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11 and 12). Their affair led to devastating results—David ordered her husband to be murdered, their child died, his family unraveled, and his leadership was repeatedly challenged. This shows the ripple effect of moral failings and selfishness with immediate and generational consequences.
- Achan’s defeat after taking spoils from Jericho when commanded not to (Joshua 7). After Israel’s victory at Jericho, God instructed them not to take any spoils of war for themselves. Achan secretly hid treasure and that act caused massive repercussions, with Israel losing in battle and Achan and his family killed for his disobedience.

These and many other accounts illustrate the “action brings consequence” pattern that karma claims. There seem to be many similarities.

In addition, we have all experienced people who sow negativity - those who are miserly, disagreeable, unhappy, "out for themselves" kind of people. They have few real friendships and are stressed and unhappy, leading miserable lives. Negative feeds on negative.

What do we do with all of this? These three arguments so far lead us in a specific direction:

We can see the similarities in the brief concepts we compared. We want to be careful, though, to make sure we understand the whole story.

It is fascinating to put these two approaches to life, consequences and future hope side- by-side. Now let’s focus on the details!

Is there a difference between the foundational basis for karma and the foundational basis for the Bible?

As we shall soon see, there is a very clear foundational difference between what drives the retribution of karma and what drives what we will clearly define as the justice of the Bible. To understand the dramatic differences between these concepts, we need to first go a bit further into understanding some of the origins of karma.

Karma dates back to around 1500 BCE, which is about the time of Moses, where it appears in ancient sacred texts of Hinduism applying to sacrificial acts performed to uphold cosmic balance. It later evolved across traditions in Hinduism, Buddhism and other world religions.

For billions of people, karma and reincarnation are deeply intertwined. Reincarnation is the cycle of rebirth—your karma determines the conditions of your next life.

Each life, it is said, is shaped by the karma of the previous one, and each action determines your next. But not everyone who believes in karma accepts reincarnation. In that case, good or bad choices tend to return in kind, within this single lifetime.

Reincarnation is another big concept interpreted in diverse ways depending on your religion, culture, society, geography and personal worldview. Briefly, the belief is some essence or consciousness survives death and enters a new body.

Some lines of thinking insist the new body must be human with the same gender, others say either gender. Others say it can be an animal or even a plant, rock or household object.

The goal is to stop cycling through lives and reach enlightenment (it has many names; we’re probably most familiar with “Nirvana” in Buddhism), but there is no set number of how many lives you go through or how much time it takes to become liberated from attachment, ignorance and karmic debt you owe.

Essentially, like Christianity, there are a lot of different ways karma is understood among those who believe in it. That is important for us to recognize and respect.

Let’s look at the pattern of the karmic belief of cycling through many different lives. Up to this point, karma and the Bible seemed to have a similar teaching, but here is where they are dramatically different.

Karma seems to operate in an undefined way, in that the cycling through different lives is very individual and (depending on the particular karma belief system) can take many lifetimes for an individual to reach a state of enlightenment. The big picture is that an individual starts in one life and hopes to stop cycling through different lives by eventually reaching enlightenment. Each pathway is very different due to the individual’s choice of conduct and the specific rules of their belief system.

In contrast, Christianity teaches that each individual has one human life that is ultimately guided by the just and loving will of God. Let’s look at how the Bible describes the process, with the differentiation between all mankind and then specifically the followers of Jesus.

First, we’ll look at all who do not currently follow Jesus:

Hebrews 9:27-28: 27 And inasmuch as it is appointed for men to die once and after this comes judgment, 28 so Christ also, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time for salvation without reference to sin, to those who eagerly await him.

After our research found so many varied details about how karma and reincarnation are supposed to work, it’s nice to see the Scriptures explain it so simply: because of sin, mankind dies. We all would have stayed in that death condition but for the fact that Christ offered himself as a ransom sacrifice, once for all: the perfect man Jesus equivalent to the perfect man Adam.

One life, one death and one judgment, and then the provisions of God’s kingdom after resurrection, which we will talk about soon. We are all part of one collective plan. Regardless of any individual’s belief system today, Jesus died for ALL.

That is the important part of this Hebrew scripture; it is appointed for men to die once—a general, broad statement—after this comes judgment. This is a panoramic view of the pattern the entire race of humanity follows in a few sentences.

For those who do not currently follow Jesus, judgment will come, but with a mediator to help them work through their challenges—another difference from karma:

1 Timothy 2:3-6: (KJV) 3 For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; 4 Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge (full discernment) of the truth. 5 For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; 6 who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.

The basis shown here is Jesus dying for all men.

They will be saved—provided a resurrection back to life, and THEN taught the truth. This process of bringing man back to God through teaching them the knowledge of the truth will be mediated by Jesus himself. This is a brief view of a pathway the entire world (all men) will follow back to God.

For those called to discipleship now, the judgment comes in our present life.

Due to our sacrifice of our earthly ambitions by following Christ, our old lives are “dead,” and we are considered freed from the sin inherited through Adam:

Romans 6:22-23: (NIV2011) 22 But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the benefit you reap leads to holiness, and the result is eternal life. 23 For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Followers of Jesus are reckoned freed from sin in this lifetime, in advance of mankind, which is an important distinction. Through Jesus, they have a relationship with God. In this case, Jesus is not the mediator sitting between God and man like the world in the future. Instead, he is described as our advocate at our side, working with us now, teaching and developing us for the work in the future kingdom.

Having already been set free, our freedom still needs the help of an advocate:

1 John 2:1-3: 1 My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; 2 and he himself is the propitiation (satisfaction) for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. 3 By this we know that we have come to know Him, if we keep His commandments.

Jesus’ sacrifice gave the provision for faithful followers now to have him as their advocate with God. Jesus will be a mediator for the “everybody else” after their resurrection in the kingdom. Jesus has a dual role, and everyone who ever lived fits into one of these two categories.

Here in Western societies, we tend to think karma requires getting what you deserve. It’s more nuanced than that. It’s more accurate to say that karma reflects the consequences of one’s actions and intentions, but not always in ways that appear fair or immediate. It’s not moral justice. It’s not someone or something deciding what's fair.

Hinduism: The quality and consequences of your actions are judged not only by what you do, but how well you fulfill your specific role in life. Even the right action won't be rewarded if it isn’t aligned with your duty. A teacher, parent and warrior each have different duties. If a warrior doesn't kill because he feels killing is wrong, abandoning his duty would generate bad karma, even with good intentions.

Buddhism: Karma is driven by intention, so even if the outcome is bad, a well-meaning act generates positive karma.

Jainism (one of India’s oldest religions): Karma is a literal substance that binds to the soul. It’s mechanical, not moral. You don’t “deserve” karma—you accumulate it through any action—and liberation comes by purifying yourself, ridding yourself of the substance.

With all the karmic views, there seems to be a mystery of exactly how a person reaches enlightenment. It seems each person must try to figure out how to do the best they can. There doesn’t appear to be a specific path.

The Bible clearly breaks down how God’s just and loving will is applied to the lives of Christians.

The gospel applies God’s grace—His unmerited favor— to lift us out of sin and death.

Is it through faith, or works?

Ephesians 2:8-10: 8 For by grace you have been saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; 9 not as a result of works, so that no one may boast. 10 For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we would walk in them.

God had in His plan the way to bring the followers of Jesus to this point. This is not arbitrary. This is defined; this is clear. The lives of true Christians are elevated to a higher level by something beyond our ability to obtain alone. It is by God’s grace, through faith.

Karma is much more of a solo endeavor, though there are differing thoughts on this. As a generalization, in Hinduism, divine intervention is possible, but rare. In Buddhism, deities do exist, but they do not override karma. They can help guide but can’t erase karma’s effects. In Jainism, karma is impersonal. It’s impossible to stop. The person cannot persuade it, or alter it because there are no deities in that religion to even help.

God’s will pervades the life of a Christian in this life and will be everywhere in the lives of the “everybody else” in the future kingdom. This is a massive difference.

These verses focus on the lives of Christians:

Ephesians 2:13-16: (NLT) 13 But now you have been united with Christ Jesus. Once you were far away from God, but now you have been brought near to Him through the blood of Christ. 14 For Christ himself has brought peace to us. He united Jews and Gentiles into one people when, in his own body on the cross, he broke down the wall of hostility that separated us. 15 He did this by ending the system of law with its commandments and regulations. He made peace between Jews and Gentiles by creating in himself one new people from the two groups. 16 Together as one body, Christ reconciled both groups to God by means of his death on the cross, and our hostility toward each other was put to death.

This is an example of the biblical approach to dealing with the difficulty of merging these two disparate groups at the time of the early church. Through belief in the sacrifice of Jesus and the will of God, the barriers between the Jews and Gentiles were broken down. Those of the Jewish faith and pagan Gentiles would never have gotten along. But people from both belief systems came together through Christianity, united with a single purpose.

God’s grace is so powerful that it can bring together under Jesus those who have forever been at odds! God’s grace is an external force that lifts us above our internal strife. It brings us up; it helps us. We do not have to find it; it is given to us.

Once grace is in place, THEN works can come into play—but grace/faith is first:

James 2:14-17: 14 What use is it, my brethren, if someone says he has faith but he has no works? Can that faith save him? 15 If a brother or sister is without clothing and in need of daily food, 16 and one of you says to them, Go in peace, be warmed and be filled, and yet you do not give them what is necessary for their body, what use is that? 17 Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead, being by itself.

The grace of God that is a gift to us through the sacrifice of Jesus is a beginning. It is a foundation. But we are required to act on it. We are elevated up, lifted up, but we still have to do the works that demonstrate our faith. Unlike karma, we are guided by God’s grace, directed and shown how to improve ourselves and to act more in Christ’s likeness.

With karmic beliefs, what a person does may or may not help them. With some belief systems, you can do the wrong thing for the right reason and generate good karma; with others, you can generate bad karma even if you do the right thing with the wrong motivation or went outside your duty in your specific role. There is no Jehovah God and His grace to help, nor His son Jesus to be an advocate and mediator.

Initially, we saw Christianity and karma agree on some principles. But when we look at the larger picture, we see a clearly-defined plan versus a concept with so many individual variables that it is almost impossible to quantify.

As the differences between karma and the gospel begin to unfold, the pattern of God’s grace and plan are beginning to shine!

With having our one life that has been touched by God’s grace in place, where do repentance and forgiveness fit into the picture?

Perhaps this is the most dramatic, practical, everyday difference between karma and the Bible. The concept of repentance and forgiveness was made plain in the Jewish Law back in the Old Testament by their needed sacrifices to atone for their various sins. Repentance and forgiveness take center stage once Jesus begins his teachings.

In researching this topic, we were getting a little overwhelmed with all of the complexities and competing explanations of karma, but then realized we don’t need to be an expert on error. We want to study the truth of the Bible, allowing us to discard whatever does not line up with that truth, much like how government agencies study real money in order to detect counterfeits. It allows them to identify fakes when they encounter them.

My wife, Trish, experienced this when she worked for a bank. Part of their training was to understand counterfeit money and to be able to not only see it, but to feel it. They were so well trained to know the feel of real dollar bills. I saw one of the tellers who worked with her counting the bills. She was going through the stack in her hand, then she stopped, nodded her head, felt that bill again, nodded again and put it on the side. It was amazing, but if we are trained on the right thing, the wrong thing becomes obvious. This is a really important concept, so we have to pay close attention to the Scriptures on this topic.

The gospel applies unmerited forgiveness for the entire world through the sacrifice of Jesus.

God is the ultimate decision-maker as to how and when He exhibits His mercy:

Romans 9:14-16: 14 What shall we say then? There is no injustice with God, is there? May it never be! 15 For He says to Moses, I WILL HAVE MERCY ON WHOM I HAVE MERCY, AND I WILL HAVE COMPASSION ON WHOM I HAVE COMPASSION. 16 So then it does not depend on the man who wills or the man who runs, but on God who has mercy.

God’s mercy is the baseline.

Karma provides individual liability for each and every “sin” for each and every person. It has to be made right. However, “sin” is really more of a Christian thought. Karma is more impersonal, as a natural law of cause and effect, not a moral indictment from a deity.

As we talk about Jehovah God, this differentiation is critical.

In Hinduism, karma is impersonal and operates independently of any god or gods who might intervene. Depending on your interpretation, there can be up to 330 million gods. In Buddhism, karma is entirely impersonal. The cycle of reincarnation is not controlled by any divine being. In fact, the goal of enlightenment is to transcend all realms, including those of divine beings.

As a Christian, listening to this makes karma seem chaotic. One’s fate is individualized depending on the karmic interpretation; there does not seem to be a predicatable method to achieve enlightenment.

In contrast, God’s decisive mercy for ALL comes through one source—Jesus. The chaos is dissolved in the clarity of the sacrifice:

John 3:16-17: 16 For God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish, but have eternal life. 17 For God did not send the son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.

God sent Jesus to save ALL of humanity. There aren’t billions of individual human paths.

It doesn’t matter where we are, or what we have ever believed. Jesus’ sacrifice is equal for each one. This is an underlying clarity instead of chaos.

The entire world will eventually benefit from Jesus’ sacrifice. How does this work?

The Apostle Paul explains the depth of this incredible gift:

Romans 5:18-21: 18 So then as through one transgression there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness there resulted justification of life to all men.

This is a clear-cut, simply stated equity: condemnation for all men came because of one man’s sin. The justification of all men will come as a result of one man’s righteousness. Justice is shown by the ransom price Jesus paid to restore humanity’s loss because of Adam’s sin. Karma doesn’t have this kind of clarity and fairness.

19 For as through the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous. 20 The Law came in so that the transgression would increase; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, 21 so that, as sin reigned in death, even so grace would reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

The Jewish Law identified sin, labeling what was sinful so Israel could see it more clearly.

The inherited sin and death we all received was canceled in a perfect and just way through a perfect life (Jesus) sacrificed for a perfect life (Adam). Yes, there is still individual liability, but first, the big problem of Adamic sin had to be resolved. We can see forgiveness clearly working here.

Karma leaves us on our own to figure things out. Many traditions believing in karma with reincarnation teach there is no memory transfer. We don’t remember past lives, so we can’t consciously “fix” past karma, but karma might influence the circumstances we are born into, like which family we are born into and our health. Teachings and teachers like gurus can help us navigate consequences and pursue liberation.

The concept of not remembering the past is difficult to understand. The person is given experiences to try to move themselves up the ladder, but they can’t remember the lessons learned from those past experiences. This means they have to figure it out from the beginning every single time.

The gospel is exactly the opposite. In God’s kingdom, Jesus tells us every man will be accountable for his own deeds. This means people will remember this life as an important learning experience. Memory is part of being human, allowing us to observe, learn and move on.

The gospel applies repentance and mutual forgiveness as tools to help us overcome our deficiencies.

Luke 17:3-4: 3 Be on your guard! If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. 4 And if he sins against you seven times a day, and returns to you seven times, saying, I repent, forgive him.

Forgiveness here means “to send the sin away from you,” but it does not mean we are sending the sin away from the person. If we do or say something bad to another person, they can forgive us. They can send that sin away from themselves, by mentally pushing it away or otherwise making it of no effect by understanding the reasons behind the bad behavior. But we still have to answer to God for our own behaviors.

Notice Jesus does not put any qualifiers on his answer in this next teaching:

Matthew 18:21-22: 21 Then Peter came and said to him, Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times? 22 Jesus said to him, I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.

If we have a forgiving attitude, we can take what someone has done against us and minimize its effect in our lives. But does that lessen the sin in God’s eyes?

With karma, me forgiving you doesn’t release you from karmic cycles. Karma is typically seen as an impersonal law of cause and effect—each action generates consequences, regardless of external forgiveness. Me forgiving you might help my own karma, though.

But with Christianity, even if I forgive someone, they are still answerable to God and the consequences He exacts. Is this really that much different from karma?

Forgiving them might make them stop to realize the grace they just received. They might admit they hurt us. It might touch their heart and help them make the decision to change from a hard heart to one who appreciates the grace they have been given. It might make the person more repentant, leading them to humbly ask for God’s forgiveness. Because we stood up and stepped out on the person’s behalf, it could change the person’s direction in a big way. It can have a great influence.

Jesus emphatically shows us how important it is to have a forgiving attitude with everyone:

Matthew 6:9-12: 9 Pray, then, in this way: Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed be Your name. 10 Your kingdom come. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. 11 Give us this day our daily bread. 12 And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

This is the well-known Lord’s Prayer. The basis of our being forgiven by God is to forgive others. Forgive us our debts—forgive what we owe. Forgive what we fall short on as we also have forgiven our debtors, those who owe us or have wronged us in some way. We rise above that wrong, which should have a positive effect on all involved. This differs from karma.

There is a basic foundational difference in how we are to deal with our hardships and hurts. The Scriptures, by God’s grace, give us direction and answers.

Looking at all of these details really uncovers the dramatic and inspiring approach the Bible has always laid out for us. Let’s appreciate what we have!

Now that we have examined the many differences between karma and the gospel, what are the final results of each approach?

One of the overwhelmingly powerful aspects of the Bible is that it has a harmonious approach to humanity’s destiny from beginning to end. As we look at an overview of that approach, let’s focus on a final and important question. Knowing what we know now, would we rather have karma rule our destiny or have God’s plan rule our destiny?

The CQ Team is in the United States. Here in the West, we are more likely to encounter karma through New Age belief systems of Paganism and Wicca. Again, there is a wide range of beliefs, but the core concept for Wicca (“white” witchcraft) is that whatever energy you send out—positive or negative—returns to you threefold. In Paganism, karma is often seen as a universal feedback loop, in that actions ripple through the world and return in kind.

Karma with reincarnation tells us that our destiny is essentially tied up in somehow learning the important lessons of life through living multiple lives with or without a memory (depending on the interpretation), in order to eventually live in an elevated state of consciousness. The person then ceases to exist as a separate entity and is beyond time and space. It is a state without suffering. Once this state is achieved, the “soul” no longer cycles through birth and death. Or it can happen while the person is still alive (without a belief in reincarnation), described as peaceful awareness, a complete liberation from craving, ignorance and karmic bondage.

However, there doesn’t seem to be a consensus as to how to reach such an elevated state of consciousness. We don’t see this commonly happening around us.

The gospel tells us that the hard lessons of sin and death are there to ultimately teach us that God’s way is the ONLY way to live for eternity. The gospel shows us how to learn these lessons!

Back to our theme text:

Galatians 6:7: Do not be deceived, God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, this he will also reap.

Tied into this discussion is the idea of generational curses, which is an interesting study in itself. We refer you to Episode #1196: “Am I Living Under a Generational Curse?” part of our three-part “Curses” series.

Similar to karma, the Bible teaches actions DO have consequences, but we are shown them in an understandable way so we know what they are, where they are applied, why they happen, how they happen and their time frame.

Let’s look at an overview of how the consequences of our actions work:

Zephaniah 3:8-9: 8 Therefore wait for Me, declares the LORD, for the day when I rise up as a witness. Indeed, My decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out on them My indignation, all My burning anger; for all the earth will be devoured by the fire of My zeal.

My indignation, all My burning anger—yes, God is angry over sin. We know He has a plan, but in reading these verses so far, we only see He is mad! Will the earth be destroyed? For all the earth will be devoured by the fire of My zeal. If we read only up to this point, this verse seems to contradict what we know of God’s plan for ALL.

We need to read the next verse to see God’s plan unfold: 9 For then I will give to the peoples purified lips, that all of them may call on the name of the LORD, to serve Him shoulder to shoulder.

This proves the literal physical earth is not going to be devoured by fire, because God’s anger brings about this beautiful condition—I will give to the peoples purified lips, that ALL of them may call on the name of the LORD.

The sacrifice of Jesus is the pivotal point of this entire plan. Once it is applied to all humanity in the future, it will be obvious to mankind what they are being taught is true and righteous because they will have a memory of this lifetime.

Here are some of the lessons mankind will cherish as a result of the sacrifice of Jesus:

Psalms 103:2-5: 2 Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget none of His benefits; 3 who pardons all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases; 4 who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with lovingkindness and compassion; 5 who satisfies your years with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle.

Listen to the incredible things laid out in these verses!

- Forget none of His benefits - He pardons all your iniquities
- Heals all your diseases - Redeems your life from the pit (from death)
- Crowns you with lovingkindness and compassion
- Satisfies your years with good things - Renews your youth… like the eagle

This is a beautiful state of being. How do the people get to this point? What direction do they follow?

Their environment will be different:

Micah 4:1-3: 1 And it will come about in the last days that the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains. It will be raised above the hills, and the peoples will stream to it. 2 Many nations will come and say, Come and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD and to the house of the God of Jacob, that He may teach us about His ways and that we may walk in His paths. For from Zion will go forth the law, even the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.

Scripturally, mountains generally symbolize governments. God rules the earth. Nations will come to His government and ask to learn. This is another fundamental difference between karma and God’s plan. God teaches the people His ways so they can learn to walk in His paths. He will give them whatever help they need to be able to fully understand and implement His plan.

What happens as a result? 3 And He will judge between many peoples and render decisions for mighty, distant nations. Then they will hammer their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks; Nation will not lift up sword against nation, and never again will they train for war.

This is the true “nirvana” everyone is looking for in the kingdom after mankind is resurrected here on earth. God will use Jesus and his faithful ones to guide them through the learning and practicing of righteousness in the kingdom.

In summary, the environment changes because rather than the chaos of this world under Satan’s influence, God’s government gives man something righteous to follow.

Instead of being left to figure it out on their own, their hearts will be educated so they can truly see life for what it is:

Jeremiah 31:33-34: 33 But this is the covenant which I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD, I will put My law within them and on their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people. 34 They will not teach again, each man his neighbor and each man his brother, saying, Know the LORD, for they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them, declares the LORD, for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin I will remember no more.

All of these transformative experiences are arranged by God to truly teach His human creation.

The judgment described in the Bible is based on the deeds of a single lifetime, not an accumulation of karma over many lives.

This principle of personal accountability for a single life challenges the concept of being reborn to pay for the deeds of a past life that one can’t even remember.

I will put My law within them and on their heart I will write it—so they can understand. This gives mankind the answers and then says, Now you have to do the work. Works are still important because they are the visible fruit of what is in the heart. God supplies the righteous environment and the training in which to grow. Mankind will have to do the work and show Him gratitude by living righteous lives for eternity.

All these transformative experiences are arranged by God to truly teach His human creation. Why? Because God loves His human creation! God created mankind so He could have a human family on this planet. There is a reason for it. It is not an endless cycle of wondering if we should do this or if we will turn into that. It is a clearly stated, directional plan that is just, wise, loving and powerful.

The bottom line: All of humanity will eventually have the benefit of remembering the hard experiences of sin AND the benefit of God’s direction through Jesus in working through and learning from those memories as they grow into righteousness.

Revelation 21:3-4: 3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne, saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is among men, and He will dwell among them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself will be among them, 4 and He will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and there will no longer be any death; there will no longer be any mourning, or crying, or pain; the first things have passed away.

We have seen that the end result of the plan of God was set up from the very beginning, from before the time the earth was created. This plan was to bring the human family to this beautiful place in the kingdom here on earth. There His son Jesus (and his faithful followers in heaven) will teach mankind. Mankind will learn and will, we believe, overwhelmingly choose to follow God through Jesus because of his sacrifice. It is a beautiful picture of everyone coming to perfection and eternity. This is the comprehensive, detailed plan for man found in the Bible.

Let’s stand for what the Scriptures teach us and not worry about trying to figure out something that can’t be explained or remembered. God’s plan is in front of us, giving us answers right now. We just need to strive to do what is expected of us in God’s honoring care.

Do we get what we deserve? We don’t. We get so much more because we do not deserve life with all of our sinfulness. We get so much more because of the sacrifice of Jesus. We get grace. And we get love. We get true justice. We get learning. We get life for eternity.

We get to learn all these things, whether now for the true disciples of Christ, or later for the entire world of mankind. EVERYBODY gets more than they deserve. WHY?

Because our Heavenly Father who created us, loves us and wants us to thrive. And that, my friends, is much better than karma!

So, do we get what we deserve?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
