### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1409-karma/

1. How does the biblical principle of “sowing and reaping” in Galatians 6:7-10, Job 4:8 and Proverbs 22:8-9 compare to the concept of karma?

2. In what areas of your life might you be “sowing to the flesh” instead of “sowing to the spirit?” Where in your life could you invest more in spiritual growth?

3. How do the teachings on reciprocity and moral accountability in Matthew 7:1-2 and Luke 6:38 reflect or differ from the logic of karma?

4. Give biblical examples where people received a clear consequence for their actions. (2 Samuel 11 and 12, Joshua 7)

*At this point, do you think that karma and Christianity are similar? Why or why not?

5. Compare the karmic cycle of reincarnation with the biblical view of life, death and judgment. How does the Bible’s “one life, one judgment” model shape our understanding of accountability and grace? (Hebrews 9:27-28, Romans 6:22-23)

6. How does the gospel’s approach to forgiveness and repentance differ from the karmic view of consequences and personal responsibility? Compare the roles of grace, mercy and memory in both. (Romans 9:14-16, John 3:16-17, Luke 17:3-4, Matthew 18:21-22)

7. When you experience hurt or injustice from others, how do you respond? How can you improve this reaction?

9. How does the understanding that God’s grace is the foundation of your salvation (Ephesians 2:8-10) affect your motivation for doing good? What is the purpose behind your service to others? How can you keep it pure and on a higher plane?

## Episode 1410 — Why Is the Book of Enoch NOT in the Bible?
Published: 2025-11-10
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1410-book-of-enoch/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/07134756/CQ_Rewind_11-10-2025_Why_is_the_Book_of_Enoch_NOT_in_the_Bible.pdf

Genesis 5:22,24: 22 …Enoch walked with God three hundred years after he became the father of Methuselah, and he had other sons and daughters. 24 Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him.

From what the Bible tells us about Enoch, he was an amazingly holy man who lived long before the Flood. To be described as one who “walked with God” is a true testimony of a life well-lived. Further, a few lines of the Book of Enoch are actually quoted in the New Testament. With such credentials, we would have to wonder why the Book of Enoch is not a part of the Bible itself. Why wouldn’t you include the writings of a man who walked with God for 300 years? Could this be an oversight… or a conspiracy? Fortunately, a clear understanding of history and the Bible gives us thorough and conclusive answers to all of these questions.

We’ve been asked several times by listeners if it is worth studying the Book of Enoch and why it isn’t in our Bibles in the first place.

There are two men named Enoch in the book of Genesis. The first was the son of Cain in

Genesis 4:17, and Cain named a city after him. The Enoch we are referring to today is the one revered in the Old and New Testaments for his faith and righteousness. He was Noah’s great grandfather.

There are actually three ancient Books of Enoch, appropriately named 1 Enoch, 2 Enoch and 3 Enoch. They were all written at different times by different authors. Scholars largely dismiss 2 Enoch and 3 Enoch from biblical canon due to being written after the correct time period and including highly imaginative, mystical content that doesn’t match theological and historical standards used to recognize accepted Scripture.

Our focus will be whether or not 1 Enoch should be part of the Bible.

What do we know about the person Enoch? Enoch was the seventh generation from Adam:

Genesis 5:18,21–24: 18 Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years, and became the father of Enoch. 21 Enoch lived sixty-five years, and became the father of Methuselah. 22 Then Enoch walked with God three hundred years after he became the father of Methuselah, and he had other sons and daughters. 23 So all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. 24 Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him.

For God took him—this is an unusual description. Where did he go?

Enoch pleased God by faith. There is a wonderful tribute to him in Hebrews:

Hebrews 11:5: By faith Enoch was taken up so that he would not see death; AND HE WAS NOT FOUND BECAUSE GOD TOOK HIM UP (quoted from Genesis 5:24); for he obtained the witness that before his being taken up he was pleasing to God.

The King James Version says he was translated, meaning moved from one place to another. The New American Standard Version (1995) says taken up. However, the word “up” is not in the original Greek; rather, it was supplied by the translator.

God “took” him. What does that mean?

Here is what we know:

1.

Enoch’s body was not found.

2. He could not have gone to heaven.

John 3:13: No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven: the Son of Man.

This plain statement by Jesus should settle any argument about Enoch being taken to heaven. He wasn’t! If he had been, Jesus, of all people, would have known. Therefore, while there is some mystery around what exactly happened to Enoch, he died like everyone else.

Watch for a future episode on three deaths the Bible describes in a unique way, with more details on Enoch, as well as Moses and Elijah.

Let’s get into the book of 1 Enoch. One of the most common arguments as to why the book SHOULD have been included in biblical canon is that the book is directly quoted in the New Testament.

Enoch warned of judgment, and his warnings were quoted in the book of Jude:

Jude 1:14–15: 14 It was also about these men that Enoch, in the seventh generation from Adam, prophesied, saying, Behold, the Lord came with many thousands of his holy ones, 15 to execute judgment upon all, and to convict all the ungodly of all their ungodly deeds which they have done in an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.

Let’s compare this with 1 Enoch:

1 Enoch 1:9: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about them: See, the Lord is coming with thousands upon thousands of his holy ones to judge everyone, and to convict all of them of all the ungodly acts they have committed in their ungodliness.

There is a striking similarity between the two passages. This is the only place in the New Testament where a passage from 1 Enoch is cited nearly verbatim, proving at least some early Christians were familiar with Enoch’s prophecy.

We do not know how many of Enoch’s prophecies were handed down through verbal communication, as was common in his day. Was Jude writing down what verbally was communicated throughout generations of Jewish history? Or was Jude quoting directly from 1 Enoch? We don’t know for sure.

CLARITY QUESTION If Enoch was such a faithful person in the Bible and a prophecy of his is directly quoted in the Bible, why would 1 Enoch NOT be part of the canon of Christian Scripture?

There are at least five distinct reasons:

1 Enoch was not in the Hebrew Bible. It was never part of the Jewish Tanakh, the Hebrew Bible which formed the Old Testament foundation for the Christian Old Testament. By the late first century, it was already excluded from the Hebrew Scriptures.

In other words, 1 Enoch was never considered authentic by the Jewish rabbis; it was never included in the Hebrew Scriptures’ canon. Just because 1 Enoch is quoted in Scripture does not mean it is automatically a validation of the whole book. The Apostle Paul quoted from Greek authors (Titus 1:12, Acts 17:28, 1 Corinthians 15:33), but that doesn’t mean those authors’ full works belong in Scripture.

Interestingly, there are a few other texts that may refer to 1 Enoch, though the source for these scriptural thoughts is not cited. In other words, credit is not specifically given to Enoch.

For example, these are two verses before our previous quote:

Jude 1:12–13: (warning against people who exploit fellowship for their own gain) 12 These are the men who are hidden reefs in your love feasts when they feast with you without fear, caring for themselves; clouds without water, carried along by winds; autumn trees without fruit, doubly dead, uprooted; 13 wild waves of the sea, casting up their own shame like foam; wandering stars, for whom the black darkness has been reserved forever.

What or who is a wandering star?

Is that quoted from 1 Enoch or referenced elsewhere?

1 Enoch 80:6–8: Many leaders of the stars will deviate from their established order.

They will change their orbits and duties and not appear at their designated seasons. The entire order of the stars will be hidden from the sinners, and the thoughts of those on the earth will be mistaken about them, leading them to go astray and even regard them as gods. Evil will be multiplied upon them, and punishment will come upon them to destroy all.

“Many leaders of the stars will deviate from their established order” sounds like wandering stars.

But could Jude have been referencing Old Testament Scripture instead?

First:

Job 38:4,7: 4 Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding, 7 When the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?

Morning stars (Jesus in his pre-human existence as the Logos and Lucifer are the only beings scripturally called by this description) sang together.

Next:

Isaiah 14:12: How you have fallen from heaven, O star of the morning, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the earth, you who have weakened the nations!

Lucifer, one of the morning stars, fell from heaven, a “wandering star”!

Finally:

Ezekiel 28:14-16: 14 You were the anointed cherub who covers, and I placed you there. You were on the holy mountain of God; you walked in the midst of the stones of fire. 15 You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created until unrighteousness was found in you. 16 By the abundance of your trade you were internally filled with violence, and you sinned; therefore I have cast you as profane from the mountain of God. And I have destroyed you, O covering cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire.

Lucifer (Satan) was cast… as profane from the mountain of God. He was a “star” no longer in the proper position.

So, we don’t have to look to 1 Enoch for the poetic description of a wandering star. It is in the Old Testament.

CLARITY QUESTION Why would a writing by such a faithful and godly man be out of consideration?

The Pseudepigrapha are ancient writings that claim to be authored by famous biblical figures—like Enoch, Moses or Isaiah—but were actually written by someone else, often centuries later. The term comes from Greek roots meaning “false inscription.” These texts were usually composed between 300 BCE and 300 CE (a 600-year period of time) and include Jewish and early Christian works that were never accepted into the official biblical canon.

By being written centuries after Enoch’s lifetime by unknown authors (see Colby Townsend (2020), Britannica.com, and James C. VanderKam (1984) for dating and authorship analysis), 1 Enoch failed the early church’s standard for prophetic or apostolic origin. A later author or authors wrote under his name to try to give that work a prophetic authority.

1 Enoch was written around 300 BCE–100 BCE (a 200-year period), long after Enoch lived. It was originally written in Aramaic and Hebrew in Judea during the Second Temple Period.

It was translated into Greek but preserved fully only in Geʽez, the classical language of Ethiopia. Its themes are angelic rebellion, the Nephilim (which we often refer to as “fallen” angels), apocalyptic judgment, heavenly calendars and moral exhortations. It contains much fantastical thinking.

CLARITY QUESTION What about the book of Enoch’s historical value?

It offers insight into the thoughts of ancient peoples during Second Temple Judaism, bridging the gap between Old and New Testament thought.

While such history has value, the Bible purposely leaves a 400-year gap between the Old and New Testaments.

Amazingly, the last words of the Old Testament introduce the first events of the New Testament:

Malachi 4:5–6: 5 Behold, I am going to send you Elijah the prophet (foreshadowing John the Baptist) before the coming of the great and terrible day of the LORD. 6 He will restore the hearts of the fathers to their children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, so that I will not come and smite the land with a curse.

The first event of the New Testament is the angel Gabriel appearing to Zacharias (Luke 1:11-20) to tell him that he and his wife were going to have a son named John. John would come in the spirit and power of Elijah, the revered prophet of old (Luke 1:17), to prepare the people to receive their Messiah.

The Old Testament ends with the prediction of what would happen next. The New Testament picks right up where the Old Testament left off, with 400 years in between. The Bible was designed with this seamless precision. There was no indication by God that unrelated writings would be provided during this intertestamental period.

While 1 Enoch may have historical value, it has questionable theology.

1 Enoch contains elaborate angelology, cosmology, and apocalyptic visions that some leaders saw as doctrinally risky or misleading.

During the 400-year period of silence between the Old and New Testaments, many biblical texts were compiled and canonized, and new genres—like apocalyptic literature and what’s called “wisdom writings”—flourished. Wisdom writings offer moral instruction and guidance for living well.

Much error crept into Judaism like angelology. (All of the fantastical details about angels is one of the reasons modern-day readers are so curious about this book.)

1 Enoch is a compilation of five distinct sections, one of which is called The Astronomical Book (also called the Book of the Heavenly Luminaries). It describes complex heavenly calendars and the movements of the sun and moon. It describes a 364-day solar calendar and envisions the heavenly bodies moving through fixed “portals” at the edges of the earth. This calendar aligns more closely with ancient Mesopotamian and Egyptian systems than with the Jewish lunar calendar of the time. While the text does show careful observation by these ancient peoples—tracking seasonal changes, lengths of days and lunar phases—it assumes a geocentric universe (earth at the center) and a flat-earth-like horizon structure, which we know is incorrect.

Interestingly, while the Bible does not come out and say the earth is not flat, it implies it:

Isaiah 40:22: (NIV2011) He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth, and its people are like grasshoppers. He stretches out the heavens like a canopy, and spreads them out like a tent to live in.

The circle (Hebrew: chûg) of the earth—implying a spherical or circular shape; not flat.

Stretches out the heavens like a canopy—the sky or atmosphere being extended across the earth, much like a canopy. This is how we view the atmosphere enveloping the planet.

Job 26:7: He stretches out the north over empty space and hangs the earth on nothing.

Hangs the earth on nothing—remarkably showing the earth is not supported by physical pillars or foundations, but is suspended in space by gravitational forces. How else but from God would Job know this at a time when ancient Mesopotamian, Egyptian and Canaanite texts often depicted earth as a flat disk supported by mountains, pillars or deities?

Scripture has a deeper understanding of scientific truths than 1 Enoch.

The period of time 1 Enoch was written also saw the rise of distinct Jewish sects such as the Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and Zealots, each offering different interpretations of the Law and messianic hope.

Influenced by Hellenistic culture (Greek with eastern influences from 323 BCE onward) and the spread of Jewish communities across the Mediterranean, Second Temple Judaism became increasingly diverse and dynamic—and corrupted—by these outside influences.

“Diverse and dynamic” might sound good, but Jesus had to continually correct the Pharisees and Sadducees. He disagreed with the Zealots. Pure Judaism was confused and writings like 1 Enoch did not help to further biblical truth. In fact, truth was being diluted and poisoned by external ideas.

CLARITY QUESTION What about the ancient manuscript evidence of 1 Enoch? Aramaic fragments of the book found among the Dead Sea Scrolls confirm pre-Christian circulation. This book existed at the time of Jesus.

1 Enoch survives complete only in the Geʽez (Ethiopic) language, with no continuous Greek or Latin manuscript tradition in the West.

Transmission establishes provenance, a complete history from its creation to when it was discovered, to determine authenticity in old manuscripts or objects. Gaps in the transmission record makes verifying authenticity more challenging.

The number of full manuscripts of 1 Enoch is relatively small—around 100+ in Geʽez, with fragments in Aramaic and Greek. Compare this with the thousands and thousands of preserved full manuscripts and fragments for the Old and New Testaments that make up the canonized books.

1 Enoch is recognized in one language with relatively few copies. It does not come close to measuring up to canonized standards.

In spite of these gaps, apocalyptic themes, the messianic “Son of Man” and angelic rebellion are all mentioned and are closely aligned with Second Temple Jewish thought and early Christian belief.

A comparison regarding the Son of Man title brings 1 Enoch back into play again:

1 Enoch 62:7: For the Son of Man was concealed from the beginning… and the Most High preserved him.

1 Enoch 69:27: And he sat on the throne of glory, and the sum of judgment was given to him.

Now compare the words of Jesus:

Matthew 25:31–32: 31 But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. 32 All the nations will be gathered before him; and he will separate them from one another, as the shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.

This might seem like Jesus is quoting from 1 Enoch. But Jesus has access to the book of Daniel, written before Enoch, so we believe he was quoting from Daniel:

Daniel 7:13–14: 13 I kept looking in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man was coming, and he came up to the Ancient of Days and was presented before Him. 14 And to him was given dominion, glory and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations and men of every language might serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion which will not pass away; and his kingdom is one which will not be destroyed.

Jesus aptly quoted from Daniel. Whoever wrote 1 Enoch centuries later could also have quoted from Daniel.

CLARITY QUESTION The acceptance of 1 Enoch in Ethiopian Orthodox canon shows that some Christian traditions have recognized it as “scripture” for centuries. Does this add credibility?

No, because this is too narrow an acceptance. We can’t say one little thread is as valuable as a massive tapestry. A single thread cannot be compared to a full tapestry.

Early councils prioritized books with widespread, continuous use across diverse Christian communities; 1 Enoch dramatically lacked this.

The fact that one Christian community uses 1 Enoch does not mean it is valid biblical canon. It simply does not have the weight of canonized Scripture.

One final scriptural instruction for us to hold tightly within our grasp as we follow in Jesus’ footsteps:

2 Timothy 2:15-16: 15 Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth. 16 But avoid worldly and empty chatter, for it will lead to further ungodliness.

We are to focus ourselves on the study of the biblical record, the word of truth, while avoiding the worldly and empty chatter even if it seems attractive and intriguing. We want to study truth, not error.

Rick, would you personally take the time to read 1 Enoch, even if just for its historical value? Is it better to read than a book of the latest fiction?

I would not pick 1 Enoch. It does have historical value, but I would absolutely not waste my time. For the historical information, we have other records that do not pretend to be part of Scripture, that were not written by a false author taking the name of somebody from thousands of years before.

Because it reads like Scripture, there is a danger of confusion and being misled. What’s the point? Why study error?

Upon gathering and reviewing the historical facts and some of the prophesies of 1 Enoch, the reasons it’s not in the Bible are clear. Actual authorship, timing and content all point to a book written with a clear basis in truth, and yet assembled with dramatic personal perspectives overriding much of that truth.

Truth can be changed and polluted to fit an agenda. For example, Satan wrapped truth in a lie when he told Eve, You will be like God, knowing good and evil. He was right! But he lied by assuring her, You surely will not die! He was wrong! (Genesis 3:4-5) We cannot waste time on polluted biblical truth.

Let us stand firm and clear upon the God-inspired words and teachings of our Bible and cautiously draw whatever godly and harmonious good we can see from other sources without diluting or polluting God’s truth!

The book of 1 Enoch does not belong in the canon of the Bible. It is not part of what we stand for or a source of truth. It is not part of what we rely upon because we do not need it. The evidence shows it is not Scripture.

The man Enoch was a wonderful example of godliness. Look what has happened to that wonderful example and how his name has actually been polluted. Stay clear of such things. Hold fast to truth!

So, why is the book of Enoch NOT in the Bible? For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1410-book-of-enoch/

1. Who was Enoch and why was he revered in the Old and New Testaments? Do we know where Enoch

was “taken” to? Do we know where he was not “taken” to? (Genesis 5:18-24, Hebrews 11:5, John 3:13)

2. What plausible routes could have led to Jude’s quoting of material that closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9?

Should we give as much credence to oral tradition as to textual quotation? (Jude 1:14-15, 1 Enoch 1:9)

3. Canon Criteria #1: Not in the Hebrew Bible – Why would 1 Enoch’s exclusion from the Tanakh

favor its exclusion from the Christian Bible? How can we explain references that appear in both 1 Enoch and the Bible? (1 Enoch 80:6-8, Jude 1:12-13, Job 38:4,7, Isaiah 14:12, Ezekiel 28:14-16)

4. CC#2 Pseudepigraphal Authorship – When was it written? Why does this cast doubt on its

authenticity? Why is the 400-year gap between the end of the Old Testament and beginning of the New, important? (Malachi 4:5-6, Luke 1:11-20)

5. CC#3 Speculative Theology – How do the elaborate angelology, cosmology and apocalyptic

visions affect the book’s theological credibility? How does 1 Enoch contrast with the Bible in the correct view of the earth? (Isaiah 40:22, Job 26:7)

6. CC#4 Transmission Gaps – How would a gap in transmission make a manuscript’s authenticity

be questionable? Why doesn’t the “Son of Man” title help with 1 Enoch’s authenticity? (1 Enoch 62:7, 69:27, Matthew 25:31-32, Daniel 7:13-14)

7. CC#5 Lack of Widespread Continuous Use – How many Christian communities have accepted 1

Enoch as part of their biblical canon? Compare the number of existing full manuscripts of 1 Enoch with the books that are part of canonized Scripture.

8. Which of the five Canon Criteria (CC#1-5) do you find most persuasive in excluding 1 Enoch from

the Bible? How does the evidence support that judgment? (Genesis 5:22,24, Hebrews 11:5)

9. How does “accurately handling the word of truth” look like in my daily study habits? What can I

do to personally guard against just following spiritual curiosity and instead focus on studying what I know to be spiritual truth from the Scriptures? (1 Timothy 2:15)

## Episode 1411 — Can One Person’s Choice Shape Generations? The Story of Ruth
Published: 2025-11-17
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1411-ruth/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/14183418/CQ_Rewind_11-17-2025_Can_One_Persons_Choice_Shape_Generations_The_Story_of_Ruth.pdf

Can One Person’s Choice Shape Generations?

The Story of Ruth

Ruth 1:16: But Ruth said, Do not urge me to leave you or turn back from following you; for where you go, I will go, and where you lodge, I will lodge.

Your people shall be my people, and your God, my God.

It is said that when Benjamin Franklin was an American Minister in Paris, he spent an evening with a group of intellectuals at a time when literary circles were known for being agnostic or even atheistic. He was called on to contribute to the entertainment and read from what he called a “charming bit of literature.” He proceeded to read the entire Book of Ruth. The normally skeptical audience was delighted and wanted to know where in ancient history such a beautiful and idealistic story could be found. They were shocked to find out it had been copied from the Bible. The story of Ruth is indeed beautiful as an endearing account of loyalty, faith and divine providence.

The account of Ruth happened during the time when judges ruled Israel. It is generally thought this happened during or shortly after the period when Gideon was judge (Judges chapters 6–8).

The story of Ruth begins with the challenges of life that were presented to her mother-in-law Naomi:

Ruth 1:1–2: 1 Now it came about in the days when the judges governed, that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the land of Moab with his wife and his two sons. 2 The name of the man was Elimelech (“God is king”), and the name of his wife, Naomi; and the names of his two sons were Mahlon (“sickly”) and Chilion (“pining,” “wasting,” “destruction”), Ephrathites of Bethlehem in Judah. Now they entered the land of Moab and remained there.

The Moabites were descendants of Abraham’s nephew, Lot. They lived east of the Dead Sea in current-day Jordan.

(Source: Wikipedia) Despite their differences, the Moabites shared cultural and religious similarities with the Canaanites. Both groups practiced polytheistic religions, and the Moabites worshiped Chemosh - Kəmōš - a deity with Canaanite influences.

Like the Canaanites, the Moabite faith included human sacrifices.

Elimelech chose to move his family out of Israel to potentially better deal with the famine. While this choice at first glance might make logical sense, he was not framing his thinking based upon God’s protection and care. His choice brought his family out from under God’s care and into an idolatrous culture. This very questionable decision sets the groundwork for Ruth, a Moabite woman, to be found and eventually be blessed by God.

It wasn’t the greatest decision from a spiritual perspective. God, however, works with our decisions even when we do not make the best choices.

Naomi’s story continues with more challenges and tragedy:

Ruth 1:3–5: 3 Then Elimelech, Naomi’s (“pleasure of Jehovah”) husband, died; and she was left with her two sons. 4 They took for themselves Moabite women as wives; the name of the one was Orpah (“wild goat”) and the name of the other Ruth (“friendship,” “refreshment.”

“satisfaction”). And they lived there about ten years. 5 Then both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and the woman was bereft of her two children and her husband.

What began as a plan to better deal with a famine ends up with this faithful Hebrew woman, Naomi, losing her husband and sons and being left with two Moabite daughters- in-law. Not what they expected to happen! Here is where we will see the providence of God clearly unfold on behalf of those who are faithful to Him, especially Naomi.

In verses 6–7, Naomi decided to return to Israel as the famine was over, so she and her two daughters-in-law packed up and started the journey back.

Naomi’s godly and faithful character shines out here!

Ruth 1:8–13: 8 And Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, Go, return each of you to her mother’s house. May the LORD deal kindly with you as you have dealt with the dead and with me. 9 May the LORD grant that you may find rest, each in the house of her husband. Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept. 10 And they said to her, No, but we will surely return with you to your people.

We can see how both daughters-in-law are really attached to her, but Naomi loves them enough to let them go. She wants them to find happiness.

11 But Naomi said, Return, my daughters. Why should you go with me? Have I yet sons in my womb, that they may be your husbands? 12 Return, my daughters! Go, for I am too old to have a husband. If I said I have hope, if I should even have a husband tonight and also bear sons, 13 would you therefore wait until they were grown? Would you therefore refrain from marrying? No, my daughters; for it is harder for me than for you, for the hand of the LORD has gone forth against me.

Naomi is feeling the stress of these losses. Her sons and her husband are gone, and she is essentially begging her daughters-in-law to not come back with her. She seems resolved to be alone.

Naomi realized the sacrifices the girls would have to make in leaving behind their families, familiar customs, and promising futures to live as foreigners in a new land where they might face discrimination. Concerned about their well-being, she urges them to return to their own people with their own religious practices, fearing their commitment to accompany her could ultimately lead to regret and hardship. She has had enough hardship!

She is looking out for them, knowing that as Moabites in Israel it would not be easy for them. She understands who they are and where they come from, even while knowing their decision to stay behind will leave her terribly lonely.

As God was drawing Ruth to eventually be one of His chosen people, Naomi, in her wisdom, offered her ample opportunity to make her own choice. Ruth could walk with Naomi into the unknown and eventually see God’s power and plan, or she could simply go back to what she knew and was comfortable with.

When we are called to Christ, we also have that opportunity to “count the cost” before committing to the unknowns of discipleship.

By looking at the lives of Naomi and Ruth, we can begin to see the parallels in our own Christian walk. We will expand this as we move through the account.

Choices were made. Orpah left to go back to her people, but Ruth wouldn’t leave Naomi’s side:

Ruth 1:14–15: 14 And they lifted up their voices and wept again; and Orpah kissed her mother- in-law, but Ruth clung to her.

Here we notice Naomi does not interrupt or minimize their sorrow. She allows space for their emotional processing. These women have been through a lot of grief in a short period of time.

15 Then she said, Behold, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; return after your sister-in-law.

Naomi’s compassion is inspiring. She is in no way forcing Ruth to stay with her. She truly wants Ruth to voluntarily choose for herself by helping her weigh the implications of her choice. She guides without demanding.

There is selflessness in that guiding. She could certainly use the help and companionship of Ruth, but she is pushing Ruth to be independent.

Our theme text:

Ruth 1:16–17: 16 But Ruth said, Do not urge me to leave you or turn back from following you; for where you go, I will go, and where you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God, my God. 17 Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. Thus may the LORD do to me, and worse, if anything but death parts you and me.

There is a beautiful song with these lyrics, and my wife’s aunt sang it at our wedding. She also embroidered a lovely scripture tapestry for us with these verses.

This was the answer Naomi needed! This decision was more powerful because it was freely chosen based on Naomi’s wise leadership. Ruth was overwhelmingly decisive regarding the direction of the rest of her life: Where you go, I will go… She is very clear.

When we are called to follow Christ, we also need to make a life-changing decision:

Matthew 4:18–20: 18 Now as Jesus was walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who was called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. 19 And he said to them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. 20 Immediately they left their nets and followed him.

We can see the parallel. Jesus calls and says, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. Immediately they left their nets and followed him. No hesitation. Ruth dropped everything to follow Naomi back to Israel. This was Ruth’s clear decision, even though her future would be uncertain. We, too, need to make this kind of decision as we begin our Christian walk following Jesus, yet not knowing all that is in store for us in the future.

So, Naomi and Ruth travel back to Bethlehem:

Ruth 1:18–19: 18 When she (Naomi) saw that she (Ruth) was determined to go with her, she said no more to her. 19 So they both went until they came to Bethlehem. And when they had come to Bethlehem, all the city was stirred because of them, and the women said, Is this Naomi?

It is moving that when Naomi saw Ruth so determined, she said no more to her. In other words, “I hear and respect your decision, so now you are with me.” Naomi accepts Ruth’s decision as final. They will move forward together.

While Naomi’s return after many years was publicly acknowledged by the women of Bethlehem, her response to them was humble and revealing:

Ruth 1:20-21: 20 She said to them, Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara (“bitter”), for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. 21 I went out full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why do you call me Naomi, since the LORD has witnessed against me and the Almighty has afflicted me?

Even the strong and the smart reach their limits! How was she to start all over at this age? Obviously, the Lord hadn’t brought her back “empty”; she had Ruth standing right next to her. To Ruth’s credit, she stays quiet. She let Naomi grieve without demanding recognition for herself. Ruth did not mention her own grief over her husband’s death. This was really selfless.

Naomi is publicly recognizing what she believes are the results of her husband’s decision all those years ago to leave their home. She is acknowledging the consequences but has no inkling of how God will, through that experience, bless her and others.

Our Christian experience has the same kind of challenges, as we often see the difficulties without knowing what God sees:

1 Peter 4:12–13: 12 Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal among you, which comes upon you for your testing, as though some strange thing were happening to you; 13 but to the degree that you share the sufferings of Christ, keep on rejoicing, so that also at the revelation of his glory you may rejoice with exultation.

How many times do we focus on and obsess over our own trials and difficulties?

This is the stage Naomi was in, not able to envision a way out. The answer for her and us is: Act wisely in accordance with God’s will.

As Naomi returns to her home with Ruth, her mind is on the hardship she has experienced. But she is also keenly aware of God’s protective power over His people.

This recognition is an important foundation for God’s providence to be built upon, as God’s will can flourish when His people have humble and contrite hearts.

There is a lot of drama unfolding here. Fortunately, where there is drama with God’s people there is also His guidance!

Now that Ruth and Naomi were back in Israel, how would these two devastated widows support themselves?

Widows in ancient Israel faced significant hardships due to the patriarchal structure of that society. Without a husband, a widow often lacked financial security, social status and legal protection. Since inheritance typically passed through male heirs, widows were frequently left without land or resources, making them vulnerable to poverty and exploitation. Chapter 1 ends with Naomi and her daughter-in-law, Ruth, returning from Moab to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Up to this point we have seen Naomi’s humility and God-centered approach. Now we will see Ruth step up and prove her dedication to Naomi:

Ruth 2:1–3: 1 Now Naomi had a kinsman (a relative) of her husband, a man of great wealth, of the family of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz (“strength”) 2 And Ruth the Moabitess said to Naomi, Please let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain after one in whose sight I may find favor. And she said to her, Go, my daughter. 3 So she departed and went and gleaned in the field after the reapers; and she happened to come to the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, who was of the family of Elimelech.

She happened to come to the portion—the Hebrew word for happened (qarah) means an unforeseen meeting or event, but it’s used in contexts where something appears accidental but is really divinely providential. This verse starts the reversal. Through this “happening,” God begins to fill what Naomi thought was empty.

This is an important piece to the story. Ruth just “happens” to go to the field belonging to Boaz, the family of her Naomi’s husband, Elimelach. Ruth did not plan to glean where she ended up, she just planned on going to work. God provided for her to be gleaning there!

Please let me go—this highlights Ruth’s humility and dedication as she sought to provide for herself and Naomi after arriving in Bethlehem. Naomi had been leading the way, but now it is up to Ruth to support them.

She worked hard gleaning leftover grain in the fields, as permitted by Jewish Law (Leviticus 23:22, Deuteronomy 24:19). The grain growing in the corners of the field, as well as grain that had been dropped by the reapers, could be gathered by any of the poor for their own use. When the landowner harvested the field, he was to leave the corners alone in order to give the less fortunate an opportunity to gather food. It was hard work but provided a source of sustenance. This shows God’s grace and compassion on the poor.

Our Christian desire should also be to willingly give of ourselves for a higher cause:

Romans 12:1: Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

Do the work of honoring God by giving.

Ruth’s best efforts to provide for herself and Naomi brought her to the place where God’s providence would guide:

Ruth 2:4: Now behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem and said to the reapers, May the LORD be with you. And they said to him, May the LORD bless you.

Imagine your employer greeting you in this way! This tells us a lot about Boaz. He noticed people. It would be very easy to not even notice the people working in his fields, but he paid attention and saw them as his equals before the Lord.

This is a big deal! He owns the field. He is a wealthy man but has genuine care and compassion for those who work for him in his fields.

Boaz notices a stranger in his fields:

Ruth 2:5–7: 5 Then Boaz said to his servant who was in charge of the reapers, Whose young woman is this? 6 The servant in charge of the reapers replied, She is the young Moabite woman who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab. 7 And she said, Please let me glean and gather after the reapers among the sheaves. Thus she came and has remained from the morning until now; she has been sitting in the house for a little while.

Boaz wants to know who this new woman is working in his field, and the foreman knows all about her. Ruth had asked to be able to gather only what the reapers left behind and nothing more, and the foreman granted her request.

Boaz is determined to provide her with a safe and profitable workspace:

Ruth 2:8–11: 8 Then Boaz said to Ruth, Listen carefully, my daughter. Do not go to glean in another field; furthermore, do not go on from this one, but stay here with my maids. 9 Let your eyes be on the field which they reap, and go after them. Indeed, I have commanded the servants not to touch you. When you are thirsty, go to the water jars and drink from what the servants draw. 10 Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground and said to him, Why have I found favor in your sight that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner? 11 Boaz replied to her, All that you have done for your mother-in-law after the death of your husband has been fully reported to me, and how you left your father and your mother and the land of your birth, and came to a people that you did not previously know.

What beautiful characters all of these individuals have! They all act with such honesty and integrity.

Boaz knows Ruth has been selfless in supporting Naomi in spite of losing her own husband. In turn, he takes care of her by allowing her to stay under his protection. He sees Ruth as having genuine humility and acting righteously before God.

Ruth puts Naomi’s needs before herself, and Boaz is protecting that effort:

Ruth 2:12–13: 12 May the LORD reward your work, and your wages be full from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to seek refuge. 13 Then she said, I have found favor in your sight, my lord, for you have comforted me and indeed have spoken kindly to your maidservant, though I am not like one of your maidservants.

The God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to seek refuge—Boaz recognizes the care God promised through the Law to the stranger in the land. He applies it to Ruth, making sure she understands.

Likewise, Ruth recognizes her lowliness and overflows with gratitude for the opportunity she is given!

Ruth was serving God by serving Naomi. As Christians, we can also be greatly blessed in our humble service:

Romans 12:10–11: 10 Be devoted to one another in brotherly love; give preference to one another in honor; 11 not lagging behind in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord.

This reminds of us Ruth! We see the giving, honor, respect and reverence. She is showing us what our Christian lives should look like.

Ruth’s blessings continue, as she was also allowed to eat with the employees. Boaz just doesn’t stop taking care of her:

Ruth 2:14: At mealtime Boaz said to her, Come here, that you may eat of the bread and dip your piece of bread in the vinegar. So she sat beside the reapers; and he served her roasted grain, and she ate and was satisfied and had some left.

It wasn’t enough for Boaz to allow her to stay close to his servants and have plenty of water to drink. He now serves her himself, and it was so much that she couldn’t finish it! He didn’t just give her a scant amount and say, “Too bad, that’s all you get.” It’s the same with the Lord. He gives us more than we expect and better than we deserve.

Ruth shows great humility and thankfulness, but we also see the thoroughness of Boaz’ leadership in this experience.

As Christians, we are also blessed by God through Jesus with spiritual abundance:

Philippians 4:19: And my God will supply all your needs according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

When we look at Boaz doing all this for this foreigner, this stranger, we can see Jesus reflected in his character. He doesn’t stop blessing. He doesn’t stop giving. He doesn’t stop looking ahead and proactively handling all the future obstacles. And he gave her more than enough!

Boaz’s blessing of Ruth doesn’t stop there. He assures her ability to fulfill her responsibility to provide for Naomi and herself:

Ruth 2:15–16: 15 When she rose to glean, Boaz commanded his servants, saying, Let her glean even among the sheaves (where there was plenty of good grain on the ground)… 16 Also you shall purposely pull out for her some grain from the bundles and leave it that she may glean…

Boaz is making sure there is plenty of grain left on the ground for Ruth. She must be able to gather enough for both her and Naomi. It is not just handed to her; she is provided an opportunity. We again see the comparison to Jesus, giving us opportunities to work and spiritually succeed.

Our Christian experience provides us all that is necessary because we have Jesus behind us:

Philippians 4:12–13: (KJV) 12 I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. 13 I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

Ruth went through hard times, but she stayed steadfast and loyal to Naomi. Now she is given this period of abundance. Boaz, picturing Jesus, provides a similar opportunity for us to spiritually prosper.

Ruth 2:17: So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it was about an ephah of barley.

(Source: tyndalehouse.com) An ephah of barley would be about 10 days' worth of food for an individual.

This was a generous amount! Ruth and Naomi were being abundantly cared for. Boaz was giving them a sense of security in a very big way. The women had just arrived back in Israel and already Boaz was blessing them abundantly.

Again, we can see the similarity to Jesus providing us a sense of spiritual security as we look to him.

Verses 18–23: Ruth returned to the city with the grain she had gleaned, and gave it to Naomi along with what was left from her meal. She is not even holding onto the leftovers from her own meal for herself! She gave everything to her mother-in-law.

Naomi was amazed at the amount Ruth had gathered. Ruth told her she was working in the field of Boaz, who encouraged her to stay close to his workers throughout the harvest.

Ruth stayed with Naomi and worked until the end of the barley and wheat harvests, which marked the times of the “firstfruits offerings.” These were celebrations of God’s provisions according to Jewish Law.

- Barley harvest: March to April. It coincided with Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Barley was the first grain harvested.
- Wheat harvest: May through June/July. It coincided with Pentecost, also called the Feast of Weeks. Wheat was considered a more valuable grain.

Ruth worked for months, doing what she was supposed to do, taking care of herself and Naomi.

Ruth did everything in her power to work at caring for Naomi and herself, and Boaz powerfully blessed and encouraged her efforts. Her work didn’t stop at barley; she continued working through the wheat harvest. Her full commitment was obvious.

We, too, should remain fully committed to our work, even as the seasons in our lives change.

The key here is that she worked through different seasons. Nothing stopped, nothing changed in her commitment to her mother-in-law or to her work. She did what she needed to do. As Christians, we need to follow this committed pattern.

Hard work fueled by humility and a godly attitude brings about blessing and providence from God through Jesus. There is nothing better than this!

Naomi has a long-term plan to secure her future and that of her daughter-in-law. How successful was her plan?

The threshing floor was a place where workers processed grain, and Boaz, as the landowner, would sleep there to protect the harvested piles of grain. Naomi instructed Ruth to approach Boaz discreetly late in the evening, as he was sleeping. She was to uncover his feet and wait for his response. In ancient Near Eastern customs, this symbolic act of uncovering the feet signified submission, humility and a request for protection. By uncovering his feet and lying down at his feet, Ruth was essentially asking Boaz to take her under his care as a “kinsman-redeemer,” a role in which he could marry her and restore her family’s lineage.

The Levirate law in the Old Testament was designed to preserve family lineage and inheritance. If a married man died without a son, his brother was obligated to marry the widow. However, the firstborn son would then carry on the deceased brother’s name and inheritance (Genesis 38:8–10, Leviticus 25:25–55, Deuteronomy 25:5–10).

This act also reflected covenantal (promise) language, as Ruth later asked Boaz to spread his garment over her (Ruth 3:9), a physical protection, representing the marriage covenant and overall protection. Boaz recognized her request as an honorable appeal rather than anything improper, praising her for her loyalty and virtue.

Ruth approaches Boaz at the threshing floor, symbolically asking him to take her under his protection:

Ruth 3:6–13: 6 So she went down to the threshing floor and did according to all that her mother-in-law had commanded her.

Notice how Ruth respectfully does whatever Naomi asks of her. It takes incredible strength of character to be a true follower! She may have felt some fear and trepidation at Naomi’s request. Even though Boaz had been kind, this was asking a lot from someone who wasn’t even an Israelite.

7 When Boaz had eaten and drunk and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain; and she came secretly, and uncovered his feet and lay down. 8 It happened in the middle of the night that the man was startled and bent forward; and behold, a woman was lying at his feet. 9 He said, Who are you? And she answered, I am Ruth your maid. So spread your covering over your maid, for you are a close relative.

This obviously doesn’t work without a high level of morality of all concerned!

She is claiming the “kinsman-redeemer” provision since Boaz is a close relative.

He is moved by her request and promises to resolve the matter, ensuring her future security: 10 Then he said, May you be blessed of the LORD, my daughter. You have shown your last kindness to be better than the first by not going after young men, whether poor or rich. 11 Now, my daughter, do not fear. I will do for you whatever you ask, for all my people in the city know that you are a woman of excellence.

Boaz is honored that she is asking for his protection! She is now known as a woman of excellence, someone with a high level of morality and integrity.

12 Now it is true I am a close relative; however, there is a relative closer than I. 13 Remain this night, and when morning comes, if he will redeem you, good; let him redeem you. But if he does not wish to redeem you, then I will redeem you, as the LORD lives. Lie down until morning.

Boaz acted in precise accordance with the Jewish Law. He planned to redeem her in an appropriate way that would honor both God and Ruth. There was a closer relative than he was, and that person had the right of first refusal.

Here we are in the middle of the night. Boaz is startled awake to find this young woman at his feet, and this is how he is thinking. What integrity!

This is why we see Boaz as a picture of Jesus in his continued examples of honoring God. We hear the echo of God’s will, and character and direction in everything Boaz does.

As Christians, we are redeemed in a similar manner by Jesus himself:

Romans 8:2–3: 2 For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and of death. 3 For what the Law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did: sending His own son in the likeness of sinful flesh and as an offering for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh.

We have redemption through Jesus. We see Boaz assure Ruth that she will be redeemed. He had to do it in exactly the right way to eliminate any doubt around her redemption. This is his promise. This is also the guarantee we have received as Christians.

Ruth complied because she knew she was in the midst of people of high godly character:

Ruth 3:14: So she lay at his feet until morning and rose before one could recognize another; and he said, Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor.

We have to appreciate Ruth so much because these were not her customs. This wasn’t her Law. The Moabites had nothing like this. She is really honoring and respecting Naomi’s wisdom.

Wasn’t this a risky plan for a beautiful young woman to go at night to sleep at the feet of Boaz? Through the lens of today’s society, this would have been reckless!

No, it was carefully guided by Naomi’s wisdom. While this situation could have been misinterpreted or lead to potential danger, Boaz’s character ensured Ruth’s safety. He recognized her virtuous intentions, praised her loyalty and took steps to protect her reputation by ensuring she left before dawn. His response highlights his integrity and respect for Ruth, reinforcing that this was not an inappropriate or reckless act; but rather, it was a culturally significant request for redemption and marriage. Boaz would make sure it was all handled above board and within the Law’s regulations.

Ruth returns to her mother-in-law and told her what had happened:

Ruth 3:15–18: 15 Again he said, Give me the cloak that is on you and hold it. So she held it, and he measured six measures of barley and laid it on her. Then she went into the city. 16 When she came to her mother-in-law, she said, How did it go, my daughter? And she told her all that the man had done for her. 17 She said, These six measures of barley he gave to me, for he said, Do not go to your mother-in-law empty-handed. 18 Then she said, Wait, my daughter, until you know how the matter turns out; for the man will not rest until he has settled it today.

Boaz shows his graciousness of character at every turn with this further gift of barley. We continue to see how he is such an accurate representation of Jesus. He took care of those in need. Naomi knows Boaz’s character and is confident he will handle the situation with godly honor.

As Christians, we are not only redeemed but blessed beyond our capacity. Just as Boaz poured out the barley, so God through Christ pours out blessings to us:

Luke 6:37–38: 37 Do not judge, and you will not be judged; and do not condemn, and you will not be condemned; pardon, and you will be pardoned. 38 Give, and it will be given to you. They will pour into your lap a good measure—pressed down, shaken together, and running over.

For by your standard of measure it will be measured to you in return.

This is the life of a Christian: blessing beyond our ability to count.

Ruth was given physical blessings of abundance from Boaz. Christians are given spiritual blessings of abundance from Jesus.

The lessons of Naomi’s humble wisdom being applied to Ruth’s humble and virtuous character—all being blessed by Boaz—truly are overflowing. God rewarded those who humbly and reverently served Him under the Jewish Law.

Our humble and reverent offering of ourselves to our Lord Jesus for his protection will bring spiritual blessings to us as well.

Let’s be like Ruth and be willing to obey and receive!

The beauty of these individuals’ characters is truly inspiring. Now we just need to observe how God’s blessings would flow to all of them.

Through the Jewish Law, God wisely provided for someone in Ruth’s situation. But who was the closest kinsman-redeemer?

In the fourth and final chapter of the book of Ruth, Boaz negotiates with a closer relative to be her redeemer. Ruth 4:1-8 describes how Boaz arranges a meeting with this closer relative and ten of the elders in the city. At first, the relative agrees to buy Ruth’s deceased husband’s household, thinking it was only land. When he finds out that he must also marry Ruth, he declines, stating that by marrying Ruth he would damage his inheritance from his own, closer family.

Having followed the Jewish Law by offering the relative the chance to purchase Naomi’s husband’s household and having the relative decline the offer in front of the ten elders, Boaz is legally free to purchase the household and marry Ruth.

We pick up the account with a public announcement:

Ruth 4:9-10: 9 Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, You are witnesses today that I have bought from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech and all that belonged to Chilion and Mahlon. 10 Furthermore, I have acquired Ruth the Moabitess, the widow of Mahlon, to be my wife in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance, so that the name of the deceased will not be eliminated from his brothers or from the court of his birth place; you are witnesses today.

Boaz restores the name of the deceased. By marrying Ruth, he ensures Mahlon’s name and inheritance continue. This is a covenant of restoration, redeeming that which was lost. Again we can see the comparison between Boaz and Jesus.

Their inheritance was lost. He redeems it. Boaz’s actions were saving the household from collapse! Without a patriarch in charge of the household, it would have been dissolved and lost. Redemption is the major theme of this whole account. Boaz redeems Ruth and all of Naomi’s family’s inheritance in exact accordance with the Law.

Jesus redeemed mankind by fulfilling the Law precisely. The true church is redeemed first by Jesus and described as his bride. Jesus then redeems the entire world.

John the Baptist was a “kinsman” of Jesus. As a representation of the Old Testament Law, he could not redeem anyone:

John 3:28–30: 28 You yourselves are my witnesses that I said, I am not the Christ, but, I have been sent ahead of him. 29 He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom's voice. So this joy of mine has been made full. 30 He must increase, but I must decrease.

We can compare John the Baptist to the other close relative. John represented the Jewish Law by preaching repentance and bringing many of the Jews back to the Law, and therefore a relationship with God. But neither John nor the Law were capable of actually redeeming the people. John directed his own followers to Jesus’ leadership.

Boaz and Ruth marry and have a son named Obed. We again have a public response to Naomi:

Ruth 4:14–17: 14 Then the women (those who not so long ago were a witness to her utter despair) said to Naomi, Blessed is the LORD who has not left you without a redeemer today, and may his name become famous in Israel. 15 May he also be to you one who restores life and sustains your old age; for your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given birth to him.

In ancient Jewish culture, having a son was one of the greatest blessings a woman could have. Ruth was better than seven sons! The grandness of God’s overruling and the redemption that came through Boaz resulted in Naomi’s renewed life and future family inheritance, which had essentially been dead. Again, we reflect on the redemption Jesus brought to all of mankind’s life and future existence.

16 Then Naomi took the child and laid him in her lap, and became his nurse. 17 And the neighbor women gave him a name, saying, A son has been born to Naomi! So they named him Obed (“worshipper”). He is the father of Jesse, the father of David.

Naomi’s loss has been restored in an unimaginable way! She had said, Call me Mara (“bitter”), for the Lord has forsaken me. This is not the Lord forsaking anyone; this is a blessing beyond imagination. She is now joyful again.

But this is not the end of the blessing. The genealogy is again repeated in the verse.

This shows us the mercy and foresight of God in the life of Ruth:

Ruth 4:18–22: 18 Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron, 19 Hezron fathered Ram, and Ram fathered Amminadab, 20 and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, and Nahshon fathered Salmon, 21 and Salmon fathered Boaz, and Boaz fathered Obed, 22 and Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.

Obed becomes the grandfather of King David, so Ruth is his great-grandmother!

Now we are not just talking about restoring a household; we are talking about King David! This is blessing beyond recognition. Ruth’s story concludes with her inclusion in the lineage of Israel’s greatest king, highlighting themes of redemption and divine providence.

Tracing the lineage further, of course, leads to none other than the Messiah, Jesus, the eternal King (Luke 1:32–33). This is how a Gentile woman came to be numbered among Jesus’ ancestors! (Matthew 1:5)

So, can the decision of one woman change generations? We just saw it happen by the grace of God!

The hand of God is evident in the lives of Naomi, Ruth and Boaz.

Their faith, humility and reverential approach to all things reminds us that God can and will work in the mundane circumstances of our lives to bring us to pathways for our highest spiritual welfare.

We first looked at the experience of Naomi and then Ruth. As a foreigner in Israel, Ruth knew little of the customs or religion of Israel except as Naomi taught her. Naomi draws her toward the living God who blessed them both through Boaz.

As a picture of Jesus, Boaz showed us the broader theme of redemption for us now as footstep followers of Christ, and eventually the whole world. Follow Jesus, learn and be blessed.

So, can one person’s choice shape generations?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
