### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1411-ruth/ See:

1. What spiritual risk did Elimelech take by moving his family to Moab? What type of comparable risks might we face in our decisions today? (Ruth 1:1-2)

2. How does Naomi’s response to tragedy reflect both her faith and her human vulnerability? In what ways was she not only a mother-in-law but also a godly example for Orpah and Ruth?

3. How does Naomi show selfless compassion and leadership in the midst of her own grief? (Ruth 1:3-21)

4. In your life, how have you gotten caught up in focusing and maybe even obsessing over your own trials and difficulties? How might you use the examples of these two women to face your challenges? (1 Peter 4:12-13)

5. What might we emulate in Ruth’s beautiful statements in Ruth 1:16-17 to enrich our own walk with Christ? (Ruth 2:1-3, Matthew 4:18-20)

6. Have you faced a decision that required you to leave behind comfort or familiarity to follow God’s leading? How did you respond? What did you learn?

7. Ruth “happened” to glean in Boaz’s field. (Ruth 2:3) How does this illustrate divine providence? What can we do to recognize God’s hand in seemingly ordinary events in our own lives?

8. How does Boaz’s treatment of Ruth reflect Christlike leadership? How does Ruth’s humility and diligence challenge our approach to service and sacrifice? What did you take away from each of these examples? (Ruth 2:5-14, Romans 12:1, Philippians 4:19)

9. How does Ruth’s story illustrate the power of one person’s choice that ended up shaping her own life and that of future generations? Also consider the various choices made by Naomi, Boaz and the unnamed “nearer kinsman.”

## Episode 1412 — What Does Leprosy Teach Us About Sin and Gratitude?
Published: 2025-11-24
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/inspiration/1412-leprosy/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/21083718/CQ_Rewind_11-24-2025_What_Does_Leprosy_Teach_Us_About_Sin_and_Gratitude.pdf

Luke 17:15-16: 15 Now one of them, when he saw that he had been healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice, 16 and he fell on his face at his feet, giving thanks to him. And he was a Samaritan.

If you haven’t noticed, our world has lost its grip on the value of gratitude in a very big way. Instead of having a thankful heart for whatever opportunities we may have and what we may receive, we seem to double down on living with a sense of entitlement. We can look at this and think, where did we go wrong? The fact is, this issue is the result of human imperfection and has been around for a very long time. The story of the ten lepers in Luke 17 reminds us of this. Leprosy—once a living death—left its victims isolated, disfigured and desperate. Yet when Jesus healed ten lepers, only one returned to give thanks. Why does thankfulness matter so deeply to God? And what does this ancient disease reveal about the spiritual condition of humanity today?

Leprosy, known medically as Hansen’s Disease, is a condition that causes numbness and physical deterioration.

The Bible frequently referenced leprosy, using it as a representation of sin’s corrupting influence.

God, in His wisdom, uses human experiences—both joyful and tragic—to teach spiritual lessons, and leprosy is no exception. Leprosy was a significant problem in biblical times.

This was not a parable; it was an actual interaction between Jesus and these men:

Luke 17:11-17: 11 While he was on the way to Jerusalem, he was passing between Samaria and Galilee. 12 And as he entered a village, ten men with leprosy who stood at a distance met him; 13 and they raised their voices, saying, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us! 14 When he saw them, he said to them, Go and show yourselves to the priests. And as they were going, they were cleansed. 15 Now one of them, when he saw that he had been healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice, 16 and he fell on his face at his feet, giving thanks to him. And he was a Samaritan. 17 But Jesus responded and said, Were there not ten cleansed? But the nine—where are they?

Such a powerful and profound question!

Before we talk about what Jesus did, let’s lay out the details of this overwhelming disease. They might be hard for us to relate to today:

Leprosy was a horrific disease of slow destruction. Skin turned pale and lifeless, limbs shriveled, and extremities—fingers, toes, even facial features—could gradually fall away. Teeth loosened and disappeared. The afflicted became ghostlike, their bodies deteriorating while they still lived. It was a living death, isolating and disfiguring, feared not only for its physical toll but for the spiritual stigma it carried.

In addition to being highly contagious and disfiguring, degeneration was progressive. The disease produces numbness, so people don’t realize they’ve injured themselves:

(Source: Dr. Paul Brand, Philip Yancey, Fearfully and Wonderfully: The Marvel of Bearing God’s Image): (One of the authors was a doctor who worked with lepers in India.)

The disease caused slow decay—hair loss, joint shrinkage and eventual loss of body parts. One traveler described lepers as “white as snow,” referencing the advanced stage of the disease.

“The disease does not spread like flesh-eating bacteria; rather, it attacks a single type of cell, the nerve cell. When the nerve cell falls silent, it no longer warns of danger, and the painless person quite literally destroys his or her own body… a person uses a hammer with a splintered handle, does not feel the pain, and an infection flares up. Another steps off a curb, spraining an ankle, and, obliviously, keeps walking. Another loses use of the nerve that triggers the eyelid to blink every few seconds for lubricating moisture; the eye dries out and the person becomes blind.

Virtually all the devastating effects of leprosy trace back to a single source: one type of nerve cell that has fallen silent.”

All this comes about because of just one type of nerve cell not doing what it is supposed to do. This has a spiritual application, as we will see.

As if the physical effects of leprosy are not enough, lepers in ancient times faced the consequences of social isolation and financial ruin. There was no known medical cure.

Social Isolation:

Lepers were legally required to live apart from society, even from their families. They had to cry out, “Unclean! Unclean!” when anyone approached. They weren’t allowed to worship in the Temple or synagogue.

Financial Ruin:

Leprosy suﬀerers were subject to ﬁnancial ruin because they couldn’t work, they couldn’t live with family unless the entire family was aﬄicted and they couldn’t shop or own property. Most lepers had to beg for a living.

No Known Medical Cure:

Leprosy had no prescribed remedy under Mosaic Law. Any healing was considered miraculous.

Imagine being cut off from family and society, forced to beg for a living, being stuck in a kind of undeserving nonexistence. This gives us a baseline understanding of what leprosy

was and the overwhelming impact it would have had not only on the individuals themselves but also on everyone around them.

Let’s review Jesus’ miraculous healing of these ten lepers in the context of the Jewish Law. The Law laid out a detailed process for dealing with leprosy, detailed primarily in Leviticus 13 and 14.

The initial examination of a potential infection was made by a priest, not a doctor:

Leviticus 13:1-3: 1 Then the Lord spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, 2 When a man has on the skin of his body a swelling or a scab or a bright spot, and it becomes an infection of leprosy on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons the priests. 3 The priest shall look at the mark on the skin of the body, and if the hair in the infection has turned white and the infection appears to be deeper than the skin of his body, it is an infection of leprosy; when the priest has looked at him, he shall pronounce him unclean.

We can see the incredible detail in all the little things the priest had to examine in order to correctly diagnose this heinous disease.

Summing up verses 4-7: If the priest couldn’t determine the nature of the mark on the skin, the person was isolated for seven days to monitor progression. Isolation could be extended another seven days if still undetermined.

Leviticus 13:8: The priest shall look, and if the scab has spread on the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is leprosy.

Once declared unclean, the person was cut off from society both spiritually and socially. They had to live alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46), wear torn clothes, leave their hair uncombed and cry, “Unclean” to warn others not to come near (Leviticus 13:45).

Each leper had to be their own warning sign, “Stay far away from me. You do not want to come near me! I’m contagious!” How difficult this must have been.

We can now see how the ten lepers were abiding by the limitations the Law had set for them:

Luke 17:11-12: 11 While he (Jesus) was on the way to Jerusalem, he was passing between Samaria and Galilee. 12 As he entered a village, ten leprous men who stood at a distance met him.

Ten men—why isn’t it nine, or thirteen? The number ten in the Bible often represents completeness. We will look further at this.

Stood at a distance—these men were essentially a small community of those whose sickness kept them separated from every aspect of normal life, in accordance with the Jewish Law.

They were really on the outside looking in. The only way to survive day-to-day was to stay together as a little community of outcasts. In the event the disease slowed to the point of

being “cured,” the person couldn’t just rejoin society. They had to return to the priest and undergo a ritual cleansing (Leviticus 14), followed by a seven-day waiting period where the person washed, shaved and waited outside their tent. On the eighth day, the person brought offerings of lambs, flour and oil.

Let’s return to the account. We left off with the ten lepers standing at a distance as Jesus approaches:

Luke 17:13: And they raised their voices, saying, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!

Isolated, helpless and hopeless, they simply cried for mercy. We would have expected them to beg for money, but instead it was, Master, have mercy on us! They recognized Jesus as someone different. This small community, completely isolated from society, still had heard of Jesus.

Talking about the awful ravages of leprosy has been depressing. How does our theme of gratitude come in? From the one leper who ran back to Jesus with thankfulness.

Sometimes our lives bring us to circumstances that are simply unfair. Sometimes we are given unexpected glimmers of hope in the face of our adversity. What will WE do with such hope? Asking for mercy is certainly a powerful beginning!

This is a powerful lesson right from the start—merely asking for mercy! Maybe our adversity is overwhelming. Asking for mercy to learn how to cope might be the first step.

In ancient times, the horror of leprosy could only find hope in grace from God. Jesus was there to deliver.

We all know what Jesus is going to do next.

The question is, how will it be received and what role will gratitude play?

We have all been desperate on some level in our lives just looking for mercy and hope. How often have we said to ourselves, if only THIS could happen then I will do or be THAT! These ten men were in such dire circumstances that their collective cry was for mercy and not coins. They recognized Jesus’ authority and compassion by calling him Master.

They appealed to someone they believed could restore them and change their condition, showing both faith and respect. They did not rush him or attempt to coerce him—just Master, have mercy on us!

Luke 17:14: When he (Jesus) saw them, he said to them, Go and show yourselves to the priests…

Think about the uniqueness of his response. Jesus did not touch them or speak even one word of healing. He simply commanded them to go show yourselves to the priests.

Jesus healed in various ways—sometimes with touch, sometimes through physical acts like mud on the eyes. Why did he tell the lepers to go to the priests before they were healed? And why no physical contact with this little community? What was the deeper significance?

To begin to answer, let’s compare with an account of Jesus healing a different leper. He touched this leper—same disease but different method of healing:

Matthew 8:1-4: 1 When Jesus came down from the mountain, large crowds followed him. 2 And a leper came to him and bowed down before him, and said, Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean. 3 Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, I am willing; be cleansed. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. 4 And Jesus said to him, See that you tell no one; but go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.

No one touched a leper! But Jesus did this time. As with the ten lepers, he told this man, show yourself to the priest.

There were two key elements needed for Jesus to heal leprosy:

1. The power of God’s spirit flowing through him. Jesus healed by God’s power.

2. The requirement of the Law to go to the priest. Jesus healed an entire small community who were impossibly sick by telling them to present themselves to the priest, be officially declared clean and return to their lives.

Why were these two healings done in different ways? We believe this particular healing of the ten was a specific picture of the larger work of Jesus—the ransom for all of mankind. We recognize that, during his first advent on earth, all his healing was temporary. Those healed by him eventually went on to die years later. But it provided a picture and foreshadowing of the future resurrection and the world being healed in Christ’s kingdom.

The community of ten lepers (ten representing completeness) pictures the entire world being healed by Jesus. They were told to go to a specific place to get the official proclamation. When Jesus died, the ransom was paid. This was long before anyone would have received actual, permanent healing in the resurrection. We believe the way Jesus healed the ten lepers—after telling them to go to the priest and they started on their way—shows what the world will go through in the future.

The world will be given the opportunity to be healed, even though they do not yet know it. We will expand on this shortly.

Following this command from Jesus to show themselves to the priest would have taken great faith:

Luke 17:14: When he saw them, he said to them, Go and show yourselves to the priests. And as they were going, they were cleansed.

Jesus was asking them to act as if they were healed, before they saw any evidence! Why would they obey when they still visibly had leprosy? The healing happened in motion, not at the command. Obedience came first, and the miracle followed.

What must that have been like after living with this condition for so long? Did they start walking and suddenly feel part of their feet touching the ground for the first time in how long?

Thinking of the bigger picture, won’t this be like the resurrection? We know in the day of judgment, mankind will be physically raised from the dead, but will have to gradually reach full healing and perfection as they are rehabilitated from sin and correct all their misdeeds from this life.

By dying on the cross, Jesus paid the ransom price for Adam, which was the first step in restoring humanity back to perfection, but God’s plan unfolds over time, not immediately. Mankind will be raised from the dead and will have to start walking in righteousness towards Jesus, being healed along the way, over time. What a wonderful picture!

1. These lepers may have had to walk a great distance to get to the priests while still visibly diseased. This journey would be a test of faith with no guarantee or timeline given—just a short instruction from Jesus.

2. There was no fanfare, no laying on of hands, and not even a command to be healed. There was only a gracious and undeserved gift these lepers had hoped for when they cried, Master, have mercy on us!

3. Jesus did have mercy, on ALL of them. His sending them back to the priests would enable them to be fully reintegrated back into family life, into society and the worship community. This will be just like the learning and encouragement of the day of judgment will bring people back into the society of being one of the children of God.

This became a process of healing. Jesus was telling them to go and get their lives back. In the bigger picture, Jesus paid the price so we ALL could get our lives back.

The gratitude from one leper burst out before he had actually been declared clean by the priest:

Luke 17:15-16: 15 Now one of them, when he saw that he had been healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice, 16 and he fell on his face at his (Jesus’) feet, giving thanks to him….

“I can’t finish this journey without expressing my gratitude. I must find Jesus! I can’t take another step without saying thank you!”

Perhaps the one thankful leper pictures the call of the church, the true followers of Jesus. This one person is different from the other nine, much like a Christian following Jesus today. The rest of the world is walking along, but those who hear the call to be a faithful follower now have an immediate response to be near Jesus because they are so thankful.

The next detail of this event is crucial. Let’s see how verse 16 ends: 16 …And he was a Samaritan.

This is important because in biblical times, Jews and Samaritans had been hostile neighbors with each other for generations. Both groups avoided contact with each other. Samaritans were considered religious outsiders by Jews, viewed as heretical and impure.

And yet it’s this “foreigner” who recognizes the source of the healing and responds with gratitude. He is the one who had the heart attitude Jesus was looking for.

Isn’t it interesting how most of those called to follow Jesus in the last 2,000 years have been “foreigners” from non-Jewish faiths, from different places, sort of outsiders looking in?

Jesus came to the house of Israel first, and his immediate apostles and disciples were Jewish. But most of those who eventually came to be Christian in the intervening centuries have not been Jewish because Jews did not recognize Jesus as Messiah.

What was the ethnicity of the other nine? While we aren’t told, the context strongly suggests they were Jewish:

- The miracle occurred “between Samaria and Galilee,” a border region where Jews and Samaritans coexisted.
- Jesus told them to show themselves to the priests (Luke 17:14), as required by Jewish Law.

This leper received a gift of unfathomable grace! His response to this gift was to express his thankfulness with passion and sincerity. The priest could wait, because his gratitude could not. Do we respond with immediate and passionate gratitude when we, as Jesus’ followers, receive such marvelous gifts? As we move about our day, it would be great if we would continually think, “I can’t take another step without saying thank you!”

This is the core value of the power of this kind of gratitude. Receiving an unmerited gift of grace from God through Jesus is mind-blowing. Such a tremendous gift should provoke a tremendous response.

Why didn’t Jesus just strike a deal with the lepers before healing them— something like, “If I heal you, will you dedicate your lives to following me?”

Who wouldn’t agree to that? Who wouldn’t promise anything to be freed from such a horrible and incurable disease? It sure seems like an easy way to gain more disciples. However, Jesus didn’t operate that way. He wasn’t looking for coerced commitment or desperate bargains. He was following the heart of the Father, who desires worshippers to come freely and worship Him in spirit and in truth (John 4:24). That’s the kind of devotion God and Jesus seek, and the kind of devotion Jesus lived and taught.

We’ve been looking at the big picture of this foreigner's gratitude for his incredible healing, while the other nine simply went to the priest for a declaration of their healing so they could get back to their lives. Let’s go back to look at how leprosy fits into this big picture.

Leprosy has been described as a “living death.” It is an apt metaphor for sin’s corrupting influence. In our big picture, we believe this shows how the world will eventually be healed from sin.

Let’s compare physical leprosy to the spiritual challenge of sin:

In ancient times, leprosy was progressive and incurable. With no medical remedy, it worsened over time. Sin is inescapable without divine intervention. Human effort alone cannot cleanse sin.

Leprosy is loathsome and disfiguring: It causes decay of skin, limbs, facial features and internal organs. Sin is corrupting and defiling: It destroys moral integrity and distorts spiritual identity.

Leprosy produces numbness: The condition worsens because the injury is often not treated right away. Sin produces numbness. When we become desensitized to sin, we have an inability to recognize the damage sin brings.

Leprosy requires isolation: Lepers lived outside the camp, cut off from family and worship. Sin means an alienation from God. Sin separates individuals from fellowship with God and others.

Clearly leprosy as a metaphor for sin is evident. See the Bonus Material for more.

Two important lessons unfold in the rest of the account:

The power of gratitude:

Luke 17:17-18: 17 Then Jesus answered and said, Were there not ten cleansed? But the nine— where are they? 18 Was no one found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?

Physical healing was truly a great gift from God. We cannot minimize the incredible gift of healing these lepers received. However, receiving that gift with gratitude and praise towards God is an even greater gift. The power of gratitude after having received mercy is the greater gift for our characters than mercy alone.

The power of faith:

Luke 17:19: And he said to him, Stand up and go; your faith has made you well <4982>.

Made you well: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4982 sōzō; to save, i.e. deliver or protect (literally or figuratively):—heal, preserve, save (self), do well, be (make) whole

Your faith has made you well is a key phrase Jesus uses only three times in the Bible. We might recognize it in its King James Version: thy faith hath made thee whole.

But what does Jesus want more—gratitude or faith?

Unequivocally, God and Jesus want faith over gratitude!

Let’s look at how the two are inextricably connected.

There is healing, and then there is transformative healing. Healing was freely given to those burdened with various sicknesses. Jesus often healed entire crowds who followed him. Transformative healing, however, took place in those whose personal effort and faith were noted by Jesus. These few individuals were blessed physically like the rest, but also spiritually.

Stand up and go; your faith has made you well—though all ten were healed physically, the Samaritan’s healing was more profound, as his gratitude expressed his deep faith that caused him to run back and give glory to God, humbly thanking Jesus.

How consistently is my faith revealed by my gratitude?

This is why God wants faith first. Gratitude is an outgrowth of true, strong, spiritual faith.

There are two other examples of Jesus using this phrase.

The woman with the hemorrhage of blood:

Matthew 9:20-22: 20 And a woman who had been suffering from a hemorrhage for twelve years, came up behind him and touched the fringe of his cloak; 21 for she was saying to herself, If I only touch his garment, I will get well. 22 But Jesus turning and seeing her said, Daughter, take courage; your faith has made you well <4982>. At once the woman was made well.

This woman’s persistence was a direct result of her faith. This combination of persistence and faith placed her in a position for physical healing and spiritual blessing. When gratitude is added, transformative healing occurs!

How consistently does my faith-driven persistence bring gratitude as one of its results? How consistently does my faith show itself through gratitude?

Are we likely to have gratitude to God in the front of our minds, ready to be expressed, as we press on to achieve a goal? Or are we more likely to congratulate ourselves on that achievement? We have to be careful to direct our gratitude upward, not toward self.

This is what the Samaritan shows us in how he expressed his gratitude before going back to his life.

Here is the third use of this phrase: (There are two blind men in the Matthew 20:29-34 account, but here Luke focuses on just one of them.)

Luke 18:35-43: 35 As Jesus was approaching Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the road begging. 36 Now hearing a crowd going by, he began to inquire what this was. 37 They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. 38 And he called out, saying, Jesus, son of David, have mercy on me! 39 Those who led the way were sternly telling him to be quiet; but he kept crying out all the more, Son of David, have mercy on me! 40 And Jesus stopped and commanded that he be brought to him; and when he came near, he questioned him, 41 What do you want me to do for you? And he said, Lord, I want to regain my sight! 42 And Jesus said to him, Receive your sight; your faith has made you well <4982>. 43 Immediately he regained his sight and began following him, glorifying God; and when all the people saw it, they gave praise to God.

The boldness of these blind men, especially Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46), was a direct result of their faith. Their transformative healing led them to follow Jesus as they received both physical and spiritual blessings. While their physical healing was wonderful, it was the transformation brought about by their gratitude and faith that led them to a whole different way of living after their healing.

Made you well carries both physical healing and spiritual salvation connotations.

Do I respond with a boldness driven by my faith when I am in a pressing situation? Does gratitude always follow? What does it mean if I DON’T express gratitude very often, giving God the credit He is due?

Before engaging in any spiritual service—such as giving a sermon, leading a Bible study, or recording each CQ episode—I take time to pray. I request my Father’s guidance and wisdom so that I can be a blessing to others by serving as His mouthpiece. The scripture that often comes to mind is Philippians 4:13, "I can do all things through him (Christ) who strengthens me," because I know I can do no good thing on my own. After asking for God’s spirit of wisdom to work through me and once I have completed my service for Him, I make it a point to return to the Creator in prayer. I thank Him for the miracle He worked through me, knowing that, regardless of the outcome, He deserves all the credit and glory.

This demonstrates how to use gratitude: ask with gratitude before the opportunity, then show gratitude afterwards for that opportunity and any good that may come from it. “Thank you, Lord, for Your guidance, Your spirit, Your providence, Your direction and Your wisdom.” Praise God.

Jesus healed the ten lepers with no strings attached. They asked for mercy, and he freely gave it to them. Upon being healed, the Samaritan immediately chose to change direction and passionately express his gratitude for his renewed life. His actions confirmed what Jesus was looking for: true, transforming faith that is real and expressible. Let us follow his example and be aware of our own need to express our gratitude as a confirmation of our faith.

I was talking to a sister in Christ who had been struggling with not trying to take control of everything in front of her, something with which we all have issues! We want to be in control and decide the outcome. We want to bend things toward what we think they should be.

She was mentally in a bad place. I was listening and thinking, I just don’t know what to say. Lord, I need to say something. Help me because I don’t know what it should be.

By God’s grace, we talked about three things.

1. Look at doing God’s will, not our will, just like Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane prayed, Yet not my will, but Yours be done… (Luke 22:42). Let’s learn to begin to let go.

2. Let’s work on healing our enemies, like Jesus did with the ear of Malchus in the Garden of Gethsemane when the Apostle Peter cut it off trying to defend Jesus. It didn’t matter that Jesus’ enemy was there to take him to crucifixion; he did the right thing and healed him. This was important to consider with this sister, because when people frustrated her, she just got mad.

3. Let’s have gratitude in being able to contribute rather than trying to control all of our situations.

Less than 12 hours later, she is driving to work with her child in the car and she gets hit by another car. Normally, this would have set her off in anger and frustration. Her child starts to cry, so she comforted the child, and they said a prayer together. Then she made sure the other driver was okay.

She finds herself encouraging him, and he is sorry. She is able to tell him, “It’s okay, it’s okay. Sometimes things happen.” She had this attitude of giving and healing. When the police came, she was able to calmly talk about what had happened.

She was able to express gratitude in the experience. While she was late to work, her co-workers covered for her. While her child was in a car accident, the child was unhurt and able to see it as not so scary. They could both see it through different eyes, because she was grateful and was able to contribute by helping both her child and the other driver.

She was talking about putting this together as a testimony for others. We thought about it, and she decided to name the testimony, “The Best Car Accident Ever,” because of the attitude that came out through the trial.

These examples show us that true, heartfelt gratitude is far more than saying thank you; it is living thankfully!

Can a lack of gratitude actually affect our ability to recognize and receive further blessings? Can it hinder our spiritual growth? Is NOT being thankful a sin?

These are important questions, and we want to be clear as to how to formulate the answers. Our gratitude to our heavenly Father through Jesus is squarely built on the foundation of our faith.

If we proclaim to have great faith and don’t often express gratitude for it, we may not be fulfilling the responsibilities of our discipleship. Faith and gratitude should always be combined in our Christian walk.

Like the leprous Samaritan, we have been healed by the merit of Jesus’ ransom. There is NOTHING that can compare with this unmerited gift.

Our faith-based gratitude, not just gratitude, for this gift can be expressed in many ways.

Faith-based gratitude puts us squarely into a frame of mind to continue to do God’s will:

Hebrews 13:15-16: 15 Through him then, let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that give thanks to His name. 16 And do not neglect doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

Thankfulness paired with service to others pleases God. One feeds the other. We are thankful for what we have been given and want to share that with others.

Our continued awareness of, and thanksgiving for, our deliverance puts us in a position to receive God’s continued providence.

How expressive am I regarding these gifts? Do I express my gratitude, or do I just mumble about it inside my head?

The Samaritan’s expression of gratitude is one of the big lessons in his response to his healing.

Faith-based gratitude brings us peace in the midst of our varied experiences:

Philippians 4:4-7: 4 Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice! 5 Let your gentle spirit be known to all men. The Lord is near. 6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. 7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Notice these gratitude steps to having peace: rejoice, live in a Christlike manner, minimize anxiety, prayerfully and thankfully commune with God.

Do I thankfully take these steps?

Faith-based gratitude is driven by God’s own faithfulness:

Lamentations 3:22-23: 22 The LORD'S lovingkindnesses indeed never cease, for His compassions never fail. 23 They are new every morning; Great is Your faithfulness.

This describes a reset button! Every morning brings a reset—God’s compassions are not recycled or worn out; they are new. We can look at each day as a gift, no matter how heavy yesterday felt. When something difficult is facing us, can we reframe our thinking when we wake up by knowing His faithfulness is already waiting for us? God’s faithfulness is waiting for us each morning! It’s just there!

God’s faithfulness is boundless, therefore our gratitude can be boundless as well:

Psalms 118:21-24: 21 I shall give thanks to You, for You have answered me, and You have become my salvation. 22 The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief corner stone (referring to Jesus) 23 This is the LORD'S doing; It is marvelous in our eyes. 24 This is the day which the LORD has made; Let us rejoice and be glad in it.

God’s mercies are new every morning, and Psalm 118 calls us to rejoice in the day He has made. In Luke, one healed leper shows us how this works—returning in gratitude for new life. His thankfulness shows us that just as God’s compassions never fail, our response should always be thanksgiving.

If we recognize that, rehearse it and remind ourselves of it regularly, we will realize that living a life truly full of gratitude makes coping with life much easier. The more we express our heartfelt gratitude to God, the more we will see His boundless care for us.

How readily and often do I express such deep gratitude?

If we want to experience God’s boundless care, work on boundless gratitude. Acknowledge these gifts from above.

Faith-based gratitude leads to a life of joy and strength.

Against all odds, after rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, the people met together to worship God:

Nehemiah 8:9-10: 9 Then Nehemiah… said to all the people, This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep. For all the people were weeping when they heard the words of the Law. 10 Then he said to them, Go, eat of the fat, drink of the sweet, and send portions to him who has nothing prepared; for this day is holy to our Lord. Do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.

The people of Israel had just heard the Law read aloud after years of neglect. Their first reaction was sorrow and weeping, realizing how far they had strayed. But instead of dwelling on their guilt and failure, they were redirected to give thanks for God’s mercy and restoration.

However far we have fallen, and however rightfully sorry we feel, that sorrow should always revert to gratitude for God's deliverance through Christ.

Even when confronted with our shortcomings, the joy of the Lord and His mercy and compassion are an overriding compensation.

Do I remember to show gratitude even in the midst of my shortcomings? What if I am falling short—including falling short in my gratitude?

There is a powerful solution for this issue, having everything to do with what Jesus did for us and how he connected us to our heavenly Father:

Hebrews 4:15-16: 15 For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin. 16 Therefore let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

How do we receive mercy and find grace to help? We have Jesus as our high priest, who understands our weaknesses. He was a human being, too! He had the humanness that we have and showed us how to deal with all that it involves.

The ten lepers were sent to the priest to be proclaimed as healed. Jesus is our high priest. He grants us the healing and then confirms it on both sides of this picture. Our gratitude is so important, and living in that gratitude is a glorious place to live our lives.

Jesus healed ten lepers, and only one came back to express his thanks. While this did not in any way minimize the gift of healing to the other nine, it did maximize the healing of the one. His physical healing and subsequent gratitude and praise to God lifted him into a life in which spiritual blessings could now begin to flow freely to him. Let us continually be reminded of our deliverance from spiritual leprosy and daily stand in awe of all we are blessed with! We have to remember to run back and say thank you, just as the Samaritan leper did.

Don’t walk. Don’t saunter. Don’t think about it. RUN BACK. The deliverance and promises we have been given to be with Jesus, to be lifted out of the mess of our own lives, all given by God’s grace through Jesus’ sacrifice, are incomprehensible!

Let us be grateful in all things, as exampled by the Samaritan leper.

2 Corinthians 9:15: Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!

So, what does leprosy teach us about sin and gratitude?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Leprosy (Physical Disease) Sin (Spiritual Condition)

Loathsome and disfiguring: Causes decay of skin, limbs, facial features and internal organs.

Corrupting and defiling: Destroys moral integrity, distorts spiritual identity.

Produces numbness: the condition worsens because the injury is often not treated right away.

Desensitization to sin: Sin produces spiritual numbness that desensitizes the conscience, allowing hidden damage to grow unchecked.

Progressive and incurable (in ancient times): No medical remedy; worsens over time.

Inescapable without divine intervention: Human effort alone cannot cleanse sin.

Highly contagious: Spread by contact and proximity.

Spiritually infectious: Influences others through behavior, culture and example.

Isolation required: Lepers lived outside the camp, cut off from family and worship.

Alienation from God: Sin separates individuals from fellowship with God and others.

Declared unclean by priests: Only priests could diagnose and pronounce healing.

Discerned by spiritual authority: Christ and the church identify and address sin.

Visible signs of uncleanness: Torn clothes, uncombed hair, public cries of “Unclean!”

Manifested through actions: Sin reveals itself in selfishness, pride and rebellion.

Healing required priestly verification: Restoration involved ritual cleansing.

Forgiveness requires spiritual cleansing: Restoration comes through Christ’s sacrifice and repentance.

One leper returned in gratitude: Demonstrated faith and worship.

Few respond with thankfulness: Many receive grace but fail to return in surrender and worship.

Cleansing ritual required.

Cleansing requires recognition of sin. Peter’s confession in Luke 5:8 and the prodigal son’s repentance in Luke 15:21 illustrate how acknowledging one’s sinful state can lead to redemption.

Once cleansed, only one said thank you.

We have been cleansed from sin and we receive life-changing blessings. Are we like the nine or the one?

There is now a medical cure.

Jesus is the Great Physician (Matthew 9:12,

Luke 5:31, Mark 5:23)

https://christianquestions.com/inspiration/1412-leprosy/

1. Compare how the physical progression of leprosy (numbness, disfigurement and isolation), mirrors the spiritual effects of sin in our lives. (Luke 17:12, Leviticus 13:45-46, Isaiah 59:2,

Romans 6:23, pages 1-3, 8, Bonus Material)

2. What does Jesus’ choosing to heal the ten lepers by sending them to the priests before they were visibly cleansed possibly indicate about obedience, faith and the process of both physical and spiritual healing? (Luke 17:14, Leviticus 14:1-9)

3. How does the one leper returning to thank Jesus reflect the heart position we should have towards the spiritual and temporal gifts we have been given? How should gratitude and faith connect? (Luke 17:15-18, Psalm 50:23, 1 Thessalonians 5:18)

4. Do I obey God’s scriptural instructions even when I don’t see immediate results or when it is terribly inconvenient to do so? In what ways can I improve my faith-driven obedience?

5. What is the significance of the thankful leper being Samaritan at the time of Jesus’ first advent? How might this be a reflection of ethnicities the Christian church attracted down through the ages? (Luke 17:16, John 4:9, Acts 10:34-35)

How was this man’s healing different from the other nine? Compare the other two instances when Jesus told someone their faith had made them whole. How was it different from the healing Jesus performed on hundreds, if not thousands, of others? (Luke 17:19, Matthew 9:20-22, Luke 18:35-43, Mark 10:46)

a. How does it affect our mind-set? (Hebrews 13:15-16)

b. What does it bring us? (Philippians 4:4-7) What are the steps for this?

c. Is based on whose example? (Lamentations 3:22-23, Psalms 118:21-24)

d. Leads to what, whether in joy or in sorrow? (Nehemiah 8:9-10, Hebrews 4:15-16)

9. How can I cultivate a lifestyle where gratitude is a natural outflow of my faith, even in adversity? (Philippians 4:6-7, Colossians 3:15-17, 2 Corinthians 9:15)

## Episode 1413 — What Really Happened to Enoch, Moses and Elijah?
Published: 2025-12-01
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1413-enoch-moses-elijah/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/30095822/CQ_Rewind_12-1-2025_What_Really_Happened-_to_Enoch_Moses_and_Elijah.pdf

Deuteronomy 34:5–6: 5 So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD. 6 And He buried him in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor; but no man knows his burial place to this day.

Reading the Bible can be confusing. After all, it is an ancient book, a collection of writings by about 40 people over a 1500-year span, that details the plan of God through history, prophecy, parables, laws, observations and life-guidance teachings. Some of the accounts of specific individuals featured in the Bible can come across as shrouded in mystery. Such is the case with the ending of the lives of Enoch, Moses and Elijah. The accounts of the deaths of these three faithful men can raise more questions than answers. What really happened to them? Was Enoch taken up to be with God? Why was the body of Moses hidden, and why did Satan seem to want it? Did Elijah really go to heaven in a fiery chariot?

Let’s begin with Moses, which at first glance seems to be the easiest of the three to explain.

Here is the account of the end of Moses’ life and God burying him in an unknown location:

Deuteronomy 34:4–8: 4 Then the LORD said to him, This is the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, I will give it to your descendants; I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there. 5 So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD. 6 And He buried him in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor; but no man knows his burial place to this day. 7 Although Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died, his eye was not dim, nor his vigor abated. 8 So the sons of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days; then the days of weeping and mourning for Moses came to an end.

Beth-peor, meaning “House of Peor,” was the center of worship for the Canaanite god Baal of Peor.

So, if Moses simply died, then what’s the big deal?

A scripture in Jude brings us a very unusual perspective regarding Moses’ body:

Jude 1:8–9: 8 Yet in the same way these men, also by dreaming, defile the flesh, and reject authority, and revile angelic majesties. 9 But Michael the archangel, when he disputed with the devil and argued about the body of Moses, did not dare pronounce against him a railing judgment, but said, The Lord rebuke you!

This is an odd peek into the spirit world—why are Michael and Satan arguing over Moses’ body?

Michael the archangel did not even consider casting a vilifying judgment over Satan; he instead left the censuring or forbidding up to God Himself. This is an important principle which comes up in a few other scriptures as well.

Why did this argument take place in the spirit realm? The Bible doesn’t tell us directly, but we can consider some ideas based on other scriptures. We know for sure Moses was dead, meaning he had ceased to exist.

Let’s verify what being dead means:

Genesis 2:16–17: 16 The LORD God commanded the man, saying, From any tree of the garden you may eat freely; 17 but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat from it you will surely die.

This is a clear command from God: In the day that you eat of it, the literal Hebrew says, dying thou shalt die. This is our starting point.

Ecclesiastes 9:10: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might; for there is no activity or planning or knowledge or wisdom in sheol (the grave) where you are going.

This is straightforward—death means lack of life.

Romans 6:23: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Note, the wages of sin are not eternal torment or somehow being more alive than ever. The wages of sin is death. We are establishing a scriptural pattern so we can understand what happened when Moses was dead and buried.

1 Corinthians 15:20–22: 20 But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who are asleep. 21 For since by a man came death, by a man also came the resurrection of the dead. 22 For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

Death is the absence of life. So, we understand Moses was dead—not alive in any way— and was buried.

What did Satan want with the dead body of Moses?

Perhaps Satan wanted to reveal Moses’ body so the Hebrews could carry it with them into the Promised Land as a remembrance of their great leader. If this were the case, what a sly maneuver it would have been to get the people to subtly lean into idolatry by worshipping Moses’ body.

This thought makes sense; after all, Moses was the bridge between slavery and freedom for millions of people—a hero of heroes. And we know the peoples’ propensity for idol worship from the golden calf experience.

There was an idolatrous background in Jewish history for generations. They were surrounded by pagans down through the years, and lived enslaved in Egypt for hundreds of years surrounded by Egyptian culture.

Also, respect for the dead and their remains was a very important part of ancient Hebrew culture, and proper burial held a high priority. When they did not know where the body of Moses was, it was difficult for them because they could not do the things they normally would have done to show respect for this venerated leader.

Remember what happened many years earlier when Joseph died:

Genesis 50:24–26: 24 Joseph said to his brothers, I am about to die, but God will surely take care of you and bring you up from this land to the land which He promised on oath to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob. 25 Then Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, God will surely take care of you, and you shall carry my bones up from here. 26 So Joseph died at the age of one hundred and ten years; and he was embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt.

The sons of Israel took Joseph’s bones with them to bury them in the Promised Land:

Joshua 24:32: Now they buried the bones of Joseph, which the sons of Israel brought up from Egypt, at Shechem, in the piece of ground which Jacob had bought from the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for one hundred pieces of money; and they became the inheritance of Joseph’s sons.

Joseph’s bones were taken with respect to the Promised Land, and the importance of that burial may have been vivid in their minds.

We could only assume Moses’ body would have been treated just as respectfully. Why would God prevent this from happening? Was it a national trial for them?

Perhaps, but we also recall how God said to Moses, I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there. Because of disobedience, Moses was not allowed to enter the Promised Land, apparently even after death.

If the people had been given Moses’ body, the temptation to use it some form of idolatry would have really grown.

Living and Dying by the Grace of God: With the evidence we have seen thus far, it is clear Moses died and was buried in a secret location of God’s own choosing. Let us reverence what God did in this experience and recognize how His decision was for the ultimate good of His people.

But what about how Moses later appears in the Mount of Transfiguration account in Matthew, Mark and Luke? Was God preserving the body of Moses so He could raise it up later with Jesus and Elijah? Some Bible commentaries say Moses and Elijah were “in the body,” meaning literally and physically present.

(Source: Biblical Commentary by Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) That Moses’ body was raised, appears from his presence with Elijah and Jesus (who were in the body) at the Transfiguration: the sample and earnest of the coming resurrection kingdom, to be ushered in by Michael’s standing up for God’s people.

Just when it looked like this would be easy, let’s remember, all Bible details are harmonious, and we just need to uncover that harmony!

Let’s move to the account of Elijah.

What REALLY happened to him at the end of his ministry with the chariot of fire?

Establishing what happened to Elijah when he turned his work over to Elisha is a really important starting point. When we look at the scriptures that define this particular experience, two things become evident: First, whatever happened was miraculous. Second, it’s very easy to draw conclusions based on that miracle that may not be supported by sound biblical principles.

Did Elijah go to heaven to be with God?

No! Why would we say that? Don’t we all remember the account of him being taken up to heaven in a chariot?

Let’s carefully examine the account to avoid potential misconceptions.

Where did Elijah go?

2 Kings 2:1: And it came about when the LORD was about to take up Elijah by a whirlwind to heaven <8064>, that Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.

Heaven: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #8064; shamayim; dual of an unused singular shameh; from an unused root meaning to be lofty; the sky (as aloft; the dual perhaps alluding to the visible arch in which the clouds move, as well as to the higher ether where the celestial bodies revolve)

Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew and English Lexicon: 1) heaven, heavens, sky 1a) visible heavens, sky 1a1) as abode of the stars 1a2) as the visible universe, the sky, atmosphere, etc. 1b) heaven (as the abode of God)

Scripturally this Hebrew word for heaven often just means the physical sky—our atmosphere that produces weather. Context can broaden it to mean our visible universe of stars, or it can be a theological description of where God resides.

Here are a few other uses of this word to demonstrate this variance in understanding:

Genesis 1:9: Then God said, Let the waters below the heavens <8064> be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear; and it was so.

Below the heavens is translated from this same Hebrew word, used here to mean the sky, the air above us.

Genesis 1:26: Then God said, Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky <8064> and over the cattle and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.

Of the sky is translated from the same Hebrew word, here meaning the same atmospheric realm, the space of birds.

One more example:

Genesis 22:17: Indeed I will greatly bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heavens <8064> and as the sand which is on the seashore; and your seed shall possess the gate of their enemies.

Stars of the heavens here refers to our visible universe of stars from our perspective from earth, the wider cosmos. It can also be used metaphorically to indicate eternity and divine order (Ecclesiastes 3:1: …And there is a time for every event under heaven, for example)

God is called the God of heaven (see Nehemiah 1:5, Daniel 2:44, Jonah 1:9 and others), meaning further than our atmosphere or the visible sky.

Psalm 11:4: The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD’s throne is in heaven <8064>…

In spite of God’s home being in heaven, we firmly believe that Elijah was taken up into the air—the sky—but NOT to God’s heavenly home. Why?

Because Jesus told us so!

John 3:12–13: 12 If I told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? 13 No one has ascended into heaven <3772>, but he who descended from heaven <3772>: the Son of Man.

The Greek term in the New Testament is essentially the direct continuation of the Hebrew idea: heaven can mean the physical sky where birds are, the starry heavens or the spiritual dwelling place of God.

Heaven: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3772 ouranos; perhaps from the same as #3735 (through the idea of elevation); the sky; by extension, heaven (as the abode of God); by implication, happiness, power, eternity; specially, the Gospel (Christianity):—air, heaven(-ly), sky

Why doesn’t the Greek Strong’s #3772 indicate the “three layers” of heaven the way the Hebrew Strong’s #8064 does? See the Bonus Material for the explanation.

Jesus was the firstborn of all creation:

Colossians 1:16: For by him all things were created, both in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things have been created through him and for him.

Jesus was also the first person to be resurrected from the dead,

Colossians 1:18: He is also head of the body, the church; and he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself will come to have first place in everything.

This provides clear proof that no human was resurrected before him, including Elijah.

If he didn’t go to be with God in heaven, where did he go? And what about the chariot?

Let’s go back to the account:

2 Kings 2:11–12: 11 As they were going along and talking, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire and horses of fire which separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind to heaven. 12 Elisha saw it and cried out, My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen! And he saw Elijah no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two pieces.

For dramatic visual impact, some of the more famous art pieces show Elijah being carried away in a fiery chariot with horses.

But the chariot was in between them. The whirlwind is what carried Elijah away, not the fiery chariot and horses.

Why a chariot? This whole thing is a miracle. Perhaps the chariot of fire comes between Elijah and Elisha to protect Elisha from the powerful whirlwind. Perhaps it was a physical indication to Elisha that he was protected, and that he would now have the authority of Elijah. Elijah was going away, and this was a separation that could not be breached.

If Elijah didn’t go to the heaven of God’s abode, where did he go and how do we know?

There are only two options:

1. He died. This was the end of his life. His work was done, and God removed him, similar to what we saw with Moses.

2. He lived. He was removed from public service as the mighty prophet he had been. His time working as God’s spokesperson was over.

The Scriptures aren’t clear as to which of the two options is correct. All we know for sure is he was not taken to the heaven of God’s abode because Jesus was the first to ascend into heaven.

Curiously, years later in 2 Chronicles, we are told King Jehoram of Judah received a letter from Elijah.

It indicted the king for his sins and predicted severe punishment:

2 Chronicles 21:11–14: 11 Moreover, he (King Jehoram) made high places in the mountains of Judah, and caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to play the harlot and led Judah astray. 12 Then a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet saying, Thus says the LORD God of your father David, Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father and the ways of Asa king of Judah, 13 but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and have caused Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to play the harlot as the house of Ahab played the harlot, and you have also killed your brothers, your own family, who were better than you, 14 behold, the LORD is going to strike your people, your sons, your wives and all your possessions with a great calamity;

As usual, what Elijah said was what happened:

2 Chronicles 21:20: He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years; and he departed with no one’s regret, and they buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

Here’s the controversy:

- In 2 Kings 2, Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind.
- In 2 Chronicles 21, years later, King Jehoram of Judah receives a letter from Elijah.

How could Elijah send a letter if he was already dead?

There are several possible explanations. Please see the Bonus Material.

In summary, we don’t know if Elijah was just taken off the scene or if his actual life was taken. What we DO know is where he did NOT go (with God in heaven) and how he did NOT get there (in a chariot)!

Living and Dying by the Grace of God: Whether Elijah died when he was taken by the whirlwind or he was simply removed from his responsibility as a major prophet is really immaterial.

No matter which details are accurate, we again see how a faithful man of God was treated by God with honor and respect after his mission was ended.

We want to be careful not to read too much into what is not in Scripture.

The similarities between Moses and Elijah are marked with a certain level of mystery. The bottom line is, God’s got it all in His control!

So, what about the Mount of Transfiguration? Doesn’t that event change our conclusions about both of these godly men?

The Mount of Transfiguration event was one of great significance. It was so unique and important that, as we shall see, Jesus told Peter, James and John NOT to speak about it until after he himself had risen from the dead. Clearly, the importance of this vision was to be received by Jesus’ followers after they were given God’s holy spirit to help them comprehend it.

For all the interesting details about the account, please see Episode #1369: “What Really Happened on the Mount of Transfiguration?”

The three accounts of the Transfiguration:

Matthew 17:1–13 (NASB77) Mark 9:2–13 (NASB77) Luke 9:28–36 (NASB77) We have combined the three accounts to get a comprehensive view of what occured.

And some eight days after these sayings, it came about that he took along Peter and John and James, and went up to the mountain to pray. And while he was praying, he was transfigured before them; the appearance of his face became different, and his face shone like the sun, and his garments became radiant and exceedingly white, as no launderer on earth can whiten them.

Transfigured: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3339; metamorphoo; to transform (literally or figuratively, "metamorphose”)—change, transfigure, transform

Meta (change) morpho (form, shape). This Greek root is where we get our English word “metamorphosis,” meaning to change or transform. In the Transfiguration scene, Jesus was still Jesus, but he transformed into a glorious representation of himself.

This word is only used in two other places, referring to a transformation from earthly to spiritual: 2 Corinthians 3:18 and Romans 12:2.

Romans 12:2: (KJV) And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed <3339> by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.

Our own transformation in Romans 12 is the transforming of a human being into the likeness of Christ as a result of God’s spirit working within us. It changes us from conforming to earthly desires to wanting to be like Jesus, a metamorphosis.

We will note an important detail as we read through the account—while it specifically says Jesus was transformed, it does not say the same about Elijah and Moses.

And Elijah appeared to them along with Moses; and they were talking with Jesus who, appearing in glory, were speaking of his departure which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Now Peter and his companions had been overcome with sleep; but when they were fully awake, they saw his glory and the two men standing with him. And it came about, as these were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, Master, it is good for us to be here; and let us make three tabernacles: one for you, and one for Moses, and one for Elijah.

This is a vivid vision! Moses and Elijah appear as representations of God’s plan working through Jesus as the centerpiece.

For he (Peter) did not know what to answer; for they became terrified. And while he was saying this, a cloud formed and began to overshadow them; and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is My son, My Chosen One; listen to him! And when the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were much afraid.

It’s interesting that both Moses and Elijah died having mysteries surrounding the end of their lives and both appear in this vision. They were two revered people in Jewish history, legendary in their importance to the Jewish nation. But here all the focus is on Jesus.

The heavenly proclamation (This is My son…) seems to have been the only audible part of this vision. It focused all the attention on Jesus as THE centerpiece of God’s glorious plan! It would now move from the Law and the prophets to the gospel of Christ as the fulfillment of God’s plan to redeem all mankind.

Witnessing such glory and hearing such a powerful proclamation can be too much for mere humans to handle. It was scary and overwhelming.

And Jesus came to them and touched them and said, Arise, and do not be afraid. And lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus himself alone. And as they were coming down from the mountain, he gave them orders not to relate to anyone what they had seen, until the Son of Man should rise from the dead. And they seized upon that statement, discussing with one another what rising from the dead might mean.

Were the literal Moses and Elijah really there like some of the Bible commentaries allude to? Were they either raised from the dead or pulled out of heaven?

We have already discussed they were not pulled out of heaven—no one was in heaven before Jesus. So, were they raised from the dead?

No! This was a vision.

How do we know? Jesus said so:

Matthew 17:9: 9 As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying, Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.

This word for vision is used 12 times in the New Testament. In every instance, it describes something supernatural from God to relay a message.

A vision is like a dream and can seem so real. You can dream of someone who died, but in the dream, it feels like they are right there.

When my wife and I were in the early years of our 45-year marriage, I was still working on building our house. Her closet in our bedroom didn’t have closet doors yet, but it had three shelves. She had a recurring dream where she saw little men on each shelf running tiny sawmills sawing wood!

One night the dream was so vivid, she grabbed my arm, sat up and said, “Look, there they are! Do you see them? Do you see them?” She was squeezing my arm, “There they are, and they don’t look very friendly!”

I just started to laugh, and she finally woke up. The dream seemed so true that she was determined to prove to me it was real.

Experiencing a vision from God must have been overwhelming beyond even the most vivid dream.

The Mount of Transfiguration was a vision with Elijah and Moses who had already died. This is not the only biblical vision to give a representation of someone who had died:

Zechariah 3:1–3: 1 Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him. 2 The LORD said to Satan, The LORD rebuke you, Satan! Indeed, the LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Is this not a brand plucked from the fire? 3 Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments and standing before the angel.

The word rebuke is used again like we saw in the Jude text we quoted about the argument over Moses’ body. Here in this vision, God is rebuking Satan over Joshua.

We don’t hear of people saying Joshua had been raised from the dead, as this clearly was a vision given to Zechariah:

Joshua 24:29–30: 29 It came about after these things that Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being one hundred and ten years old. 30 And they buried him in the territory of his inheritance…

Joshua had been dead for generations before Zechariah. Again, this was a vision; the literal Joshua was not raised from the dead (or pulled out of heaven) to appear. Having another text showing a vision with someone who died helps put the Mount of Transfiguration in its appropriate perspective.

The Mount of Transfiguration vision was to show the disciples a snapshot of the glory of God’s kingdom and in no way supported the idea that Moses and Elijah were risen beings:

Moses representing the design of deliverance by God and His Law—Moses

delivered the people. Jesus later fulfilled the Law to pay the ransom sacrifice for Adam.

Elijah representing the support of deliverance—those who stood for and spoke for

God’s way, meaning the prophets of old (Elijah himself) and those who paved the way for the Messiah (John the Baptist and the true church, both of whom Elijah represented).

Jesus as the deliverance—the centerpiece of God’s plan, the ransom for all.

Living and Dying by the Grace of God: It is revealing that both Moses and Elijah had secrecy surrounding the end of their lives of service and yet these two men of faith were incredible representations of what their lives meant in the Mount of Transfiguration vision. It is as if God is saying that their personal lives were reverential, direct links to the Messiah who would deliver ALL mankind.

Moses represented the Law (which Jesus would fulfill perfectly). Elijah represented the prophets (with the prophecies of Jesus as the Messiah.) It was about their connection to Messiah the Deliverer.

The Mount of Transfiguration fits very well into the overall account of living and dying and the mysteries God allows us to see in Scripture.

Moses and Elijah were truly great servants of God whose lives, right down to the ending of their contributions, showed us what faith and obedience look like!

So, we’ve examined the reality of the deaths of Moses and Elijah and have learned some powerful lessons. What about Enoch?

The most dramatic difference with Enoch is how little we know about him. Moses’ life is reflected in several Old Testament books and Elijah’s life covers many chapters. When it comes to Enoch, we have very few scriptures to rely upon. However, examining these reveals his amazing life. We now need to determine what happened when God took him.

Please listen to Episode #1410: “Why is the Book of Enoch Not in the Bible?” We examined the Book of Enoch in relation to the canon of Scripture.

There are only three references to Enoch in the entire Bible.

We know his genealogy. Enoch was the seventh generation from Adam:

Genesis 5:21–24: 21 Enoch lived sixty-five years, and became the father of Methuselah. 22 Then Enoch walked with God three hundred years after he became the father of Methuselah, and he had other sons and daughters. 23 So all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. 24 Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took <3947> him.

Took: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3947; laqach; a primitive root; to take (in the widest variety of applications)

God took him—this is an unusual description. Where did he go?

The Old Testament word for took is used over 900 times in the Old Testament. It has a very general meaning, so we can’t use that to authentically build a dramatic meaning into such a common word. We would need more scriptural support.

Let’s look at two other scriptures to show how broadly took is used:

Genesis 2:23: (KJV) And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken <3947> out of Man.

She was taken from Adam to become her own person.

Job 1:21: (KJV) And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away<3947>; blessed be the name of the LORD.

The Lord gives life. The Lord takes life.

We can see from these two examples that the word is broadly used. We can’t draw any specific conclusions from examining the word itself.

The New Testament reveals that Enoch pleased God by faith:

Hebrews 11:5: By faith Enoch was taken up so that he would not see death; AND HE WAS NOT FOUND BECAUSE GOD TOOK HIM UP (quoted from Genesis 5:24); for he obtained the witness that before his being taken up he was pleasing to God.

The King James Version says he was translated, meaning moved from one place to another. The New American Standard Version (1995) says taken up. However, the word “up” is not in the original Greek; rather, it was supplied by the translator. This is a little deceptive. We have to be careful of words supplied to fit a preconceived idea.

God took him. His body was not found. We know he could not have gone to heaven:

John 3:13: No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven: the Son of Man.

Again, this is how we know Enoch, Moses and Elijah and anyone else who died before Jesus were not taken up to heaven, meaning the abode of God.

Another text to describe death:

2 Peter 3:4: And saying, where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all continues just as it was from the beginning of creation.

Moses, Elijah and Enoch are still asleep in death, and we need to leave them there until the resurrection! They are the fathers.

Enoch warned of judgment. His warnings are quoted by Jude in Jude 1:14–15. This doesn’t relate to our topic today, but we discussed this in detail in Episode #1410.

What does Enoch being taken (not “taken up”) by God really mean?

Hebrews 11:5: (KJV) By faith Enoch was translated <3346> that he should not see <1492> death; and was not found, because God had translated <3346> him: for before his translation <3331> he had this testimony, that he pleased God.

The word for translated or taken means to transfer, change or remove; to cause a change of place or condition; to transfer from one state to another.

Translated (verb): Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3346; metatithemi; to transfer, i.e. (literally) transport, (by implication) exchange (reflexively) change sides, or (figuratively) pervert

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) to transpose (two things, one of which is put in place of the other) 1a) to transfer 1b) to change

This word is used six times in the New Testament. Translated seems to give this basic word an unwarranted, mysterious slant.

Removed (noun): Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3331; metathesis; from #3346; transposition, i.e. transferal (to heaven), disestablishment (of a law)

Same word, but one is a verb and one is a noun.

Here is another use:

Galatians 1:6: (KJV) I marvel that ye are <3346> so soon removed <3346> from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel:

Ye are removed—you have been taken from being in the gospel of Christ through Paul’s teaching, to some other place or state of being where you are now in danger. (Those Paul is talking to were being influenced by Jewish Christians who led them to believe salvation was through Jesus Christ, but only if they kept the Law. This was another gospel, not the one he taught them.) There is nothing mysterious about this.

One more example of how the word is used:

Hebrews 12:27: (KJV) And this word, Yet once more, signifieth the removing <3331> of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain.

Interestingly, when we look at the root words, part of the root means “to place in the widest application, literally and figuratively, properly in a passive or horizontal posture… different from… an upright and active position.” Perhaps this alludes to Enoch being taken by God in death passively, horizontally, like in his sleep.

#5087 is the root verb behind “taken/translated” in #3346 when combined with the prefix #3326:

Taken: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3326; meta; a primary preposition (often used adverbially); properly, denoting accompaniment; “amid”

Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5087; tithemi; a prolonged form of a primary theo (which is used only as alternate in certain tenses); to place (in the widest application, literally and figuratively; properly, in a passive or horizontal posture, and thus different from 2476, which properly denotes

an upright and active position, while 2749 is properly reflexive and utterly prostrate)

Enoch was taken by God— not “taken up,” but we believe taken passively in death:

Hebrews 11:5: (KJV) By faith Enoch was translated <3346> that he should not see <1492> death.

See/Perceive: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1492 horáō; (eido in King James Version) properly, to stare at (compare 3700), i.e. (by implication) to discern clearly (physically or mentally); by extension, to attend to; by Hebraism, to experience; passively, to appear:—behold, perceive, see, take heed

The word see <1492> in this verse means to perceive, to clearly discern; not physically using our eyeballs. “See” in our English translations can have different meanings as they are from different Greek words.

How did Enoch not “see”—perceive, discern—death? Perhaps it was unexpected. God took Enoch's life at a “young” age (365 years) compared to his peers. Compared to Adam (930 years) and Methuselah (969 years), for example, he was very young. Perhaps he didn’t anticipate dying so young.

After speaking the Parable of the Sower, Jesus’ disciples asked him why he taught in parables. His answer was based on Isaiah 6:9–10.

Jesus uses this prophecy to teach us about seeing and perceiving—two separate words:

Matthew 13:14: 14 In their case the prophecy of Isaiah is being fulfilled, which says, YOU WILL KEEP ON HEARING, BUT WILL NOT UNDERSTAND; YOU WILL KEEP ON SEEING <991>, BUT WILL NOT PERCEIVE <1492>;

Seeing: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #991 blepō; a primary verb; to look at (literally or figuratively):—behold, beware, lie, look (on, to), perceive, regard, see, sight, take heed

You will keep on seeing (with your eyes), but will not perceive (understand, comprehend what is happening). Jesus was teaching the basic lessons of seeing and then of elevating ourselves to perceiving.

Hebrews 11:5 says he (Enoch) should not see (perceive, understand) death. Perhaps he died in his sleep or was otherwise not expected to die, by not being injured or sick, etc.

Similarly, we know Moses was seemingly healthy when he died—his eye was not dim, nor his vigor abated (Deuteronomy 34:7).

Living and Dying by the Grace of God: Moses, Elijah and Enoch all had powerful faith and obedience when it came to following God’s will. These three men shared a unique mystery in the ending of their service to God. Not exactly knowing the details of their singular experiences helps us remember that God is sovereign. What He does and how He does it is always for the purpose of the eternal good of His plan. Let us rejoice in what we do know, as God’s plan goes grandly forward!

Human nature likes to create drama where it shouldn’t be. We want to respect and reverence how the Scriptures are written to show us the lives of these faithful individuals. We appreciate who they were, how they served God, and how God treated them in the context of His plan. Life is life, death is death. Jesus died so that all who died can be raised to life. Enoch, Moses and Elijah were not exceptions to that rule.

So, what really happened to Enoch, Moses and Elijah?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!
