------------------------------------ Why doesn’t the Greek Strong’s #3772 indicate the “three layers” of heaven the way the Hebrew Strong’s #8064 does?

Hebrew (#8064 – shamayim)

- Notice the “-im” ending. In Hebrew that’s a plural ending (like “-s” in English). The word itself is grammatically plural, even when it refers to a single “heaven.” It naturally carries the idea of multiple layers or realms of heaven.
- Hebrew cosmology often speaks of “heavens of heavens” (for example, Nehemiah 9:6), so the lexicon reflects that layered concept: atmosphere, starry heavens and God’s dwelling.

Greek (#3772 – ouranos)

- The word is singular and rooted in the idea of “height” or “elevation.”
- Greek thought doesn’t build the same grammatical layering into the word. Instead, the New Testament context supplies the distinctions (such as Paul’s “third heaven” in 2 Corinthians 12:2).
- The Strong’s definition focuses on “sky, heaven, air” and then extends by implication to “eternity, power, happiness the Gospel.” It doesn’t list three layers because the Greek term itself doesn’t grammatically demand them.

Summary:

- Shamayim (#8064): The word is plural with multiple layers implied.
- Ouranos (#3772): The word is singular. Layers must be inferred from contextual usage (like “third heaven”), not from the lexicon entry.

------------------------------------

How could Elijah send a letter if he was already gone?

Explanation #1: The whirlwind transported him to another location, like being moved by a tornado, and didn’t die. It signaled the end of his public ministry, and he wrote the letter to the king. Similar to what happened to Philip in Acts 8:39.

Explanation #2: Being a prophet of God, Elijah foretold these events of Jehoran’s specific sins and had the letter sent years after his own death. God could have directed him what to write in the letter, before those events actually happened.

Explanation #3: Another possible explanation scholars consider is, whoever wrote Chronicles used Elijah’s name to emphasize authority. Elijah’s name functions symbolically as the prophetic voice confronting Jehoram’s sins. Even though Elijah was gone, his prophetic authority still speaks against idolatry and injustice. Just as Moses represents the Law, Elijah represents the Prophets, and together they symbolize God’s unbroken word confronting human rebellion.

Explanation #4: (which we at CQ find reasonable and natural) Elijah wrote the letter while King Jehoram of Judah reigned, before the whirlwind. The biblical timeline is complex, as the narrative of 2 Kings chapters 1,2 and 3 does not give us the precise sequence. At one point, both Israel in the north and Judah in the south had kings named Jehoram/Joram ruling at the same time (2 Kings 8:16). The whirlwind happened during Jehoram of Israel’s reign. But Elijah was still alive when Jehoram of Judah came to power.

Elijah could have written the letter to Judah’s king before the whirlwind because he was alive during the overlap of both kings. The letter could then have been delivered later (perhaps by Elisha or another prophet), explaining why it appears in the narrative of 2 Chronicles after Elijah’s departure. The Bible doesn’t say exactly when Jehoram of Judah received Elijah’s letter.

We focus on three kings of the northern kingdom of Israel—namely Ahab, Ahaziah and Jehoram—and the narrative in 2 Kings chapters 1, 2 and 3.

Before 2 Kings, Ahab died and Ahaziah replaced him. Ahaziah then reigned for parts of two years. Ahaziah's reign then ended at the close of 2 Kings 1. Because his reign ended there, then his successor Jehoram necessarily began then, even though the narrative does not yet mention Jehoram.

So, Jehoram was king of Israel by the end of chapter 1. In chapter 2, Jehoram would have been king during the time when Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind.

In what year of Jehoram’s reign would this have occurred? The narrative does not specify, but it could have been at any time during the time Jehoram of Israel was ruler.

Later, in 2 Chronicles 21:12, "There came a writing... from Elijah the prophet," this letter came to the other Jehoram, the king of Judah. Jehoram of Israel came to the throne first. Jehoram of Judah came to the throne during year five of Jehoram of Israel’s 12-year reign.

Evidently, Elijah had not yet been taken up in the whirlwind by that time. He was taken up sometime in the reign of Jehoram of Israel (because it was after the passing of his predecessor Ahaziah), but no text specifies when exactly during Jehoram of Judah’s reign Elijah was taken up.

It may have been after Jehoram of Israel’s fifth year, when Jehoram of Judah reigned as well. In summary, Elijah could have written and sent the letter to the king of Judah before the whirlwind, or it could have been delivered later. This would explain why it appears in Chronicles after Elijah’s departure without requiring him to reappear. – Thank you to CQ volunteer David Rice for this explanation.

Matthew 17:13: Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist. Luke 9:36–37: 36 …And they kept silent, and reported to no one in those days any of the things which they had seen. 37 On the next day, when they came down from the mountain, a large crowd met him.

### Study Questions

## Episode 1414 — Did Jesus Die for Every Single Human Being?
Published: 2025-12-08
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1414-salvation-for-all/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/05110646/CQ_Rewind_12-05-2025_Did_Jesus_Die_for_Every_Single_Human_Being.pdf

Romans 6:23: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

As Christians, we deeply appreciate the price that Jesus paid for us to be released from the grip of the sin of Adam. To say this has given us a new opportunity for life is a dramatic understatement, and all we can really do is be profoundly thankful as we diligently follow in his footsteps. However, one question many Christians find uncomfortable to face is what happens to “everybody else”? According to the Bible, what really happens to everyone who does not follow Jesus? What effect did Jesus’ life, death and resurrection have on those who are atheists, Muslims or Hindus? If we say they are essentially doomed, the question of true justice needs to be addressed. How fair would it be to condemn people to eternal death who, in many cases, never, ever really knew the name of Jesus? Precisely what effect does Jesus’ sacrifice have on these people?

Did Jesus die for EVERY single human being?

First, the Bible is clear that ALL of humanity was doomed to death through Adam:

Genesis 2:15-17: 15 Then the LORD God took the man and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate it and keep it. 16 The LORD God commanded the man, saying, From any tree of the garden you may eat freely; 17 but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat from it you will surely die.

(Young’s Literal Translation): 17 …for in the day of thine eating of it— dying thou dost die.

This describes the gradual dying process. We know Adam chose to sin after Satan deceived Eve. The consequence of this direct disobedience was the dying process. This consequence was clear and just.

God describes the death sentence for Adam:

Genesis 3:17-19: 17 Then to Adam He said, Because you… have eaten from the tree about which I commanded you, saying, You shall not eat from it; cursed is the ground because of you; in toil you will eat of it all the days of your life. 18 Both thorns and thistles it shall grow for you; and you will eat the plants of the field; 19 By the sweat of your face you will eat bread, till you return to the ground, because from it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.

These verses show the beginning of the dying process. Adam and Eve were removed from the Garden and its Tree of Life. They would now need to work hard to raise their food. They were taken from the dust of the ground and eventually would return to that dust.

This death penalty removed Adam from God’s freely given life-sustaining environment. He would eventually die and return to the earth’s elements.

It all looks pretty sad and hopeless—or does it?

When God pronounced judgment upon Satan, He did so in a prophetic way which brought great hope to a terminal situation:

Genesis 3:15: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; he shall bruise you on the head, and you shall bruise him on the heel.

There is a little glimmer of hope! The seed of the woman will take Satan out. So, Satan’s deception and Adam’s sin were not the end of everything. All hope for mankind was not over. God subtly shows us this was a step the longer process of redemption.

Satan, represented as a serpent, would suffer a fatal wound from the “seed of the woman”—a crushing of his head, which a snake could not survive. There is a faint hint that something is going to change.

What do we have so far? It’s simple and unequivocal: the death sentence has been pronounced, but then a hope of deliverance is shown.

When we jump to the New Testament, the sentence of death and the hope of deliverance are clearly summed up in Romans:

Romans 6:23: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Now, that’s a free gift everyone will sign up for! The wages of sin is death. We are all “earning” those wages, but there is a free gift attached.

How does this work?

Who is saved from death in Adam by Jesus, and how do we know?

The Bible emphatically answers this question in several places and in several ways. We will sum up a few of them in this episode.

1 Corinthians 15:20-22: 20 But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who are asleep. 21 For since by a man (Adam) came death, by a man (Jesus) also came the resurrection of the dead. 22 For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

This sounds like everyone. How do we know that ALL are included and not just those who follow Jesus? Many in Christianity say only those who follow Jesus now are included in this. How do we know this is more inclusive? We need to pull in more scriptures.

In Genesis, the gospel’s foundation was made plain through the faithful life of Abraham, exemplified by his willingness to sacrifice his son Isaac.

Speaking as God’s mouthpiece, here is what the angel of God relayed to Abraham:

Genesis 22:17-18: 17 Indeed I will greatly bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heavens and as the sand which is on the seashore; and your seed shall possess the gate of their enemies. 18 In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice.

In hindsight, we know Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice Isaac is a picture of God willingly offering His son, Jesus, for the recovery of humanity from sin. Jesus is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). While God mercifully stopped Abraham from sacrificing his son Isaac, Abraham's willingness to do so ultimately proved his loyalty, allowing him to receive the promise.

God had no intention of letting Abraham kill his son. He set up this test of faithfulness to show a picture of something so much larger that we can barely comprehend it. God PROMISES that through Abraham, ALL of humanity will be blessed.

A dramatic hint of the fulfillment of this promise was given at Jesus’ birth:

Luke 2:9-11: 9 And an angel of the Lord suddenly stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them; and they were terribly frightened. 10 But the angel said to them, Do not be afraid; for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be for all the people; 11 for today in the city of David there has been born for you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.

But a savior of whom? A savior only of those who would follow Jesus now? No, that’s not what it says. A savior of only the Jews? Only the Gentiles? Again, NO!

This scripture, often quoted at Christmas, is simple, and yet we gloss right over this powerful point. It highlights that Jesus is a savior for ALL people. ALL the nations of the earth will be blessed.

Jesus is further confirmed as THE centerpiece—THE subject of this whole blessing process:

Galatians 3:16: Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, and to seeds, as referring to many, but rather to one, and to your seed, that is, Christ.

To one, and to your seed, that is, Christ—the Apostle Paul is telling us the promise given to Abraham specifically refers to Jesus.

We are seeing the all the people concept of redemption work appears in the Scriptures in different ways and in different places.

Let’s go further.

First, this is the will of God. This is what God proclaims will happen:

1 Timothy 2:3-4: (KJV) 3 For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; 4 Who will have <2309> all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.

Will have: Strong’s Exhaustive Condordance #2309 thelō Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to will, have in mind, intend 1a) to be resolved or determined, to purpose 1b) to desire, to wish 1c) to love

Since God will have all to be saved, is He capable of achieving His vision? Of course He is!

Colossians 1:19-20: 19 For it was the Father’s good pleasure for all the fullness to dwell in him, 20 and through him to reconcile all things to Himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross; through him, I say, whether things on earth or things in heaven.

The words good pleasure are the same as those found in Matthew 3:17 at Jesus' baptism. This is My beloved son in whom I am well pleased. God was pleased from the beginning of Jesus' ministry until the end of his ministry at the cross.

The fact that Jesus’ sacrifice made peace tells us that God’s justice had been completely satisfied. When God’s justice requires something to be fulfilled, it requires something to be entirely fulfilled. Colossians tells us the blood of Jesus (his sacrifice) made peace—to reconcile all things to Himself. God’s justice is completely, utterly, totally and unequivocally satisfied. What a powerful statement: Jesus’ ransom sacrifice was for ALL.

Repeating our first question, who is saved from death in Adam by Jesus, and how do we know?

The scriptures we have reviewed thus far show us EVERYONE is included under the value of Jesus’ sacrifice! This is said in so many different ways:

All the nations of the earth shall be blessed.

A savior for all people.

It is God’s will that all will be saved.

All will be reconciled to God through Jesus’ blood.

When are the redeemed delivered from death in Adam, and how do we know?

The redeemed are delivered at different times, so there are two parts to this answer:

1. Faithful followers of Jesus, his true disciples, are delivered now, in this lifetime.

2. Everyone else is delivered later, in God’s future kingdom.

Understanding this requires us to pay attention to the details:

WHY “THE SAVING OF THOSE WHO ARE FOLLOWERS OF JESUS” COMES FIRST.

We already saw Jesus identified as Abraham’s seed who blesses all mankind. His disciples are also included in that blessing:

Galatians 3:29: And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's descendants, heirs according to promise.

This reminds us of Hebrews 12:23, which says, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. So, the church of the firstborn is judged in advance of the world. They are “born” first. They are older and are supposed to take care of the younger ones. If we belong to Christ and are Jesus’ followers, then we are also heirs according to the promise. We inherit the blessing of blessing others!

As Jesus’ disciples, we are privileged to work with him to bless all the families of the earth. (Genesis 12:3)

Because we are made right by Jesus’ sacrifice here and now, Jesus is by our side helping us:

1 John 2:1-2: 1 My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; 2 and he himself is the propitiation (meaning, satisfaction) for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world.

An advocate is someone who sits with you on your side and pleads your case before a judge.

Note the two parts:

1. Jesus is the advocate working at the side of his true followers, the church of the firstborn since his first advent.

2. But he is also the propitiation—the satisfaction—for the sins of the whole world. For EVERYBODY. That comes later. The price has been paid, but the fulfillment of saving everyone comes later.

THE SAVING OF ALL MEN LATER.

Back to 1 Timothy, repeating verse 4 and adding verses 5-6:

1 Timothy 2:4-6: (KJV) 4 Who will have <2309> (in other words, God is determined) all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge <1922> of the truth. 5 For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; 6 who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.

Knowledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1922 epignōsis; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment

Two observations:

All men will be able to understand and have complete knowledge or full discernment. Full discernment means truly understanding—not just hearing and nodding and going along, but mind comprehension. All men will be able to understand the truth.

The mediation of Moses for the Jewish people foreshadowed Jesus as mankind’s Savior, giving ALL a true opportunity.

For “everyone else” (all of mankind other than Jesus’ true followers), Jesus will guide and mediate between them and God, to lead them to a full understanding of God’s plan and their part in it. Over time with education in His principles, people will once again be able to achieve a full relationship with God as Adam once had.

For the firstborn (Jesus’ true followers now), he works with them as an advocate. Along with God’s holy spirit within them, he helps the true church (Jesus’ faithful followers) discern God’s will for them in this lifetime. They are preparing to help bring the world back to God.

Each group is coming from a different place, but all will receive the benefit of Christ’s sacrifice eventually—either now if they are followers of Jesus and are studying and learning in this day and age, or in the future under the guidance of Jesus and the church.

The world, in all its mess and all its madness, is waiting for the faithfulness of the followers of Jesus to be completed in heaven. They just don’t know it yet!

Romans 8:19-21: 19 For the anxious longing of the creation waits eagerly for the revealing of the sons of God.

We certainly live in an anxious time, with people longing for answers and solutions to the fear, death, disease and war faced by fragile societies.

20 For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it, in hope 21 that the creation itself also will be set free from its slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

Into the freedom of the glory of the children of God—referring to the called-out ones who have been following Jesus since his first advent (the church). Once those followers are trained and perfected, they will be “revealed,” and then the creation itself will also be set free from its slavery to corruption. This is telling us every single human being (the creation) is going to have the same freedom that has been given to those Jesus advocates for right now. The turn for “everybody else” is coming later. And it will provide them with the freedom from sin and corruption that they have never known before.

Romans 5 tells the whole story, beginning with the necessity for justice first, so grace could be applied:

Romans 5:12-14: 12 Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, because all sinned— (sin and death are an INEVITABLE inheritance from Adam) 13 for until the Law sin was in the world, but sin is not imputed when there is no Law. 14 Nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the offense of Adam, who is a type of him who was to come.

Before the Law and after the Law, sin still reigned. No matter when a person lived, as human beings, we were under the reign of sin because we inherited it from Adam.

Death was inevitable from the very beginning, even before the Law was given. This is what Paul was describing. The Law was God’s tool to show man how deeply humanity had fallen into the depths of sin. All were doomed!

That is why God gave the Law to Israel. It taught the Jews they could not live up to it, but it identified the requirements of God and how far we are from being able to obey them. There is such a void between us! We need to be continually looking upward. The Law required so many sacrifices as a picture of what was required to right the scales of justice.

So far, Paul has established that sin and death are inevitable to all and are clearly identified by the Law (Romans 5:12-14).

Now the solution will be presented that fulfills the need for justice:

Romans 5:15-16: 15 But the free gift is not like the transgression. For if by the transgression of the one the many died, (“the many” refers to all humanity according to the previous context) much more did the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many.

This is the same “the many”—all humanity.

16 The gift is not like that which came through the one who sinned; for on the one hand the judgment arose from one transgression resulting in condemnation, but on the other hand the free gift arose from many transgressions resulting in justification.

From these verses we see there was one transgression (Adam’s), and so all his progeny sin (the many) and are stuck in death (condemnation).

BUT, there comes this free gift (from Jesus) which covers many transgressions which results in justification of the many.

This doesn’t sound fair—how can Jesus pay for all (the “many’s”) transgressions?

It is fair because every human being inherited sin from the one transgression—the one sin of Adam. One sin produced death and transgressions in all, and Jesus canceled all of it out.

We have the free gift of Jesus as the ransom pictured on one end, balancing the transgression of Adam, pictured on the other end.

When Adam sinned, the scales were way out of whack. Jesus came and gave up his human life, this evened them out exactly as they needed to be in order to satisfy God’s justice.

Therefore, what happened to all through Adam is counteracted by the redeeming balance of Jesus as the ransom. This was God's plan from the very beginning!

A perfect man, Adam, for a perfect man, Jesus. Justice was satisfied. If Jesus hadn’t been a perfect man who didn’t sin in his earthly life, there would have been no justice. God’s justice is precise, complete and overreaching. It covers everything.

Earlier we looked at Colossians 1:20: And through him to reconcile all things to Himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross… This is what the apostle is talking about.

Paul next brings out the differences in salvation’s application:

Romans 5:17: For if by the transgression of the one, death reigned through the one, (again, who did death reign over? Everyone! The many!) much more those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ.

Paul again shows the called-out ones reigning with Jesus and being given authority alongside him.

This group of called-out ones will be the blessers of the world! It’s hard to wrap our minds around this—if we are faithful in our Christian walk, we can be a blesser alongside Jesus. It is an incredible gift. Think of all the gifts we are being given here!

Jesus came and fulfilled that Law and gave himself as a fair price for Adam—a life for a life, balancing the scales:

Romans 5:18-19: 18 So then as through one transgression there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness there resulted justification of life to all men. 19 For as through the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.

EVERYONE BENEFITS FROM JESUS’ SACRIFICE! So, what part of the word ALL do we not understand?

It is so simple and straightforward. Let’s allow God’s grace be God’s grace. It is perfect justice. God’s got this. He’s got everyone covered because of His son’s dedication and loyalty. What a perfect plan! We are in awe of His plan. Amen.

The 22nd Psalm details the suffering of Jesus on the cross, starting with My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? It goes through all the horrific details of the cross. Reading these verses, we are struck by the horror of what Jesus suffered for our sake.

But we can’t forget to read the end of the Psalm that represents the victory that follows the cross:

Psalms 22:27-28: 27 All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations will worship before You. 28 For the kingdom is the LORD'S and He rules over the nations.

All the ends of the earth will remember… and all the families of the nations will worship. The fact that this comes after the pain and suffering of the cross shows us what Jesus’ suffering and sacrifice accomplish. It shows us the glory of God’s plan because of the dedication and focus of Jesus’ sacrifice.

We can sum up the plan of redemption for all of humanity in three statements:

1. It is simple: Restore the harmony between God and mankind that was lost.

2. It is just: All those lost because of Adam’s sin will be given a full and fair opportunity to live.

3. It is eternal: As Adam was designed to live eternally under God’s care so will all of humanity be granted that same privilege.

Thank you, Jesus!

We see how the scriptures come together to show us this incredible plan God determined would happen, how Jesus came and made it happen, and how it covers every single human being without exception.

Those who are resurrected will have to learn and prove they can walk righteously, but that is a subject for another episode.

Here we see the beauty of the ransom. What a wonderful story and opportunity for all of humanity!

So, did Jesus die for every single human being?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Jesus will preside over the raising of all mankind from death in Adam:

Israel and Jerusalem will be the source of earthly blessing:

All of this is for the opportunity of every human who has ever lived to benefit from Jesus sacrifice:

Isaiah 42:1-4: 1 Behold, My servant, whom I uphold; My chosen one in whom My soul delights. I have put My spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations. 2 He will not cry out or raise his voice, nor make his voice heard in the street. 3 A bruised reed he will not break and a dimly burning wick he will not extinguish; he will faithfully bring forth justice. 4 He will not be disheartened or crushed until he has established justice in the earth; And the coastlands will wait expectantly for his law.

Isaiah 62:1-2: 1 For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not keep quiet, until her righteousness goes forth like brightness, and her salvation like a torch that is burning. 2 The nations will see your righteousness, and all kings your glory; and you will be called by a new name which the mouth of the LORD will designate.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1414-salvation-for-all/

1. Describe how the lives of Adam of Eve were changed by the death sentence given to them as a result of

Adam’s sin. Who else is under the death penalty caused by Adam’s sin? Why? (Genesis 2:15-17, 3:17-19)

2. What does the prophecy of the “seed of the woman” crushing the serpent’s head foreshadow? Why is this

a glimmer of hope to Adam and Eve (and to us all)? (Genesis 3:15)

3. How do Paul’s writings connect the inevitability of death in Adam with the hope of resurrection in

Christ? What does this imply about the scope of salvation? (Romans 6:23, 1 Corinthians 15:20-22)

4. How does the Abrahamic promise of blessing “all nations” through Abraham’s seed find its fulfillment in

Christ? What does this teach us about God’s plan for all humanity? (Genesis 22:17-18, Galatians 3:16)

5. Discuss how the angel’s proclamation of “good news… for all people” in Luke 2:10-11, and Paul’s

declaration that “God will have all men to be saved” in 1 Timothy 2:3-6, reinforce the concept of the universality of Jesus’ role as Savior.

‘

6. In what way did Jesus’ sacrifice “make peace” and allow him “to reconcile all things” to the Father? How

does this balance the scales of justice which were out of balance due to Adam’s sin? (Colossians 1:19-20,

Romans 5:12-19)

7. Explain the two parts of the promise in 1 John 2:1-2. (1 Timothy 2:4, Romans 8:19-21, Psalms 22:27-28)

8. What role do the “sons of God” play in the process of blessing mankind in bringing them back to God?

(Romans 5:17-19, 8:19-21)

9. How do the resurrection of judgment and the ministry of reconciliation together illustrate the fairness of

God’s plan, ensuring all people receive a full opportunity to respond to Christ? (John 5:28-29,

Acts 17:30-31, 2 Corinthians 5:17-19)

10. As Jesus truly is the Savior for “all people,” how will this shape the way you interact with those of different

faiths, backgrounds or even those who reject Christianity?

11. How does knowing you will, as a faithful follower of Jesus, be working with these people to bless them in

God’s future kingdom, change how you think of them today?

## Episode 1415 — Does Our Preaching Really Save Those Who Hear?
Published: 2025-12-15
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1415-preach-the-gospel/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/12200100/CQ_Rewind_12-15-2025_Does_Our_Preaching_Really_Save_Those_Who_Hear.pdf

Matthew 28:19: Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit.

So, what is the real mission of Christianity? Are we tasked with converting the world? Are we responsible to preach the good news of the gospel wherever we go, to anyone and everyone? Is the eternal destiny of those we come in contact with heavily dependent upon our delivering the message of salvation? All Christians would agree that at his ascension, Jesus commanded us to be part of preaching the gospel throughout the world. Where we differ is in the outcome of this preaching. The bottom-line question: do we as Christians bear the responsibility of saving sinners from the wrath of God right here and right now in this age, or do we preach for another reason?

Why don't we answer the question right up front and then get into the scriptural proofs? Does our preaching really save those who hear? Yes and no!

Here is more of the context of what Jesus said at his ascension in our theme verse:

Acts 1:6–8: 6 So when they had come together, they were asking him, saying, Lord, is it at this time you are restoring the kingdom to Israel? 7 He said to them, It is not for you to know times or epochs which the Father has fixed by his own authority; 8 but you will receive power when the holy spirit has come upon you; and you shall be my witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the remotest part of the earth.

It is not for you to know—while his disciples were not to know the big events of the future, they were to systematically expand the reach of the gospel, beginning in Jerusalem. The disciples were already in Jerusalem to celebrate Pentecost.

…and in all Judea and Samaria—over time, the gospel would be spread even to the remotest part of the earth.

So, they were to expand the gospel, but for what reason?

Matthew 28:18–20: 18 …All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. 19 Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit, 20 teaching them to observe all that I commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.

There is a great comfort at the end of the verse, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. “Even when I am not here where you can see me, I am still with you.”

Notice how Jesus said this: make disciples of all nations, not “make all nations my disciples.” After you make disciples from all nations, (back to Acts 1:6) then the nation of Israel will be restored. This was a long-term project.

While specifically commanded to spread the gospel throughout the whole world, we are not specifically commanded that our objective is to convert everyone.

How can we be sure that worldwide conversion is not our responsibility here and now? The Bible teaches us in many scriptures and in many ways what our preaching is for.

One example: Jesus, in the Parable of the Sower, reveals a profoundly important truth regarding the gospel and those who are exposed to it.

This parable is unusual in that Jesus interprets it after he speaks it:

Luke 8:4–5: 4 When a large crowd was coming together, and those from the various cities were journeying to him, he spoke by way of a parable: 5 The sower went out to sow his seed…

In the parable, Jesus says a farmer goes out to sow seeds. Some fall along the path, some onto stony places, some onto thorny places, and some into good ground.

Luke 8:11: Now the parable is this: the seed is the word of God.

The seed, representing the word of God, falls on different kinds of soils. Only one ends up producing fruitage. Jesus does not define the sower in detail, but the implication is he himself is sowing the word of God during his ministry. Through additional teachings (Matthew 28:19-20, Mark 4:26-29), we get the sense that his followers are also sowers.

The Apostle Paul confirms this interpretation many years later:

1 Corinthians 3:6–9: 6 I planted, Apollos watered, but God was causing the growth. 7 So then neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who causes the growth. 8 Now he who plants and he who waters are one; but each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. 9 For we are God's fellow workers; you are God’s field…

Paul planted, Apollos watered (the seed Paul planted), and we are all God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field.

In the Parable of the Sower, the good ground was the field that grew the seed into fruit.

The Apostle Paul uses similar horticulture analogies to say the followers of Christ plant and water, sowing the gospel message. They are all part of the same field.

Focusing on one specific aspect of this parable helps us see what happens as a result of our sowing the seeds of the gospel. Remember, most of the ground the seed fell onto did not properly nurture the seed, and it did not grow well.

Jesus explained the meaning of the seed falling on or beside the path:

Matthew 13:19: When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand <4920> it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is the one on whom seed was sown beside the road.

Understand: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4920, suniemi; to put together, i.e. (mentally) to comprehend; by implication, to act piously

This is all about hearing God's word but not understanding the kingdom. Many Christians don't talk about the kingdom. This reminds me of when I was in line at my local doughnut shop for some doughnuts. While I was in line, I was fellowshipping with a Christian woman, and our discussion came around to how terrible things are in the world. I said, “We really need the kingdom!” She asked, “What kingdom?” I told her, “The kingdom Jesus told us to pray for—Thy kingdom come on earth, as it is in heaven.” She looked at me strangely, and our conversation ended.

God’s kingdom was the heart of Jesus’ message, appearing over 60 times in Matthew, Mark and Luke. Many of his parables start with the kingdom of heaven is like (the mustard seed, the leaven, the hidden treasure, the pearl of great price, the dragnet—Matthew 13). He spoke of the kingdom in his Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3) and in many other teachings.

The verse we just read in Matthew 13:19 tells us, when anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, then Satan comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart.

If it were true that it is our responsibility to convert the world now with our preaching, why would a simple lack of understanding of the word of God give Satan the ability to take away what we taught them? Is that fair?

How can someone reject what they haven’t even understood? It’s like telling a seven-year- old he can’t have his dinner because he didn’t understand the calculus we taught him. Well, we taught him calculus —he just didn’t get it. Too bad!

People can’t truly reject a doctrine unless they have a full understanding of it. In Matthew 13:19, Jesus does not mention rejection of the kingdom message as a reason for not accepting it. If individuals really understood this message and dismissed it through free and informed choice, then why blame Satan as Jesus does in this verse?

The answer lies in what Jesus explained after he spoke the parable to the people, and before he explained it to his disciples:

Matthew 13:10–12: 10 And the disciples came and said to him, Why do you speak to them in parables? 11 Jesus answered… To you it has been granted to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been granted. 12 For whoever has, to him more shall be given, and he will have an abundance; but whoever does not have, even what he has shall be taken away from him.

This certainly wouldn’t be fair if everyone has to be converted in this lifetime!

To his disciples, his specially chosen followers, it has been granted to know the mysteries… but to them (most of those listening) it has not… ? Why wouldn’t Jesus explain his teachings to the crowd at large? Why only to his close disciples?

While we ARE to preach to the world, we also need to realize the fact that this is Satan’s world, and his influence is very powerful in most lives. He CAN undo the power of the gospel, but only temporarily!

Even though Satan can only temporarily snatch away the message of the gospel from many, Jesus makes it clear Satan is doing this extensively during this age of gospel expansion.

Let’s look at the practicality of why we are to preach to the world even though Satan is taking away much of the “seed” we are sowing.

Jesus is God’s gift of salvation for the world:

John 3:16–17: 16 For God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish, but have eternal life. 17 For God did not send the son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him.

John 6:44: (KJV) No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.

It doesn’t sound like God is saving the world if only a few are drawn to Him! Is this a contradiction?

Matthew 7:13–14: 13 Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. 14 For the gate is small and the way is narrow that leads to life, and there are few who find it.

Those few who find it refers back to those who in Matthew 28:19 were called to be disciples of all the nations. Only a few walk what Jesus calls the narrow way. Again, this seems contradictory to saving the whole world.

We used to have an atheist friend named Don call into our live program on the radio many years ago. He would call just to try to trip us up by quoting scripture to contradict what we were saying. We loved talking to him. But we would answer him and say, “There you go again, Don, reading other people’s mail. Why are you trying to interpret that which wasn’t even addressed to you? You’ve said you don’t want to believe any of this, so leave it to those it was addressed to!”

Why wouldn’t God draw ALL men to Him? Because there are two groups of people referenced: those to which the Bible is NOT addressed, and those of us to which it IS addressed—the followers of Jesus.

God does not draw all men to Himself now because His plan works in two stages—this eliminates any thought of there being a contradiction.

The first stage is the calling to follow Jesus; this is when these statements of Jesus referring to the narrow way apply. God calls only a few to know the mysteries. We will refer to these called-out ones as “disciples” for this episode.

These few disciples have a mission to be faithful NOW for the benefit of all others later:

1 Peter 2:9,12: 9 But you are A CHOSEN RACE, A royal PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION, A PEOPLE FOR God’s OWN POSSESSION, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light;

A priesthood exists to serve others. They are to proclaim God’s excellencies (His plans, deeds and mercies) to others—there is privilege, but there is also responsibility. This scripture is written to the few disciples now.

How are those disciples supposed to act compared to everyone else?

12 Keep your behavior excellent among the Gentiles, so that in the thing in which they slander you as evildoers, they may because of your good deeds, as they observe them, glorify God in the day of visitation.

Gentiles—the rest of the world; those who aren’t faithful followers of Jesus in this lifetime. They will slander us but will still see (take note of) our good deeds. And they will also glorify God—when? In the day of visitation, (the day of judgment) which we will address in a few minutes.

The key here, though, is that these two groups (the disciples and the Gentiles—the rest of the world) will both glorify God! They look like they are at odds at the beginning, but by the end they are in harmony. How does that happen?

The world waits for the faithfulness of the followers of Jesus to be completed:

Romans 8:19–21: 19 For the anxious longing of the creation (the rest of the world) waits eagerly for the revealing of the sons of God (the disciples). 20 For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it, in hope...

What kinds of answers will we get if we go out on the street and take a survey of 100 people, asking, “Are you waiting for the revealing of the sons of God, Jesus’ disciples?” They won’t know what we are talking about!

But we know they are looking for answers to the myriad of unsolvable problems that exist in the world. They are looking for a way to find harmony and unity and to get rid of all the injustice and horror in this world. The sons of God will bring all of that, so they are waiting for them, but they just don’t know it; they only know they want the good results.

21 that the creation itself also will be set free from its slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

So, the rest of the world will be given freedom from the futility of trying to solve all the problems without God. Their future freedom will come as a result of the disciples.

Let’s look back at the true disciples of Jesus:

Romans 8:28: And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.

People often quote just the first part of this verse, All things work together for good to those who love God. But it is specifically to those who are called...

At this point in time, this verse only applies to those few called-out disciples who are walking in Jesus’ footsteps. It does not pertain to the average “fan” of Jesus, someone who maybe loves what Jesus stands for but is not changing their life to a life of sacrifice like his.

It is for those few who, like the apostles, are walking the way Jesus walked. They have a special privilege, and yet a heavy responsibility, to sacrifice their earthly ambitions during their lifetime.

We are not converting the world right here and now!

But we are assured that in the future, both groups—the disciples and everybody else—will glorify God!

God’s plan of redemption for every human being works through true Christians. They are called to be a faithful and royal priesthood for the benefit of the whole world. We preach to find those who are called according to His purpose.

We preach to find those who feel a calling by God, but along the way, like Jonathan’s experience in the doughnut shop, we are given an opportunity for the kingdom to be revealed. Most people won’t understand our words or think further on them, but we can still give them the hope of the peace of God’s future kingdom.

Is the world given a “free pass”? Do they just get away with all of their sinful behavior? No!

2 Peter 3:9: (KJV) The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance <3341>.

Repentance: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3341, metanoia; from #3340; (subjectively) compunction (for guilt, including reformation); by implication reversal (of [another’s] decision)

Notice it doesn't say “all come to eternal life.” It says, all should come to repentance so they can learn what is required for eternal life. That’s what the kingdom on earth is for.

God is not willing that any should perish, BUT that all should come to repentance. They will not get a “Get out of jail FREE” card, obtaining eternal life no matter what.

They will have to be educated as to what past behavior needs repentance. They will need to understand what they did wrong and how they harmed others. They will have to recognize the need to make amends for all their sins.

How does this true repentance happen? Through a complete education regarding God’s truth:

1 Timothy 2:4–6: (KJV) 4 Who will have <2309> all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge <1922> of the truth.

Will have: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2309 thelō Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to will, have in mind, intend 1a) to be resolved or determined

Knowledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1922 epignōsis; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment

That word for knowledge means full discernment, full understanding. Remember in the Parable of the Sower, some heard the gospel but didn't understand. Satan was able to “snatch” away what has been sown in his heart. He took the gospel of the kingdom they had heard away from them. 1 Timothy 2:4 shows a time when they actually will understand.

5 For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; 6 who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.

It wasn’t “fair” that Satan took away the good news of the gospel from some people. They were given the truth, but Satan’s influence was too strong and he perverted and “took away” what had been sown in their hearts before it had even sunk in.

But, what IS fair is that God will have all men to be saved to come unto the knowledge, the full discernment, of the truth in His kingdom! ALL men will be able to understand fully what they cannot now. It’s okay if they don’t understand now; they will later if they do the work needed to fully discern God’s plan and repent.

Jesus will mediate between God and mankind to give ALL a true opportunity for life.

We preach good news of great joy for ALL people (Luke 2:10)!

It's good news for the disciples, the true followers of Jesus. But it’s also good news for the rest of the world!

This opportunity will include ALL, providing an appropriate period of testing after they have fully learned what is expected of them.

When will all this happen?

2 Peter 2:9: (KJV) The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment <2920> to be punished <2849>

Judgment: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2920 krisis Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon #2920: 1) a separating, sundering, separation 1a) a trial, contest

2) selection 3) judgment

Punish: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2849 kolazo Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon #2849: 1) to lop or prune, as trees and wings

2) to curb, check, restrain

The day of judgment is the day of visitation from 1 Peter 2:12 we read earlier.

The Greek word here for punish isn't what we may think; it means to lop or prune; to curb, check or restrain.

Lopping, pruning, judgment, separation of the godly and unjust, trial—all of these are difficult. But if we use an analogy of surgery, we get a better understanding. When someone goes through a knee reconstruction, they wake up and the doctor comes in to tell them the good news. They are going to be fine—able to use the knee better than before. But wait! To get to the point of being “fine,” they will need to go through serious physical therapy. That therapy is painful and difficult. Is this person willing to go through the pain and difficulty so they can walk again freely and eventually be pain free? Of course!

Salvation will be enacted by walking the world through accountability, so people will be able to stand before God forever on their own individual merit of righteousness. It will be a difficult process of unlearning error, making amends and transforming their selfish hearts. But they will eventually reach the point of being “fine,” able to fully appreciate the good news of the gospel. It will take great effort!

We prepare the world for the message of hope by planting the seeds of the gospel message.

The time when Jesus mediates will have an entirely different basis for operation than the world does today:

Acts 3:20–21: 20 and that He may send Jesus, the Christ appointed for you, 21 whom heaven must receive until the period of restoration of all things about which God spoke by the mouth of His holy prophets from ancient time.

The period of restoration of all things is not going to operate like our societies today. Jesus’ mediation is a future time of universal restoration.

We preach to show how good God is, as He will have all to be saved and come back into harmony with Him. They will have the ability, with full knowledge, to choose everlasting life.

But see what happens before the period of restoration:

Zephaniah 3:8-9: 8 Therefore wait for Me, declares the LORD, For the day when I rise up as a witness. Indeed, My decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out on them My indignation, all My burning anger; for all the earth will be devoured by the fire of My zeal.

However, once the time of trouble and Armageddon are over, the landscape changes dramatically as the removal of the broken systems of imperfect human government open the door to true learning. Read the next verse!

9 For then I will give to the peoples purified lips, that all of them may call on the name of the LORD, to serve Him shoulder to shoulder.

We preach to prepare mankind for the time when they will all speak one language, praising God. Can you imagine?

But it gets even bigger!

Micah 4:3–4: 3 And He will judge between many peoples and render decisions for mighty, distant nations. Then they will hammer their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks; nation will not lift up sword against nation, and never again will they train for war. 4 Each of them will sit under his vine and under his fig tree, with no one to make them afraid, for the mouth of the LORD of hosts has spoken.

No more war! For the mouth of the LORD of hosts has spoken.

We preach to praise God for guaranteed permanent peace, safety, food and shelter for all. God is good!

Revelation 21:3–4: (KJV) 3 And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself shall be with them, and He their God. 4 And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

God Himself shall be with them and be their God—this sounds like the Garden of Eden. God was with Adam and Eve, but they lost that communion. Mankind’s relationship with God will return and all pain and suffering will be removed.

God is still calling out those who would answer His call to walk in Jesus’ footsteps. Our mission IS to preach, to spread the seeds of the gospel, find those who would answer God’s call and to spread hope to any and all who will accept it. Our preaching the gospel in its original form helps, encourages and brings praise and honor to our God and to our Lord Jesus!

Does our preaching really save those who hear? No. But it does give the hope in the gospel that Jesus saves everyone. Most will dismiss it, but the message will draw some (few) to follow in Jesus’ footsteps. Regardless, the gospel applies to all.

The preaching of the gospel is to fulfill the commandment to draw disciples from the nations. It is also to give hope to the rest of the world because their salvation is coming. Thy Kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is done in heaven.

This is why we preach.

So, does our preaching really save those who hear?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

More on the Parable of the Sower: Mark 4 begins with Jesus addressing a “great multitude” of people. One of the lessons he taught them was the Parable of the Sower (Mark 4:2-9). In the parable, a sower (a farmer) sows a parcel of seeds. Different things happen to the seeds. Some are eaten by birds (Mark 4:4). Some land on stony ground where, although they sprout, they don’t have enough earth to take root, and are burned away by the sun (Mark 4:5-6). Others fall into ground where thorns grow, and the thorns choke them and prevent them from growing (Mark 4:7). Some, though, fall on good ground and produce fruit. The amount of fruit is described as different from plant to plant, but all the plants growing from the good ground are considered to have delivered “an increase” (Mark 4:8).

The different soils reflect why individuals fail to retain or act on the divine message, which often correlates to three major paths of failure:

- Roadside (Lack of Knowledge): The seed does not penetrate because the heart is hardened or lacks knowledge, allowing Satan to snatch it away.
- Rocky Ground (Immaturity): The seed springs up with joy but has no firm root. When affliction or persecution arises, the immature heart quickly falls away, lacking the endurance needed to overcome trials.
- Thorns (Weakness/Distraction): The word is choked out by the worries of the world, deceitful riches and desires for worldly things. This inability to choose the spiritual over the convenient illustrates failure due to weakness.

After the crowds left, the apostles asked Jesus to explain the parable to them (Mark 4:10). Jesus explained that the seeds represented the word of God (Mark 4:14). The parable teaches that different people have different reactions to God’s word. Some hear God’s word and immediately respond positively to it; however, they take no further action to develop their understanding of it, or allow it to change their minds and hearts into something more pleasing to God. In the parable, these are the “seeds” that fell on the stony ground, and, without being able to take root, were soon “burned away” (Mark 4:16- 17). Others hear God’s word, but allow worldly pursuits and priorities to dominate their time, and eventually their hearts. These are like the plants that tried to grow among the thorns. Worldly pursuits often take a great deal of one’s time and energy, leaving a smaller amount of time and energy to pursuing God’s word. Christian growth is often stifled and choked under these conditions, just like the thorns stifled and choked the growing plants (Mark 4:18-19). There are other people, however, who not only hear God’s word, but “receive it” (Mark 4:20). These are “the seeds sown on good ground,” who devote their time and energy to God, and in so doing, grow into something pleasing to him; each according to their own individual ability (“some thirtyfold, some sixty, and some an hundred”—Mark 4:20).

Jesus continues to emphasize this expectation that receipt of God’s word is expected to cause one to work toward growing closer to God by pointing out that a candle, once lit, is expected to be placed in a place of prominence, where it can give light, not hidden away under a bushel or under a bed (Mark 4:21). God’s word, like the light of the candle or the seeds sown on the ground, is expected to take a place of prominence in one’s mind and heart, and not be buried under the priorities of the world, causing spiritual growth to be choked out like so many seedlings among a patch of thorns. To highlight the importance of this lesson, Jesus warns that a lack of appreciation for God’s word will not be something that one can hide from God (Mark 4:22). God has a work that needs appreciative and diligent workers to complete. One’s spiritual progression can only be accomplished through focus, sincerity, priority and love.

Those who hear God’s word but do not allow “the seed” to “take root,” or who allow it to whither or be overtaken may expect that sooner than later, the opportunity to serve Him

will be taken from the unappreciative heart (“take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete”—in other words, take care to respond with an appreciative heart and a mind and will that devotes time and energy to serve God—Mark 4:24 KJV). The opportunities to work and grow in God’s service will be taken from those who do not respond to God appropriately and given to those who joyfully do so (“unto you that hear shall more be given”).

Here are a few more scriptures that further paint the picture of the hope of our preaching.

This learning for the world begins with the resurrection:

Acts 24:14–15: 14 But this I admit to you, that according to the Way which they call a sect I do serve the God of our fathers, believing everything that is in accordance with the Law and that is written in the Prophets; 15 having a hope in God, which these men cherish themselves, that there shall certainly be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.

The righteous are those who followed Christ (the called-out ones) and the wicked are those who died in their sins (the everybody else). This is the point at which the world’s reconciliation begins.

Now the gospel begins to shine with the dramatic process of removing sin and infusing perfection!

Isaiah 35:5–10: 5 Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. 6 Then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will shout for joy. For waters will break forth in the wilderness and streams in the Arabah. 7 The scorched land will become a pool and the thirsty ground springs of water; in the haunt of jackals, its resting place, grass becomes reeds and rushes.

Along with the correction of all physical maladies comes the correction of sinful thoughts and actions, pictured in the progress made by moving towards a destination: 8 A highway will be there, a roadway, and it will be called the Highway of Holiness. The unclean will not travel on it, but it will be for him who walks that way, and fools will not wander on it. 9 No lion will be there, nor will any vicious beast go up on it; these will not be found there. But the redeemed will walk there, 10 and the ransomed of the LORD will return and come with joyful shouting to Zion, with everlasting joy upon their heads. They will find gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.

God clearly shows us through prophecy that the rules will go from inheriting generational sins to being fully accountable for past personal sins. This prophecy is focused on Israel’s restoration:

Jeremiah 31:29–34: 29 In those days they will not say again, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge. 30 But everyone will die for his own iniquity; each man who eats the sour grapes, his teeth will be set on edge.

This is the personal accountability Jesus will mediate between God and man: 31 Behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a New Covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, 32 not like the covenant which I made with their fathers….

The Law WAS temporary, and now with the ransom for Adam paid, a New Covenant will be in place. Remember, just as the Old Covenant needed mediation, so this New Covenant will need mediation.

33 But this is the covenant which I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD, I will put My law within them and on their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people. 34 They will not teach again, each man his neighbor and each man his brother, saying, Know the LORD, for they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them, declares the LORD, for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin I will remember no more.

Through Jesus, THIS covenant will produce heart-driven obedience to the sovereignty of God!

Israel and Jerusalem will be the source of earthly blessing:

Isaiah 2:3: And many peoples will come and say, Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob; that He may teach us concerning His ways and that we may walk in His paths. For the law will go forth from Zion and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.

All of this is for the opportunity of every human who has ever lived to benefit from Jesus’ sacrifice:

Isaiah 42:1–4: 1 Behold, My servant, whom I uphold; My chosen one in whom My soul delights. I have put My spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations. 2 He will not cry out or raise his voice, nor make his voice heard in the street. 3 A bruised reed he will not break and a dimly burning wick he will not extinguish; he will faithfully bring forth justice. 4 He will not be disheartened or crushed until he has established justice in the earth; and the coastlands will wait expectantly for his law.

## Episode 1416 — How Did God’s Spirit Inspire Those Surrounding Jesus’ Birth?
Published: 2025-12-22
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/inspiration/1416-jesus-birth/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/19183158/CQ_Rewind_12-22-2025_How_Did_Gods_Spirit_Inspire_Those_Surrounding_Jesus_Birth.pdf

Luke 1:31-33: 31 And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall name him Jesus. 32 He will be great and will be called the son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David; 33 and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and his kingdom will have no end.

We all love to tell the story of Jesus’ birth. We love the vulnerability behind God’s choice of Mary, the young woman who was engaged to Joseph to be Jesus’ mother. We love the humility of his being born in a stable because there was no room at the inn. We love the magnificence of the angel announcing his birth to shepherds and then having the heavenly host of angels praising and glorifying God. We love the reverential sobriety of the wise men coming with gifts for the small child Jesus. Some of the things we don’t focus as much attention on are how God used specific individuals surrounding all of these events to speak in a prophetic way and outline in great detail what this series of incredible experiences would mean. Today we pause and consider the words of Zacharias and Elizabeth, the parents of John the Baptist; Mary, the mother of Jesus; Simeon the prophet and Anna the prophetess.

At Christmas, we often focus on the nativity scene with baby Jesus and the shepherds, and that’s great. But as we will see, God gave us wonderful lessons with these other people who also played an important part.

As we begin with Zacharias, we need to remember how the Old Testament ended 400 years before these events:

Malachi 4:5-6: 5 Behold, I am going to send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the LORD. 6 He will restore the hearts of the fathers to their children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, so that I will not come and smite the land with a curse.

These last words of the Old Testament were the last words of hope and prophecy for 400 silent years. They foretold how the New Testament would start with the coming of one who would prepare the people for the Messiah by doing the work of Elijah, the Old Testament prophet.

Zacharias and Elizabeth were righteous in the sight of God and as a result were chosen to be John the Baptist’s parents. Zacharias served the people as a priest of God.

They were aging and childless and had lost hope of having children, until one day when Zacharias was serving in the Temple:

Luke 1:11-13: 11... an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the altar of incense. 12 Zacharias was troubled when he saw the angel, and fear gripped him. 13 But the angel said to him, Do not be afraid, Zacharias, for your petition has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will give him the name John.

Zacharias’ mind must have begun to race as the initial fear began to subside and be replaced by questions. How could this be? Why me? Why here? Why now? Why the angel?

The angel continued:

Luke 1:14-15: 14 You will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth. 15 For he will be great in the sight of the Lord; and he will drink no wine or liquor, and he will be filled with the holy spirit while yet in his mother’s womb.

His son was to be named John, who would be a great man filled with the holy spirit. What a revelation for Zacharias who was just going about his business serving in the Temple!

This angel poured out incredible details about John’s life, the son Zacharias never expected:

Luke 1:16-17: 16 And he will turn many of the sons of Israel back to the Lord their God. 17 It is he who will go as a forerunner before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers back to the children, and the disobedient to the attitude of the righteous, so as to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.

Zacharias undoubtedly recognized that the angel was quoting from the prophet Malachi, the last spoken words of a prophet in over 400 years! These words were a prophecy of the coming of Messiah and this angel had just announced Zacharias’ son would be the forerunner of the Messiah.

The impossibility of all this must have overwhelmed Zacharias:

Luke 1:18: Zacharias said to the angel, How will I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her years.

The angel Gabriel was quick to respond:

Luke 1:19: …I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news.

Gabriel identifies himself as an angel. Perhaps Zacharias realizes it sounds like he’s actually doubting the angel’s message.

Gabriel continued:

Luke 1:20: And behold, you shall be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their proper time.

God’s word will be fulfilled, regardless of human disbelief. Zacharias’ silence would be temporary but transformative, turning doubt into reflection—and as we shall see— reflection into praise.

Zacharias did doubt because he knew he and Elizabeth were too old to have children. Doubt in the face of God’s power and mercy does bring a consequence. But even our doubt does not cancel God’s power and mercy.

Was Zacharias being punished? It seems like it was more a chance for preparation. God knew Zacharias needed time because this pronouncement of what would happen was beyond anything he could conceive. He was struck mute that he might contemplate these things.

A now silent Zacharias finishes his cycle of priestly service and returns home:

Luke 1:23-25: 23 When the days of his priestly service were ended, he went back home. 24 After these days Elizabeth his wife became pregnant, and she kept herself in seclusion for five months, saying, 25 This is the way the Lord has dealt with me in the days when He looked with favor upon me, to take away my disgrace among men.

My disgrace among men—the social humiliation of being childless, considered in that society as a personal sorrow and social stigma of divine disfavor.

Even in the face of a long forgotten hope and under the circumstances of unlikely events, God’s blessing would take root and grow. God was gathering these faithful ones to unfold His glorious plan.

Elizabeth and Zacharias were the first two faithful ones God put in place in the New Testament to unfold His plan. They loved and served God and were given this incredible opportunity. We can assume they privately discussed what all of this meant. Even though Zacharias couldn’t speak, he could still write.

Jumping ahead to the birth of John the Baptist and his circumcision eight days later:

Luke 1:57-63: 57 Now the time had come for Elizabeth to give birth, and she gave birth to a son. 58 Her neighbors and her relatives heard that the Lord had displayed His great mercy toward her; and they were rejoicing with her. 59 And it happened that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were going to call him Zacharias, after his father. 60 But his mother answered and said, No indeed; but he shall be called John. 61 And they said to her, There is no one among your relatives who is called by that name. 62 And they made signs to his father, as to what he wanted him called. 63 And he asked for a tablet and wrote as follows, His name is John. And they were all astonished.

The rite of circumcision set Israel apart from surrounding nations. The holy spirit was dramatically expressed at this pivotal point.

We see Gabriel’s instructions were followed in the naming of the baby. Zacharias cannot speak, but Elizabeth knows the truth and announces his name will be John. When the neighbors object and remind her of the family naming custom, Zacharias writes clearly on a tablet, His name is John. The couple faithfully followed Gabriel’s instructions from God.

Circumcision of a male child was done on the eighth day of life. (Modern science shows that a newborn’s natural clotting ability, supported by vitamin K and prothrombin levels, peaks around that time, making it the safest day biologically for such a procedure.)

This was a reverential ceremony honoring God, representing the nation of Israel being set apart as God’s people from the rest of the world.

This part of Zacharias’ story is all about obedience and humility before angelic authority. Though he didn’t speak a word over those many months, Zacharias’ faithfulness was evident. He precisely carried out the angel’s instructions, even though they went against tradition.

What had been a secret between Elizabeth and Zacharias was now beginning to be revealed to all others. What a blessing beginning to unfold!

Now that Zacharias had effectively communicated the angel’s instruction, what would be his next task?

Think about the learning and maturing that Zacharias would have experienced over those many months. His last spoken words were questioning Gabriel, a mighty messenger of God, about how he will know for certain that they would have a son who would pave the way for the Messiah. Now this son was born and appropriately named.

The faithfulness of Zacharias while he was silent would be made plain by the power of his first words after the birth of his son:

Luke 1:64-66: 64 And at once his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he began to speak in praise of God.

Think about the suspense, how nine months of his silence actually amplified his voice when it finally returned! “He’s talking! What is he going to say? He last talked to an angel!” People would know these were not going to be ordinary words; instead, they would be the culmination of God’s promise.

The first words out of his mouth were overwhelming praise to God for these events.

As Zacharias was speaking and the people were listening: 65 Fear came on all those living around them; and all these matters were being talked about in all the hill country of Judea. 66 All who heard them kept them in mind, saying, What then will this child turn out to be? For the hand of the Lord was certainly with him.

The people had just witnessed miraculous events—Elizabeth conceiving in old age, Zacharias struck mute for nine months, and his speech suddenly restored when he obeyed Gabriel’s command. God was clearly involved, and they knew it.

Think of the chatter among the people around these events and the powerful reverence they would all experience as they were hearing of these God-directed developments regarding this child. It makes sense it would cause some fear—they were witnessing impossible, holy events!

The people wonder what’s happening, and Zacharias is going to explain what Gabriel prophesied to him:

Luke 1:67-71: 67 And his father Zacharias was filled with the holy spirit, and prophesied, saying:

We can see his faithfulness! This prophecy would be firmly grounded in Old Testament truth.

68 Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for He has visited us and accomplished redemption for His people, 69 and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David His servant— 70 As He spoke by the mouth of His holy prophets from of old—71 Salvation FROM OUR ENEMIES, and FROM THE HAND OF ALL WHO HATE US.

Zacharias talks about a horn of salvation in the house of David being God’s ultimate deliverance, fulfilling what the prophets had long ago declared. Horns are a symbol of power, and we know Jesus was from the royal line of David.

This praise is very similar to:

Psalms 18:1-2: (KJV) 1 I will love thee, O LORD, my strength. 2 The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.

We believe Zacharias referred to this Psalm to express his praise. We can see God’s spirit working in him, connecting the familiar Old Testament scriptures and prophecies with what will happen in his son’s life and the foreshadowing of Jesus, the Messiah.

Zacharias also quotes the deliverance from Egypt:

Psalms 106:9-10: (KJV) 9 He rebuked the Red Sea also, and it was dried up: so He led them through the depths, as through the wilderness. 10 And He saved them from the hand of him that hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.

By using the imagery of the horn of salvation, giving praise and honor to God and talking about the deliverance from Egypt, Zacharias is painting the big picture of Jesus coming as the Messiah. We don’t yet see how John fits into this picture, but he is broadly showing us the overview through Old Testament scriptures.

Zacharias doesn’t stop there:

Luke 1:72-75: 72 To show mercy toward our fathers, and to remember His holy covenant, 73 The oath which He swore to Abraham our father, 74 to grant us that we, being rescued from the hand of our enemies, might serve Him without fear, 75 in holiness and righteousness before Him all our days.

Zacharias moves from the Davidic Covenant of Israel’s king back to the Abrahamic Covenant which promised the seed of Abraham would bless all the families of the earth in

Genesis 22:18. The arrival of Jesus wasn’t a new plan! It was promised throughout the centuries.

Zacharias recognizes that the foundation of ALL promises of salvation and blessing come from the Abrahamic Covenant:

Psalms 105:8-10: (KJV) 8 He hath remembered His covenant for ever, the word which He commanded to a thousand generations. 9 Which covenant He made with Abraham, and His oath unto Isaac; 10 and confirmed the same unto Jacob for a law, and to Israel for an everlasting covenant.

This strongly suggests Zacharias spent those nine months meditating on Scripture. Remember, he was a priest, so his mind would naturally turn to the covenant promises and prophecies in the Torah, Psalms and the Prophets.

During his time of silence, aided by God’s spirit, Zacharias was able to weave together the prophecies he had long studied. Gabriel’s announcement compelled him to revisit those scriptures, for the angel himself had spoken in the very language of the Old Testament. With every reason to trust the message, Zacharias carefully traced how the promises he had known all his life now converged into this new, unfolding reality—until at last he was ready to proclaim it.

Luke 1:76: And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High…

What a prophecy from a father to his son, speaking to him when he is only eight days old! He is foretelling what John will become.

Jesus would describe John as a prophet many years later:

Matthew 11:9-10: 9 But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and one who is more than a prophet. 10 This is the one about whom it is written, BEHOLD, I SEND MY MESSENGER AHEAD OF YOU, WHO WILL PREPARE YOUR WAY BEFORE YOU.

Zacharias’ prophecy was fulfilled.

Luke 1:76-77: 76 …For you will go on BEFORE THE LORD TO PREPARE HIS WAYS; 77 To give to His people the knowledge of salvation by the forgiveness of their sins…

John would grow up to announce the one who will bring deliverance.

Zacharias is quoting from Malachi:

Malachi 3:1: (KJV) Behold, I will send my messenger (John the Baptist), and he shall prepare the way before me (Jesus): and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.

Through Zacharias, we in our day know these Old Testament verses apply to Jesus and John. It shows us how to study the Bible—we need both Old and New Testaments for the full picture.

It’s interesting that Gabriel announced himself as an angel—a messenger—of God. Here

Zacharias applies Malachi 3:1 to his son as a messenger to prepare the way for Jesus. This is another remarkable application of Old Testament prophecies

Zacharias continues with more of what Gabriel told him:

Luke 1:17: It is he who will go as a forerunner before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, TO TURN THE HEARTS OF THE FATHERS BACK TO THE CHILDREN, and the disobedient to the attitude of the righteous, so as to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.

Gabriel’s words and the Hebrew Scriptures already in Zacharias’ heart and mind just needed God’s spirit to put the pieces together. He was able to publicly declare his son’s future role in relation to the Messiah.

That is what God revealed through Zacharias at this moment:

Luke 1:78-79: 78 Because of the tender mercy of our God, with which the sunrise from on high will visit us, 79 TO SHINE UPON THOSE WHO SIT IN DARKNESS AND THE SHADOW OF DEATH, to guide our feet into the way of peace.

Zacharias again quotes from Malachi, now about Jesus:
