Malachi 4:2: (KJV) But unto you that fear My name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.

When Zacharias spoke (Luke 1:78), he said, with which the sunrise from on high will visit us. He is showing us these words of Malachi are real and would happen right there in Israel.

Next, he quotes from Isaiah about the light of Jesus:

Isaiah 9:2: The people who walk in darkness will see a great light; Those who live in a dark land, the light will shine on them.

Luke 1:80: And the child continued to grow and to become strong in spirit, and he lived in the deserts until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

Zacharias’ prophecy has ended, and we learn John continued to grow and to become strong in spirit.

We notice the similar description of Jesus as a boy:

Luke 2:51-52: 51 And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he continued in subjection to them; and his mother treasured all these things in her heart. 52 And Jesus kept increasing in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

John grew strong in spirit; Jesus kept increasing in wisdom and stature. God’s power and influence worked in both of their lives.

It is easy to see why Zacharias was chosen to be the father of John the Baptist. His zeal for God, his knowledge of the Scriptures, his life dedication as a priest and his prophesying through God’s spirit, all led up to John having a powerful example of dedication to follow.

Zacharias was the right man for this very important mission. When God’s spirit influences one of His faithful servants, it is easy to see how powerful the results can be!

Now that we have seen God’s power influence the father of John, what did it look like when His power influenced the mother of John and the mother of Jesus?

The fact that Elizabeth and Mary were cousins and that Elizabeth in her old age was six months pregnant with John when young Mary came to see her, begs for our attention. These two women would in turn mother the greatest messenger among men and the Messiah of Israel and the Savior of the world. Neither had any previous clue that they would be in such a position!

It will become obvious God handpicked these mothers with such wonderful characters so John and Jesus could grow into the men they became. Elizabeth and Mary were both given great blessing and great responsibility.

Let’s review the message Gabriel delivered to Mary and observe her strong and grounded faith:

Luke 1:26-29: 26 Now in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city ...called Nazareth, 27 to a virgin engaged to a man whose name was Joseph… and the virgin’s name was Mary. 28 And coming in, he said to her, Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you. 29 But she was very perplexed at this statement, and kept pondering what kind of salutation this was.

Wouldn’t we all be perplexed?

The angel Gabriel’s greeting to Mary was one of great favor yet her reaction was confused and fearful. Gabriel continued:

Luke 1:30-33: 30 ...Do not be afraid, Mary; for you have found favor with God. 31 And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall name him Jesus.

This was similar to what Zacharias was told.

32 He will be great and will be called the son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David; 33 and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and his kingdom will have no end.

Gabriel revealed all the hopes the Israelites had been waiting for. Mary was chosen by God to give birth to the Messiah!

Her response was calm and logical:

Luke 1:34: Mary said to the angel, How can this be, since I am a virgin?

Gabriel answered:

Luke 1:35-49: 35 …The holy spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and for that reason the holy child shall be called the son of God. 36 And behold, even your relative Elizabeth has also conceived a son in her old age; and she who was called barren is now in her sixth month. 37 For nothing will be impossible with God.

Mary asked and the angel answered. She would now need to heavily rely on her faith, but there is no indication she doubted.

Gabriel’s last words must have rung true in the deepest recesses of her young heart—for nothing will be impossible with God.

She answered: 38 And Mary said, Behold, the bondslave of the Lord; may it be done to me according to your word. And the angel departed from her.

Mary’s great faith opened the door for God’s world-changing miracle to take place.

We aren’t told how old Mary was at this time, but it’s generally assumed she was a teenager. It was Jewish practice at the time to be engaged soon after puberty, so perhaps she was anywhere from 12- to 16-years old.

https://www.britannica.com/topic/How-Old-Was-Mary-When-She-Had-Jesus

To have this kind of faith at her young age is remarkable.

Gabriel tells her that her older relative, Elizabeth, is six months pregnant. This would have verified God’s hand in both their circumstances.

Mary’s faith drove her to immediately seek out Elizabeth: 39 Now at this time Mary arose and went in a hurry to the hill country, to a city of Judah, 40 and entered the house of Zacharias and greeted Elizabeth. 41 When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb; and Elizabeth was filled with the holy spirit. 42 And she cried out with a loud voice and said, Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!

Elizabeth was blessed with God’s spirit and understanding! She knew her baby, who would be named John, would clear the path for Mary’s baby, Jesus, who would save the world!

Elizabeth was filled with the holy spirit—again we have God’s power and influence helping someone, this time Elizabeth, to respond in a way where the events can be told before they actually happen. This allows us to appreciate God’s foresight.

As we go further, Elizabeth’s humility would be obvious: 43 And how has it happened to me, that the mother of my Lord would come to me? 44 For behold, when the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby leaped in my womb for joy. 45 And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what had been spoken to her by the Lord.

These were definitely the right women for the task. Can we imagine if Elizabeth were bitter that she was so close to carrying the actual Messiah but her relative got the privileged blessing instead? That never crossed her mind. She was thrilled for Mary. She recognized Mary’s faith and the power of God in this experience.

Mary’s response was one of faith, humility and praise. She recognized her own honored position: 46 And Mary said: My soul exalts the Lord, 47 and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior. 48 For He has had regard for the humble state of His bondslave; for behold, from this time on all generations will count me blessed. 49 For the Mighty One has done great things for me; And holy is His name.

While this doesn’t explicitly say Mary was filled with the holy spirit, we can definitely see God’s power and influence driving her in her remarkable response.

She recognizes this is a very specific, surprise blessing.

Mary’s praise reminds us of Hannah’s praise in the Old Testament. Hannah asked the Lord for a child, promising she would dedicate him to God’s service. She gave birth to Samuel, who would be a prophet.

Here is Hannah’s praise—listen to the similarity with Mary’s:

1 Samuel 2:1-2: (KJV) 1 And Hannah prayed, and said, My heart rejoiceth in the LORD, mine horn is exalted in the LORD: my mouth is enlarged over mine enemies; because I rejoice in Thy salvation. 2 There is none holy as the LORD: for there is none beside Thee: neither is there any rock like our God.

There’s that horn imagery again, representing strength and deliverance from Hannah’s public shame of barrenness. This was another woman of outstanding character.

We see how many Old Testaments events unfold as New Testament truths in God’s plan.

Here is what happens:

Mary recognized the power of God’s mercy upon all men, especially Israel:

Luke 1:50: And His mercy is upon generation after generation toward those who fear Him.

No surprise, Mary is quoting the Old Testament:

Psalms 103:17-18: 17 But the lovingkindness of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear Him, and His righteousness to children's children, 18 To those who keep His covenant and remember His precepts to do them.

Old Testament prophecies are fulfilled as the New Testament events unfold.

Mary recognized the power of God’s strength over all men:

Luke 1:51: He has done mighty deeds with His arm; He has scattered those who were proud in the thoughts of their heart.

She is singing praises to God and talking about His strength in their lives.

Again, no surprise, back to the Old Testament:

Psalms 98:1-2: 1 O sing to the LORD a new song, for He has done wonderful things, His right hand and His holy arm have gained the victory for Him. 2 The LORD has made known His salvation; He has revealed His righteousness in the sight of the nations.

Mary recognized the power of God’s capacity to restore balance in the earth:

Luke 1:52-53: 52 He has brought down rulers from their thrones, and has exalted those who were humble. 53 He has filled the hungry with good things; and sent away the rich empty- handed.

This sounds like Psalm 107:

Psalm 107:9: For He has satisfied the thirsty soul, and the hungry soul He has filled with what is good.

(This theme of restoring balance repeats in Psalms 113:7-8, 147:6, Proverbs 3:34, and

Ezekiel 21:26.)

Mary recognized the power of God’s loyalty to those who serve Him:

Luke 1:54-55: 54 He has given help to Israel His servant, in remembrance of His mercy, 55 as He spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.

Many scriptures show God’s loyalty to His people. Mary is reminding us of that loyalty.

These two blessed women encouraged each other for about three months until right about the time John was born:

Luke 1:56: And Mary stayed with her about three months, and then returned to her home.

Three months of support and praise. Zacharias must have been smiling the whole time! He couldn’t talk, but we imagine him listening to the women prepare for these monumental births, seeing the power of God unfolding before his eyes in such a grand way.

Again, it was Gabriel’s words and insights that guided all three of these individuals as they navigated these incredible miracles in their lives.

For Elizabeth and Mary, the power of God’s influence in their lives was first manifested by physical events. However, the power of these physical things was fully supplemented by the power of understanding that God graciously opened up for them. They could both now see beyond the miracles and appreciate what the results of those miracles would bring.

Experiencing a miracle is incredible, but even more vital is seeing the bigger picture of what that miracle points to, and focusing on that as the larger story. Even in the midst of a life-changing experience, their focus on the future showed their faith, humility and perspective.

These two women are powerful examples for every one of us in their display of humbly receiving God’s gifts while being able to see the big picture as well!

All of these spirit-driven proclamations were made by these individuals before Jesus’ birth. What about after his birth?

God did not stop allowing broad explanations of Jesus’ mission to be revealed. Very much along the lines of Zacharias being able to speak when his son John was circumcised on the eighth day, so we see more spirit-driven prophecy come out on the eighth day when Jesus was circumcised, this time by Simeon.

The striking example of Simeon the prophet shows us the peace a God-centered life brings. Here is the context:

Luke 2:21,22-24: 21 And when eight days had passed, before his circumcision, his name was then called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. 22 And when the days for their purification... were completed, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord… 24 and to offer a sacrifice according to what was said in the Law of the Lord...

Mary, Joseph and Jesus were given no special entitlement or dispensation; they were simply given opportunity to obediently show their faith like everyone else. On the eighth day after Jesus is born, they offered the required Jewish sacrifices to fulfill the Law.

This humble acquiescence to God’s will and God’s way is evident by their doing what was expected.

Let’s see the role Simeon plays:

Luke 2:25-26: 25 And there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, looking for the consolation of Israel; and the holy spirit was upon him. 26 And it had been revealed to him by the holy spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

It is interesting to see how often God’s holy spirit directly influences the events around Jesus’ birth. His power and influence worked through these devout people to reveal the mind of God. God was setting everything in order while these two children were mere infants. Remember, Jesus did not start preaching for 30 years after this, but his role in saving the world is revealed long before.

What a revealing! Even at his advanced age, Simeon never forgot hope or allowed doubt or fear to rule his heart. He lived in anticipation and expectation of God’s gift, having been promised he would see the Messiah before he died.

Luke 2:27-29: 27 And he came in the spirit into the temple; and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to carry out for him the custom of the Law, 28 then he took him into his arms, and blessed God, and said, 29 Now Lord, You are releasing Your bond-servant to depart in peace, according to Your word.

Simeon was granted just a glimpse of God’s gift of redemption. He sees the baby, takes him in his arms and knows that his own life is now fulfilled. “In my arms I hold the hope of the world. I can die fulfilled because of what You have given me and all of us.”

We can feel Simeon’s emotion as he held the baby Jesus:

Luke 2:30-31: 30 For my eyes have seen Your salvation, 31 which You have prepared in the presence of all peoples.

He alluded to the Old Testament:

Isaiah 52:10: The LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations, that all the ends of the earth may see the salvation of our God.

Simeon is the first one able to proclaim, I have seen Your salvation, which would be revealed to everybody else later.

Luke 2:32: A light of revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of Your people Israel.

It’s telling that he saw this Messiah had purpose beyond saving Simeon’s own Israel. Jesus would be a light of revelation to the Gentiles, meaning to ALL people, even beyond Israel. How could Simeon have anticipated this without the holy spirit?

This helps us to see God’s intricate pre-planning of each part of His plan.

Simeon quoted from Isaiah 9 at Jesus’ circumcision, just as Zacharias did at John’s:

Isaiah 9:2-3: 2 The people who walk in darkness will see a great light; those who live in a dark land, the light will shine on them. 3 You shall multiply the nation, you shall increase their gladness; they will be glad in your presence as with the gladness of harvest, as men rejoice when they divide the spoil.

Simeon prophesied the full import of redemption—I have seen your salvation with my own eyes! Jesus is a light that reaches the Gentiles, not just the favored people of Israel. He is the light, AND he is the glory of Israel as well. This is an important truth revealed!

Remember, every prophetic statement refers back to what God’s holy prophets have already said. The New Testament is a fulfillment of the Old Testament. We must put the two together to better gain understanding of each.

What happened next:

Luke 2:33: And his father and mother were amazed at the things which were being said about him.

Jesus, just a newborn baby, was publicly revealed as the hope of the world.

Who all was observing and hearing these profound truths? We imagine this was a relatively public event at the Temple. People would have been going about their business and perhaps these prophecies were heard by others.

Simeon speaks some more, but it takes a different turn. Up until this point things have been magnificent and beautiful:

Luke 2:34-38: 34 And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rise of many in Israel, and for a sign to be opposed—35 and a sword will pierce even your own soul—to the end that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.

Simeon also knew that fulfilling the plan of God would bring great sacrifice to Jesus as he stood for righteousness while revealing the hearts of men. Mary would have to suffer the

loss of her son so many years later. Sadly, Simeon revealed there would be future conflict and heartbreak for Mary.

Anna the prophetess appears on the scene: 36 And there was a prophetess, Anna the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years and had lived with her husband seven years after her marriage, 37 and then as a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple, serving night and day with fastings and prayers. 38 At that very moment she came up and began giving thanks to God, and continued to speak of Him to all those who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem.

Anna is another example of God blessing a faithful woman. As an old lady, she got to be one of the first to publicly testify to the identity of the Messiah. Her specific words are not recorded, but Anna was also a blessed vessel of revealed truth as she continued what Simeon had started.

It’s interesting we see three women of different ages, from the teenaged Mary, middle- aged Elizabeth and the senior Anna. God is revealing that no matter the age of a woman, she is reflected in the glory of God when He brings His plan to pass. Each of these women had incredible faith, humility and a sense of doing God’s will.

Anna is speaking about those looking for the redemption of Jerusalem. She is encouraging them—it’s coming!

The accounts surrounding the birth of Jesus contain so much more than the record of his birth. They contain several details of the comprehensiveness of God’s incredible plan that brings all of humanity back into harmony with God.

Zacharias, Elizabeth, Mary, Simeon and Anna were individuals blessed to be tools of God at the beginning of John and Jesus’ lives, lives that would change the world.

These five individuals were not only given the privilege to participate in the lives of John and Jesus; they were given the privilege to speak the words of God through His spirit to show what God was doing. What a powerful privilege!

Going back to Isaiah 9, the chapter that both Zacharias and Simeon referred to:

Isaiah 9:6-7: (NIV2011) 6 For to us a child is born, to us a son is given, and the government will be on his shoulders. And he will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. 7 Of the greatness of his government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on David’s throne and over his kingdom, establishing and upholding it with justice and righteousness from that time on and forever. The zeal of the LORD Almighty will accomplish this.

We can see the Lord’s zeal accomplishing this by telling us beforehand through His spirit, working in faithful individuals, what was going to happen. What a God we have! What a plan it is!

So, how did God’s spirit inspire those surrounding Jesus’ birth?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Bonus Material and Study Questions Recommended additional study:

Ep.1312: How Do We Know Jesus Is the Promised Messiah? (Part I) Jewish skepticism and key Old Testament identifiers of the Messiah https://christianquestions.com/program/1312-messiah/

Ep.1209: How Do We Keep Christmas About Jesus?

Remembering the inspiring events surrounding the birth of Jesus https://christianquestions.com/program/1209-christmas/

For children, parents and Bible class teachers, continue your studies on this topic with these short, animated videos for kids at ChristianQuestions.com/YouTube:

- What is the story of Jesus’ birth? https://christianquestions.com/cq-videos/videos-cq-kids/jesus-birth/
- Who was Simeon? https://christianquestions.com/cq-videos/videos-cq-kids/who-was-simeon/
- Why did God choose Mary to be the mother of Jesus? https://christianquestions.com/cq-videos/videos-cq-kids/mary-the-mother-of-jesus/

The birth of Jesus was such a big event and such a humble process:

Luke 2:1-2,4: (KJV) 1 And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed… 3 And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city. 4 And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem;...

One wonders if Joseph and Mary were aware of the prophecy in Micah and if they used that prophecy as motivation for their journey:

Micah 5:2: (NIV2011) But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times.

This journey is said to be about 90 miles by way of the winding roads of the day. Traveling at the speed of a donkey, this meant it would probably take five days or so.

It would have been a grueling trip, especially for a woman ready to give birth:

Luke 2:5-6: (KJV) 5 To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child. 6 And so it was, that, while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered.

Outside of the miraculous conception, the angelic visit and the dreams of angels giving direction, the experiences of Mary and Joseph were unremarkable.

There were no special provisions, no special exemptions, no special circumstances—they were required to do what everyone else did, travel where everyone else traveled and pay what everyone else paid.

Luke 2:7: (KJV) And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.

To be born in a stable and to be laid in a manger among the animals was in fact the most fitting of places for the Lord of men to enter the world. After all, Jesus would live these humble beginnings each and every day for 33 and a half years, for it was through this humility that he would be able to pay the ransom price.

As Mary is going through the pains of delivering her child, there are not far away shepherds tending their flocks. These men were just humbly going about their own business.

Their lives were about to take an unexpected turn:

Luke 2:8-14: (KJV) 8 And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. 9 And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid.

When an angel of God appears out of nowhere, being afraid is not only natural, it’s healthy. It shows respect and awe for that which is bigger than we are.

The next step is to listen and learn: 10 And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. 11 For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord. 12 And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.

The fulfillment of prophecy—in this case it required an angelic announcement to a most humble audience of shepherds. How fitting an audience, as the baby Jesus was just born in the city of David who was a shepherd himself.

And then it was full of music—the thundering chorus of heavenly angelic voices singing praise: 13 And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, 14 Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.

Humility does not preclude heavenly celebration; rather, it provokes it! It was in this manner that our Lord Jesus was born and announced.

Okay, you are a shepherd and you have just heard this amazing message. What do you do now?

Luke 2:15-16: 15 When the angels had gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds began saying to one another, Let us go straight to Bethlehem then, and see this thing that has happened which the Lord has made known to us. 16 So they came in a hurry and found their way to Mary and Joseph, and the baby as he lay in the manger.

These shepherds knew that they were part of something much bigger than they had ever conceived to be possible. They acted in faith, and they acted right away, and they found Mary and Joseph. The baby lay quietly in a manger. Think of the tranquility and peace of the moment as they cast their eyes on their future Savior and played the chorus of the heavenly host again and again in their minds.

This was Jesus, the one who would save the world:

Luke 2:17-18: 17 When they had seen this, they made known the statement which had been told them about this child. 18 And all who heard it wondered at the things which were told them by the shepherds.

To go and see him was one thing, but to take this miracle and publish it amongst the people, that was on another level! These were just shepherds, but they were emboldened to speak out about the stunning event and the miraculous announcement that they had been a part of.

How about us? Are we emboldened to speak out about the good news of Christ?

We too have seen the grandeur of the gospel message, and we too have been invited to be a part of that message:

Luke 2:19-20: 19 But Mary treasured all these things, pondering them in her heart. 20 The shepherds went back, glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, just as had been told them.

For Mary, this was a time of awe-struck wonder. She had been living in faith for the last nine months, and now that Jesus was born, her faith would begin to take on new meaning.

## Episode 1417 — How Do I Know if I Am REALLY Following Jesus? (Part I)
Published: 2025-12-29
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1417-follow-jesus-part-i/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/26150706/CQ_Rewind_12-29-2025_How_Do_I_Know_if_I_Am_Really_Following_Jesus_Part_I.pdf

Romans 12:1: Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

As Christians, we love Jesus. All who claim that Jesus is their Lord and Savior do so because they have acknowledged their own sinful state and have realized the power of forgiveness that comes from Jesus’ sacrifice. It is easy for us to fellowship about what we have been freely given. What may not be as easy for us to define is what we are giving. A true disciple of Jesus receives redemption. That same true disciple is also required to give back as a result of that gift. Wait a minute! Isn’t Jesus’ gift freely given with no strings attached? Yes, it is free with no strings attached. Because we received that gift, we are “required” to care for it. As we shall soon see, this “required care” thought is the very essence of being a true and genuine follower of Christ.

In this episode, we focus on Romans 12:1 to help us define what it REALLY means to follow Jesus:

Romans 12:1: Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

In Part II, we will focus on Romans 12:2 and the transformation that discipleship brings:

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

How do we know if we are REALLY following Jesus? We receive a lot of correspondence through our email: inspiration@ChristianQuestions.com. Some listeners express their love for Jesus, but they don’t understand what it means to actually follow Jesus. It’s not just about loving Jesus, which may sound strange. Instead, it is about following Jesus, whom we love.

Romans 12:1 begins with the word therefore. So we have to ask, what is it “there for”?

The previous chapter is all about the casting off of Israel from God’s exclusive favor. Let’s look at the end of Romans 11 to see what the therefore at the beginning of chapter 12 is referring to.

Paul is teaching us how Israel’s sin brought tremendous privilege to unbelievers (those outside of the Jewish faith at the time):

Romans 11:28–32: (KJV) 28 As concerning the gospel, they (the Jews) are enemies for your sakes (the Gentile Christians): but as touching the election, they (the Jews) are beloved for the fathers’ sakes.

Cast off, yet beloved? That's interesting.

Though natural Israel became enemies of the gospel because the nation rejected Jesus, that nation was still beloved by God for the sake of Israel’s faithful fathers—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Moses. God made a covenant with and through these fathers, so God still loved Israel despite the nation rejecting Jesus.

Continuing: 29 For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.

God was not repentant—not even slightly regretful—of the grace He had given Israel as a nation. He didn’t look back and think what a waste of time that was. His gifts do not fail; they are for a much bigger purpose. What is that purpose?

30 For as ye in times past have not believed God, yet have now obtained mercy through their unbelief:

Up until the time Israel as a nation rejected Jesus, every Gentile believer had been outside of God’s favor because God only had a relationship with the Jewish nation. God’s favor had to come through Israel. But Israel’s rejection of Jesus extended mercy to all those who accepted Jesus, those who would otherwise have no idea how to obtain such mercy.

This beautiful, amazing gift developed out of a very tragic set of circumstances.

Continuing: 31 Even so have these also now not believed, that through your mercy they also may obtain mercy.

Cornelius was the first non-Jewish convert, along with his entire household. Cornelius sets the stage for a dramatic shift in how God’s favor would move forward.

Yes, we see how God’s favor shifted from being solely with Israel to now being with the Gentiles. But we can’t forget what Paul says in the rest of the verse—through your mercy they also may obtain mercy. The mercy Gentile Christians received will bring mercy back to Israel!

It is not that Israel is forgotten; it is that for a time, Israel is set—outside of God’s favor— because of their unbelief in Jesus. But the gifts... of God are without repentance. He is not regretting His past relationship with Israel, determined never to repeat it. Through true Christians, that relationship will be developed again according to His plan.

Let’s continue: 32 For God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that He might have mercy upon all.

Why were they left in unbelief? So God could have mercy on every one of them!

When we look at these verses, thinking this is about the tragic rejection of Israel because they rejected Jesus, we have to realize this is NOT a tragic ending to a tragic circumstance. There will be a beautiful ending of having mercy upon all. That plan all happens through the calling of Gentile Christians to help make this happen.

This is what following Jesus is really all about.

Let’s conclude this section with the following verse:

Romans 11:33: (KJV) O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!

How unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out!

Because God’s wisdom is so profound and inclusive, we Gentile Christians have been given a place in God’s master plan. This is a privilege beyond comprehension. What a gift!

The call to follow Christ requires maintenance to prevent it from losing value. For example, in my past job, I had to polish silver for a client to maintain its brilliant shine. Silver easily tarnishes. I had to use cotton gloves while polishing so the salt and oils from my fingers wouldn’t mark the silver. It was hard to do, but it was worth the effort to keep its value.

That is a great illustration of what following Jesus requires. We are given this beautiful, remarkable gift, but it needs maintenance. It needs us to pay attention.

Required Care for the Gift of Discipleship:

True discipleship begins with the recognition that we, as sinful humans, are not and never were in harmony with God. His willingness to open the door through Jesus for us to become followers of Christ defies all earthly logic and probability. This gift is beyond our ability to comprehend!

It is really important, especially at the outset of our walk with Jesus, to recognize how big and how far beyond us this gift is.

Finally, we’ve reached the first word in our theme text—therefore:

Romans 12:1: (KJV) I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.

Romans 12:1: (NASB95) Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

Because we have been given this gift we do not deserve, and because it came to us as a result of others’ difficulties, and because it is such a great and wonderful gift that is so big and incomprehensible, Therefore…

Let’s take this verse apart piece by piece to help us understand what it means to truly follow Jesus: I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God…

REQUIRED CARE FOCUS (OUR MAINTENANCE FOCUS) IS THREE PIECES

o Awe

o Gratitude

o Humility

Awe: 1 Peter 2:9–10: 9 But you are A CHOSEN RACE, A royal PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION, A PEOPLE FOR God’s OWN POSSESSION, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light; 10 for you once were NOT A PEOPLE, but now you are THE PEOPLE OF GOD; you had NOT RECEIVED MERCY, but now you have RECEIVED MERCY.

This highlights the incredible grace and mercy that God extends to us, even though we don’t deserve it. To be called out of darkness into His light is truly an undeserved gift for eternity! We need to be faithful to that gift. We are in awe of this. It is magnificent; it is like the greatest masterpiece we could have ever imagined.

Gratitude: Ephesians 2:8: For by grace you have been saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God.

How can we show our thankfulness to Him for this gift? One way is to answer the call and follow His son. In addition, we can go back and recognize the gift again and again. Even after many years, it is as exciting as it was at the beginning. Part of having gratitude is reflecting back to recognize what we have been given.

Humility: 1 Corinthians 1:26–31: 26 For consider your calling, brethren, that there were not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble; 27 but God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God has chosen the weak things of the world to shame the things which are strong, 28 and the base things of the world and the despised God has chosen, the things that are not, so that He may nullify the things that are, (why?) 29 so that no man may boast before God.

Followers of Jesus cannot boast of being called because they are so great—this is the opposite of what these texts are saying.

30 But by His doing you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption, 31 so that, just as it is written, LET HIM WHO BOASTS, BOAST IN THE LORD.

There's no place for pride here—just humility.

Awe, gratitude and humility have to be part of the foundation built on the recognition of our own worthlessness.

Required Care for the Gift of Discipleship:

The gift of discipleship is lofty and precious, and it requires us to be profoundly appreciative. Standing in this appreciation sets us up for what needs to follow. Let us be careful not to overlook the foundational importance of living in awe, gratitude and humility as disciples of Jesus.

Learning to be a true disciple of Jesus is likely a much bigger and more complex lesson than we might generally expect!

All Christians agree that having a basis of recognition, awe, gratitude and humility for our Christian walk is reasonable. What comes next?

The next steps towards true discipleship are where many of us may begin to have second thoughts. When Jesus called individuals to follow him, one thing he did NOT promise was an easy path to take. On the contrary, he promised difficulty!

Our text unfolds this difficulty in a straightforward way:

Romans 12:1: (KJV) …ye present your bodies a living sacrifice…

REQUIRED CARE FOCUS:

Intentional Self-Denial

Jesus made this concept of being a living sacrifice abundantly clear:

Luke 9:23: And he was saying to them all, If anyone wishes to come after me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow me.

Following in Jesus' footsteps requires sacrificing our own will. It means setting aside self- will in favor of God's will. It is not that God makes us do it—we need to intentionally take up our cross and follow Jesus. Why would Jesus say this? Because he took up his cross and died on it. We follow in his steps in the denial of our own wills in sacrifice.

What does this mean?

1 Peter 2:11: Beloved, I urge you as aliens and strangers to abstain from fleshly lusts which wage war against the soul.

To abstain here means to voluntarily hold back from things that are sinful. Not delay doing them, not doing less of them, but to stop and walk away from them. This is not easy!

On several occasions, Jesus in his ministry discouraged the masses from following him. Why would he do that? Because it was hard!

One example:

Luke 14:25–28: 25 Now large crowds were going along with him; and he turned and said to them, 26 If anyone comes to me, and does not hate (meaning, to love less) his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. 27 Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. 28 For which one of you, when he wants to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost to see if he has enough to complete it?

We call this principle “counting the cost.” Essentially, Jesus is saying that to follow him, we must love him and follow him more than any person or circumstance in our lives. If we are not going to take up our cross, we cannot come and follow him. He says we need to count the cost to see if we are ready to take such a dramatic step. When Jesus said this to the crowds, many of them didn’t like it. They felt he was asking too much. But this is what Jesus was (and is) looking for.

Jesus was testing their motives. Why were they following after him? Did they want to be part of something impressive, miraculous and newsworthy? This is the man who performs the miracles. Here is the guy whose words mesmerize! This is the man who can speak to the Pharisees, and they don’t know how to answer him! Did they follow him for the exciting show?

Or were they aspiring to be part of something profoundly difficult and life-changing? That is what Jesus was looking for. There is a big difference between these two motivations.

What did Jesus show us about this intentional self-denial, about presenting your bodies a living sacrifice?

Jesus himself had to abandon his own will as a man whenever the will of God stood above it:

Psalms 40:7–8: 7 Then I said, Behold, I come; In the scroll of the book it is written of me. 8 I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your Law is within my heart.

Sometimes that “delighting” isn’t as delightful as we would like it to be.

Let’s look at an example of Jesus abandoning his own will when the Father’s will was higher:

Matthew 26:39: And he went a little beyond them, and fell on his face and prayed, saying, my Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as You will.

Now that's intentional self-denial, even with the pressure he was under. What an example! It is because he delighted to do his Father’s will that he could acquiesce when it was contrary to what he himself wanted.

That’s the beauty of delighting in doing the Father’s will—when it gets difficult, we still do it because we know it is the direction we ultimately want to go.

Further, Jesus NEEDED to suffer for the sake of fulfilling his redemptive work:

Hebrews 5:8: (KJV) Though he were a son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered <3958>.

Suffered: Strongs Exhaustive Concordance #3958; pascho; to experience a sensation or impression (usually painful)

Jesus was not “suffering” in a painful way every day of his life, though he was sacrificing his own will every day; in many cases, it was a joyful experience. He lived in obedience to his Father every day of his life. This intentional self-denial is our example to follow.

We, therefore, must also suffer and live in obedience to God our Father as Jesus did:

Philippians 1:29: For to you it has been granted for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer <3958> for his sake.

It's important to remember that Jesus wasn't suffering every day of his life. We shouldn’t expect that for ourselves either. The same Greek word for suffer is used to describe Jesus in

Hebrews 5:8 and his followers in Philippians 1:29. We can expect suffering, but because we are so imperfect, we can get more easily worn out by our trials and challenges. We might feel we do not have the strength.

However, our trials and challenges must be weighed against the value of eternity:

2 Corinthians 4:16–17: 16 Therefore we do not lose heart, but though our outer man is decaying, yet our inner man is being renewed day by day. 17 For momentary, light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory far beyond all comparison.

Not only do we receive the gift of the calling to follow in Jesus’ footsteps, but if we remain faithful to this gift, if we maintain it, if we do the work of required care, God promises an even greater future gift of glory.

Discipleship requires that we take up our own cross and follow the pathway to this glory. It is not handed to us on a silver platter; gaining it requires trial and tribulation.

Part of our suffering and trials includes being very different from those around us:

2 Corinthians 6:14–16: 14 Do not be bound together with unbelievers; for what partnership have righteousness and lawlessness, or what fellowship has light with darkness? 15 Or what harmony has Christ with Belial, or what has a believer in common with an unbeliever? 16 Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God…

There is great privilege in this intentional self-denial. Do my thoughts, actions and beliefs reveal the sacredness of the call by which I am being transformed? Do they truly reflect God’s holiness in the midst of an unholy world? Am I living in a way that genuinely represents Him? We are to be IN the world, but not OF the world. We are to rise above those things around us.

We really do need, as best as we can, to walk in Jesus’ footsteps:

Romans 8:16–17: 16 The spirit itself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God, 17 and if children, heirs also, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with <4841> him so that we may also be glorified with him.

Suffer with: Strongs Exhaustive Concordance #4841; sumpascho; (including its alternate); to experience pain jointly or of the same kind (specifically, persecution; to “sympathize”)

Just as Jesus intentionally denied everything earthly, we are to do similarly in our own small way. We suffer with him means to experience pain jointly or of the same kind. We are supposed to be like Jesus, but of course on a much smaller scale.

Required Care for the Gift of Discipleship:

Along with being blessed by God, answering the call to follow Jesus will walk us through hardship, contradiction, brokenness, failure, ridicule, and even isolation from worldly influences. If we claim to be disciples of Jesus, then let us embrace all that comes our way with thankfulness for God’s providence and mercy!

We want to be careful that our dedication to our calling is firmly grounded in Scripture, not in what some Christian traditions may say. We need to follow the words of Jesus and of the apostles, and the actions of both, so we can be going in the right direction.

How are my Christian brethren helping me with intentional self-denial? Are we in an environment where intentional self-denial is being encouraged and worked on jointly?

Now we see the pathway of Christianity showing us the uncomfortable side of things. Are we still willing to forge ahead?

With intentional self-denial in focus, it seems like the discipleship challenge is already more than formidable! What else is there to add?

It is really important to remind ourselves that walking in Jesus’ footsteps is an amazing privilege given only to those called to follow. And yes, there is more to add. As we shall soon see, self-denial is not an end result. On the contrary, it is a powerful step that paves the way for truly being able to grasp and follow God’s will.

This reminds us of Jesus' baptism when God said, This is My beloved son in whom I am well pleased. What is required for us to be holy and acceptable? We must adopt a new mindset.

Romans 12:1: (KJV) …holy <40>, acceptable (fully agreeable, well–pleasing) unto God…

Holy: Strongs Exhaustive Concordance #40; hagios; from hagos (an awful thing); sacred (physically, pure, morally blameless or religious, ceremonially, consecrated)

REQUIRED CARE FOCUS:

Adopting a NEW Mindset

Before Jesus was crucified, he told his followers that God’s spirit was coming to them.

The magnitude of this change was expressed in Ephesians long after Jesus told them about it:

Ephesians 1:13–14: (WEY) 13 And in him you Gentiles also, after listening to the message of the truth, the good news of your salvation—having believed in him—were sealed with the promised holy <40> spirit; 14 that spirit being a pledge and foretaste of our inheritance, in anticipation of its full redemption—the inheritance which he has purchased to be specially his for the extolling of his glory.

The spirit was given as a pledge and foretaste of our inheritance. It was given as a down payment on the future gift that will be even greater than what we have now. The word holy is important. The holy in holy spirit means sacred. Remember that word as we go through the following few scriptures on adopting this new mindset—it will play an important role.

This gift of the holy spirit is God’s assurance to every true follower of Jesus that they are called to a remarkable new life and a remarkable new mindset! We can’t live a new life without changing our mindset. We have to put the old away and adopt the new.

Paul further in Ephesians helps us understand the import of who we have become with God’s spirit within us:

Ephesians 2:19–22: 19 So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints <40> (the same word translated as holy. We are fellow citizens with the holy ones), and are of God’s household, 20 having been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the corner stone, 21 in whom the whole building, being fitted together, is growing into a holy <40> temple in the Lord, 22 in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling of God in the spirit.

We are becoming fellow citizens with the saints (holy ones). This is what following Christ actually looks like.

Our new mindset is driven by God’s own holy influence—His spirit—towards His own holy things. We are a holy temple in the Lord. We are different from how we were before.

When I answered the call to follow Christ and changed my mindset (which needed a lot of work), all my friends from the past asked, “What’s going on with you? Where did Jon, the person we used to know, go? You have become some kind of religious fanatic!” By the way, I decided to go by my given name, Jonathan, after that.

It was a way for you to put old things behind you and set your mind on things that were new. You changed the way you saw yourself, and you wouldn’t answer to Jon anymore. You were Jonathan. I know that when I just met you, there were a few times I called you Jon, and you said, “No, it’s Jonathan.” I thought, He’s a little bit fanatical about that! It took me a while to figure out why it was important to you. But it’s a powerful and beautiful statement of what it means to really follow Jesus and leave the past behind.

This holy temple in the Lord is defining us as a dwelling place for God’s spirit:

1 Corinthians 3:16–17: 16 Do you not know that you are a temple of God and that the spirit of God dwells in you? 17 If any man destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him, for the temple of God is holy <40>, and that is what you are.

The temple of God is holy; it is sacred, which means we are sacred. We are God’s definition of sacred—not mankind’s definition of sacred.

Our holy and well-pleasing lives before God should grow into reflecting powerful spiritual maturity:

Romans 5:1–5: 1 Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 through whom also we have obtained our introduction by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we exult in hope of the glory of God. 3 And not only this, (and now comes the work!) but we also exult in our tribulations, knowing that tribulation brings about perseverance; 4 and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope; 5 and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out within our hearts through the holy <40> spirit (which) was given to us.

Tribulation brings about perseverance… proven character… and hope. All of these things are what the growth of spiritual maturity looks like.

Our new mindset points us to an unshakable hope in God’s plan, and God’s spirit feeds that hope. It is a beautiful, higher mindset. A different mindset. We have to leave behind what once was.

Our new mindset is driven by following the mindset that Jesus had, even before he came to earth!

Philippians 2:3–8: 3 Do nothing from selfishness or empty conceit, but with humility of mind regard one another as more important than yourselves; 4 do not merely look out for your own personal interests, but also for the interests of others. 5 Have this attitude in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, 6 who, although he existed in the form of God (although he existed spiritually), did not regard equality with God a thing to be grasped, 7 but emptied himself,

taking the form of a bond-servant, and being made in the likeness of men. 8 Being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

Jesus showed his willingness to humble himself and become a man because it was the will of God. We attempt to follow the mindset of Jesus, who saw God as the Father, the ultimate, and would serve Him in any way he possibly could. To do so, he reduced himself to a human being, and then he gave himself as a sacrifice for all humanity. That is the beauty of his mindset.

This mindset from Jesus encapsulates everything we’ve talked about— the recognition of the gifts of God, awe, gratitude, humility and the intentional self-denial necessary to be fully engaged in doing God’s will each and every day.

This new mindset in us never stops seeking and learning a better understanding of God’s plan and will. There’s work involved.

This mindset constantly works towards godliness in our daily lives:

2 Timothy 2:15–16: 15 Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth. 16 But avoid worldly and empty chatter, for it will lead to further ungodliness,

Accurately handling the word of truth, not just arbitrarily reading a scripture and feeling good. That’s nice to do—we’re not discouraging that. But we want to read a scripture, understand its context and true meaning so that it can transform us. So it can help us be stronger in the Lord, in the power of His might, and stand against the things of this world, because we have to be about our Father’s business, just like Jesus was.

Required Care for the Gift of Discipleship:

As true followers of Jesus, we must be open to embracing a spiritually focused mindset fueled by God’s spirit prompting and guiding us.

His holy word is our primary source of learning. Our primary objective is to become usable in God’s hands for His purposes and NOT our own!

Being a follower of Jesus means so much more than simply loving him! It requires the focusing of our very being on walking in his footsteps.

Recognition, awe, gratitude, humility, self-denial and adopting a new mindset. How do we fully embrace all of these things as integrated parts of our lives?

Fully embracing discipleship is the main point of what Paul is teaching us in Romans 12:1. Each phrase he’s written adds another dimension to the depth of his teaching, and his next statement will conclude this aspect of our call. This conclusion is almost surprising in its simplicity.

Romans 12:1: (KJV) …which is your reasonable <3050> service <2999>.

REQUIRED CARE FOCUS:

Full Engagement

What exactly does reasonable service mean? Or as it says in the NASB translation, spiritual service of worship? “Reasonable” means rational and logical. “Service” means a service rendered, for hire or any service or ministration, even to serving God.

Reasonable: Strongs Exhaustive Concordance #3050; logikos; rational (“logical”)

Service: Strongs Exhaustive Concordance #2999; latreia; ministration or God, i.e. worship

Thayer's Greek-English Lexicon: 1) service rendered for hire 1a) any service or ministration: the service of God

The New American Standard Version translates this as, your spiritual service of worship. But it is something rational and logical—not dramatic. It does not require a strong emotional push to follow this reasonable service.

The Psalms sets the stage for our full engagement:

Psalm 116:12–15: 12 What shall I render to the LORD for all His benefits toward me? 13 I shall lift up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the LORD. 14 I shall pay my vows to the LORD, oh may it be in the presence of all His people. 15 Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His godly ones.

Full engagement says I will pay what I owe for the gift I've been given. I will do the maintenance, like wearing the cotton gloves and scrubbing and cleaning that tarnished silver so it shows its luster. And the next time it begins to tarnish, I will do the maintenance again so the gift shines as it is meant to.

We have to give because of what we’ve been given. How can we help it? It is such an incredible gift. True discipleship changes all of us from who we were into what we have become. Jesus accepts us—we can come to him as we are, but we cannot stay as we are. We need to conform to spiritual behaviors as soon as we understand them.

If we are intent on staying as we are, we are in the wrong place. It’s really that simple.

Galatians 3:27–29: 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. 28 There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29 And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s descendants, heirs according to promise.

To have clothed yourself with Christ is to be covered by his sacrifice, to be fully engaged as a part of him.

In my own life experience, I believed I was called to follow God when I was only 16 years old. I remember being at a young people’s Bible seminar at age 15, and it was in my mind that the Lord wanted something from me. I just couldn’t get it out of my head. We were sitting around the campfire in the evening, and the leader was doing the talking. I was sitting there staring at this big, beautiful fire. The logs sometimes crumble in the middle of the fire as they are consumed, and I was watching one of them crumble. One of its embers rolled out of the fire about a foot away from it. It was glowing red hot. I watched the ember, knowing what was going to happen. As I watched it (I remember this as if it were yesterday, even though it was 52 years ago), the ember stopped glowing and eventually turned black and cold.

I remember looking at that saying, I don’t want to be that. I need to stay in the fire. I need to be consumed by what God is drawing me to. There was an overwhelming sense that this was where I belonged. Don’t allow the fire to go out. Stay where the fire is burning. Be covered by his sacrifice. Be fully engaged to be part of him. In my experience, and I remember it well, it was a powerful lesson for me. It took another year to actually say, Lord, I’m going to give you my life because I was counting the cost. But that experience was the catalyst.

The Apostle Paul further describes how our fully engaged lives should interact with other followers:

1 Corinthians 12:14–16: 14 For the body is not one member, but many. 15 If the foot says, Because I am not a hand, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body. 16 And if the ear says, Because I am not an eye, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body.

Paul is saying that one part of the body cannot function without the other. Just because this part doesn’t have as much glory as that part doesn’t mean it’s not functional or vital.

This illustration helps us see the importance of what we are called to, regardless of our abilities.

1 Corinthians 12:17–20: 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body, just as He desired. 19 If they were all one member, where would the body be? 20 But now there are many members, but one body.

We all contribute in our own unique way.

Each member of the body is vital, as the object is to be a complete, self-sustaining, mutually supportive unit, all under the head who is Christ! That’s what it means to be fully engaged!

We need each other for this mission in Christ. We must surround ourselves with like- minded followers to build us up, to help us in the narrow way.

From a practical standpoint, we’ve been working on Christian Questions for 27 years, and there is a team of the brotherhood that volunteers their time. Over 40 people do their part each week to make this work. They just came on their own, asked what they could do and went to work. This is what makes it functional.

God is looking for our full engagement. Full engagement gives us the capacity to prioritize our lives from a clear spiritual perspective—the highest perspective.

Requoting:

2 Corinthians 4:16–17: 16 Therefore we do not lose heart, but though our outer man is decaying, yet our inner man is being renewed day by day. 17 For momentary, light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory far beyond all comparison,

We see that getting our priorities straight from a spiritual perspective may be costly in this life, but it is an investment in eternity. Something costly for a short period of time may be difficult, but it is certainly worth it. This is what Jesus did. This is what the Apostles Paul and Peter did. This is what the rest of the apostles and many in the early church did, and it is what we are called to do.

Our full engagement provokes us to let go of all that we used to be and to press forward:

Philippians 3:13–14: 13 Brethren, I do not regard myself as having laid hold of it yet; but one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, 14 I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

This is full engagement! We're running to what lies ahead, leaving behind who and what we were. It no longer has importance because this is where we are going.

Our full engagement brings us to an absolutely clear vision of our life priorities:

Philippians 1:21: For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.

This doesn't mean we forget our family responsibilities or our health and legal responsibilities. It means we do ALL to the glory of God!

If we are parents, we parent to the glory of God. We must take care of those children. If we have a job, we do it well because we are essentially working for God. That is the way we want to see that, to be consumed by doing things in a God-honoring way. For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain because it will eventually bring eternity, by God’s grace.

Our full engagement enables us to capture our highest priority. We began with Romans 11. Let’s end with the last verse of that chapter—remember, this comes right before the word Therefore.

Romans 11:36: For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever. Amen.

It is all about honoring God. To Him be the glory forever. That is what following Jesus is all about: putting us in the right mindset.

Required Care for the Gift of Discipleship:

We can tell if we are really following Jesus by recognizing the call to discipleship and having awe, gratitude and humility regarding the answering of that call. Further, our true following of Jesus requires us to intentionally engage in self-denial as well as embracing and adopting a new mindset.

All of this requires the full engagement of our heart, mind, soul and strength. To follow Jesus is to walk towards God as our Father!

Let’s go back to our original question: How do I know if I am really following Jesus?

In Part II, we will cover the power of transformation as expressed in the next verse:

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

This builds on our discussion of intentional self-sacrifice, a new mindset and full engagement. How does this all come about? By God’s spirit making us different, transforming us. We will discuss how this all works in our next episode. Until then, think about the power of walking in Jesus’ footsteps.

So, how do I know if I am REALLY following Jesus?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
